(p-٢٢٢٩) Surat al-An'am

(p-٢٢٣٠) In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

6. Surat al-An'am

It is Meccan, and it has one hundred and sixty-five verses.

Al-Awfi, Ikrimah and Ata' narrated from Ibn Abbas that he said: "Surat al-An'am was revealed in Mecca."

Abu Salih narrated from Ibn Abbas that he said: "It is Meccan. It was revealed all at once, at night, and they wrote it down that same night, except for six verses of it, which are Medinan. They are His statement, exalted is He: ﴿Say, "Come, I will recite what your Lord has prohibited to you"﴾ [al-An'am: 151] to the end of the three verses; His statement, exalted is He: ﴿And they did not appraise Allah with the appraisal due to Him﴾ [al-An'am: 91] (p-٢٢٣١) and the verse; and His statement, exalted is He: ﴿And who is more unjust than one who invents a lie against Allah﴾ [al-An'am: 93] to the end of the two verses."

Muqatil mentioned something similar, but added two verses: His statement, exalted is He: ﴿Those to whom We have given the Scripture know that it is sent down from your Lord﴾ [al-An'am: 114], and the verse; and His statement, exalted is He: ﴿Those to whom We have given the Scripture recognize it﴾ [al-An'am: 20], and the verse.

It is also narrated from Ibn Abbas and Qatada that they both said: "It is Meccan except for two verses, which were revealed in Medina: His statement, ﴿And they did not appraise Allah with the appraisal due to Him﴾ [al-An'am: 91], and His statement, ﴿And it is He who produces gardens﴾ [al-An'am: 141], and the verse."

(p-٢٢٣٢) Al-Bayhaqi said in (al-Dala'il): "Among the surahs revealed in Mecca there are verses that were revealed in Medina, which were then joined to them." Ibn al-Hassar said likewise: "Every category of the Meccan and the Medinan contains verses that are exceptions." He said: "However, some people relied on ijtihad (independent reasoning) rather than transmission in determining the exceptions." Then he discussed these verses, and said: "No transmission supports them, especially what is reported that they were revealed all at once."

Al-Suyuti replied to him that the transmission from Ibn Abbas is sound, with the exception of: ﴿Say, "Come"﴾ [al-An'am: 151] and the three verses that follow. As for the rest: ﴿And they did not appraise Allah with the appraisal due to Him﴾ [al-An'am: 91], this is because Ibn Abi Hatim reported that it was revealed concerning Malik ibn al-Sayf. And His statement, exalted is He: ﴿And who is more unjust than one who invents a lie against Allah﴾ [al-An'am: 93], the two verses were revealed concerning Musaylima. And His statement: ﴿Those to whom We have given the Scripture recognize it﴾ [al-An'am: 20], and His statement: ﴿Those to whom We have given the Scripture know that it is sent down from your Lord in truth﴾ [al-An'am: 114].

Abu al-Shaykh reported from al-Kalbi that he said: "All of Surat al-An'am was revealed in Mecca, except for two verses which were revealed in Medina concerning a man of the Jews, and he is the one who said: ﴿Allah has not sent down anything to a human being﴾ [al-An'am: 91]." Thus it is in (al-Lubab) and (al-Itqan).

Among the distinctive features of this surah is what al-Tabarani reported from Ibn Abbas, who said: "Surat al-An'am was revealed in Mecca at night, all at once, and around it were seventy thousand angels, glorifying with loud voices."

(p-٢٢٣٣) Al-Suddi narrated from Ibn Mas'ud that he said: "Surat al-An'am was revealed, and seventy thousand angels escorted it." Something similar was narrated from him through another chain as well.

Al-Hakim reported in (al-Mustadrak) from Jabir that he said: "When Surat al-An'am was revealed, the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) glorified Allah, then said: 'Seventy thousand angels escorted this surah, filling the horizon.'" Then he said: "It is sound according to the condition of Muslim."

Ibn Mardawayh reported it from Anas, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Surat al-An'am was revealed with a procession of angels filling what lies between the two horizons. For them there is a loud sound of glorification, and the earth quakes because of them, while the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) was saying: 'Glory be to Allah, the Mighty! Glory be to Allah, the Mighty!'"

He also reported from Ibn Umar that he said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Surat al-An'am was revealed to me all at once, and seventy thousand angels escorted it, for them there is a loud sound of glorification and praise."

Al-Razi said: The usulis (scholars of the foundations of jurisprudence) said: "This surah is distinguished by two kinds of excellence:

One of them: that it was revealed in a single installment.

The second: that seventy thousand angels escorted it. The reason for this is that it includes the proofs of tawhid (monotheism), justice, prophethood, the return, and the refutation of the doctrines of the misguided and the atheists. This indicates that the science of the foundations (usul al-din) is of the highest grandeur and rank. Also, the revelation of what pertains to rulings may be sent down by Allah, exalted is He, in measure with their need and according to events and occurrences. As for what pertains to the science of the foundations, Allah, exalted is He, sent it down all at once. This indicates that learning the science of the foundations is obligatory immediately, not with delay."

Al-Darimi reported in (his Musnad) from Umar, may Allah be pleased with him, that he said: "Al-An'am is among the essentials (nawajib) of the Qur'an."

In the (Qamus): "The najaʼib (choicest parts) of the Qur'an are its best and purest; its nawajib are its essence." End of quotation.

It is named (Surat al-An'am) because most of its rulings, and the ignorance of the polytheists, and their drawing near to their idols with cattle (an'am), are mentioned in it.

(p-٢٢٣٤) In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

Discussion of the interpretation of His statement, exalted is He:

[1] ﴿All praise is due to Allah, who created the heavens and the earth and made darknesses and light. Yet those who disbelieve equate [others] with their Lord.﴾

﴿All praise is due to Allah﴾ means: all praises belong to Him, whether those with which He praised Himself, or those with which His creation praised Him, or those with which some of them praised their Lord; it is exclusively His. Then He informed of His complete power, which is required by His deserving all praise, by His statement: ﴿who created the heavens and the earth﴾. He singled out these two for mention because they are the greatest of created things as seen by the servants, and in them are lessons and benefits; for the heavens, with their configurations and motions, are the causes of the generated and corruptible beings, which are the manifestations of divine perfections, while the earth comprises the receptive capacities of generation and corruption, which are the effects caused.

﴿And made darknesses and light﴾ means: He brought them into existence as a benefit to His servants, in their night and their day.

Here are some subtleties:

The first: the purpose of the verse is to alert that the One who bestowed these great blessings is the one truly deserving of praise and worship, not anything else.

The second: the word (ja'ala) (made) is transitive to one object when it means "to create and originate," as here; and to two objects when it means "to render," as in His statement: ﴿And they have made the angels, who are the servants of the Most Merciful, females﴾ [al-Zukhruf: 19]. The difference between (khalaqa) (created) and (ja'ala) (made) is that (khalq) carries the sense of determining measure, while (ja'l) carries the sense of transformation, such as producing one thing from another, or rendering one thing into another, or moving something from one place to another. Among this is: (p-٢٢٣٥) ﴿And made from it its mate﴾ [al-A'raf: 189], ﴿Has he made the gods one God?﴾ [Sad: 5]. The word (ja'l) is appropriate here because light and darkness alternate, so that each of them seems to have come into being from the other, as al-Razi said, and al-Zamakhshari preceded him to this. Al-Nasir said in (al-Intisaf): "The words (ja'ala) and (khalaqa) have occurred in a single context: (khalaqa) occurs in: ﴿and created from it its mate﴾, and (ja'ala) occurs in: ﴿and made from it its mate﴾. This is clearly synonymy. However, the mind inclines toward the distinction that al-Zamakhshari proposed. What supports it is that (ja'ala) was not used with the heavens and the earth, while (khalaqa) is bound to them. In the attribution of (khalq) in this verse to the heavens and the earth, and of (ja'l) to the darknesses and light, there is a confirmation of the distinction between them, and Allah knows best."

The third: If it is asked: why are the heavens put in the plural while the earth is not, even though they are alike, as in His statement: (p-٢٢٣٦) ﴿and of the earth the like of them﴾ [al-Talaq: 12], and in the hadith: "Do you know what this is?" They said: "This is the earth." He said: "Do you know what is beneath it?" They said: "Allah and His Messenger know best." He said: "Another earth, and between them is a journey of five hundred years," until he counted seven earths, between each earth and the next a journey of five hundred years." Related by al-Tirmidhi and Abu al-Shaykh from Abu Hurayra, may Allah be pleased with him.

(p-٢٢٣٧) The answer: the heavens are layers that differ in their essence, distinct in their reality, unlike the earths, as al-Baydawi stated.

Al-Razi said: The heaven functions as the agent, and the earth functions as the recipient. If the heaven were one, the effect would be uniform, and that would disrupt the interests of this world. But if they are many, the celestial connections differ, and by means of them arise the four seasons and the other varying conditions, and by means of these differences arise the interests of this world. As for the earth, it is receptive to the effect, and one receptive entity suffices for receiving. End of quotation.

He put the heavens first for their nobility and the loftiness of their place.

The fourth: the apparent meaning of (the darknesses and the light) is that they refer to the two matters perceptible to the sense of sight. What strengthens this is that the word is literal in both, and the principle is to keep a word on its literal meaning. Also, when (the darknesses and the light) are joined with the heavens and the earth, nothing is understood from them except the two perceptible matters. It is reported from some of the early scholars (salaf) that they meant by them disbelief and faith.

Al-Razi preferred the first, for the reason mentioned.

Some have construed the second as follows: the meaning is that when He created the heavens and the earth, He set up the proofs for knowing Him and His unity. Then He explained the path of misguidance and the path of guidance, by sending down the laws and the heavenly books. Then ﴿those who disbelieve equate [others] with their Lord﴾, so the particle (then) (thumma) is suitable here for expressing remoteness (istib'ad), since it is far from a rational observer, after the proof has been established, to choose falsehood. End of quotation.

Accordingly, the plural (darknesses) and the singular (light) are evident, because guidance is one, while misguidance is multiple, as He said at the end of this surah: ﴿And that this is My path, straight, so follow it, and do not follow other ways, lest you be separated from His way﴾ [al-An'am: 153].

(p-٢٢٣٨) On the first view, the plural is due to the evident multiplicity of their causes and their locations among people, for every body has darkness, but not every body has light. As for their being mentioned first, it is because they precede light in measure and in actuality.

There is a report: "Indeed Allah created the creation in darkness, then sprinkled upon them of His light."

His statement, exalted is He: ﴿Then those who disbelieve equate [others] with their Lord﴾ is coordinated with the preceding sentence, which states the things that required His exclusive right to praise, which calls for limiting worship to Him. It is brought to deny what the disbelievers adhere to, and to consider remote their opposition to its content and their audacity toward what the self-evident intellect (p-٢٢٣٩) judges to be false. The meaning is that He, exalted is He, is exclusively entitled to praise and worship, both by virtue of His essence and by virtue of what has been detailed of His great, specific affairs, which necessitate restricting praise and worship to Him. Then these disbelievers do not act according to this requirement, and they equate others with Him, exalted is He. That is: they make others equal to Him in worship, which is the highest end of gratitude, whose head is praise, although everything other than Him is His creation and is not characterized by any of the foundations of praise. The particle (then) (thumma) is for expressing the remoteness of polytheism after the clarity of the cosmic signs mentioned, which demand its falsity. The particle (bi) (with/by) is connected to (ya'dilun) (equate), and (the Lord) (al-Rabb) is placed in the position of His pronoun, for the sake of added reproach and condemnation. Its fronting is for greater emphasis and haste toward establishing the axis of denial and remoteness, and to preserve the rhyme (fawasil). The object is omitted for its evidence, or to direct the denial toward the act itself, by treating it as intransitive, signaling that it is the basis of the remoteness, not the specificity of the object. This is what befits the eloquence of the revelation; so said Abu al-Su'ud.

Then he discussed what occurred to the exegetes here that contradicts this. Consult it.

The root of (adl) is making one thing equal to another. The meaning is that they assign to Him equals from His creation, which have no power over anything, so they worship stones, while acknowledging that Allah created the heavens and the earth.

Al-Nadr ibn Shumayl said: the particle (bi) here means (an), that is: they turn away from their Lord and deviate, from the sense of (al-'udul 'an al-shay') (turning away from a thing).

Subtle point:

Commentary of al-Qasimi (Mahasin al-Ta'wil) on surah 6, verse 1 (part 2 of 2):

Ibn 'Atiyya, may Allah have mercy on him, said: "(Thumma, "then") indicates the ugliness of the act of those who disbelieved, because the meaning is that His creating of the heavens has been established, His signs have shone forth, and His bounty through that has become clear; then, after all of this, they have set up equals to their Lord. This is like your saying: 'I gave you, and I did good to you, then you insult me?' Had the conjunction in this and similar cases been with (wa, "and"), the rebuke would not have been necessary as it is with (thumma, "then"). End of quotation." That is: in it there is the indication of rebuke and denunciation, as well as of wonder.

Abu Hayyan said: "What Ibn 'Atiyya held, that (thumma) is for rebuke, and what al-Zamakhshari held, that it is for remoteness (istib'ad), is understood from the context of the speech, not from the denotation of (thumma)." End of quotation.

And (thumma) was not interpreted as indicating temporal delay (al-tarakhi), despite its being sound, because remoteness (istib'ad) is more fitting to the context; for temporal delay is already known in it, so there is no benefit in mentioning it.

The Interpretation of His Words, the Exalted:

[2] ﴿It is He who created you from clay, then decreed a term; and there is a specified term with Him; yet you still doubt.﴾

﴿It is He who created you from clay﴾ is a resumptive sentence, brought to demonstrate the falsehood of their disbelief in the Resurrection, despite their witnessing what necessitates belief in it, following the demonstration of the falsehood of their associating partners with Him, the Exalted, despite their direct observation of what necessitates His Oneness. The specification of their creation for mention, from among the rest of the proofs for the validity of the Resurrection, although what He mentioned of the creation of the heavens and the earth is among the clearest and most manifest of them, as occurs in His words: ﴿Is not He who created the heavens and the earth able to create the likes of them?﴾ [Ya-Sin: 81], is because the locus of dispute is their resurrection. Thus the indication of the beginning of their creation upon that is more evident, and they are more knowledgeable regarding the affairs of their own selves, and turning a blind eye to the luminous proof is more repugnant. The shift (iltifat) is for added censure and rebuke. That is: He began your creation from it (clay), for it is the first material for all things, since it is the origin of Adam, who is the father of mankind. The creation is attributed to the addressees and not to Adam, peace be upon him, although he is the one actually created from it, such that it is said: "He is the One who created your father..." etc. Together with the sufficiency of their knowledge of his, peace be upon him, creation from it, in necessitating belief in the Resurrection and the falsehood of doubt, for the clarification of the method of analogy, and for the sake of exaggeration in removing confusion and ambiguity. Along with this is the realization of the truth and an alert to a hidden wisdom: that every individual of mankind has a share of his creation, peace be upon him, from it (p-2241) since his wondrous natural disposition was not confined to himself, but was a model encompassing the natural disposition of all the individuals of the species, in a general (ijmali) encompassing, entailing that its effects flow over all. Thus his creation, peace be upon him, from clay was a creation of each one of his descendants from it. And since his creation was in this pattern, flowing to all the individuals of his offspring, it is more fitting than that this be confined to himself, as is the understanding from the attribution of the aforementioned creation to him, and more indicative of the magnitude of the power of the All-Creating, the All-Knowing, and the perfection of His knowledge and wisdom. And the beginning of the state of the addressees is more worthy to be a standard for its end, so He did what He did. How excellent is the affair of the Revelation! Upon this secret rests His words, the Exalted: ﴿And We created you, then We formed you﴾ [al-A'raf: 11], etc., and His words, the Exalted: ﴿And I created you before, when you were nothing﴾ [Maryam: 9], as will come.

It is said: the meaning is "He created your father from it," with an elided modifier. It is also said: the meaning of "He created you from it" is that He created you from the drop (nutfah) resulting from foods formed from the earth. Whichever is the case, there is in it, from the clarity of the indication of His complete power over the Resurrection, what is not hidden; for whoever is able to bring back to life that which has never tasted the scent of life at all, is more manifestly able to bring back to life that which has been associated with it for a period. This was conveyed by Abu al-Su'ud.

In "al-'Inayah": in the verse there is an iltifat, because the address—though it may be valid that it is general—is specific to those who disbelieved, as indicated by: "yet you still doubt." Its subtle point is that the evidence from the selves is closer to the observer than the evidence from the horizons in the preceding verse, and gratitude for it is more obligatory. Both proofs have pointed to the origin and the return, and what lies between them. End.

(p-2242) Abu Dawud and al-Tirmidhi narrated from Abu Musa al-Ash'ari, who said: I heard the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) say: "Indeed Allah created Adam from a handful He took from all of the earth, so the children of Adam came according to the proportion of the earth. Among them came the red, the white, and the black, and what is between that; and the easy and the difficult, and the wicked and the good."

His words, the Exalted: ﴿then decreed a term﴾ means: He ordained for the death of each one of you a term specific to him, that is, a determined limit of time at whose arrival he perishes. Or, He ordained, for the period between the birth of each one of you and the day of his death, a term.

﴿And there is a specified term with Him﴾ means: and a determined limit for your resurrection all together, fixed and specified in His knowledge, which does not accept change, and no one knows the time of its arrival. Like His words, the Exalted: ﴿Its knowledge is with my Lord; none will reveal it at its time but He﴾ [al-A'raf: 187]. So the meaning of "with Him" is that He alone is independent in its knowledge. And "a term" is the subject (mubtada') because it is specified by the descriptive phrase, and because it occurs in the position of detailing. Its tanwin is for magnifying its matter and emphasizing its gravity; for this reason its placement before the predicate "with Him" was preferred, although the common practice in such constructions is postponement, as if it were said: "And what specified term is in His knowledge that no one knows, neither in summary nor in detail?" As for the term of death, it is known in summary and approximately, based on the manifestation of its signs, or on what is customary in human lifespans.

﴿Yet you still doubt﴾ is a expression of wonder and disapproval at their doubt concerning the Resurrection, after witnessing the dazzling proofs indicating it that have been mentioned (p-2243), that is: you doubt its occurrence and its realization in itself, despite your observing within yourselves what cuts off the basis of doubt; for whoever is able to create substances, gather them, and originate life in them, and sustain them as He wills, is more able to gather those substances and bring them back to life a second time.

The Discussion on the Interpretation of His Saying, Exalted is He:

[3] ﴿And He is Allah in the heavens and on the earth; He knows your secret and your open, and He knows what you earn.﴾

﴿And He is Allah in the heavens and on the earth﴾ — meaning: the one worshipped in them. ﴿He knows your secret and your open﴾ — meaning: of speech, or of the inner motives and turnings of the heart, and of the deeds of the limbs. ﴿And He knows what you earn﴾ — meaning: what you do of good or evil, so He rewards for it and punishes for it. Mentioning it specifically, although it is included in what preceded, according to the second interpretation of "secret" and "open," is to show complete concern with it, since reward depends upon it. And this is the reason for repeating "He knows" (ya'lamu).

Al-Nasir said in al-Intisaf: These two noble verses — meaning this verse and the verse of al-Zukhruf, which is His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And He is the one who is God in the heaven and God on the earth﴾ [al-Zukhruf: 84] — are twins. For the praise in the verse of al-Zukhruf is made with the same praise made here: the power to restore, the exclusive knowledge of the Hour, and being the sole deity, and His being the one worshipped in the heavens and the earth.

Imam Ibn Kathir, may Allah have mercy on him, said: The exegetes have several opinions on this verse, after their agreement in rejecting the first view of the Jahmiyya, who say — exalted is He far above what they say — that He is in every place, for they took the verse to mean that. The most correct of the opinions is that He is the one called upon in the heavens and the earth, that is: (p-2244) those in the heavens and those in the earth worship Him, declare His oneness, and acknowledge His divinity, and they call Him Allah, and they call upon Him: ﴿and they call upon Us with hope and fear﴾. Except those among the jinn and humankind who disbelieve. This verse, according to this view, is like His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And He is the one who is God in the heaven and God on the earth﴾ [al-Zukhruf: 84], that is: He is the God of those in the heaven and the God of those on the earth. According to this, His saying "He knows your secret and your open" is a predicate or a circumstantial clause.

The second opinion: The meaning is that He is Allah, who knows what is in the heavens and what is on the earth of secret and open. Then His saying "He knows" is connected to His saying "in the heavens and on the earth," its implied sense being: "And He is Allah who knows your secret and your open in the heavens...," and so on.

The third opinion: His saying "And He is Allah in the heavens" is a complete pause, then He resumes the predicate, saying: "and on the earth; He knows your secret and your open." This is the choice of Ibn Jarir. End.

Ibn 'Atiyya preferred, regarding the verse, that He is the one who is called Allah in both. He said: This, in my view, is the best of the opinions, and the most comprehensive in eloquence of wording and sublimity of meaning. Its clarification: He intended to indicate His creation, the signs of His power, His encompassing and dominion, and similar attributes. So He gathered all of these in His saying "And He is Allah," to whom all of these belong, "in the heavens and on the earth," as if He said: "And He is the Creator, the Provider, the Giver of life and the Giver of death in both."

Note:

Al-Razi said: The verse indicates that man acquires (iktisab) the act, and acquisition is the act that leads to bringing about a benefit or repelling a harm. For this reason, the act of Allah is not described as acquisition, since He, exalted is He, is far above bringing about benefit or repelling harm. And Allah knows best.

Commentary of al-Qasimi (Mahasin al-Ta'wil) on surah 6, verse 4:

(p-2245) The discussion on the interpretation of His saying, exalted is He:

[4] ﴿And there does not come to them any sign from the signs of their Lord except that they are from it turning away.﴾

﴿And there does not come to them any sign from the signs of their Lord﴾ meaning: there does not appear to the disbelievers of Makkah any proof among the proofs that call for reflection and consideration, or any miracle among the miracles, or any sign of the signs of the Qur'an, among which are the preceding signs, which speak of the wondrous works of His creation and His power over resurrection. ﴿Except that they are from it turning away﴾ i.e., in the manner of denial and mockery, due to their little fear and their lack of contemplation of the outcomes.

The discussion of His words, Exalted is He:

[5] ﴿So they have denied the truth when it came to them, but there will come to them the news of that which they used to mock.﴾

﴿So they have denied the truth when it came to them﴾ means: the Qur'an, with which they were challenged and were unable to match. ﴿But there will come to them the news of that which they used to mock﴾ means: the fulfilment of the news of the truth which they used to deny in a mocking manner. Its "news" refers to the swift punishments that will befall them. It is therefore a severe warning to them that they must surely taste its consequence. They did taste it on the Day of Badr and at other times.

**On the interpretation of His saying, Exalted is He:**

[6] ﴿Have they not seen how many generations We destroyed before them, whom We had established on the earth as We have not established you, and We sent down abundant rain upon them and made rivers flow beneath them? Then We destroyed them for their sins and brought into being after them other generations.﴾

﴿Have they not seen﴾ means: have they not known with a knowledge resembling sight with the eye, since they heard by mass transmission (tawatur) of the coming of the mockers before them, and the reports of them, many times over? ﴿How many generations We destroyed before them﴾ means: how many communities. We left none of them remaining, such as the people of Noah, ʿAd, Thamud, and others of the past nations and bygone centuries. ﴿Whom We had established on the earth﴾ means: We settled them and made them firm on the earth. ﴿As We have not established you﴾ means: We did not grant you the same abundance, comfort, and long lives, O people of Makkah. ﴿And We sent down the sky﴾ means: the rain. Al-Mahayimi said: this is more emphatic in indicating abundance than "We sent down (anzalna)." ﴿Abundant upon them﴾ means: plentiful. ﴿And We made the rivers flow beneath them﴾ means: beneath their trees, so they lived in fertility among the rivers and fruits and the watering of abundant rain. ﴿Then We destroyed them for their sins﴾ means: because of their sins, their disbelief, and their denial of their messengers. We made them into tales, and what they had been in did not avail them. That is: the like of the punishment that befell them will likewise befall these people. ﴿And brought into being after them other generations﴾ means: as replacements for those who perished. The meaning is that nothing is too great for Him, Exalted is He, to destroy these people, empty their dwellings of them, and bring into being a different community. They are not more honored in the sight of God than those were. The Messenger whom they denied is more honored before God than their messengers, so they are more deserving of punishment and of sudden retribution, were it not for His gentleness and kindness.

Then Exalted is He explained the severity of their obstinacy after their turning away, by His saying, Glorified is He:

The discussion of His words, exalted is He:

[7] ﴿And even if We had sent down to you a written scroll on paper, and they had touched it with their hands, those who disbelieve would have said, "This is nothing but evident magic."﴾

﴿And even if We had sent down to you a book on paper﴾, meaning written on a sheet. ﴿And they had touched it with their hands﴾, meaning they had handled it. ﴿Those who disbelieve would have said, "This is nothing"﴾, meaning this magnificent thing is not, with these evident aspects indicating that it could only come from God, ﴿but evident magic﴾, out of obstinacy and stubbornness. The specification of "touching" (*lams*) is because forgery cannot occur in it, so they could not say, "Only our eyes were bewitched," and because sight precedes it, where there is no obstacle. Restricting it to "hands" (*al-aydi*) removes figurative usage, for it may be used figuratively for examining, as in His words: ﴿And we have touched the heaven﴾ (72:8). This was stated by al-Baydawi (*al-Bayḍawi*, the commentator).

(p-٢٢٤٧) Al-Nasir said in *al-Intisaf*: The apparent purpose of adding "with their hands" is to confirm the reading at close range, that is, they read it while it was in their hands, not far from them, and still they would not have believed.

Ibn Kathir said: This is as He, exalted is He, said, reporting their denial of what is perceptible to the senses: ﴿And even if We opened for them a gate from the heaven, and they continued ascending through it﴾ (15:14), ﴿they would surely say, "Our eyes have only been dazzled; rather, we are a people bewitched"﴾ (15:15). And His words, exalted is He: ﴿And if they should see a fragment of the heaven falling down, they would say, "Layered clouds"﴾ (52:44).

**The interpretation of His saying, exalted is He:**

[8] ﴿They say, "Why has an angel not been sent down to him?" Had We sent down an angel, the matter would have been decided, and then they would not be reprieved.﴾

﴿They say, "Why has an angel not been sent down to him?"﴾ That is: so that it would accompany him, speak to us, and affirm that he is a prophet, as in His saying: ﴿"Why has an angel not been sent down to him to be a warner alongside him?"﴾ [Al-Furqan: 7].

﴿Had We sent down an angel, the matter would have been decided﴾ is a reply to their proposal and a statement of what prevents it, namely God's sparing of them, so that they would not be like one who seeks his own destruction with his own hoof. The meaning is: if an angel were sent down to the Messenger of God (ﷺ) in his own form, which is a sign more manifest and certain than anything, and they still did not believe, the punishment would have overtaken them and the matter would have been finished. For God's custom (sunnah) regarding the disbelievers is that whenever they propose a sign and then do not believe, they are uprooted by punishment, as He, exalted is He, said: ﴿We do not send down the angels except with truth, and they would then not be reprieved﴾ [Al-Hijr: 8], and His saying, exalted is He: ﴿On the Day they see the angels, there will be no good news that Day for the criminals﴾ [Al-Furqan: 22].

﴿Then they would not be reprieved﴾ means: they would not be given respite after its descent for the blink of an eye, let alone be warned by it. The meaning of "then" (thumma) here: the gap between the two matters, the decision of the matter and the absence of respite, is great. He made the absence of respite more severe than the decision of the matter, because the sudden arrival of severity is more severe than severity itself.

**Note:**

Al-Zamakhshari mentioned a second reason for hastening their punishment upon the descent of the angels: that choice (ikhtiyar), which is the basis of moral responsibility (taklif), would cease, and so their destruction becomes obligatory. In *al-Kashshaf* it is said: "Choice is the basis of responsibility, and this is a compelling sign." He, exalted is He, said: ﴿But their faith did not benefit them when they saw Our might﴾ [Ghafir: 85]. Therefore their destruction became obligatory, lest their existence remain devoid of wisdom, since they were created only to be tested by responsibility, and this does not persist alongside compulsion. This is his explanation according to their school, and it is not free from difficulty. End of quotation. Within it is an indication that it is not in accordance with the principles of the sunnah. The likely source of its difficulty is that it occurs in the Qur'an, and the actual event contradicts it, as in His saying: ﴿Or like the one who passed by a town﴾ [Al-Baqarah: 259]. So it is in *al-Inayah*.

Al-Zamakhshari also mentioned a third reason: that when they witness an angel in his form, their souls depart from the terror of what they witness.

In *al-Intisaf*, it is said: This reason is strengthened by His saying: ﴿Had We made him an angel, We would have made him a man﴾ [Al-An'am: 9]. Ibn Abbas said: "So that they could see him and not perish from witnessing his form." End of quotation.

Abu al-Su'ud preferred this third reason in *al-Taqdim*, where he said: That is, had We sent down an angel in his own shape as they proposed, while the situation is that, because of the terror of the sight, the powers of ordinary humans cannot endure witnessing it. Do you not see that the prophets, peace be upon them, used to witness the angels and converse with them in human form, like the guests of Abraham and Lot, and the adversaries of David, peace be upon them, and others? Since their condition was thus, and they were supported by holy powers, what do you think about those other than them from the common people? Had they witnessed him in that manner, the matter of their destruction would have been decided completely, and his being made a warner would have become impossible. This, besides being contrary to what they seek, entails the concealment from the world of that upon which the order of this world and the next depends, namely the sending of messengers and the establishment of laws. And He, glorified is He, said: ﴿We would never punish until We send a messenger﴾ [Al-Isra': 15]. End of quotation.

In *al-Inayah* it is said that the third reason does not fit His saying, ﴿then they would not be reprieved,﴾ because it indicates their destruction, not their ruin by seeing the angel, except with forced interpretation.

Al-Nasir (Ibn al-Munir) said in *al-Intisaf*: According to the first reason, it is not fitting to make the cause of their immediate destruction the clarity of the sign in the descent of the angel. For this statement may give the impression that the signs whose faith is obligatory for them are less clear than the descent of an angel, and this is not the case. The reason, and God knows best, is that the cause of hastening their punishment, assuming the angel's descent and their non-belief, is that they proposed something upon which the obligation of belief does not depend. For what the obligation depends upon is the miracle as a miracle, not a particular miracle. ﴿When they are answered according to their proposal, but it does not benefit them,﴾ they are then at an extreme of firmness in obstinacy, which is appropriate to the absence of respite. And God knows best.

Al-Mahayimi said: There is no proof of prophethood except the testimony of the angel, and the descent of an angel in his angelic form ends the matter of responsibility, since faith does not benefit after the unveiling of the realm of the angelic kingdom (malakut). So they are not given respite, because respite is for reflection. A miracle, though it conveys a necessary knowledge, is not free from some obscurity that requires minimal reflection, but there is no obscurity with the unveiling of the realm of the angelic kingdom. So there is no reason for respite for reflection, and faith is not accepted with it, so accountability must follow immediately. End of quotation. So let it be considered.

Commentary of al-Qasimi (Mahasin al-Ta'wil) on surah 6, verse 9:

The discussion of the interpretation of His saying, exalted is He:

[9] ﴿And if We had made him an angel, We would have made him a man, and We would have confused them as they confuse themselves.﴾

﴿And if We had made him an angel, We would have made him a man﴾ is a second answer. That is: if We had made the warner whom they proposed an angel (malik), We would have given him the form of a man (rajul), because of what has passed concerning the inability of individuals to witness the angel in his own form, which is of light. Rather, individuals among the prophets saw him in that form by virtue of their holy (qudsiyyah) strength. ﴿And We would have confused them as they confuse themselves﴾ is an omitted answer (jawab mahdhuf). That is: if We had made him a man, We would have confused them about what they confuse themselves with at that time, by saying to him: "You are only a human being, and you are not an angel." And if he had argued for his angelhood by the inimitable Qur'an, which speaks of it, or by other miracles that do not compel assent, they would have denied him, just as they denied the Prophet, may God's blessings and peace be upon him. And if he had shown them his original form, what has been mentioned of the decree of the matter would have followed.

Remarks:

First: The choice of "rajul" (man) over "bashar" (human being) indicates that the making is by way of representation (tamthil), not by way of changing the reality, and it specifies that by which the representation occurs.

Second: The verse contains a demonstration of His mercy toward His creatures, namely that He sends to every kind of creature messengers from among them, so that some of them may call others, and so that some of them may benefit from others in address and questioning. As He, exalted is He, said: ﴿Certainly God conferred a favor upon the believers when He sent among them a messenger from themselves, reciting to them His verses and purifying them﴾ [Al 'Imran: 164], to the end of the verse. And He, exalted is He, said: ﴿Say: Had there been upon the earth angels walking securely, We would have sent down to them from the heaven an angel as a messenger﴾ [al-Isra': 95].

Third: The expression of His representing Himself as a man by "confusion" (al-labs) is either because it is in the form of confusion, or because it is a cause of their confusion, or because it occurs in its company by way of mushakalah (correspondence of terms). In it is an emphasis on the impossibility of making the warner an angel, as if it were said: if We did that, we would do what is unbecoming of Our dignity, namely confusing the matter for them. Abu al-Su'ud stated this.

Fourth: Some scholars permitted a second aspect for His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And if We had made him an angel﴾, namely that it be an answer to a second proposal, with the pronoun referring to the Messenger, not to their earlier proposal. He said: because they sometimes say: "Why was an angel not sent down to him?" and sometimes say: "If our Lord had willed, He would have sent down angels." The meaning: if We had made the Messenger an angel, We would have represented him as a man. The apparent view is the first aspect.

The discussion of the words of God Most High:

[10] ﴿And indeed, messengers before you were mocked, but those who mocked them were engulfed by that which they used to mock.﴾

His words, Exalted is He: ﴿And indeed, messengers before you were mocked, but those who mocked them were engulfed by that which they used to mock.﴾ are a consolation to the Messenger of God (ﷺ) for what he suffers from his people, and a promise to him and to the believers in him of victory and a good end in this world and the Hereafter. And (ḥāqa) means "to descend" and "to alight," and it is hardly used except for evil. So there descended upon them the consequence of their mockery, or the punishment they used to mock when they were warned of it, for they perished in this world in the most abhorrent manner, and then they were returned to the most dreadful punishment forever and ever. And He placed the messengers in the highest stations of nearness to the Lord of the worlds.

Then God Most High commanded that he (the Prophet) openly declare to them that they should travel about the earth, in case they doubted what was widely transmitted, or closed their eyes to what they had seen, with His words:

The discourse on the interpretation of His saying, exalted is He:

[11] ﴿Say: Travel through the earth, then observe how was the end of those who denied.﴾

﴿Say: Travel through the earth, then observe how was the end of those who denied.﴾ That is: travel through the earth to come to know the conditions of those nations, and reflect on how they were destroyed when they denied the Messengers and opposed them, so that you may recognize the truth of what you are being admonished with. In travelling through the earth, journeying through the lands, and beholding those ruins fallen upon their foundations, there is a completion of taking heed (i'tibar, drawing lessons) and a strengthening of insight (istibsar). That is: do not be deceived by what you enjoy of the pleasures of this world and its appetites.

In this verse there is also a completion of consolation, through what it contains of a subtle promise that there will befall them the like of what befell their counterparts who denied, and this has been fulfilled magnificently on the Day of Badr.

A subtle point (latifah):

Here occurred "thumma unzuru" (then observe), while in an-Naml occurs: ﴿Say: Travel through the earth, then observe﴾ [an-Naml: 69], and likewise in al-'Ankabut. Some have laboured to distinguish the instance here by "thumma" (then), as is expounded in al-'Inayah, along with what is objectionable in it. It is related from some of them that the travelling is one in both places, but it is a matter extended in time, which is conjoined with "fa" (so) on occasion, regarding its end, and with "thumma" (then) regarding its beginning; and there is no difference between them.

In al-Intisaf: The more apparent view is that the command to travel in both places is one, so that it becomes a cause for observation. Wherever "fa" enters, it is to show causation; and wherever "thumma" enters, it is to alert that observation is the intended aim of travel, and that travel is merely a means to it, and nothing more. How vast is the difference between the aim and the means. And Allah knows best.

**Commentary on the interpretation of His words, Exalted is He:**

﴿Say: "To whom belongs whatever is in the heavens and the earth?" Say: "To Allah."﴾

﴿Say: "To whom belongs whatever is in the heavens and the earth?"﴾ That is, in creation and in ownership. This is a question of rebuke and reproach. ﴿Say: "To Allah."﴾ is a confirmation of the answer on their behalf. That is: it is Allah. There is no dispute between me and you, and you cannot attribute any part of it to anything else. This points to the answer being determined by agreement, as in His words, Exalted is He: ﴿And if you asked them who created the heavens and the earth, they would surely say, "Allah."﴾ [Luqman: 25]. It is established that commanding the questioner to give the answer is only appropriate in a situation where the answer has become so evident that no denier can deny it and no challenger can refute it, as here. It has been said: this also indicates that they were slow to answer, although the answer was determined, because they were confounded.

His words, Exalted is He: ﴿He has prescribed for Himself mercy﴾ form an independent sentence within the command, expressing that His vast mercy encompasses all creation, just as His dominion and power encompass everything. It is brought to explain that He, Exalted is He, is kind to His servants. He does not hasten to punish them, and He accepts from them repentance and return. What was mentioned before and what followed of the rulings of wrath is not among the requirements of His essence, Exalted is He, but comes from the side of creation. How could it not be so? Among His mercy is that He created them upon the sound innate nature (al-fitrah, the natural disposition toward recognizing the Creator), and guided them to knowing and affirming His oneness, by setting up signs within themselves and in the horizons, sending messengers, and sending down books filled with the call to what brings about His good pleasure and with warning against what brings about His anger. Yet they changed the nature of Allah, ﴿a change﴾, turned away from the signs entirely, denied the books, and mocked the messengers. ﴿We did not wrong them, but they were wrongdoers themselves.﴾ Were it not for the comprehensiveness of His mercy, they would have been treated in the same way as the bygone peoples.

The meaning of ﴿He has prescribed for Himself mercy﴾ is that He, Exalted is He, made it obligatory and decreed it upon His sacred essence by way of bounty and kindness, directly, without any intermediary at all. In expressing the essence by "the self" (al-nafs) there is evidence against those who claim that the word "self" (nafs) is not applied to Allah, Exalted is He. Even if it is intended to mean the essence, this is only for the sake of parallelism (mushakalah, matching of wording), given the absence of such parallelism here. This was stated by Abu al-Su'ud.

His words, Exalted is He: ﴿He will surely gather you﴾ are the answer to an implied oath. The sentence is a resumption, brought as a threat, regarding their associating partners with Allah and their neglect of reflection. For when He had shown the perfection of His divinity by His words, ﴿Say: "To whom belongs whatever is in the heavens and the earth?" Say: "To Allah."﴾, and then informed that He shows mercy to them in this world by granting respite and averting the punishment of annihilation, He made known that He will gather them for that Day and call them to account for everything they did. For a wise king does not neglect the affairs of his subjects, and it is not befitting his wisdom to treat the obedient and the disobedient alike. It has been said: ﴿He will surely gather you﴾ is the answer to His words, "He has prescribed," because it functions in the place of an oath.

It has also been said: ﴿He will surely gather you﴾ is a substitute (badal) for "mercy," a substitute of part (badal al-ba'd). Al-Mahayimi said: The perfection of mercy lies in the recompense, for without it the hardships of the knowledge of God and righteous deeds would be wasted, and injustices would go unpunished. There is no recompense in the abode of this world, because recompense is a consequence of obligation (taklif), and the abode of obligation cannot be the abode of recompense, for witnessing it would prevent obligation. End of quote.

The particle "ila" (to) here has the meaning of "li" (for), as in His words: "You are gathering people for a Day," ﴿about which there is no doubt﴾, meaning: concerning the Day, or concerning the gathering.

﴿Those who have lost their souls﴾ means: by squandering their capital, which is the original innate nature (al-fitrah), sound reason, the close readiness that comes from witnessing the Messenger, peace and blessings be upon him, hearing the revelation, and other effects of mercy.

﴿So they do not believe﴾ means: they do not affirm the Return (al-ma'ad), and they do not fear the evil of that Day.

Abu al-Su'ud said: The "fa" (so) is used because the subject contains the meaning of a condition, and to indicate that their not believing is due to their loss. For the nullification of reason through following the senses, immersion in imitation, and neglect of reflection led them to persist in disbelief and to refuse faith. The sentence is a concluding statement (tadhyil) coming from Him, Exalted is He, to denounce their state, and it is not included within the command.

**Note:**

It is related about the meaning of this verse from Abu Hurayrah, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "When Allah created the creation, He wrote in a book, which is with Him above the Throne: 'Indeed My mercy overcomes My wrath.'" Narrated by the two Shaykhs (al-Bukhari and Muslim).

In al-Bukhari: "Allah wrote a book before He created the creation: 'Indeed My mercy precedes My wrath.' It is written with Him, over the Throne."

In another narration of both: "When Allah created the creation."

(p-٢٢٥٧) In Muslim: "When Allah decreed the creation, He wrote in a book which He wrote concerning Himself, and it is placed with Him." Al-Bukhari added: "over the Throne." Then both agreed: "Indeed My mercy overcomes My wrath."

If Allah wills, we will mention a portion of the hadiths on mercy near the verse: "Your Lord has prescribed for Himself mercy," shortly.

Abu al-Su'ud said: The meaning of the precedence and overcoming of mercy is that it is more ancient in its connection to creation, and more extensive in reaching them, along with the fact that it is among the requirements of the essence, which overflows with goodness.

Commentary of al-Qasimi (Mahasin al-Ta'wil) on surah 6, verse 13:

(p-2258) The discussion on the interpretation of His statement, exalted is He:

[13] ﴿And to Him belongs whatever rests in the night and the day, and He is the All-Hearing, the All-Knowing.﴾

﴿And to Him﴾, i.e., and to Allah, mighty and majestic: ﴿whatever rests in the night and the day﴾, i.e., whatever settles and dwells, from the sukna (dwelling) in the sense of ḥulūl (residing). Like His statement, exalted is He: ﴿and you dwelt in the dwellings of those who wronged themselves﴾ [Ibrahim: 45]. The meaning: to Him, exalted is He, belongs everything that occurs in the night and the day, of what the sun rises upon or sets upon. He likened the settling in time to settling in place, so the term used for place is applied to it. Or sakana is from sukūn, the opposite of movement; i.e., whatever is still in them and whatever moves, and He suffices with one of the two opposites over the other, as in His statement: ﴿garments that protect you from the heat﴾ [al-Nahl: 81]; because that is known from the context. Accordingly, He mentioned only stillness to the exclusion of its opposite and not the reverse, because stillness is more frequent in existence, and the blessing in it is greater.

Some of them said: there is no need for the claim of sufficiency (iktifa'), for "whatever rests" encompasses all created things, since none of them is free of the attribute of stillness, even the moving thing while it is moving, according to what has been verified in theological discussion: that the variation of motions in speed and slowness is due to the paucity or abundance of the intervening pauses.

A subtle point:

Abu Muslim al-Isfahani said: In the first verse He mentioned the heavens and the earth, since there is no place other than them. In this verse He mentioned the night and the day, since there is no time other than them. So time and place are receptacles (ẓarfān) for created things, and He, glorified is He, informed that He is the owner of place and what is in place, and the owner of time and what is in time. This is an explanation of the utmost grandeur.

Al-Razi said: Here is another subtle point: the beginning was with the mention of place and what is in place, then He mentioned after it time and what is in time. That is because place and what is in place are closer to the intellects and thoughts than time and what is in time, due to subtleties mentioned in the pure rational sciences. Complete instruction is that which begins with the more evident, then the more evident, ascending to the less evident, and this is part of the secret of the arrangement of the verse with what precedes it.

﴿And He is the All-Hearing, the All-Knowing﴾: He hears every thing heard and knows every thing known, so nothing is hidden from Him of what the two realms (al-malawān: night and day) contain.

Commentary of al-Qasimi (Mahasin al-Ta'wil) on surah 6, verse 14:

The discussion of His saying, exalted is He:

[14] ﴿Say: "Shall I take as a protector other than God, the Originator of the heavens and the earth, while He feeds and is not fed?" Say: "Indeed I have been commanded to be the first to submit, and never be of the polytheists."﴾

﴿Say﴾, i.e., to the disbelievers of Makkah, who are rebuked by what preceded: ﴿Shall I take as a protector other than God﴾, i.e., as an object of worship. Like His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Say: "Do you order me to worship other than God, you ignorant ones?"﴾ [al-Zumar: 64]. The meaning is: I do not take as a protector anyone but God alone. ﴿the Originator of the heavens and the earth﴾, i.e., their Creator and Innovator, without a precedent pattern. It is in the genitive (bi-al-jarr) as an attribute of the Name of Majesty (al-Jalalah), emphasizing the denial.

﴿while He feeds and is not fed﴾, i.e., He provides sustenance and is not provided for; that is, all benefits come from Him, and benefiting from Him is impossible. That is, it is incumbent to take Him as a protector so that He is worshipped in gratitude for His favors and for His sufficiency in meeting needs without requesting any return. It was said: the intended meaning of "feeding" (al-tu'm) is provision (al-rizq) in its linguistic sense, which is everything from which one benefits, as evidenced by its being set in opposition to it in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿I do not desire any provision from them, nor do I desire that they should feed Me﴾ [al-Dhariyat: 57]. So He expressed the general by the specific figuratively, because it is the greatest and most abundant of it, given the intensity of need for it. And He dispensed with the general, because from the negation of this is understood the negation of everything else.

(p-2260) ﴿Say: "Indeed I have been commanded to be the first to submit"﴾, i.e., to turn my face to God, sincere to Him, so that I become the one followed by the rest. Like His saying: ﴿And I have been commanded thus, and I am the first of the Muslims﴾ [al-An'am: 163], and like Moses' saying: ﴿Glory be to You; I have repented to You, and I am the first of the believers﴾ [al-A'raf: 143].

﴿and never be of the polytheists﴾, i.e., and it was said to me: "and never be." It is conjoined to "I have been commanded," with the meaning: I have been commanded to submit to Islam and forbidden from polytheism explicitly and emphatically, after the prohibition implicit in the command. The prohibition addressed to the one followed is a prohibition to those who follow. It is also permissible to conjoin it to "Say." The verse contains guidance that every commander should himself act upon what he commands, since he is their exemplar. It was said: this verse is for encouragement, as a king commands his subjects with a matter and then says: "I am the first to do that," so as to move them to comply.

The discussion of the saying of His, exalted is He:

[15] ﴿Say: Indeed, I fear, if I disobey my Lord, the punishment of a tremendous day.﴾

﴿Say: Indeed, I fear, if I disobey my Lord﴾ meaning: by violating His command and His prohibition, whatever the disobedience. Thus what has been mentioned enters into it as a primary entry. ﴿the punishment of a tremendous day﴾ meaning: the punishment of the Day of Resurrection, in which the greatness of the divine dominance becomes manifest. In the verse there is another emphasis in cutting off their hopes, and an allusion to them that they are disobedient and deserving of the great punishment. The manner of the allusion is the attribution of what is known to be impossible, by means of (in) which indicates doubt, as an allusion. The past tense is used to present it in the form of something already occurring by way of supposition, as an allusion to those from whom that proceeded. Since it is an allusion to them, and the intent is to frighten them should that proceed from them, it contains no indication that the Prophet ﷺ himself fears disobedience for his own soul, although he is infallible. Just as such a thing is not to be imagined in His saying: ﴿If you associate partners with Allah, your deeds will surely be nullified﴾ [al-Zumar: 65]. And at that point there is no need for what has been answered regarding its apparent indication of what was mentioned, namely that the fear is attached to disobedience whose occurrence is ordinarily impossible, so it indicates only that he would fear if disobedience proceeded from him, and this does not indicate that the fear has occurred.

Some of them said: It cannot be said that on the assumption of disobedience, the response would be the deserving of punishment, not fear. Because we say: there is no contradiction between them. The fear is either in its literal sense, or a metonym for deserving. End.

Commentary of al-Qasimi (Mahasin al-Ta'wil) on surah 6, verse 16:

The discussion of His saying, may He be exalted:

[16] ﴿Whoever is turned away from it on that Day, He has indeed had mercy on him. That is the manifest triumph.﴾

﴿Whoever is turned away﴾ is in the passive form, meaning: the punishment is turned away ﴿from him on that Day, He has indeed had mercy on him﴾, i.e., He saved him and bestowed favor upon him, or caused him to enter Paradise, in accordance with His saying: ﴿So whoever is drawn away from the Fire and admitted into Paradise [has succeeded]﴾ [Al 'Imran: 185], and His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿He admits whom He wills into His mercy﴾ [al-Insan: 31]. The clause is independent (mustani'afah), serving to emphasize the terror of the punishment.

﴿And that﴾, i.e., the turning away or the mercy, ﴿is the manifest triumph﴾, i.e., the evident one.

Then He, may He be exalted, mentioned another proof that it is not permissible for a person of sound intellect to take as a protector (waliyy) other than Allah, may He be exalted, by His saying:

(p-2262) The discussion of the interpretation of His saying, Exalted is He:

[17] ﴿And if Allah touches you with adversity, there is no remover of it except Him. And if He touches you with good, then He is over all things competent.﴾

﴿And if Allah touches you with adversity﴾ i.e., with an affliction, such as poverty, sickness, and the like. And (al-ḍurr) (adversity): a comprehensive term for whatever befalls a person of harm. ﴿there is no remover of it except Him﴾ i.e., none is able to repel it except Him alone. ﴿And if He touches you with good﴾ such as well-being, ease, and the like. And (al-khayr) (good): a comprehensive term for whatever befalls a person of what is beloved to him. ﴿then He is over all things competent﴾ i.e., and this is among the totality of things over which He has power; so He holds it [i.e., the good] fast for you and preserves it for you, with none able to repel it or remove it. Like His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿So there is no one to repel His bounty﴾ [Yunus: 107], and like His saying, Glorified is He: ﴿Whatever Allah grants to people of mercy, none can withhold; and whatever He withholds, none can release thereafter﴾ [Fatir: 2].

And in the Sahih it is narrated that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) used to say: "O Allah, there is none who can withhold what You have given, and none who can give what You have withheld, and the fortune of the fortunate will not benefit them against You."

(p-2263) And from Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him, who said: "I was behind the Prophet (ﷺ) when he said: 'O boy! I will teach you some words: Guard Allah and He will guard you; guard Allah and you will find Him before you. When you ask, ask Allah; and when you seek help, seek help from Allah. Know that if the whole nation gathered to benefit you with something, they would not benefit you except with something Allah the Exalted has already written for you; and if they gathered to harm you with something, they would not harm you except with something Allah the Exalted has already written against you. The pens have been lifted and the pages have dried.'" Narrated by al-Tirmidhi, who said: hasan sahih.

Commentary of al-Qasimi (Mahasin al-Ta'wil) on surah 6, verse 18:

The discussion of the interpretation of His saying, Exalted is He:

[18] ﴿And He is the Subduer over His servants, and He is the Wise, the All-Aware.﴾

﴿And He is the Subduer over His servants, and He is the Wise, the All-Aware.﴾ That is: He is the Overpowering by His power, the One exalted above His servants. He manages their affairs as He wills, so there befalls them that which is hard upon them, burdensome, distressing and saddening, and none of them can repel His management or escape from under His dominion and decree.

Abu al-Baqa' said: In (fawqa, "above") there are two aspects:

The first: it is in a position of accusative (nasb) as a circumstantial state (hal) of the pronoun in al-Qahir; that is, "exalted" and "overpowering."

The second: it is in a position of nominative (raf') as an apposition (badal) of al-Qahir, or as a second predicate (khabar thani).

The Interpretation of His Words, Exalted Is He:

[19] ﴿Say: "What thing is greatest as testimony?" Say: "God is witness between me and you. This Qur'an has been revealed to me so that I may warn you by it, and whomever it reaches." Do you truly testify that there are other gods with God?" Say: "I do not testify to that." Say: "He is only one God, and I am innocent of what you associate with Him."﴾

﴿Say: "What thing is greatest as testimony?"﴾ That is, such that nothing equal to it can be set against it. ﴿Say: "God"﴾ [p. 2264], that is, He is the greatest testimony, since there is no possibility at all that falsehood could enter His report, exalted is His majesty. He commanded the Prophet (ﷺ) to give the answer himself, either to signify that it is specific (to God), and that they are unable to answer with anything else, or because they might stammer over it. This is not because they doubt that He, exalted is He, is greater than everything, but rather regarding His being a witness in this matter.

His words, Exalted is He, ﴿God is witness between me and you﴾ are a predicate of an omitted subject, or a predicate of the word "Allah" (the Name of God). It indicates the answer to "what thing" (ayy) by way of meaning, because if He, exalted is He, is the witness between him and them, then He is the greatest thing as testimony, being a witness to him. This is the wise method (al-uslub al-hakim), since he turned away from the answer that comes immediately to mind, in order to show that the greatest testimony is the witness to the Messenger, for God is the greatest thing as testimony, and God is a witness to him, so the conclusion is that He is the greatest testimony for him. The syllogism mentioned is of the third figure (al-shakl al-thalith), because the middle term is the subject in both premises, not the second figure, as al-Shihab fell into in his *al-Inaya*, and this is among the basic axioms of logic (al-mizan).

Some have said: The purpose of the question "What thing is greatest as testimony?" is that my witness is the greatest testimony. So His words "He is witness…" etc. are an explicit statement of this, and the question does not need an answer, since it is known and clear to the opponent. Its sum is that God, who is the greatest testimony, is famous for that. End of quote.

The meaning of "witness" (shahid) is an intensifier of testimony to my prophethood, such that it ends the dispute between me and you, since He, glorified is He, testified by speech in the books He sent down to the earlier ones, and by action in what appeared at my hands of miracles, especially the miracle of the Qur'an, as He, exalted is He, said:

﴿And this Qur'an has been revealed to me﴾, that is, which comprises the knowledge needed in matters of belief and law, in brief words, at the highest levels of beauty and eloquence, a miracle bearing witness to the truth of my messengership, because you are the eloquent and the masters of speech, and you have been unable to produce its like. ﴿so that I may warn you by it﴾, that is, by what it contains of threat, ﴿and whomever it reaches﴾ is conjoined to the pronoun of those addressed, meaning: "so that I may warn you by it, O people of Makkah, and all the rest of mankind whom it reaches." So he is a warner to everyone it reaches, as in His words: ﴿And whoever among the factions disbelieves in it, the Fire is his promised place﴾ [Hud: 17].

﴿Do you truly testify that there are other gods with God?﴾ is a statement to them, together with denial and astonishment.

﴿Say: "I do not testify to that"﴾, that is, to what you testify. ﴿Say: "He is only one God"﴾, that is, rather, I testify that there is no god but Him, not shared in His divinity nor in the attributes of His perfection. ﴿And I am innocent of what you associate with Him﴾, meaning: the idols.

In this verse there are several issues:

The first: The majority (al-jumhur) cited His words, ﴿Say: "God"﴾, in answer to "What thing is greatest as testimony?" as evidence for the permissibility of applying the term "thing" (shay') to God, exalted is He. Likewise His words, glorified and exalted is He, ﴿Everything perishes except His Face﴾ [al-Qasas: 88], since the exception must fall under the thing excepted. This is because "thing" is the most general of general terms, as Sibawayh said, since it applies to everything that can be known and spoken of. Al-Zamakhshari chose that it includes even the impossible. Many of the verifiers (al-muhaqqiqun) explicitly stated that it is restricted to the existent, and they weakened the view of those who applied it to the non-existent, arguing that it is refuted by the Arabs' non-use of it in that way, as is known from inductive study of their speech, and by such verses as ﴿Everything perishes except His Face﴾ [al-Qasas: 88], since the non-existent does not have the attribute of perishing, and by such verses as ﴿And there is nothing that does not glorify Him with His praise﴾ [al-Isra': 44], since glorification cannot be conceived from the non-existent.

Al-Nasir (Ibn al-Munayyir) said in *al-Intisaf*: This question is counted among the science of kalam in one respect, but this inquiry is linguistic, and the judgment in it belongs to the people of language. The apparent sense of their saying "I was angry at nothing (la shay')" and the verse:

"When he sees other than a thing, he thinks it a man"

is that "thing" is applied only to the existent. For if "thing" were everything that can be known, whether non-existent or existent, possible or impossible, it would not be true of any matter that it is "not a thing." The matter in this is close. End of quote.

This is so. Those who prohibited applying it to Him, exalted is He, held to His words: ﴿And to God belong the most beautiful names, so call on Him by them﴾ [al-A'raf: 180]. A name is only beautiful by the beauty of what it names, namely that it indicates an attribute of perfection and a description of majesty. The word "thing" is the most general of things, so what it names is found in the best of things and in the basest of them. When that is so, the one named by this term is not an attribute of perfection, and so we must not permit calling on God by this name, since it is not among the beautiful names, and He commanded that He be called upon by them. It was answered: That it is not among the beautiful names is because these are tawqifi (determined only by revelation), and that it is not to be called upon by it because it has not been transmitted does not conflict with its including the exalted essences by way of general inclusion. What is meant by applying it to Him, exalted is He, in what preceded, is its inclusiveness, not naming Him by it. In sum: it does not follow that its not being among the beautiful names means it does not include the sacred essence in a universal way. How could it not, when it is among the general terms? The judgment on that belongs to the linguists, as we have previously stated.

The second: What we have already mentioned, that what is meant by the testimony is His testimony to the establishing of prophethood for him (ﷺ), is the view to which most inclined. It seems the polytheists of Makkah asked him (ﷺ) for a witness to his prophethood. So it was said to them: The greatest thing as testimony is God, exalted is He, and He has testified to my prophethood, since He revealed this Qur'an to me, and challenged you to produce its like, and you were unable, though you are at the level of eloquence. Since it is a miracle, its being manifested by Him, exalted is He, in accordance with my claim, is a testimony from Him to my truthfulness in prophethood.

For some there is another view, namely that what is meant is His testimony to the establishing of His oneness, and His transcendence above rivals and likenesses. This is reinforced by the completion of the verse, namely His words, ﴿Do you truly testify…﴾ etc., and His words, ﴿God testifies that there is no god but Him﴾ [Al 'Imran: 18], and His words, exalted is He, ﴿If they testify, then do not testify with them﴾ [al-An'am: 150], [which indicates] that testimony, wherever it occurs in revelation, is meant to establish oneness. The Qur'an explains part of it by part. And God knows best.

The third: He limited himself to warning in His words, ﴿so that I may warn you by it﴾, because the address is to the disbelievers of Makkah, and there was none among them who would be given good tidings. Or it is sufficient for this, rather than mentioning good tidings, in the manner of: ﴿garments that protect you from the heat﴾ [al-Nahl: 81].

The fourth: It was cited by His words, ﴿so that I may warn you by it and whomever it reaches﴾, as evidence that he (ﷺ) was sent to all mankind and to the jinn.

The fifth: It was also cited as evidence that the rulings of the Qur'an apply to those present at the time of its revelation and to whoever will exist after that until the Day of Resurrection, except that this is by way of implication (ibarah) for all, according to the Hanbalis, and by consensus (ijma') in our view for those not present and those not obligated at that time. This was conveyed by Abu al-Su'ud.

The sixth: Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Muhammad ibn Ka'b regarding His words, ﴿and whomever it reaches﴾: "Whoever the Qur'an reaches, it is as if he saw the Prophet (ﷺ) and spoke with him." Ibn Jarir narrated it from him with the wording: "Whoever the Qur'an reaches, Muhammad (ﷺ) has conveyed to him."

Abd al-Razzaq narrated from Qatada regarding this verse that the Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: "Convey from God; whoever has had a verse of the Book of God reach him, the command of God has reached him."

Al-Rabi' ibn Anas said: It is incumbent upon whoever follows the Messenger of God (ﷺ) that he call as the Messenger of God (ﷺ) called, and warn with what he warned.

The seventh: His words, ﴿Say: "He is only one God"﴾ and His words, ﴿And I am innocent of what you associate with Him﴾ indicate the establishing of monotheism by the greatest means of clarification and the most eloquent forms of emphasis, since "only" (innama) conveys restriction, and "one" (wahid) is explicit in negating partners. Then he explicitly declared his disavowal of establishing partners. Al-Shafi'i recommended that whoever embraces Islam, after bringing the two testimonies, should disavow every religion other than the religion of Islam, based on His words, ﴿And I am innocent of what you associate with Him﴾ immediately after the explicit declaration of monotheism.

"The Word concerning His saying, exalted is He:

[20] ﴿Those to whom We gave the Book recognize him as they recognize their own sons. Those who have lost their souls—they do not believe.﴾

As for His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Those to whom We gave the Book﴾, meaning the Jews and the Christians, ﴿recognize him﴾, i.e., they recognize the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) by his description and attributes which are established in the two Books, ﴿as they recognize their own sons﴾ by their features and characteristics, so that they are not concealed from them and are not confused with others.

Al-Mahayimi said: Because the Prophet (ﷺ) was mentioned in the Book with his description. And although it does not establish his specific identity by color, form, time, or place, he is specified by the indications of the miracles. Thus the persistence of the remote possibility regarding him is like its persistence regarding a child, in that it is possible that he is other than the one his wife bore, or that it results from immorality, despite the indications that she is free from forgery and immorality. So he, just as they recognize their sons, the remote possibility is removed by the indications of their innocence.

Al-Zamakhshari said: This is an argument to the people of Makkah from the recognition of the People of the Book, and for the validity of his prophethood.

Then Allah, exalted is He, explained that denying him is a loss of what they recognized and of what they were commanded to adhere to, by His saying: ﴿Those who have lost their souls﴾, i.e., among the polytheists, ﴿they do not believe﴾, i.e., in this clear and manifest matter which the Prophets gave glad tidings of and proclaimed, because it is sealed upon their hearts."

Commentary of al-Qasimi (Mahasin al-Ta'wil) on surah 6, verse 21:

The discussion of His saying, may He be exalted:

[21] ﴿And who is more unjust than one who invents a lie against Allah or denies His signs? Indeed, the wrongdoers will not succeed.﴾

﴿And who is more unjust than one who invents a lie against Allah⁠﴾ like their saying: "The angels are the daughters of Allah," and "These are our intercessors with Allah." Allah, the Exalted, said: ﴿And when they commit an immorality, they say, "We found our fathers upon it, and Allah has commanded us with it."﴾ [al-A'raf: 28]

(p-2271) ﴿Or denies His signs⁠﴾ i.e., the Qur'an and the miracles, by calling them magic. He said "or," although they combined both matters, to alert that each of them alone reaches the utmost extreme of wrongdoing against oneself. So how much more so when they have combined the two? For they affirmed what Allah, the Exalted, had negated, and negated what He had affirmed.

﴿Indeed, the wrongdoers will not succeed⁠﴾ i.e., they will not be saved from what is disliked, nor will they attain what they seek. If this is the condition of the wrongdoers, then how about one than whom no one is more unjust?

Note:

What we have mentioned, that the relative pronoun refers metonymically to the polytheists, is the apparent meaning, because the surah is Meccan and the address is with its polytheist inhabitants. Al-Baydawi took it to refer to them and to the People of the Scripture, adhering to the general wording of the expression; al-Mahayimi took it to refer specifically to the People of the Scripture, linking the verse to what precedes it. The first reading is apparent, for the reason we have stated. The wording of al-Mahayimi: "Those who have lost their own selves by forfeiting what they were given of the Book and what they were commanded, so they do not believe. And how would they not lose, when they are wrongdoers, and every wrongdoer is a loser?" We said they are wrongdoers because they distort the Book of Allah in wording or meaning, thereby inventing lies against Allah, and they deny the signs of Allah in their Book and the miracles of Muhammad ﷺ and his Book. They sometimes conceal part of what is in their Book, and that too is denial. They did all of this because it is not possible for them to abandon belief in Muhammad ﷺ without one of these matters.

He said regarding His saying, ﴿And who is more unjust⁠﴾ etc.: because through distortion they claim divinity for themselves, and through denial they intend to make Allah incapable of confirming His messengers, and they attribute the origination of these things to other than Allah, despite their need for complete power. We said every wrongdoer is a loser because every wrongdoer does not succeed, as Allah, the Exalted, said: ﴿Indeed, the wrongdoers will not succeed⁠﴾ i.e., they will not succeed in this world, through the cutting off of proof from them and the victory of the Muslims over them. This contains an indication that the claimant to prophethood, if he were a liar, would be one who invents against Allah, and so he would not succeed, and thus would not be a cause of the well-being of the world, nor a locus for the manifestation of miracles. End.

(p-٢٢٧٢) The discussion on the interpretation of His statement, exalted is He:

[22] ﴿And on the Day We gather them all, then We will say to those who associated others with Allah, "Where are your partners whom you used to claim?"﴾

﴿And on the Day We gather them﴾, i.e., mankind, the jinn and the devils. It is governed by an implied verb, to magnify the matter. ﴿All﴾, so that those wrongdoers who will not prosper are further disgraced, and the successful appear in complete honor.

﴿Then We will say to those who associated﴾, i.e., those who persisted in polytheism, dying upon it, and who testified that there were other gods besides Allah: ﴿Where are your partners﴾, i.e., those whom you made into partners with Us, who are your partners in worship. So said al-Mahayimi. According to this, the idafah (the grammatical annexation construction) is in its proper sense.

In al-Inaya: the idafah here is for the slightest connection, as the qadi indicated with his words: "i.e., your gods that you made partners with Allah, because there is no partnership between them, and they only named them partners. For this connection they were annexed to them."

It has been said: the statement of Allah, exalted is He, ﴿Gather those who did wrong and their companions and what they used to worship﴾ [al-Saffat: 22] requires their presence with them at the place of gathering, while "ayna" (أين, "where") is used to ask about what is not present. It is answered that there is an implied annexed noun, i.e., "Where is their benefit and their intercession?" Or they are treated as absent, because what they hoped for from them of intercession is nonexistent. In either case, the purpose of the question is to rebuke and reproach them, and to establish in their souls that what they were hoping for is hopeless. This is also a warning to them in the worldly life about the corruption of this path.
