His statement, exalted is He, ﴿that you used to claim﴾, i.e., you claimed them to be partners from your own selves. That is, by this you intended the action of those who corrupt the kingdom by assigning it to other than its rightful owner.

The Interpretation of His Words, Exalted is He:

[23] ﴿Then their trial will be only that they say, "By Allah, our Lord, we were not polytheists."﴾

﴿Then their trial will not be﴾ meaning: the answer to what was raised as an objection to their trial, which is the testimony that there are other gods along with Allah. He expressed their answer as a "trial" (fitnah) because it is a lie. ﴿Only that they say, "By Allah, our Lord, we were not polytheists."﴾ They pleaded in excuse for their idols by denying them, emphasizing it with an oath by the all-encompassing Name (Allah), together with attributing lordship (rububiyyah) to Him, Exalted is He, and not to anything else, as an exaggeration in disavowing association (shirk). So this excuse was another sin, confirming their fabrication of the association which they denied. As Allah, Exalted is He, said:

The discussion of the interpretation of His words, may He be exalted:

[24] ﴿Look how they lied against themselves, and what they used to invent has forsaken them.﴾

﴿Look how they lied against themselves﴾: that is, by denying association (with God) before the All-Knowing of the unseen, in the presence of witnesses without number. ﴿and what they used to invent has forsaken them﴾: that is, how it was lost and vanished. ﴿what they used to invent﴾: that is, the associates, which did not avail them anything, so they lost what they had hoped for from their intercession and their support for them, as in His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿They will say, "Where are those you used to call upon besides God?" They will say, "They have forsaken us."﴾ [al-A'raf: 37]. Here "ma" (what) is a relative pronoun, a metonymy for the associates. And the attribution of invention (iftira') to them, although in reality it falls upon their states of divinity, partnership, intercession and the like, is for the sake of emphasis on their matter, as if they themselves were the thing invented.

(p-2274) Remarks:

The first: what we have mentioned, that He expressed their answer as "fitna" (trial, test), is the most apparent. The meaning is: the answer consisting of what is a lie, because it is the cause of the trial; so "fitna" is used figuratively for it, the effect being named for its cause, or it is a metaphor. It has been said: "fitna" means "excuse", because linguistically it is the freeing from deceit, and an excuse frees one from sin, so it is borrowed for it. It has been said: it means "disbelief", because the trial (fitna) is that by which one is tested and which pleases you, and they were pleased with their disbelief, proud of it, and thought it to be something; so its outcome was nothing but loss and disavowal of it. This is not on the assumption of an elided noun; rather, the outcome of the thing is made to be the thing itself, by claim.

Al-Zajjaj said: The interpretation of this verse is sound in the language, and none knows it except one who knows the meanings of speech and the varied usages of the Arabs in this. That is because God, exalted, explained that the polytheists were tested by their polytheism, utterly enamoured of its love; so He informed in this verse that their being tested by their polytheism, and their persistence in it, was only that they disowned it and distanced themselves from it, and they swore that they had not been polytheists. An example: you see a person who loves a deviant man of blameworthy way; then when he falls into an ordeal because of him, he disowns him, and it is said to him: "Your love for so-and-so was nothing but that you disowned him."

Al-Khafaji said, after quoting what has been mentioned: This is not of the kind of your rebuking the sword, nor of the assumption of an elided noun; and if it is sound, memorize it, for it is among the marvellous and splendid things.

The second: what we have explained, that "ma" in His saying, may He be exalted, ﴿and what they used to invent has forsaken them﴾ is a relative pronoun, a metonymy for the associates, in the sense of their not availing them, is the one that agrees with the second verse we have brought. It is permitted that it be verbal-noun (masdariyya), meaning: Look how their inventing (of partnership) went away and vanished from them, until they denied its issuance from them altogether and disowned it entirely.

Moreover, al-Nasir in "al-Intisaf" took "dalla" to mean that they were deprived of knowledge of it, as if they had forgotten it and become dazed in bewilderment. This is far, for it does not match the other verse, and the Revelation explains one part of it by another. His wording: (p-2275) In the verse there is clear evidence that informing about a thing contrary to what it is, is a lie, even if the informant does not know the divergence of his report from its object. Do you not see that He made their informing and disowning a lie, although He, exalted, informed that what they used to invent had forsaken them? That is, they were deprived of its knowledge at that time through bewilderment and perplexity. That did not remove the application of the term "lie" to them. End.

The third: al-Zamakhshari said: If you say: how can it be correct that they lie when they witness the realities of affairs, and that lying and denial have no benefit?

I say: the one being tested speaks with what benefits him and with what does not benefit him, without distinguishing between them, out of bewilderment and dazzlement. Do you not see them saying: ﴿Our Lord, bring us out of it; then if we return, we will indeed be wrongdoers﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 107], though they had become certain of eternity and had no doubt about it; and ﴿They will call, "O Malik, let your Lord put an end to us"﴾ [al-Zukhruf: 77], though they knew that no end would be decreed for them.

As for the saying of one who says: its meaning is: "We were not polytheists in our own selves, and we did not know that we were in error in our belief," and taking His saying ﴿Look how they lied against themselves﴾ to mean in this world, that is a far-fetched contrivance, a distortion of the most eloquent speech toward what is an incapacity and a silencing; for the meaning they went to is not what this speech translates, nor does it apply to it, and it is far removed from it. I do not know what he who holds that interpretation will do with His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿On the day God raises them all, they will swear to Him as they swear to you, and they think they are upon something. Indeed, they are the liars﴾ [al-Mujadila: 18], after His saying: ﴿and they swear upon falsehood while they know﴾ [al-Mujadila: 14]; for their lying in the Hereafter is compared with their lying in this world. End.

The saying mentioned, and the interpretation he contested, originate with Abu 'Ali al-Jubba'i and the judge (al-Qadi), for they both held that the people of the Resurrection cannot venture upon lying, and they argued with feeble arguments set forth by al-Razi. Let it be considered there; for we do not blacken the faces of our pages with what involves subjecting transmission to the judgement of reason.

Then He, may He be exalted, explained some of what used to proceed from the polytheists of Makkah, by which a seal was set upon their hearts, saying, may He be glorified:

Commentary on the interpretation of His words, Exalted is He:

[25] ﴿And among them are those who listen to you, but We have placed over their hearts coverings, lest they understand it, and in their ears deafness. And if they see every sign, they will not believe in it. Until, when they come to you disputing with you, those who disbelieve say, "This is nothing but the fables of the former peoples."﴾

﴿And among them are those who listen to you﴾ — i.e., they lend their ears while you recite the Qur'an, but this benefits them nothing, because they do not reflect upon it so as to perceive its inimitability (i'jaz) and so that guidance (irshad) takes effect on them. ﴿And We have placed over their hearts coverings﴾ — i.e., veils (hijab), the plural of kinan, like ghita' and aghita', both in wording and meaning. ﴿Lest they understand it﴾ — i.e., out of aversion to understanding with the inner depths of their hearts its inner meanings, through which lie its inimitability and its guidance, by establishing the proofs and removing doubts. ﴿And in their ears deafness﴾ — i.e., and We have placed in their ears, which are the path of access to the inner depths of the hearts, a deafness preventing beneficial hearing from reaching them. The verification of this has already passed at the beginning of al-Baqarah, so reflect upon it!

As for His words, Exalted is He: ﴿And if they see every sign, they will not believe in it﴾ — this is an indication that what has been mentioned of them is not restricted to the Qur'an on account of their seeing a deficiency in it; rather, whatever signs and proofs they see that indicate the truthfulness of the Messenger, they will not believe in them, and they will interpret them as sorcery, due to the extremity of their obstinacy and the firmness of imitation (taqlid) among them, so there is neither understanding nor fairness with them. Like His words, Exalted is He: ﴿And had Allah known any good in them, He would have made them hear﴾ [al-Anfal: 23].

﴿Until, when they come to you disputing with you﴾ — i.e., their denial of the signs has reached the point that when they come to you, they argue with you and debate with you about the truth by means of falsehood. Then he explained the disputing with His words: ﴿Those who disbelieve say, "This is nothing but the fables of the former peoples"﴾ — (p-2277) i.e., their falsehoods and their tales that have no order. And counting the best of speech and its truest, among the category of falsehoods: "Falsehood does not come to it from before it or from behind it" [Fussilat: 42] — is a degree of disbelief beyond which there is no further limit.

The discussion of the words of the Exalted:

[26] ﴿And they forbid it, and they keep away from it; and they destroy none but themselves, and they perceive not.﴾

﴿And they forbid it﴾ means: they are not content with what has been mentioned of their denial of it, but they also forbid people from listening to it.

Al-Mahayimi said: They, seeing the sweetness of its composition above their prose and poetry, together with the solidity of its meanings, know that reflecting upon it leads to perceiving its inimitability. So they fear its effect upon the hearts of creatures. Therefore they forbid it, that is, forbid [people] from reciting and listening to it, lest it call them to reflect upon it, thereby spoiling their corrupt aims.

﴿And they keep away from it﴾ means: they keep themselves far from it, displaying the utmost of their aversion to it and emphasising their prohibition of it. For avoiding the one who forbids from what is forbidden is among the completions of the prohibition. Perhaps this is the secret in placing (al-na'y, "keeping away") after (al-nahy, "forbidding"). This was noted by Abu al-Su'ud.

Since this indicated that they seek to harm the Messenger of Allah ﷺ and the believers, out of fear of the power of the revelation's effect upon hearts, He followed it by stating that this aim will not be achieved for them, because Allah is the perfecter of His light and the manifester of His religion. And the calamity turns back upon them, by His saying: ﴿and they destroy none but themselves﴾ by exposing themselves to the severest punishment, both immediately and in the future. ﴿And they perceive not﴾ means: of that.

Admonition:

Al-Hakim and others narrated, from a group of the Successors, that this verse was revealed concerning Abu Talib, who used to forbid people from harming the Prophet ﷺ and keep away from him, not believing in him. His collectivity at that time was considered in terms of his leading his followers.

Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Sa'id ibn Jubayr that it was revealed concerning the paternal uncles of the Prophet ﷺ, who were ten. They were the most of people with him in public, and the most against him in secret. It is not hidden that the wording of the revelation is applicable to what has been mentioned and does not contradict it, and this is what is meant by "revelation" — as we have stated many times before. Abu Talib addressed the Prophet ﷺ, saying:

By Allah, they shall never reach you with their gathering until I am laid in the dust, buried.
So proclaim your command; no reproach shall fall upon you, and rejoice in it, and let it cool the eyes.
You called me, and you claimed that you were a sincere advisor, and you have indeed spoken truly, and you were trustworthy there.
And you presented a religion, which is undoubtedly among the best religions of mankind.
Were it not for blame, or my fear of a disgrace, you would have found me generous in that, clearly declaring it.

In (yanhawna) and (yan'awna) there is a wonderful paronomasia (tajnis).

When the Exalted informed that they destroy themselves, He explained the manner of it together with a statement of what will proceed from them in the Hereafter, of the speech contradicting their worldly conviction, by His saying, glorified is He:

Commentary of al-Qasimi (Mahasin al-Ta'wil) on surah 6, verse 27:

The discussion of the interpretation of His saying, exalted is He:

[27] ﴿And if you could see when they are made to stand before the Fire, and they say, "Oh, would that we were returned, and would not deny the signs of our Lord, and would be among the believers."﴾

﴿And if you could see when they are made to stand before the Fire﴾ That is: they are made to look upon it and witness it. It is said: "He made so-and-so stand over his sin (waqafa), meaning he made him aware of it." Or: they are made to enter it and come to know the punishment within it. It is said: "I came to know (waqaftu 'ala) what so-and-so has," meaning: I understood it and clarified it. The "standing over" (al-waqf 'alayhi) is figurative, or it is literal in the sense of standing. As for "upon" ('ala), it may be in its literal sense, meaning: they are caused to stand over the Fire upon the Sirat, which is a bridge above Hell. Or it may carry the sense of "in" (fi), meaning: they are caused to stand within the Fire and are immersed in it, while it encompasses them. In that case, the sense of elevation is sound because the Fire consists of levels and tiers, some above others.

﴿Then they say, "Oh, would that we were returned, and would not deny the signs of our Lord, and would be among the believers"﴾ They wish for a return to the world when there is no return, promising that they would not deny what has come to them and would be among the believers, that is, believers in His signs, acting in accordance with their requirements, so that they would not see this terrifying standing. Or [it means] among the company of believers who are saved from the punishment and who attain a good final return.

Note of caution:

The answer to "law" (if) is omitted, for the purpose of magnifying the matter and exalting its importance, and its omission is permissible because the addressee knows it. Such omissions are numerous in the Qur'an and in poetry. If you were to supply the answer, it would be: "you would see the evil of their end." Omitting the answer in this case is more eloquent in meaning than stating it. Do you not see that if you said to your servant, "By God, if I come to you," and then remained silent about the answer, his mind would go to all kinds of hateful things: beating, killing, breaking, and his fear would grow great, not knowing which of the possibilities you intend? But if you said, "I will surely beat you," and gave the answer, he would be safe from anything but beating, and no other kind of harm would come to his mind. Thus it is established that omitting the answer has a stronger effect in producing fear, as al-Razi stated. Its summary: the omission of the answer is based on confidence in its being evident, and a notice that expression falls short of detailing it.

The Interpretation of His Words, Exalted Is He:

[28] ﴿But there has become apparent to them what they used to conceal before. And even if they were returned, they would return to what they were forbidden, and indeed they are liars.﴾

﴿But there has become apparent to them what they used to conceal before﴾ This is a turning away (idrab) from what their wish for the false promise (of belief) indicates, namely their affirmation and faith. That is, it is not due to a sound resolve and sincere conviction; rather it is due to another cause, which is that there became apparent to them what they had been hiding within themselves of disbelief and polytheism, through their saying: "By God, our Lord, we were not polytheists" (6:23), and they came to know that they would perish because of their polytheism, so they wished for that. Or (it refers to) the testimony of their own limbs against them, or what they used to conceal within themselves in the world of the truthfulness of what the Messenger (ﷺ) brought, even though they would outwardly display the opposite to their followers. This is like His saying, Exalted is He, reporting about Moses that he said to Pharaoh: ﴿You certainly know that none has sent these down except the Lord of the heavens and the earth as clear evidence﴾ (17:102), and the verse. And like His saying, Exalted is He, reporting about Pharaoh and his people: ﴿And they denied them, though their souls were convinced of them, out of wrongdoing and arrogance﴾ (27:14). Or this verse is a report about the state of the hypocrites, and that their hypocrisy, which they used to keep secret, will become apparent. This does not contradict the sura being Meccan, for hypocrisy only arose among some people of Madinah and the Bedouins around it after the Hijrah; because God, Exalted is He, mentioned the occurrence of hypocrisy in a Meccan sura, which is (al-'Ankabut), saying: ﴿And God will surely make evident those who believed, and He will surely make evident the hypocrites﴾ (29:11). This is what they have mentioned of what the noble wording can be applied to, given its generality. Al-'Allamah Abu al-Su'ud has discussed all of this, and he adopted that what is meant by "what they used to conceal in the world" is the Fire upon which they will be made to stand; since it is the Fire whose matter the speech is driven to magnify, and to express wonder at the horror of the state of those made to stand before it, and (by "concealing it") their denial of it, for denying a thing is disbelief in it and certainly concealing it. This is preferred over the explicit denial found in His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿This is Hell which the criminals used to deny﴾ (55:43) and His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿This is the Fire which you used to deny﴾ (52:14), while being more fitting with what precedes it, namely their saying: (p-2281) ﴿and we would not deny the signs of our Lord﴾ (6:27), for the sake of observing what is opposed to it in terms of manifestation. This is what the eloquence of the noble composition demands.

Then he said, regarding the previously mentioned aspects: after overlooking in each of them what is forced and flawed, there is no path to any of that at all. This is because you have come to know that the driving of the noble composition is to magnify the matter of the Fire and to make horrible the state of its people, and it has been mentioned that they are made to stand upon it, and it has been indicated that there overcame them at that time fear, dread, bewilderment and astonishment that description cannot encompass. He ordered upon it their aforementioned wish with the (fa') which denotes that what precedes it is the cause of what follows it. So the omission of the Fire after that from that causal relation, while it itself is the greatest of calamities and the strongest of deterrents, and attributing it to one of the aforementioned matters which are lesser than it in terror and deterrence, while its mention has not been carried along there, is a matter whose sanctuary of revelation must be exempted from such things. As for what has been said, that what is meant is the recompense for what they used to conceal, it is of the kind of entering houses from their backs while their doors are open. So reflect.

I say: There is no doubt about the eloquence of what he established and its excellence, were it not for his strain in bearing the concealment upon what he mentioned, which is not apparent in it, and for which there are no parallels in the noble revelation. Therefore its figurative nature is then from the side of the enigmatic. As for the earlier aspects, keeping it upon its literal meaning without strain, and its encompassing them, is not far-fetched, because in each of them there is what supports it, as we have explained. The only point is that what he established is a wondrous aspect among them. As for it being the sole meaning, beneath it is the uprooting of thorns—and God knows best the secrets of His Book.

﴿And if they were returned﴾, that is, from their position that to the world as they wished, and what they had witnessed of the terrors had left them: ﴿they would return to what they were forbidden﴾ of disbelief and polytheism: ﴿and indeed they are liars﴾ in their promise of faith, or their habit is lying in their states.

(p-2282) On the interpretation of His saying, exalted is He:

[29] ﴿And they said, "There is no life except our worldly life, and we will not be resurrected."﴾

﴿And they said﴾ is a conjunction with (لَعادُوا) [they would surely return to what they were forbidden], or it is a resumption (isti'naf) of speech. ﴿There is no﴾: i.e., "what is life" — the pronoun (هِيَ, "it") refers to what follows it. ﴿except our worldly life﴾ — meaning: the life in which resurrection is imagined, and in which return is imagined, is none other than our first life. ﴿And we will not be resurrected﴾ — i.e., after our departure from this life.

The discussion on the interpretation of His saying, exalted is He:

[30] ﴿If only you could see when they are made to stand before their Lord. He will say, "Is this not the truth?" They will say, "Yes, by our Lord." He will say, "Then taste the punishment for what you used to disbelieve."﴾

﴿If only you could see when they are made to stand before their Lord.﴾ Al-Jalal said: that is, they are presented to Him. Ibn Kathir said: that is, they are made to stand before Him. ﴿He will say, "Is this not"﴾, that is, the Resurrection, ﴿"the truth?"﴾ as a rebuke to them and a refutation of what they had imagined at the time of the return. ﴿They will say, "Yes, by our Lord."﴾ That is, it is indeed the truth, not falsehood, as we used to suppose. They emphasized their acknowledgment with an oath, to show the completeness of their certainty of its truth, and to indicate that this acknowledgment came from them with willingness and eagerness, hoping for its benefit. ﴿He will say, "Then taste the punishment for what you used to disbelieve."﴾

**Commentary of al-Qasimi (Mahasin al-Ta'wil) on Surah 6, Verse 31**

On the interpretation of His words, exalted is He:

[31] ﴿Those have lost who denied the meeting with Allah, until when the Hour comes upon them suddenly, they say, "Oh, our regret over what we neglected concerning it!" while they carry their burdens upon their backs. Unquestionably, evil is what they carry.﴾

﴿Those have lost who denied the meeting with Allah﴾: that is, [denied] the arrival at the Hereafter and what is connected to it. Or it may be taken according to its apparent meaning, because one who denies resurrection also denies seeing [Allah]. This is what al-Nasafi said. The second is the correct view, although many have restricted themselves to the first and made it a figurative metaphor (*isti'ara tamthiliyya*, a metaphor by representation) for their situation, compared to a servant who came before his master after a period of time, and the master had become aware of his conditions. Then the master either meets him with delight at what pleases him of his actions, or with anger at what angers him of them. This is a Mu'tazili tendency, and there is no departure to metaphor so long as the literal meaning is possible.

In al-Nasafi's words there is an indication that *liqa'* (meeting) means seeing, and this is what is in the *al-Qamus*. Its commentator al-Zubaydi said: "This is among what they criticized, and they extended the discussion on it and prohibited it. They said: seeing does not necessarily entail meeting, nor the reverse."

Al-Raghib said: it is the facing of a thing and its encountering together, and it is used to express each of the two. It is said of perception through the senses and sight.

**A subtle point:**

Al-Khafaji said in *al-Inaya*: It is said that it was narrated from 'Ali, may Allah be pleased with him, that he composed verses in accordance with this verse and its meaning, and they are:

*The astrologer and the physician, both of them, claim: "Bodies will not be resurrected." I say: "Those two are for you both."*

*If your statement is correct, I am not a loser; but if my statement is correct, then the loss is upon you both.*

Al-Khafaji said: I do not know which of the two is more wondrous, the transmission or the understanding? For this poetry belongs to Abu al-'Ala' al-Ma'arri in his *Diwan*, and it is:

*The astrologer and the physician, both of them, said: "Bodies will not be resurrected." I said: "Those two are for you both."*

*If your statement is correct, I am not a loser; but if my statement is correct, then the loss is upon you both.*

*Virtue and evil have been wrestling in this world; which of them is more righteous in your sight?*

*I purified my garment for prayer, and before it my body; so where is the purity of your two bodies?*

*I remembered my Lord in hearts, seeking His companionship; my heart was content with that, so let your two hearts be lonely.*

*I rose early in the two coverings, seeking mercy from Him, and you two are not mindful in your two coverings.*

*If the benefits of what I bring do not return to my hand, then is there any returner to your two hands?*

*The garment of the pious, though its weave has become thin, is better, by the knowledge of Allah, than your two garments.*

Ibn al-Sayyid said in his commentary: This is versified from what was narrated from 'Ali, may Allah be pleased with him, that he said to someone who doubted resurrection and the Hereafter: "If the matter is as you say, that there is no Resurrection, then we have all been saved; and if the matter is not as you say, then we have been saved and you have perished." They mention that he silenced him, and he returned from his belief. This statement, although it comes out in the form of doubt, is in fact an affirmation of the addressee's own statement, and a sign of his scant attention to reflection and his lack of caution for himself, while the interlocutor is confident in his position. It is a kind of disputation.

His words "*ilaykuma*" (to you two) is an expression meant to restrain and rebuke. Its meaning is: "Stop what you are saying." Its real sense is: "Your speech is turned back to you; I have no need for it." End of quote.

Whoever has knowledge of composing poetry knows that this is a later-composed poem (*shi'r muwallad*).

Then al-Khafaji drew attention to the fact that this kind of thing is called *istidraj* (leading on by degrees).

In *al-Mathal al-sa'ir* (by Ibn al-Athir) it is said: *Istidraj* is a kind of eloquence that I extracted from the Book of Allah, the Exalted. It is the deceptions of speech that take the place of deceptions of action, whereby the opponent is led on until he submits and yields. It is close to sophistry (*mughalata*), but it is not of it. Like His words, exalted is He: ﴿Will you kill a man because he says, "My Lord is Allah," and he has brought you clear proofs from your Lord? And if he is a liar, upon him is his lie; but if he is truthful, there will afflict you some of what he promises you. Indeed, Allah does not guide one who is a transgressor and a liar.﴾ [Ghafir: 28]. Do you not see the subtlety of his argument by the method of division, with His words: "If he is a liar, then his lie is upon him; and if he is truthful, there will afflict you some of what he has promised you." In it is what of fairness and courtesy is not hidden. For he is a truthful Prophet, so all that he promised must befall them, not some of it; but he came with what is more effective for their acceptance and acknowledgment, because of the gentleness in advice that it contains, with a fair speech that is neither extreme nor harsh. He showed them that he had not given his claim its full due, nor had he been partisan for it or defended it, so that they would not flee from him. For this reason he put first "*kadhiban*" (a liar), then he concluded with His words: "Indeed, Allah does not guide..." meaning: he is a Prophet upon guidance, and had he not been so, Allah would not have given him prophethood and supported him. In it is what of deceiving and leading on the opponent is not hidden. End of quote.

His words, exalted is He: ﴿until when the Hour comes upon them suddenly﴾: that is, the Resurrection comes upon them unexpectedly. The Resurrection was named "the Hour" (*sa'a*) because it overtakes people suddenly at an hour that no one knows except Him, exalted is He. The meaning: their death comes upon them. This is because the intended "Hour" is the lesser one. Al-Raghib said: the Greater Hour is the raising of people for reckoning, and the lesser is a person's death; so the hour of each person is his death, and this is what is indicated by His words, exalted is He: ﴿Those have lost who denied the meeting with Allah, until when the Hour comes upon them suddenly﴾. It is known that the gathering reaches a person at his death. End of quote.

(*Baghtatan*) is a verbal noun (*masdar*) in the position of a circumstantial state (*hal*), that is: "suddenly" (*mubaghatatan*), or a verbal noun for an omitted verb, that is: "it overtakes them," or for the mentioned verb, since "*ja'at-hum*" means "*baghat-hum*" (it overtook them).

(p-2286) ﴿They say﴾: that is, the deniers of resurrection, who are the Quraysh disbelievers and whoever followed their path in disbelief and belief: ﴿"Oh, our regret!"﴾: that is, "Oh, our remorse!" *Al-hasra* is grief over a thing that has passed. It is mentioned in the form of a call for emphasis. The purpose is to alert the addressees to the regret that has befallen them. ﴿over what we neglected﴾: that is, we fell short, ﴿concerning it﴾: that is, in the worldly life. The pronoun is implied though it has not been mentioned, because it is known: that is, "over what we wasted in it, since we did not acquire from beliefs, morals, and deeds that which would save us." Or the pronoun refers to the Hour, that is, "over what we neglected regarding it, and of observing its right, preparing for it, believing in it, and acquiring righteous deeds."

Ibn Jarir said: the pronoun refers to the transaction indicated by His words, "Those have lost..." since loss only happens in a transaction of sale that has taken place. He said: the meaning is: "Those who denied the meeting with Allah have been cheated, by exchanging the faith through which they would deserve from Allah His good pleasure and Paradise, for the disbelief through which they would deserve from Him His wrath and punishment. And they do not perceive the loss that is upon them in that, until the Hour comes. So when the Hour comes upon them suddenly, and they see the loss that has reached them in their exchange, they will say then, in remorse: 'Oh, our regret over what we neglected!'"

His words, exalted is He: ﴿while they carry their burdens upon their backs﴾ is a circumstantial clause (*hal*) from the subject of "*qalu*" (they say). Its benefit is to announce that their punishment is not restricted to what has been mentioned of regret over what has passed and gone, but rather they also suffer, together with that, the bearing of heavy burdens. It also hints that this regret is of such intensity that it does not cease or get forgotten, due to what they undergo of various kinds of punishment. Abu al-Sa'ud said this.

*Awzar* is the plural of *wizr*, which originally means a heavy load; the sin was named by it because of its weight upon its bearer. It has been said: He made them carried upon the backs as a figurative metaphor (*isti'ara tamthiliyya*), like their being attached to them in a way that does not separate from them. He specified the back because carrying loads upon it is what is customary, just as earning is customarily done by the hands.

(p-2287) It has also been said: it is literal, based on what was narrated from al-Suddi that he said: "There is no oppressive man who dies and enters his grave, except that there comes to him a man with an ugly face, black in color, foul in smell, wearing filthy garments, until he enters the grave with him. When he sees him, he says to him, 'How ugly your face is!' He says, 'Likewise was your deed ugly.' He says, 'How foul your smell is!' He says, 'Likewise was your deed foul.' He says, 'How filthy your garments are!' He says, 'Indeed your deed was filthy.' He says, 'Who are you?' He says, 'I am your deed.' So he remains with him in his grave. When he is raised on the Day of Resurrection, he says to him, 'I used to carry you in the world with pleasures and desires, and today you carry me.' So he rides upon his back and drives him until he enters him into the Fire. That is His words: ﴿and they carry﴾..." the verse.

Al-Khafaji said: Perhaps this is also a representation (*tamthil*). Close to this is what has been said: whoever affirms the Scale and believes in the weighing of deeds, does not say that it is a representation. End of quote.

﴿Unquestionably, evil is what they carry﴾: that is, wretched is what they carry.

The discussion of the interpretation of His words, Exalted is He:

[32] ﴿And the life of this world is but amusement and diversion. And the Home of the Hereafter is better for those who fear Allah. Then will you not reason?﴾

﴿And the life of this world is but amusement﴾ i.e., jest, and deeds that yield no benefit; ﴿and diversion﴾ i.e., occupation with desire and merriment, and that which wisdom does not require, and that which distracts a person from what concerns him, [consisting of] what he takes pleasure in and then passes away.

﴿And the Home of the Hereafter is better for those who fear Allah﴾ because of its permanence, and the purity of its benefits and pleasures from harms and pains.

﴿Then will you not reason?﴾ That is, so that you might fear what you are upon of disbelief and sins, and not prefer the lowly and perishing over the high and enduring.

Here are some subtle points (laṭā'if):

The first: al-Razi said: Know that those who deny resurrection and the Last Day have an intense desire for this world and for attaining its pleasures. So Allah mentioned this verse to draw attention to its baseness and vileness. Know also that this life itself cannot be condemned, because the immediate life is the only place in which the attainment of the felicities of the Hereafter is valid. For this reason, two opinions arose concerning the interpretation of this verse:

The first: that what is meant is the life of the disbeliever. Ibn ʿAbbas said: He means the life of the people of polytheism and hypocrisy. The reason for describing their life with this attribute is that the life of the believer contains righteous deeds, so it is not amusement and diversion.

The second opinion: that this is general, encompassing the life of both believer and disbeliever. What is meant by it is the pleasures found in this life and the good things sought in this life. He called them (amusement and diversion) because a person, while occupied with amusement and diversion, takes pleasure in it; then, when it ends and passes, nothing remains of it but regret. Thus is this life: when it ceases, nothing remains but grief and remorse.

The second: al-Khafaji said: He combined "diversion" (lahw) and "amusement" (la'ib) in several verses. Sometimes He puts "amusement" first, as here, and sometimes He puts "diversion" first, as in al-ʿAnkabut. For this variation there is a point mentioned in "Durrat al-Ta'wil," in summary: the difference between lahw and la'ib, although they share that both are occupation with what does not concern the rational person and does not matter to him of desire or merriment, whether it is forbidden or not, is that lahw is more general than la'ib; every la'ib is lahw, but not vice versa. Listening to musical instruments is lahw, and is not la'ib. They have also distinguished between them by saying that la'ib is that which is intended to hasten gladness and relaxation through it, while lahw is everything that occupies one with desire and merriment, even if it is not intended for that, as is related from the lexicographers. They said: lahw, when used absolutely, means seeking delight through women, as Imru' al-Qays said:

"Has Basbasa claimed today that I have grown old, and that men like me cannot do well in diversion?"

Qatadah said: In the dialect of Yemen, lahw means "the woman." It was said: la'ib is the seeking of gladness and joy through what is not fitting to seek through; and lahw is the diverting of worry through what is not fitting to divert through.

Since the verse was a refutation of the disbelievers in their denial of the Hereafter and their restriction of life to the life of this world, and since in their belief there is nothing but the immediate gladness of the adornment of the perishing world, He placed first "la'ib," which indicates this, and completed it with "lahw." As for in al-ʿAnkabut, the context is mention of the brevity of the duration of life and its belittlement in comparison with the Hereafter; therefore it was mentioned with the demonstrative noun, which conveys belittlement. Occupation with lahw is something by which time is shortened, and it is more inclusive than la'ib in this regard. And the days of joy are short, as one said:

"A night, one of the bright nights, was but a twilight and a dawn."

The third: In His words, Exalted is He: "for those who fear Allah," there is an alert that whatever is not among the deeds of the God-fearing is amusement and diversion.

The discussion of the interpretation (*ta'wil*, the explanation of meaning) of His saying, Exalted is He:

[33] ﴿We certainly know that what they say grieves you. Yet it is not you they call a liar, but it is the signs of Allah that the wrongdoers deny.﴾

As for His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿We certainly know that it grieves you﴾, it is read with a *fatha* and with a *damma* on the *ya'* (of *yahzunuka* and *yahzunuka*, i.e., the two readings of the verb). ﴿what they say﴾ means: what they say about you, that you are a liar, or a sorcerer, or a poet, or a madman.

Abu al-Su'ud said: This is a resumptive sentence (*isti'naf*), directed at consoling him, peace and blessings be upon him, for the grief that overtook him because of what was related about the disbelievers, namely their persistence in denial and their exaggeration in it. It shows that he, peace and blessings be upon him, holds a station with Allah, Mighty and Majestic, and that what they do against him ultimately returns to Allah, Exalted, and that He will take vengeance upon them with the most severe vengeance. The word *qad* (indeed) serves to emphasise the knowledge of what has been mentioned, which conveys the emphasis of the warning.

As for His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿Yet it is not you they call a liar, but it is the signs of Allah that the wrongdoers deny﴾, the *fa'* (so/for) here indicates causation (*ta'lil*), because His saying ﴿We certainly know﴾ carries the meaning of "do not grieve," as is said in contexts of prohibition and rebuke: "We know what you are doing!" The point of the causation in His consoling him, peace and blessings be upon him, is that the denial is in reality directed at Me, and I am the Forbearing, the Patient. So adopt My character.

Abu al-Su'ud said: This indicates that he, peace and blessings be upon him, attained a rank of great dignity, elevated status, and nearness to Allah, Mighty and Majestic, to a degree beyond which there is no further limit. For Allah did not confine Himself to making their denial of him a denial of His signs, in the manner of His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Whoever obeys the Messenger has obeyed Allah﴾ [al-Nisa: 80]. Rather, He negated their denial of him altogether and affirmed it as directed at His own signs, in the manner of His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Indeed, those who pledge allegiance to you, they are pledging allegiance only to Allah﴾ [al-Fath: 10]. This was an announcement of the perfection of his nearness, and of the dissolution of his own affairs, peace and blessings be upon him, into the affair of Allah, Mighty and Majestic. It also contains an expression of the enormity of their offence, and indicates the magnitude of their punishment.

It has been said: The meaning is: they do not deny you in their hearts, but they repudiate with their tongues, out of obstinacy or arrogance. This is supported by what al-Thawri narrated from Abu Ishaq, from Najiyah, from Ali, may Allah be pleased with him, who said: Abu Jahl said to the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him: "We do not call you a liar, but we call a liar what you have brought." So Allah revealed: ﴿Indeed, it is not you they call a liar﴾, the verse. Al-Hakim related it and declared it authentic.

Ibn Jarir related from al-Suddi, who said: When the day of Badr came, al-Akhnas met Abu Jahl privately and said: "O Abu al-Hakam! Tell me about Muhammad: is he truthful or a liar? For there is none here from Quraysh besides you and me to hear our conversation." Abu Jahl said: "Woe to you! By Allah, Muhammad is truly truthful, and Muhammad has never lied. But when the Banu Qusayy take the banner, the water-supply (*al-siqayah*), the keeping of the Ka'bah (*al-hijabah*) and prophethood, what will remain for the rest of Quraysh?" That is His saying: ﴿Yet it is not you they call a liar, but it is the signs of Allah that the wrongdoers deny﴾. So the signs of Allah are Muhammad, peace and blessings be upon him.

Al-Razi said: This view is not unlikely. Its parallel is His saying, Exalted is He, concerning the story of Musa: ﴿They denied them, though their souls were convinced of them, out of wrongdoing and arrogance﴾ [al-Naml: 14].

It has also been said: The meaning is: they do not call you a liar, because you are, in their view, the truthful one, known for truthfulness. But they deny the signs of Allah. This is as is reported: Abu Jahl used to say to the Messenger of Allah, peace and blessings be upon him: "We do not call you a liar, and you are truthful in our eyes, but we call a liar what you have brought us."

Abu al-Su'ud said: It seems that the truthfulness of the informant, in the view of the wicked, lies in the correspondence of his report to his own belief. The first interpretation is the one demanded by the eloquence of the revelation (*al-jazalah al-tanzilah*). It has also been read as: *la yukadhdhibunaka* (from *akdhaba*), meaning: they found him to be a liar, or they attributed lying to him, or they demonstrated his lie. And it was said: *akdhaba* and *kadhdhaba* have the same meaning. Thus is it in the *al-Qamus* and its commentary.

**The discussion on the interpretation of His saying, exalted is He:**

[34] ﴿And messengers were denied before you, but they endured patiently what they were denied and what they were harmed by, until Our help reached them. There is none who can alter the words of Allah. And there has certainly come to you some of the news of the messengers.﴾

﴿And messengers were denied before you﴾ is a variation in consoling him, peace and blessings be upon him, since the generality of an affliction may somewhat lessen its weight. It also guides him (ﷺ) to follow the noble messengers before him in their patience with the various kinds of harm their peoples inflicted on them. It is an implicit promise to him (ﷺ) of the same victory that they were granted. The opening of the speech with an oath serves to emphasize the consolation. The tanwin (nunation, the "-un" ending) on "messengers" (rusul) is for glorification and multiplicity. This is what Abu al-Su'ud conveyed.

Al-Zamakhshari said: In His saying, ﴿And messengers were denied﴾, there is evidence that His saying, ﴿Indeed, they do not deny you﴾ [al-An'am: 33], is not a negation of their denial of him. Rather, it is like your saying to your servant: "They did not insult you, but they insulted me!" End of quote.

Al-Nasir criticized him in "al-Intisaf," saying: There is no evidence in it, because it is also consistent with the negation of denial, and its position then is clearer in virtue. That is: these people have not denied you, so it is your right to be patient with them, and their affair should not grieve you. And if those prophets before you were denied by their peoples and they endured patiently with them, then you, since they have not denied you, are more deserving of patience. Thus it agrees, as you see, with both interpretations together. However, it comes from a direction other than the one used as evidence, and in it is an approximation to what he (al-Zamakhshari) chose. That is because this kind of consolation has been stated explicitly (p-2293) in such as His saying, ﴿And if they deny you, then messengers were denied before you﴾ [Fatir: 4], so He consoled him about their denial of him by the denial of other nations toward their prophets. This is nothing but a fine interpretation that corresponds to reality, supported by the apparent meaning. And Allah knows best.

﴿But they endured patiently what they were denied and what they were harmed by﴾, that is: at their denial and their harming, so follow their example: ﴿until Our help reached them. There is none who can alter the words of Allah﴾, that is: His promises, from His saying, ﴿And Our word had already preceded to Our servants, the messengers﴾ [al-Saffat: 171], ﴿that they would surely be helped﴾ [al-Saffat: 172], and His saying, ﴿Allah has decreed: "I will surely prevail, I and My messengers"﴾ [al-Mujadila: 21].

﴿And there has certainly come to you some of the news of the messengers﴾, that is: some of their account in enduring patiently against the disbelievers, and what they were granted of victory. So We must remove your grief by destroying them, and their being given respite is not neglect of them, but rather due to the continuation of His established way (sunnah), exalted is He, in the realization of the patience and gratitude of the messengers.

Commentary on the Words of Allah, the Exalted:

[35] ﴿And if their turning away is grievous to you, then if you are able to seek a tunnel in the earth or a ladder into the sky to bring them a sign—(you may do so). And had Allah willed, He would have brought them together upon guidance. So do not be among the ignorant.﴾

﴿And if their turning away is grievous to you﴾ meaning: it is hard and heavy upon you, ﴿their turning away﴾ meaning: from belief in what you have brought of the Qur'an, their keeping away from it, and their forbidding people from it. ﴿Then if you are able to seek a tunnel in the earth﴾ meaning: a passage and an outlet through which you can penetrate to what is beneath the earth, so that you may bring forth for them a sign by which they would believe (p-2294) ﴿or a ladder into the sky﴾ meaning: a means of ascent by which you could climb into it ﴿to bring them a sign﴾ meaning: of what they have proposed—then do it. The omission of the answer (to the conditional) is fine, since the listener knows it. That is, but Allah has not granted you this ability, for faith would then become compulsory and no longer beneficial.

﴿And had Allah willed, He would have brought them together upon guidance﴾ meaning: but He willed, in accordance with His majesty and beauty, to manifest the utmost of His subjugation and the utmost of His gentleness. ﴿So do not be﴾ meaning: through eagerness for their faith, or inclination toward sending down what they have proposed, ﴿among the ignorant﴾ meaning: regarding what the affairs of the Exalted require, of which is what has been mentioned: that His will, exalted is He, is not attached to their faith. Either by choice, since they do not turn toward it, or by compulsion, since that would take it out of the legislative wisdom founded upon testing.

Remarks:

First: In this verse there is clear indication of the extent of his ﷺ eagerness for the Islam of his people and his intense concern for it, to the degree that if he were able to bring them a sign from beneath the earth or from above the sky, he would have brought it, hoping for their faith and out of compassion for them.

Second: Al-Nasir said in al-Intisaf: This verse serves as a refutation of the Qadariyyah in their claim that Allah, the Exalted, willed to gather all people upon guidance, but it did not happen. Do you not see that the sentence is introduced with "law" (lau), whose implication is the impossibility of its answer, because of the impossibility of what follows it? So the impossibility of their being gathered upon guidance is only because the will was impossible. Hence you see al-Zamakhshari interpreting the will as subduing them upon guidance by a compelling sign, such that faith would not be by choice in that case; and so it is established for him that this aspect of will did not occur, and that His will to gather them upon guidance by their own choice is established and not impossible, but its object did not occur. These are among his hidden depths and secrets, so beware of them. And Allah is the Granter of success.

Third: He did not say "do not be ignorant," but rather "among those who are attributed to ignorance," out of veneration for His Prophet ﷺ, by not ascribing ignorance to him, for the sake of emphasizing its negation from him. And the severity of address in it has the purpose of keeping his noble station far from eagerness for what will not happen and from anxiety in situations requiring patience, things that befit only the ignorant.

The discussion of His words, exalted is He:

[36] ﴿Only those who listen will respond, while the dead—Allah will raise them up; then to Him they will be returned.﴾

His words, exalted is He: ﴿Only those who listen will respond, while the dead—Allah will raise them up; then to Him they will be returned.﴾ are a confirmation of what passed, that upon their hearts are coverings (akinnah), and a verification that they, by this, are of the category of the dead, from whom faith is not conceivable at all. That is: only the living who hear what is conveyed to them—hearing with understanding (sama' tafahhum)—respond to you by accepting your call to faith, not the dead, of whom these are among. This is like His words, exalted is He: ﴿Indeed, you cannot make the dead hear﴾ [al-Naml: 80]. Even though they are alive with animal life, they are dead in relation to humanity, because their hearts have died from the poisons of corrupt beliefs and vile characters.

And: "the dead" (al-mawta) is the subject (mubtada'). That is: the disbelievers who do not hear and do not respond. Allah will raise them on the Day of Resurrection, then to Him they will be returned, and He will recompense them for their deeds. So "the dead" is a metaphor for the disbelievers, as it has been said:

"Let not the ignorant man be impressed by his finery; for he is a corpse, and his garments are a shroud."

It has been said: in this there is an allusion that their guidance is like raising the dead, which none can do except Allah; thus there is in it a discouragement to the Messenger ﷺ regarding their faith. And in calling them "the dead" there is mockery of them and disparagement of them, which is not hidden.

(p-2296) The discussion of the interpretation of His saying, exalted is He:

[37] ﴿They say: "Why has not a sign been sent down to him from his Lord?" Say: "Indeed, Allah is able to send down a sign, but most of them do not know."﴾

﴿And they say﴾, meaning: the polytheists of Makkah. This is an explanation of another kind of their obstinacy, since they were not satisfied with the clear proofs they had witnessed, by which the mountains would crumble. ﴿"Why has not a sign been sent down to him from his Lord?"﴾ That is, an extraordinary sign, according to what they wished and what they used to demand in their obstinacy. Like their saying: ﴿"We will not believe you until you cause a spring to gush forth for us from the earth"﴾ [al-Isra: 90], and so on.

﴿Say: "Indeed, Allah is able to send down a sign, but most of them do not know"﴾, that is: their demand is ignorance, because sending down such a sign would uproot the foundation of obligation (taklif), which is built upon the principle of free choice. Or (it would lead to) their complete annihilation, for among the necessary consequences of denying a compelling sign is destruction, in accordance with His established way (sunnah) concerning the earlier nations. The restriction of the lack of knowledge to most of them is because some of them are aware of the true state of affairs, and they only act as they do out of arrogance and stubborn opposition.

[p. 2297]

**On the interpretation of His words, exalted is He:**

[38] ﴿There is no creature crawling on the earth, nor bird flying on its two wings, but they are communities like you. We have not neglected anything in the Book. Then to their Lord they will be gathered.﴾

﴿There is no creature crawling on the earth﴾, meaning: settled upon it, not rising above it. ﴿Nor a bird﴾ that rises above it ﴿flying on its two wings, but they are communities like you﴾, meaning: kinds classified in governing their affairs, in not neglecting any of them, in managing their concerns, and in determining their provisions.

[p. 2297] ﴿We have not neglected in the Book﴾, meaning: We have not left out or overlooked in the Preserved Tablet (lawh al-qada', the Tablet of Decree) ﴿anything﴾, meaning anything great or small, for it contains what occurs in the world, and no matter has been left unattended in it. The meaning is that the knowledge of all of them is with Allah, and He forgets none of them in regard to their provision and management. This is like His words: ﴿There is no creature on the earth but that its provision is upon Allah, and He knows its place of rest and its place of storage. All is in a clear Book﴾ [Hud: 6], meaning: it makes clear their names, their numbers and their places, and it encompasses their movements and their stillness. ﴿Then to their Lord they will be gathered﴾, meaning: all the communities, of beasts and birds, so that He will bring justice between them, to the extent that from His justice He takes for the hornless (animal) from the horned. The pronoun referring to them is in the form of the plural for rational beings, because they are treated as such.

**Remarks:**

**First:** Al-Zamakhshari said: If you ask, "What is the purpose of mentioning this?" I answer: it indicates the greatness of His power, the subtlety of His knowledge, the vastness of His dominion, and His management of those creatures that differ in kinds and are numerous in types, while He guards what belongs to them and what is upon them, and watches over their conditions. No matter preoccupies Him from another, and the accountable (humans) are not singled out for this, to the exclusion of the rest of the animals. Al-Razi said: The aim is that Allah's care is attached to these animals. So if the manifestation of a compelling sign were beneficial, He would manifest it, and this serves as evidence that He is able to send down a sign.

Al-Qadi said: When He, exalted is He, had mentioned the unbelievers and explained that they will return to Allah and be gathered, He then explained, by His words ﴿There is no creature…﴾ and so on, that the resurrection also applies to the beasts.

**Second:** The addition of ﴿min﴾ in His words ﴿There is no creature on the earth﴾ is for emphasizing comprehensiveness. And ﴿fi﴾ (in) is attached to an omitted element which is a descriptive phrase for ﴿creature﴾, conveying further generalization, as if it were said: "No single individual of the creatures settles in any region of the regions of the earth." Likewise, the addition of the description in His words ﴿flying on its two wings﴾.

Al-Intisaf (by Ibn al-Munayyir) said: As regards the purpose of the addition of generalization: the position of His words ﴿on the earth﴾ and ﴿flying on its two wings﴾ is the position of a general description, and the description of the general is general, by necessity of correspondence. So it is as if, along with the addition of the attribute, two general attributes have combined.

**Third:** Al-Zamakhshari said: If you ask, "How is it said ﴿communities﴾ when ﴿creature﴾ and ﴿bird﴾ are singular?" I answer: since His words, exalted is He, ﴿There is no creature on the earth nor a bird﴾ indicate the meaning of comprehensiveness, and dispense with saying "no beasts and no birds," His words ﴿but communities﴾ are treated according to meaning.

**Fourth:** The verse indicates that every kind of beast is a community. It is reported in a hadith: "Were it not that dogs are a community among the communities, I would have ordered them to be killed." Narrated by Abu Dawud and al-Tirmidhi from Abdullah ibn Mughaffal, may Allah be pleased with him.

**Fifth:** What we have mentioned regarding the meaning of the communities' resemblance to us, in Allah's management of their affairs, His undertaking of their provision, and the non-neglect of anything of them, which shows the comprehensiveness of power and the breadth of knowledge, is the most apparent, in agreement with His words, exalted is He: ﴿There is no creature on the earth but that its provision is upon Allah, and He knows﴾ [Hud: 6], the verse. And the Qur'an explains one part by another. Al-Wahidi reported from Ibn Abbas that the resemblance lies in their knowledge of Allah, His unity, and their glorifying and praising Him, as in His words, exalted is He: ﴿There is nothing but that it glorifies Him with His praise﴾ [al-Isra': 44], and His words: ﴿Each has known its prayer and its glorification﴾ [al-Nur: 41].

It is reported from Abu al-Darda', who said: The intellects of beasts are restricted from everything except four things: knowledge of God, seeking provision, knowledge of the male and the female, and each one's readiness for its mate.

It was said: the resemblance is that they will be gathered on the Day of Resurrection like people.

I say: There is no doubt in the soundness of both views in themselves, and in the truthfulness of the resemblance in both. But inclining toward them is distanced by their lack of agreement with the other verse. So what is closest, in support of parallel texts, is what we mentioned first. And Allah knows best.

**Sixth:** What we have explained regarding the meaning of ﴿the Book﴾, that it is the Preserved Tablet in the Throne and the world of the heavens, which contains all the conditions of created things in complete detail, is the most apparent, because it agrees with the verse we mentioned, in support of the Qur'anic parallels. Imam Ibn Kathir did not mention anything other than this, despite his breadth of scope.

It was said: what is meant by it is the Qur'an, as in His words, exalted is He: ﴿And We have sent down to you the Book as an explanation of all things﴾ [al-Nahl: 89]. Al-Khafaji said: It was said that taking it to mean the Qur'an does not fit what comes before and after it. This is answered by saying that the meaning is: We have not left out any of the proofs and other things except that We mentioned it, so how would one need another sign of what they have proposed, while they deny Our signs? Thus the discourse is, without doubt, holding one part to another.

Abu al-Su'ud said: That is, We have not left out in the Qur'an any of the important matters, among which is the explanation that He, exalted is He, takes into account the interests of all His creatures.

Al-Shihab, regarding al-Baydawi's words ("for it has recorded in it what is needed of the matters of religion, in detail or in summary"), said: This points to the fact that what is established by the three proofs is established by the Qur'an, by its indication through such words as ﴿So take warning, O people of insight﴾ [al-Hashr: 2], pointing to analogical reasoning (qiyas), and His words ﴿And whatever the Messenger gives you, take it﴾ [al-Hashr: 7], pointing to the Sunnah. Indeed, it has been said that by this method all things can be deduced from it. Just as one of the atheists asked some others where the cooking of sweets is mentioned in the Qur'an, and they said: in His words, exalted is He: ﴿So ask the people of remembrance if you do not know﴾ [al-Nahl: 43]. End.

Al-Razi inclined to the view that what is meant by "the Book" is the Qur'an, and argued that when the definite article is attached to a singular noun, it refers to the previously known referent, and the previously known "Book" for the Muslims is the Qur'an. Therefore, the intended meaning of "the Book" in this verse must be the Qur'an. Given this, one may say: how did He, exalted is He, say ﴿We have not neglected in the Book anything﴾ when it does not contain the detailed content of medical science, the detailed content of mathematics, nor the detailed content of many of the investigations and sciences? Nor does it contain the detailed positions of people's schools of thought and their proofs in the science of principles (usul) and branches (furu')?

The answer: His words ﴿We have not neglected in the Book anything﴾ must be restricted to clarifying the matters that must be known and comprehended, and its clarification is in two respects:

The first: the term "neglect" (tafrit) is not used, affirmatively or negatively, except regarding what must be made clear, because no one is blamed for neglect or shortcoming in not doing what there is no need for. This term is only mentioned where one has fallen short in what is needed.

The second: that all, or most, of the verses of the Qur'an indicate, by direct meaning, by inclusion, or by necessary implication, that the purpose of sending down this Book is the explanation of religion, the knowledge of Allah, and the knowledge of Allah's rulings. And when this restriction is known from the whole Qur'an, the unrestricted here is to be understood in terms of that restricted meaning. As for the claim that this Book does not comprise all the sciences of principles and branches, we say: as for the science of principles, it is wholly present in it, because the fundamental proofs are mentioned in it in the most eloquent manner. As for the reports of schools and the details of opinions, there is no need for them. As for the detailed sciences of the branches, the scholars said: the Qur'an indicates that consensus (ijma'), single-narrator reports (khabar al-wahid), and analogical reasoning (qiyas) are proofs in the Shari'ah. So whatever is indicated by any of these three principles is, in reality, present in the Qur'an.

Al-Wahidi, may Allah have mercy on him, gave three examples for this meaning:

**The first example:** It is reported that Ibn Mas'ud used to say: "Why should I not curse one whom Allah has cursed in His Book?" meaning the woman who tattoos and the one who has herself tattooed, and the woman who connects hair and the one who has it connected.

It is reported that a woman recited the Qur'an, then came to him and said: "O son of Umm Abd! Last night I recited what is between the two covers, and I did not find in it a curse on the tattooing woman and the one who has herself tattooed!" He said: "If you had recited it, you would have found it. Allah, exalted is He, says: ﴿And whatever the Messenger gives you, take it﴾ [al-Hashr: 7], and among what the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) has given us is that he said: 'Allah has cursed the tattooing woman and the one who has herself tattooed.'"

Al-Razi said: I say: this meaning can be found in the Book of Allah in a clearer way than that. For He, exalted is He, said in Surat al-Nisa': ﴿They invoke none but a rebellious Satan﴾ [al-Nisa': 117], ﴿whom Allah has cursed﴾ [al-Nisa': 118]. So He passed judgment on him with the curse, then enumerated after that his evil deeds, and mentioned among them his words: ﴿and I will surely command them, and they will change the creation of Allah.﴾ The apparent meaning of this verse requires that changing the creation incurs the curse. End.

I say: the continuation of the hadith also supports that. Its wording is: "Allah has cursed the tattooing women and those who have themselves tattooed, and the women who pluck their facial hair and those who have it plucked, and those who file their teeth for beauty, who change Allah's creation." Narrated by Imam Ahmad, the two Shaykhs (al-Bukhari and Muslim), and the authors of the Sunan, from Ibn Mas'ud.

Then al-Razi said:

**The second example:** It is mentioned that al-Shafi'i, may Allah have mercy on him, was sitting in the Masjid al-Haram and said: "Do not ask me about anything except that I will answer you concerning it from the Book of Allah, exalted is He." A man said: "What do you say about the muhrim (one in the state of ihram) who kills a wasp?" He said: "There is nothing upon him." The man said: "Where is this in the Book of Allah?" He said: "Allah, exalted is He, says: ﴿And whatever the Messenger gives you, take it﴾ [al-Hashr: 7]." Then he cited a chain of narration to the Prophet (ﷺ) that he said: "Hold fast to my Sunnah and the Sunnah of the rightly guided caliphs after me." Then he cited a chain of narration to Umar, may Allah be pleased with him, that he said: "For the muhrim, killing a wasp is permitted." Al-Wahidi said: So he answered him from the Book of Allah by deriving the ruling through three levels.

I say: here there is another way closer than that, namely that the original state of the property of Muslims is inviolability. Allah, exalted is He, says: ﴿For it is what it has earned, and against it is what it has deserved﴾ [al-Baqarah: 286], and He says: ﴿And He will not ask you for your wealth﴾ [Muhammad: 36], and He says: ﴿Do not consume your wealth among yourselves in falsehood, except it be trade by mutual consent among you﴾ [al-Nisa': 29]. So He forbade consuming people's property, except by way of trade. When there is no trade, it must remain under the original prohibition. These general texts require that the muhrim who killed the wasp bears nothing; for holding to these general texts requires judgment at a single level.

**The third example:** Al-Wahidi said: It is reported in the hadith of the hired laborer who committed fornication: "His father said to the Prophet (ﷺ): 'Judge between us by the Book of Allah.' He, peace be upon him, said: 'By Him in whose hand is my soul! I will certainly judge between you two by the Book of Allah.' Then he decreed the lashing and banishment for the laborer, and stoning for the woman if she confessed." Al-Wahidi said: There is no mention of lashing and banishment in the text of the Book. This indicates that everything the Prophet (ﷺ) judged by is itself the Book of Allah. Al-Razi said: This is true, for He, exalted is He, said: ﴿that you may explain to the people what has been sent down to them﴾, and everything the Messenger (peace be upon him) explained falls under this verse. End.

Commentary of al-Qasimi (Mahasin al-Ta'wil) on surah 6, verse 38 (part 2 of 2):

In summary, the Noble Qur'an is the totality of the Shari'ah (the sacred law), and within it are gathered universal principles (kulliyyat). Since the Shari'ah was completed with the completion of its revelation, when we examine how the Shari'ah's particulars return to its universal principles, we find that the Qur'an has comprehended them in full. Al-'Allamah al-Shatibi has thoroughly investigated this important question in his *al-Muwafaqat*, in its second part, with the evidences in detail. So refer to it.
We have quoted a fragment from it in the introduction to this tafsir, so remember!

Seventh: Abu al-Baqa' said: The "min" in His Exalted words ﴿مِن شَيْءٍ﴾ ("of anything") is extra (za'idah), and "shay'" here stands in the position of a verbal noun (masdar), meaning "neglect" (tafriṭan). On this interpretation, there remains in the verse no proof for one who thinks that the Book explicitly contains mention of everything. A parallel to this is ﴿لا يَضُرُّكم كَيْدُهم شَيْئًا﴾ ("Their plotting will not harm you at all"), meaning: harm (ḍararan) [p. 2306]. We have mentioned parallels to it. It is not permissible for "shay'" to be a direct object, because "faraṭnā" is transitive by itself only with a preposition, not directly; and it has been made transitive by "fī" to "al-Kitab," so it is not made transitive by another preposition. Nor is it correct that the meaning is: "We did not leave out anything from the Book," because the meaning would then be contrary to this. Thus it becomes clear that the interpretation is what we have mentioned. End.

Al-Khafaji said: Tafrīṭ means shortcoming (taqṣīr). Its original usage is to be transitive with "fī," but here it has been given the sense of "we neglected and left out" (aghfalnā wa-taraknā). So "min shay'" is in the position of the direct object, and "min" is extra. The meaning: We did not leave in the Book anything that is needed from the evidences of divinity and the obligations.

This is what Abu Hayyan and al-Zamakhshari approved, but al-Baydawi departed from it, because it is not transitive. So he made the estimate "tafriṭan," the verbal noun was deleted, and "shay'" was placed in its stead. He followed Abu al-Baqa' in this, since he chose this view, and he raised an objection to it in *al-Multaqaṭ*, that it is not as he described. For when the negation applies to the verbal noun, it becomes negated in a general sense, and it entails negating all types of the verbal noun and all of its instances. This is not right, because he means that the meaning then is: all kinds of neglect are negated from the Qur'an, which is beyond doubt, and it does not entail that everything must be mentioned in it, as would be required on the other reading, so that interpretation would be needed. Just as negating its transitivity does not harm one who says it is a direct object through implicit meaning (tadmin), as has passed. As for what has been said, that "faraṭa" is transitive by itself, based on what occurs in the *Qamus* ("faraṭa al-shay'", and "faraṭa fihi tafriṭan": he wasted it, showed weakness in it, and fell short and was negligent in it), we do not concede that it is transitive by itself. The singular view of the author of the *Qamus* on a matter is not to be heeded against al-Zamakhshari and others. Moreover, it is possible that its transitivity mentioned therein is not inherent but figurative, or by way of implicit meaning. End of al-Shihab's words.

I say: What al-Majd (al-Fayruzabadi) has in the *Qamus* is not among his unique or personal opinions, since lexicography is based on transmission (sama'), not individual reasoning [p. 2307]. His weighing between al-Zamakhshari and others is from the category of recognizing truth by men, whereas the correct approach is the reverse. Moreover, there is nothing in the *Kashshaf* that requires what he claimed. The commentator on the *Qamus*, al-Zubaydi, cited as evidence for its transitivity by itself, in support of the words of al-Majd, the verse of Sakhr al-Ghayy:

*That is my armor, so I will not neglect it, lest they fulfill what they have promised.*

Ibn Sida said: He means: I will not waste it. His saying "bazzi" means "my weapons." Then al-Zubaydi said: Abu 'Amr said: "I neglected you in such-and-such," meaning "I left you." And it is also interpreted this way for the verse of Sakhr. End. And Abu al-Su'ud recited the verse of Sa'idah ibn Ju'ayyah:

*With him a waterskin whose load he does not neglect*

meaning: he does not leave it. By this it is known that what Abu al-Baqa' said falls, and the claim that its original usage is transitivity with "fī" falls, and the earlier claim of implicit meaning falls, and the burden of making "shay'" stand in the position of a verbal noun falls.

Furthermore, it is read "faraṭnā" with light pronunciation (takhfīf), and it has the same meaning as the emphatic form. We have only gone beyond what has been narrated according to the second view on the meaning of "the Book," because of the fame of the verse in this sense, though the first is more apparent, for what we have mentioned, and because the surah is Meccan, and its rulings are not complete. And Allah knows best.

Eighth: The verse indicates the gathering (hashr) of all beasts, animals, and birds, that is, their resurrection on the Day of Resurrection, like His Exalted words: ﴿وَإِذَا الوُحُوشُ حُشِرَتْ﴾ ("And when the wild beasts are gathered") [al-Takwir: 5].

Imam Ahmad narrated from Abu Dharr, may Allah be pleased with him, that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) saw two sheep butting each other, and said: "O Abu Dharr! Do you know why they are butting?" He said: "No." He said: "But Allah knows, and He will judge between them." Abd al-Razzaq and Ibn Jarir also narrated it, and they added: "And the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) left us, and no bird flaps its wings in the sky except that he mentioned to us knowledge of it."

Abd Allah ibn Imam Ahmad narrated in the *Musnad* of his father from Uthman that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Indeed the hornless sheep will be given retribution from the horned on the Day of Resurrection."

Abd al-Razzaq narrated from Abu Hurayrah regarding this verse, he said: "All creatures will be gathered on the Day of Resurrection: the beasts, the animals, the birds, and everything. So Allah's justice will reach such a point on that day that He will take retribution for the hornless from the horned. Then He will say: 'Be dust!' That is why the disbelievers will say: 'Would that I were dust!'" This has also been narrated as a raised (marfu') report in the hadith of the Trumpet. Ibn Kathir reported this.

I say: Imam Ahmad, al-Bukhari in *al-Adab al-Mufrad*, Muslim, and al-Tirmidhi narrated from Abu Hurayrah that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Rights will certainly be returned to their owners on the Day of Resurrection, even to the hornless sheep from the horned sheep that gored it."

[p. 2309] Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Ikrimah, from Ibn Abbas, regarding the verse, that he said: "Death gathers them." The same has been narrated from Mujahid and al-Dahhak. The first is more apparent.

Ninth: In *al-Iklil*: This verse has been cited as evidence for another issue. Abu al-Shaykh narrated from Anas that he was asked: "Who takes the souls of animals?" He said: "The Angel of Death." This reached al-Hasan, and he said: "He is right! And that is in the Book of Allah." Then he recited this verse.

The Interpretation of His Words, Exalted is He:

[39] ﴿Those who deny Our signs are deaf and dumb, in darkness. Whomever Allah wills, He leaves astray; and whomever He wills, He places on a straight path.﴾

﴿Those who deny Our signs are deaf and dumb, in darkness﴾ That is: they are like [those who are] in their ignorance, their lack of understanding, and their wretched state. "Deaf" (ṣumm, plural of aṣamm, the one who does not hear) and "dumb" (bukm, plural of abkam, the one who does not speak). Moreover, they are in darkness, not seeing. How then could such people find the way, or emerge from what they are in? The Revelation has frequently likened them to this, to make clear the extent of their deep-rootedness in ignorance and the complete closing of the door of understanding and of making others understand.

Then He indicated that they are among those sealed [in their hearts] by His words: ﴿Whomever Allah wills, He leaves astray; and whomever He wills, He places on a straight path﴾. That is: He is the one who disposes of His creation as He wills. Whoever He loves to guide, He enables by His grace and bounty to believe; and whoever He wills to be misguided, He leaves in his disbelief, "and whomever Allah does not give light, for him there is no light."

Then Allah, Exalted is He, commanded His Messenger to rebuke them with something they have no way to deny, by making clear that when calamity befalls them, they turn to Him, Exalted is He, and not to the idols. So Allah, Exalted is He, said:

The discussion concerning His words, may He be exalted:

[40] ﴿Say: "Tell Me, if the punishment of Allah should come upon you, or the Hour should come upon you, would you call upon other than Allah, if you should be truthful?"﴾

﴿Say: "Tell Me"﴾ i.e., inform me: ﴿if the punishment of Allah should come upon you﴾ i.e., like what befell the past disbelieving nations, ﴿or the Hour should come upon you﴾ meaning the Resurrection, ﴿would you call upon other than Allah﴾ i.e., to remove the punishment from you? This is the point of rebuke (al-tabkit), i.e., do you single out your gods for supplication to lift that severity? Rather, you do not call upon them even alongside Allah. ﴿if you should be truthful﴾ is connected to "Tell Me" and serves to emphasize the rebuke, exposing their falsehood.

Discussion on the interpretation of His saying, exalted is He:

[41] ﴿Rather, it is Him you call upon, and He removes that for which you call upon Him, if He wills, and you forget what you associate (with Him).﴾

﴿Rather, it is Him you call upon﴾: that is, you single Him out in supplication. ﴿And He removes that for which you call upon Him, if He wills﴾: that is, if He wills to remove it. The restriction by His will (mashi'ah) is to show that their answer is not constant; rather it follows His will, exalted is He, which is based on wisdoms He has reserved knowledge of for Himself. ﴿And you forget what you associate﴾: that is, you abandon completely what you associate (with Him), because you know that they neither harm nor benefit. It is coordinated (ma'tuf) upon "you call upon." The placement of the removal (kashf) between the two, despite their being juxtaposed, and the delay of the removal after them, serve to show the complete concern for the matter of the removal and to signal that it follows upon supplication specifically.

Then Exalted is He explained that among the disbelievers of the earlier nations were those who reached such hardness that they were seized by calamities in order that they would humble themselves and turn to Allah, exalted is He, but they did not do so. As a consolation to His Prophet (ﷺ), He said:

Commentary of al-Qasimi (Mahasin al-Ta'wil) on surah 6, verse 42:

The explanation of His saying, exalted is He:

[42] ﴿And We certainly sent [messengers] to nations before you, and We seized them with adversity and hardship, that they might humble themselves.﴾

﴿And We certainly sent [messengers] to nations before you﴾, i.e., messengers, "so they denied them and did not care," because they were in ease (al-rakhaa'). ﴿So We seized them with adversity (al-ba'saa')﴾, i.e., severity and famine, ﴿and hardship (al-darraa')﴾, i.e., sickness and loss of lives and wealth, ﴿that they might humble themselves (yatadarra'un)﴾, i.e., that they might abase themselves, become submissive to their Lord, and repent to Him from their disbelief and their sins, for souls grow humble when calamities descend.
