The discussion of the interpretation of His saying, Exalted is He:

[43] ﴿So why, when Our punishment came upon them, did they not humble themselves? But their hearts became hardened, and Satan made attractive to them what they used to do.﴾

﴿So why, when Our punishment came upon them, did they not humble themselves?﴾ That is: with repentance and submissiveness. Its meaning is the negation of humbling themselves.

It is as if it were said: "So they did not humble themselves." The particle (lawla) is used to convey that they had no excuse for abandoning humility except their obstinacy, as He said: ﴿But their hearts became hardened﴾, so there was in them no softness that would necessitate humbling themselves, and they did not refrain, but were only afflicted with it. ﴿And Satan made attractive to them what they used to do﴾, that is, of polytheism. So the statement "but" is a corrective to the sense, to explain what turned them away from humbling themselves, and that there was nothing preventing them except the hardness of their hearts and their admiration for their deeds, which had been made attractive to them.

A subtle point (laṭīfa):

If you say: Here God attributed the beautifying (tazyīn) to Satan, and He attributed it to Himself in His saying: ﴿Thus We made attractive to every nation their deeds﴾. Is it literally true of both, or of one of them? I say: The beautifying occurs in many contexts. Sometimes it is attributed to Satan, as in the first verse; sometimes to Himself, as in the second; and sometimes to humans, as in His saying: ﴿And thus many of the polytheists had their partners make attractive to them the killing of their children﴾ (in one reading); and sometimes it is in the passive, with no mentioned agent, as in His saying: ﴿It was made attractive to those who transgress﴾. This is because beautifying has meanings attested by usage and by language:

First: bringing a thing into being as good and beautified in reality, as in His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿We have adorned the lowest heaven﴾ [al-Saffat: 6].

Second: making a thing appear beautified without bringing it into being, as the bridal attendant beautifies the bride.

Third: making a thing beloved to the soul and desired by the disposition, even if it is not so in itself. If this means creating inclination in the soul and disposition, it is attributed only to God, since He is the true agent of it, by His bringing it into being, and linguistically and grammatically because it is a quality of His creation. If it means merely embellishing and promoting it through speech and what resembles it, such as whispering and seduction, then it is not attributed to Him, Exalted is He, literally; rather it is attributed to humans or to Satan. And when its agent is not mentioned, the appropriate agent is supplied in each place.

Thus in al-'Inaya.

**The interpretation of His saying, exalted is He:**

[44] ﴿So when they forgot what they had been reminded of, We opened for them the gates of everything, until, when they rejoiced in what they had been given, We seized them suddenly, and then they were in despair.﴾

﴿When they forgot what they had been reminded of﴾, i.e., of the hardship (*al-ba'sa'*) and adversity (*al-darra'*), meaning they abandoned taking heed from it. ﴿We opened for them the gates of everything﴾, i.e., of blessings, such as health, abundance, ease of mind, security, and all kinds of their desires, as *istidraj* (a gradual drawing toward ruin) and *imla'* (respite) and a scheme against them. We seek refuge in Allah from His scheme. ﴿Until, when they rejoiced in what they had been given﴾ of their aims and desires, while still in polytheism: ﴿We seized them﴾, i.e., with a total punishment that uproots them. ﴿Suddenly﴾, i.e., unexpectedly, without any prior warner, since the warning did not benefit them the first time. ﴿And then they were in despair﴾, i.e., regretful and grieving, despairing of every good.

The interpretation of His saying, exalted be He:

[45] ﴿So the last remnant of the people who did wrong was cut off. And praise be to God, Lord of the worlds.﴾

﴿So the last remnant of the people who did wrong was cut off﴾: i.e., their last ones (ākhiruhum). It is a metaphor (kināyah) for total annihilation (al-istiʾṣāl), because the going of the last part of a thing necessarily entails the going of what precedes it. It derives from (dabara-hu) when one follows him, so he was at his dubur (rear), i.e., behind him. Thus al-dābir (the remnant) is what comes after the others, and it is applied to it figuratively. Abu ʿUbayd said: "The dābir of a people is their last." Al-Aṣmaʿi said: "Al-dābir is the root (al-aṣl)," and from it: "God cut off his dābir," meaning his root.

﴿And praise be to God, Lord of the worlds﴾: i.e., for what befell them of destruction. The destruction of the disbelievers and the disobedient, insofar as it is a deliverance for the people of the earth from the ill omen of their beliefs and deeds, is a great blessing deserving that God be praised for it, especially with what it contains of elevating the word of truth which their messengers, peace be upon them, proclaimed.

(p-2314) Admonitions:

The first: Reports and narrations have been related concerning this verse. Among them is what Imam Ahmad transmitted from ʿUqbah ibn ʿAmir, from the Prophet (ﷺ), who said: "When you see God giving a servant of the world what he loves despite his sins, then it is only a gradual leading (istidrāj)." Then the Messenger of God (ﷺ) recited: ﴿So when they forgot what they had been reminded of﴾ [al-Anʿam: 44] – up to: ﴿they were struck dumb in despair﴾ [al-Anʿam: 44]. Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim related it from him.

Ibn Abi Hatim also related from ʿUbadah ibn al-Samit that "the Messenger of God (ﷺ) used to say: 'When God wills to cut off a people, He opens for them (or He opens upon them) the door of treachery, until when they rejoice in what they have been given, We seize them suddenly' – the verse." Ahmad and others related it.

Al-Hasan al-Basri said: "Whoever is granted abundance by God and does not think he is being tested by it has no judgment. And whoever is restricted and does not think he is being given respite has no judgment." Then he recited: ﴿So when they forgot﴾ [al-Anʿam: 44], the verse. Al-Hasan said: "They were deceived concerning the people, by the Lord of the Kaʿbah! They were given their wants and then they were seized."

Qatadah said: "The command of God overtook the people suddenly, and God never seized a people except at the height of their intoxication, their heedlessness, and their blessing. So do not be deceived by God, for none is deceived by God except the defiant people." Ibn Abi Hatim related this.

The second: al-Razi said: The people of meanings (ahl al-maʿani) said: They were seized in a state of ease and comfort so that it would be more severe, because of their regret over what had escaped them of safety and well-being.

The third: al-Zamakhshari said: In His saying, exalted be He: ﴿And praise be to God, Lord of the worlds﴾ is an announcement of the obligation of praise at the destruction of the wrongdoers, and that it is among the greatest blessings and most abundant portions. That is, it is a statement with the meaning of a command, as instruction for the servants.

(p-2315) Al-Nasir said in "al-Intisaf": A parallel to it is His saying, exalted be He: ﴿And We rained down upon them a rain; evil was the rain of those who were warned﴾ [al-Naml: 58] ﴿Say: Praise be to God, and peace upon His servants whom He has chosen﴾ [al-Naml: 59]. Regarding one who stops here and makes the praise upon the destruction of the tyrants mentioned above, and among them is one who stops at "those who were warned" and makes the praise connected to what follows of establishing proofs for God's oneness, and that He, majestic is His majesty, is better than what they associate. So according to the first, the praise is a conclusion, and according to the second, an opening, and it is used in both legally, but in the verse of al-Naml it is more evident as an opening for what follows, while in the verse of al-An'am it is definitively a conclusion of what precedes it, since the context requires nothing else. End.

I say: If we follow what is most sound among the verses in terms of harmonizing parallels, it requires reading the verse of al-Naml in the sense of what is here, and claiming it is more evident there is disputed, for revelation explains one part by another. So reflect. Then God, exalted be He, commanded His Messenger to repeat the rebuke against them and to reiterate the argument.

The commentary of al-Qasimi (Mahasin al-Ta'wil) on surah 6, verse 46:

On the interpretation (*ta'wil*) of His saying, exalted is He:

[46] ﴿Say: "Have you considered? If God were to take away your hearing and your sight and seal your hearts, who is a god other than God to bring them back to you? Look how We vary the signs; yet they turn away."﴾

He, exalted is He, says: ﴿Say: "Have you considered? If God were to take away your hearing and your sight"﴾ by making you deaf and blind, ﴿"and seal your hearts"﴾ by covering them with that which removes your reason and understanding. ﴿"Who is a god other than God to bring them back to you?"﴾ That is, to bring back what was taken. These three organs were singled out for mention because they are the most noble of a human being's organs. When they are disabled, the human order is disrupted, his affairs are corrupted, and his interests in religion and in this world are nullified.

﴿Look how We vary the signs﴾ That is, We present them in various ways, like the variation of the winds. The word *unzur* (look), here, indicates astonishment at their lack of response to the stupendous signs they have witnessed.

[p. 2316] ﴿Yet they turn away.﴾ That is, after seeing the signs varied, they turn away from them and do not reflect upon them, out of obstinacy, envy and arrogance.

Notes:

The first: By "the signs" may be meant either all the Qur'anic proofs in general, or what has been mentioned from the beginning of the surah up to this point, or what was mentioned before this of the rational premises indicating the existence of the Creator and His oneness, referred to by His saying, ﴿If the punishment of God comes upon you...﴾ (6:47), and of the encouragement expressed by His saying, ﴿so that He removes what you call upon Him for﴾, and of the warning expressed by His saying, ﴿If God were to take away your hearing...﴾, and of the admonition and reminder with the conditions of earlier peoples. Some commentators took each of these views, and the general wording covers all of them without contradiction.

The second: Some commentators from the Zaydiyya (a Shi'i school) said: the verse indicates the permissibility of argumentation in matters of religion. End of quotation. This is evident.

The third: The purpose of this verse is to show that the one capable of granting these three faculties and protecting them from afflictions is none other than God, exalted is He. If that is the case, then the one who bestowed these lofty blessings and excellent goods is God, exalted is He. Therefore it is necessary to say: the one deserving glorification, praise and worship is none other than God, exalted is He. This indicates that the worship of idols is a false and corrupt path, as al-Razi (may God have mercy on him) established.

Then God, exalted is He, pointed to another rebuke of them, by compelling them to acknowledge that the punishment is specific to them, in His saying, glorified is He:

(p-2317) The discussion on the ta'wil (interpretation) of His saying, exalted is He:

[47] ﴿Say: Have you considered: if the punishment of God comes upon you suddenly or openly, will anyone be destroyed except the wrongdoing people?﴾

﴿Say: Have you considered, if it comes upon you﴾ because of your turning away from the signs after they have been made clear: ﴿the punishment of God﴾, i.e., the one that uproots you; ﴿suddenly﴾, i.e., unexpectedly, without any preceding sign that would give notice of it, since what came before did not benefit them; ﴿or openly﴾, by being preceded by a sign, as an exaggeration in removing excuse. It was said: at night or by day, as in His saying: ﴿by night or by day﴾ [Yunus: 50], because what comes at night is generally sudden, and what comes by day is generally open. ﴿Will anyone be destroyed except the wrongdoing people?﴾, i.e., will anyone be destroyed by that punishment except you? The apparent noun was placed in the position of the pronoun, to record wrongdoing against them, and to indicate that the basis of their destruction is their wrongdoing, which is their turning away from the signs that God has made clear, in place of faith.

Then the Exalted pointed to the function of the messengers and the fulfilment of what is incumbent upon them, to show that what the disbelievers propose to him (ﷺ) is not at all related to the message, by His saying, glorified is He:

The discussion of the interpretation of His words, exalted is He:

[48] ﴿We send not the messengers except as bearers of good news and warners. So whoever believes and makes amends, there will be no fear for them, nor will they grieve.﴾

﴿We send not the messengers except as bearers of good news﴾ of reward for the people of faith and righteous deeds, ﴿and warners﴾ of punishment for the people of disbelief and disobedience. ﴿So whoever believes and makes amends﴾ in deeds and conduct, these are the people of glad tidings. ﴿There will be no fear for them﴾, i.e., of the punishment with which they were warned, both in this world and in the Hereafter. ﴿Nor will they grieve﴾, i.e., over the loss of what they were given good news of, of reward both immediate and deferred.

(p-2318) The discussion of the interpretation of His saying, exalted is He:

[49] ﴿And those who denied Our signs, the punishment will touch them for what they used to defiantly disobey.﴾

﴿And those who denied Our signs, the punishment will touch them﴾ i.e., the punishment with which they were warned, whether soon or later. ﴿For what they used to defiantly disobey﴾ i.e., departing from the command of Allah by abandoning faith, engaging in corrupt deeds, and acquiring vile character traits.

The discussion of the Almighty's words:

[50] ﴿Say: I do not tell you that with me are the treasuries of God, nor do I know the unseen, nor do I tell you that I am an angel. I only follow what is revealed to me. Say: Are the blind and the seeing alike? Will you not then reflect?﴾

His words, exalted is He: ﴿Say: I do not tell you that with me are the treasuries of God﴾, meaning: Say to these polytheists who propose to you at times the sending down of signs, and at other times other things: I do not claim that the treasures of God's provision have been entrusted to me, so that I give you from them whatever you wish, such as turning the mountains into gold, and other such things.

[The treasuries (al-khaza'in) is the plural of khizana, which is the name of the place where a thing is stored. The storing of a thing (khazn al-shay') is its safeguarding in such a way that hands cannot reach it.]

﴿nor do I know the unseen﴾, meaning: of His acts, exalted is He, so that you ask me about the time of the Hour, or the time of the descent of punishment, or the like.

﴿nor do I tell you that I am an angel﴾, meaning: so that you burden me with supernatural acts beyond what humans can bear, such as ascending into the sky and the like, or consider my not having their attributes a flaw in my affair, as their saying indicates: "What is this messenger who eats food and walks in the markets?" The meaning is: I do not claim any of these three things, so that you propose to me what is among their effects and rulings, and make my not responding to that a proof of the invalidity of what I claim of prophethood, which has no connection whatsoever with any of what was mentioned. Rather, it is merely an expression of receiving revelation from God, mighty and majestic, and knowledge of its requirements only, as His saying indicates: ﴿I only follow what is revealed to me﴾, meaning: In what I say to you, I follow only what is revealed to me from Him, exalted is He, who honoured me with it and bestowed it upon me, as He unveils the angels to me so that they inform me.

Then He repeated the matter, as a second rebuke, with His saying:

﴿Say: Are the blind and the seeing alike?﴾ This is an example for the misguided and the guided in general. The interrogation is denunciatory, and what is meant is denying the equality of one who does not know the realities mentioned with one who knows them. In it is an indication of the complete clarity of these realities, and of the aversion from misguidance and the encouragement to guidance, which is not hidden. This was conveyed by Abu al-Su'ud.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Will you not then reflect?﴾ is a reproach and rebuke included under the command. That is: Will you not reflect so that you may be guided, and not be misguided like the blind?

Notes:

First: Some exegetes took His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Say: I do not tell you that with me are the treasuries of God, nor do I know the unseen﴾ as a disavowal of the claim of divinity, since the distribution of provision among the servants and the knowledge of the unseen are specific to Him, exalted is He. He said: That is why He repeated the phrase "nor do I tell you" in the case of angelhood. The meaning: I do not claim divinity nor angelhood.

It was objected to this that the intended meaning is: I do not have the power to do what you wish of what you propose, and the intent is not a disavowal of the claim of divinity; otherwise it would have said: "I do not tell you that I am a god," just as it said: "nor do I tell you that I am an angel." Also, the expression of divinity by "with me are the treasuries of God" contains what is not hidden of its offensiveness. Rather, it is an answer to their proposal to him, peace be upon him, that he widen the good things of this world for them. Thus in al-'Inayah.

Abu al-Su'ud said: To make this a disavowal of the claim of divinity is something for which there is absolutely no basis.

Second: Al-Jubba'i said: The verse indicates that the angel is superior to the prophets, because the meaning is: I do not claim a station above my station. Had the angel not been superior, that would not be valid. Al-Qadi said: If the purpose of what is negated is the manner of humility, then the closer view is that this indicates the angel is superior; but if the intent is negating his capacity for acts which only angels can perform, it does not indicate that they are superior.

Al-Zamakhshari affirmed the first view in support of his school, saying in the interpretation of the verse: That is: I do not claim what is deemed unlikely in minds, that a human should possess the treasuries of God, which are His distribution among creation and His provisions, and knowledge of the unseen; and I am not of the angels, who are the noblest and most excellent kind God created, and nearest in rank to Him. That is: I did not claim divinity nor angelhood, for there is no rank above the angels' rank after divinity, so that you would find my claim unlikely and deny it; rather I claim what many humans have, namely prophethood. End.

Al-Nasir in "al-Intisaf" criticised him, saying: This is built upon the principle he stated earlier, of the angels' superiority over the prophets. By my life, the apparent meaning of this verse supports it, which is why he seized the opportunity to argue from it. But his opponent may say: The verse was revealed as a reply to the unbelievers in their saying: "What is this messenger who eats food and walks in the markets? Why was not an angel sent down to him to be with him a warner, or a treasure thrown down to him..." (the verse). So He answered their saying, "What is this messenger who eats food," by saying he is a human, and that is the nature of humans, and he did not claim to be an angel, so that his eating food would be a matter of surprise. In that case it does not necessarily follow that the angels are superior to the prophets, since there is no dispute that the prophets eat food and the angels do not; the distinction in this respect is agreed upon, and it does not require agreement that the angels are superior to the prophets.

Likewise, He answered their saying, "or a treasure be thrown down to him," by saying he does not possess the treasuries of God, so that he could bring them a treasure from them according to their proposal, and he did not say that to them, so that the proof could be established against him by it.

Then al-Nasir, may God have mercy on him, said: Al-Zamakhshari did not express himself well in his saying: "There is no rank above the angels' rank after divinity," for he made divinity one of the ranks like angelhood, and such a generalisation is not permissible. A rank (manzilah) is an expression for the place where God causes the servant to dwell, in height or otherwise, so applying it to divinity is a distortion. And God is the Granter of success to what is right.

Third: Al-Razi said: The apparent meaning of His saying, exalted is He: ﴿I only follow what is revealed to me﴾ indicates that he, peace be upon him, acts only by revelation, and this indicates two rulings:

The first: This text indicates that he, peace be upon him, did not judge by his own accord in any of the rulings, and that he did not exercise independent reasoning (ijtihad), but rather all his rulings proceed from revelation. This is reinforced by His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Nor does he speak from desire﴾ [al-Najm: 3] ﴿It is only a revelation revealed﴾ [al-Najm: 4].

The second: The opponents of analogy (qiyas) said: It has been established by this text that he, peace be upon him, did not act except by the revelation sent down to him, so it is necessary that no one of his community be permitted to act except by the revelation sent down to him, by His saying: "follow him," and this negates the permissibility of acting by analogy. Then He emphasised this statement with His saying: ﴿Say: Are the blind and the seeing alike?﴾, because acting without revelation proceeds in the manner of the blind man's action, while acting in accordance with the descent of revelation proceeds in the manner of the seeing man's knowledge. Then He said: ﴿Will you not then reflect?﴾, and what is meant by it is an alert that the intelligent person must know the difference between these two domains, and not be heedless of knowing it. End.

In "Fath al-Rahman": Whoever does not affirm the independent reasoning of the prophets held to this, acting on what the restriction in this verse conveys.

The matter is recorded in the books of legal theory (usul). It is authentically related from him, peace be upon him, that he said: "I have been given the Qur'an and its like with it."

Then, when God, exalted is He, informed that those polytheists are like the deaf, dumb and blind, rather the dead, since they were not admonished by the clear diversification of the signs, He commanded the delivery of warning to those who are affected by what is revealed to him, disregarding those wicked ones. So He said, exalted is He:

(p-2322) On the interpretation of His saying, exalted is He:

[51] ﴿And warn thereby those who fear that they will be gathered to their Lord, having besides Him no protector and no intercessor, that they may become righteous.﴾

﴿And warn thereby﴾ i.e., with what is revealed, previously mentioned: ﴿those who fear that they will be gathered to their Lord, having besides Him﴾ meaning, besides Allah, exalted is He: ﴿no protector﴾, i.e., a helper who would support them; ﴿and no intercessor﴾ who would intercede for them and save them from the punishment, other than Him, exalted is He. ﴿That they may become righteous﴾, i.e., [may abandon] corrupt beliefs, wicked deeds, and bad morals.

Al-Qasimi said in "al-'Inayah" (al-Ināya): He singled out these people for mention because they are the ones whom warning benefits and whom it leads to piety. The intent is not restriction, such that it could be objected that warning others is also obligatory. End of quote.

The clause ﴿having besides Him no protector and no intercessor﴾ is in the position of a circumstantial clause (ḥāl) relative to ﴿they will be gathered﴾, since what is feared is the gathering in this state. By "protector" (walī) and "intercessor" (shafī') is meant the deities which the polytheists claimed were their intercessors. In that case, there is no indication in the verse negating intercession for the Muslims, because the intercession of the Messengers on that day will only be by His permission, exalted is He, so it is in effect from Him, exalted is He.

**(p-2323)** The discussion on the interpretation (*ta'wil*) of His saying:

[52] ﴿And do not drive away those who call upon their Lord morning and evening, seeking His face. Nothing of their account is upon you, and nothing of your account is upon them, so that you would drive them away and thus be among the wrongdoers.﴾

Imam Muslim narrated from Sa'd ibn Abi Waqqas (may Allah be pleased with him), who said: "We were with the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), six men. The polytheists said to him: 'Drive these away, lest they become bold against us!' He said: I was there, and Ibn Mas'ud, a man from Hudhayl, Bilal, and two other men whose names I will not mention. Something came into the soul of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) that Allah willed to occur, so he spoke to himself, and Allah the Exalted revealed: ﴿And do not drive away those who...﴾, the verse..."

Al-Hakim and Ibn Hibban narrated something similar in their *Sahihs*.

Imam Ahmad narrated from Ibn Mas'ud, who said: "A group of the chieftains of Quraysh passed by the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), and with him were Khabbab, Suhayb, Bilal, and Ammar. They said: 'O Muhammad! Are you content with these?' So the Qur'an was revealed to him: ﴿And warn therewith those who fear that they will be gathered to their Lord...﴾ up to His saying: ﴿Is not Allah most knowing of the grateful?﴾ [al-An'am: 53]."

Ibn Jarir also narrated it from Ibn Mas'ud, who said: "A group of the chieftains of Quraysh passed by the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), and with him were Suhayb, Bilal, Ammar, Khabbab, and others of the weak among the Muslims."

**(p-2324)** In it: they said: "O Muhammad! Are you content with these from your people? Are these the ones on whom Allah has bestowed favour from among us, while we would be followers of these? Drive them away; perhaps if you drive them away, we will follow you!" So this verse was revealed: ﴿And do not drive away those who call upon their Lord morning and evening...﴾, the verse.

Beyond what we have mentioned, there are narrations that are not authentic and cannot be relied upon.

When you know this, it becomes clear that he (ﷺ) did not actually drive them away. Rather, he only intended to distance them from his assembly at the time of those people's arrival, in order to win them over, so that this might lead them to faith. Then Allah forbade him from carrying out that intention. As for what al-Razi mentioned, that the Prophet (ﷺ) drove them away and then began to labour to answer it, because it contradicts infallibility (*'ismah*) in his view, it is built upon something weak. The established principle is that investigating a report is a branch of its authenticity; otherwise, falsehood is refuted by the fact that it is false. I have clarified this in my book *Qawa'id al-Tahdith min Funun Mustalah al-Hadith* (The Principles of Narration from the Sciences of the Terminology of Hadith).

The meaning is: do not distance from yourself those who possess these attributes; rather, make them your companions and intimates. This is like His saying: ﴿And restrain yourself to be with those who call upon their Lord morning and evening, seeking His face. And let not your eyes overlook them, desiring the adornment of the worldly life. And do not obey one whose heart We have made heedless of Our remembrance, who follows his desire and whose affair has become excess﴾ [al-Kahf: 28].

As for His saying: ﴿who call upon their Lord﴾, i.e., they worship Him and ask Him, ﴿morning and evening﴾: Sa'id ibn al-Musayyib and others said that what is meant is the obligatory prayer (*al-salah al-maktubah*).

As for His saying: ﴿seeking His face﴾, what is meant by "face" is the Essence (*al-dhat*), as in His saying: ﴿Everything will perish except His Face﴾ [al-Qasas: 88]. The meaning of seeking the Essence is sincerity toward it. The phrase is a circumstantial clause (*hal*) relating to "call upon" (*yad'una*), i.e., they call upon their Lord sincerely for Him in it. Its restriction by this phrase serves to emphasise the cause (*'illiyyah*) of the prohibition, since sincerity is among the strongest causes for honouring, which is the opposite of driving away.

As for His saying: ﴿Nothing of their account is upon you, and nothing of your account is upon them﴾, **(p-2325)** it is like the saying of Noah (peace be upon him) concerning those who said: ﴿Shall we believe you when the lowest have followed you?﴾ [al-Shu'ara': 111]. He said: ﴿And what is my knowledge of what they used to do?﴾ [al-Shu'ara': 112]. ﴿Their account is only upon my Lord, if you could perceive﴾ [al-Shu'ara': 113]. That is: their account is only with Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, and nothing of their account is upon me, just as nothing of my account is upon them.

The scholar Abu al-Su'ud said: The sentence is a parenthetical clause (*i'tiradh*) placed between the prohibition and its answer, confirming it and repelling what might be imagined as a justification for driving them away, from the words of those who disparaged their religion, as was the habit of the people of Noah when they said: ﴿And we do not see you followed except by those who are the lowest of us, at first glance﴾ [Hud: 27]. That is: nothing of the account of their faith and their inner deeds is upon you, so that you should concern yourself with it and build upon it the rulings you see. Your duty, as is the nature of the station of prophethood, is only to take note of outward deeds and to apply rulings according to what they require. As for the inner realities of affairs, their account rests with the All-Knowing of what is in the breasts, as in His saying: ﴿Their account is only upon my Lord﴾ [al-Shu'ara': 113]. He mentioned His saying: ﴿nor is there upon you any account of theirs﴾ even though the answer was already complete with what preceded it, for the sake of emphasis in showing the negation of their account being upon him (ﷺ), by placing it in the same series as what has no doubt at all, namely the negation of his (peace be upon him) account being upon them. This follows the manner of His saying: ﴿They cannot delay an hour nor advance it﴾ [al-A'raf: 34]. As for what has been said, that this is to make the two sentences function as one sentence conveying one meaning, in the manner of His saying: ﴿And no bearer of burdens will bear the burden of another﴾ [Fatir: 18], it is not fitting for the dignity of the revelation. End of quote.

The statement mentioned belongs to al-Zamakhshari, who held that the two sentences are equivalent to one sentence, performing the function of: "And no bearer of burdens will bear..." and that both are necessary.

Furthermore, it has been said: the pronoun refers to the polytheists, and the meaning is: they will not be held accountable for your account, nor will you be held accountable for theirs, so that their faith would concern you and eagerness for it would drive you to drive away the believers.

Al-Mahayimi went too far when he said: The rebellious, because they are people of rank and wealth, dislike sitting with them because of their lack of rank and wealth. So He, the Mighty and Majestic, said to the most noble of people: ﴿Nothing of their account is upon you﴾, i.e., nothing of their lack of rank and wealth returns to you, nor are they upon you. If their deficiency does not reach you, and they do not take away your perfection by stripping it from you, then there is no reason to drive them away. End of quote.

There is distance in this, because it does not connect with the earlier verse about Noah. And the observance of parallels (*nazha'ir*) is not hidden.

In *al-'Inayah*: He placed the address to him (ﷺ) first in both positions, as an honour to him. Otherwise the apparent form would have been: "and nothing of your account is upon them" with "upon them" and its object placed first, as in the first. In the arrangement there is a return of the last part to the first (*radd al-'ajuz 'ala al-sadr*), as in the saying: "The customs of the nobles, the nobles of customs."

As for His saying: ﴿so that you would drive them away and thus be among the wrongdoers﴾: wrongdoing (*al-zulm*) is placing a thing in other than its proper place. That is: do not intend to drive them away from you, lest you place a thing in other than its proper position.

The discussion on the interpretation of His words, exalted is He:

[53] ﴿And thus We tried some of them by means of others, that they might say, "Are these the ones on whom Allah has bestowed favor from among us? Is not Allah most knowing of those who are grateful?"﴾

﴿And thus We tried some of them﴾ refers to the nobles, ﴿by means of others﴾ refers to the oppressed (mustad'afun), because We bestowed favor upon them with faith. His words ﴿that they might say﴾ mean the nobles, ﴿"Are these..."﴾ means the oppressed, ﴿"...the ones on whom Allah has bestowed favor from among us?"﴾ means by the nobility of faith, even though the nobles, by their own claim, have more right to every nobility. Thus, if it were a nobility, the matter would have been reversed. This is a denial that these people should be singled out from among them for reaching the truth and for precedence in goodness, like their saying: "If it had been good, they would not have preceded us to it" (al-Ahqaf 46:11).

Then God, exalted is He, pointed out that He bestowed upon them only the blessing of faith, because He knew that they recognize the worth of this blessing and thank Him for it as it deserves. As for those others, they do not recognize its worth and so do not give thanks for it. This is in His words, glorified is He: ﴿Is not Allah most knowing of those who are grateful?﴾ It is a rebuttal of their saying and an invalidation of it, and an indication that the basis for deserving favor is knowing the worth of the blessing and acknowledging the right of the Benefactor. Furthermore, there is in it an indication that those oppressed people recognize the right of Allah's blessings in the revelation of the Qur'an and in being guided to faith, and that they give thanks to Him for that, along with an implicit allusion that the speakers are far removed from all of that, which is not hidden.

Al-Hafiz Ibn Kathir said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) at the beginning of his mission was followed mostly by the weak among the people, men and women, slaves and maids, and only a few of the nobles followed him, as the people of Noah said to Noah: ﴿And we do not see you followed except by those who are the lowest among us, immature in judgment﴾ [Hud: 27], and so on. And as Heraclius, the king of the Romans, asked Abu Sufyan, when he asked him about those matters: [Are the nobles of the people following him, or their weak?" He said, "Rather, their weak." He said, "They are the followers of the messengers."] The polytheists of Mecca used to mock those among their weak who believed, and torment whoever among them they could, and they would say: "Are these the ones on whom Allah has bestowed favor from among us?" like His words: ﴿If it had been good, they would not have preceded us to it﴾ [al-Ahqaf: 11], and His words, exalted is He: ﴿And when Our clear verses are recited to them, those who disbelieved say to those who believed, "Which of the two groups is better in position and better in assembly?"﴾ [Maryam: 73]. Allah, exalted is He, answered that: ﴿And how many generations We destroyed before them, who were better in possessions and appearance?﴾ [Maryam: 74]. And He said in answer to them here: ﴿Is not Allah most knowing of those who are grateful?﴾, that is, He knows them with their statements, their deeds, and their inner intentions, so He grants them success, guides them to the ways of peace, and brings them out of darkness into light by His permission, and guides them to a straight path. As He, exalted is He, said: ﴿And those who strive in Our cause - We will surely guide them to Our ways. And indeed, Allah is with the doers of good﴾ [al-'Ankabut: 69].

In the authentic hadith: "Indeed Allah does not look at your forms, nor at your colors, but He looks at your hearts and your deeds."

Ibn Jarir narrated from Ikrima who said: Utba ibn Rabi'a, Shayba ibn Rabi'a, Mut'im ibn 'Adiy, al-Harith ibn Nawfal, and Qarazah ibn 'Abd 'Amr ibn Nawfal, among nobles of the Banu 'Abd Manaf, from the disbelievers, came to Abu Talib and said: "O Abu Talib! If only your nephew would drive away from himself our clients and allies, for they are only our slaves and our low-born. That would be greater in our hearts, more obedient to him in our view, and nearer to our following him and believing him." So Abu Talib came to the Prophet (ﷺ) and told him what they had said to him. 'Umar ibn al-Khattab said: "If you did that, you would watch to see what they intend and where their words lead!" So Allah, mighty and majestic, revealed this verse: ﴿And warn thereby those who fear that they will be gathered to their Lord﴾ [al-An'am: 51], up to His words: ﴿Is not Allah most knowing of those who are grateful?" He said: And they were: Bilal, 'Ammar ibn Yasir, Salim the freedman of Abu Hudhayfa, and Suhayb the freedman of Usayd. And among the allies: Ibn Mas'ud, al-Miqdad ibn 'Amr, Mas'ud ibn al-Qari, Waqid ibn 'Abd Allah al-Hanzali, 'Amr ibn 'Amr Dhu al-Shimalayn, Mirthad ibn Abi Mirthad, and Abu Mirthad ibn Ghanim, ally of Hamza ibn 'Abd al-Muttalib, and their likes among the allies. And [the verse] ﴿And thus We tried some of them﴾ was revealed concerning the leaders of disbelief among the Quraysh, the clients, and the allies, up to the end of the verse. When it was revealed, 'Umar came and apologized for his statement, so Allah, mighty and majestic, revealed: ﴿And when those who believe in Our verses come to you﴾ [al-An'am: 54], to the end of the verse.

Notes and benefits:

Some of the commentators said:

1. It is obligatory in supplication to be sincere in it, because He, exalted is He, said: "they desire His face." This is what al-Hakim said, and so it is with all acts of obedience: they should not be for the sake of worldly purpose. Al-Nafs al-Zakiyya (peace be upon him) said: If the imam makes a call and then finds someone better than him, it is obligatory upon him to hand over the matter to that person. If he does not do so, he has committed transgression, because if he does not do so, it indicates that he seeks the world.

2. It indicates that the morning and evening have a particular excellence for good deeds and supplication, and therefore He singled them out for mention.

3. It indicates that excellence lies in deeds. As for what is excluded from preference that is not a matter of religion, such as equality (kafa'a) in marriage, that is due to a specific reason, like his peace be upon him saying: "The Arabs are equal to one another in marriage."

4. It indicates that no one is taken to account for the sin of another, as in His words: ﴿No bearer of burdens will bear the burden of another﴾ [Fatir: 18]. And what has been mentioned before has already been covered regarding what was reported that the dead is punished for the weeping of his family, with the understanding that this applies when he has instructed them to do so.

5. It indicates that the inner talk of the self (hadith al-nafs) is not held against a person, because it has been reported that he (ﷺ) intended such a thing.

6. It indicates that poverty does not affect the state of the believer. It has been reported in a hadith from him (ﷺ): "The poor among the believers will enter Paradise before their rich by so many years." And it has been reported that "the last of the Companions to enter Paradise will be 'Abd al-Rahman ibn 'Awf because of the abundance of his wealth." And it has been reported that 'Ali (peace be upon him) left nothing behind after his death. So said the Tahdhib, and the account ends.

I say: The first hadith was narrated by al-Tirmidhi from Abu Hurayra, and he said: "hasan sahih." Its wording is: "The poor will enter Paradise before the rich by five hundred years." As for the hadith: "The last of the Companions to enter Paradise..." etc., I have not found it with this wording.

Al-Bazzar and Abu Nu'aym narrated from Anas from the Prophet (ﷺ): "The first of the rich of my community to enter Paradise is 'Abd al-Rahman ibn 'Awf. By the One in whose hand is Muhammad's soul, he will not enter it except crawling." Al-Suyuti said: its chain is weak. So it is in "Muntakhab Kanz al-'Ummal" in the biography of 'Abd al-Rahman ibn 'Awf (may Allah be pleased with him), in "Fada'il al-Sahaba."

7. Furthermore, Ibn al-Faras said: It may be derived from this verse that one should not prevent anyone who reminds people of Allah and the matters of the Hereafter in a mosque, a road, or elsewhere. He said: The later scholars have differed concerning a muezzin who calls to prayer at dawn and pleads with supplication, repeating that until morning, and the neighbors are harmed by it: is he to be prevented? Those who said he should not be prevented argued with this verse and with His words: ﴿And who is more unjust than one who prevents the mosques of Allah﴾ [al-Baqara: 114], and so on. End of quote.

8. Ibn 'Amir recited "bil-ghudwa" with a waw and a damma on the ghayn, here and in Surat al-Kahf, while the rest recited with an alif and a fatha on the ghayn. This is the reading of al-Hasan, Malik ibn Dinar, Abu Raja' al-'Utaridi, and others.

Abu 'Ubayd said: Ibn 'Amir and Abu 'Abd al-Rahman al-Sulami recited "bil-ghudwa," while the majority recited "bil-ghada'" (bil-ghadāt). We believe they recited it following the written form, because it is written with a waw in all the codices, like "al-salat" and "al-zakat." The presence of the waw in the writing is not evidence that it is the recitation, because they wrote "al-salat" and "al-zakat" with a waw while they are pronounced without it. Likewise "al-ghada," and so we find the words of the Arabs. End of quote.

Abu 'Ali al-Farisi said: The correct reading is the majority's "bil-ghada'," because it is used as an indefinite noun, so it is possible to make it definite by adding the definite article to it. As for "ghudwatan," it is definite, a proper name formed for it, and in that case the definite article cannot be attached to it, like other definites. Writing it with a waw does not indicate their pronunciation. End of quote.

Al-Shihab replied and argued: Although the known view regarding "ghudwa" is that it is a generic proper noun (ism jins 'alam), prohibited from taking tanwin, not taking the definite article, and not admitting a construct, so one does not say "ghudwat yawm al-Khamis" as al-Farra' said, yet it has also been heard as a common noun (ism jins), indefinite and taking tanwin, so the definite article can be attached to it. Sibawayh transmitted this in his book from al-Khalil, and a great many of the people of language and grammar mentioned it. So there is no weight to the saying of Abu 'Ubayd that whoever recited with the waw erred, and that he followed the written form, because "al-ghada" is written with a waw like "al-salat" and "al-zakat," and it is a generic proper noun not admitting the definite article, and the one who errs is in error for what has passed. Al-Mubarrad mentioned from the Arabs its indefiniteness, its taking tanwin, and the attachment of the definite article to it when it does not mean a specific morning. Whoever has memorized is a proof against whoever has not memorized, and its occurrence in the widely transmitted recitation is sufficient proof. So there is no need for what was said: that it is a proper noun but was made indefinite, because making a generic proper noun indefinite is not known. Nor that it is definite and the definite article was attached to it for the sake of matching "al-'ashiyy" (the evening), as in his saying: "I saw al-Walid ibn al-Yazid blessed," where "al-Yazid" was used because of the proximity of "al-Walid." From this you learn that matching (mushakala) may be literal. End of quote.

9. In the Qamus: "al-ghudwa" with a damma is "al-bukra" (early morning), or what lies between the dawn prayer and sunrise, like "al-ghada." "Al-'ashiyy" and "al-'ashiyya" are the end of the day.

In al-Sihah: from the maghrib prayer until 'atama (the night prayer).

Al-Azhari said: "al-'ashiyy" applies to the period between the decline of the sun and sunset.

10. Al-Zamakhshari made "dhalika" (that) a reference to this trial mentioned, where he said: "And like that [great trial], We tried some people by means of others," that is, We tested them through them. He expressed it with "that" to signal its magnification, like your saying: "I struck Zayd that blow." It does not necessarily imply comparing a thing with itself, because the likeness is not intended; it is only brought in for emphasis, as one says "that is like that." So said the 'Allama (al-Taftazani) in clarifying this. He means: just as the comparison is made a metaphor for continuity, because what has similars has its kind continuing by the renewal of its similars, as the commentators of the Hamasa indicated in the verse:

"Thus does time pass, and knowledge perishes in it, and traces are effaced."

Continuity requires certainty and establishment and entails it, so in such cases, through the use of the demonstrative for the distant, it is made an expression for the certainty of a great matter. Its being great is derived from the word "that" pointing to this nearby trial mentioned, and the kaf in it is not superfluous. Whoever said it is inserted meant that comparison is not intended in it, but rather its implied meaning, either metonymic or metaphorical, is meant. Al-Zamakhshari, because of the eloquence and precision of this view, chose it in the places where "thus" occurs. So said [al-Taftazani] in "al-'Inaya."

Abu al-Su'ud said: "that" is a reference to the verbal noun of what follows it of the verb, and its original position is in the accusative as an adjective to an omitted emphatic verbal noun. The sense is: "We tried some of them by means of others with a trial like that trial," and the kaf is inserted to emphasize what the demonstrative conveys of grandeur, so it becomes the emphatic verbal noun itself, not an adjective to it. The meaning: "We tried with that complete trial."

Al-Shihab said: This insertion for emphasis is common in the usage of both Arabs and non-Arabs. End of quote.

It is also said: the kaf is not superfluous (za'ida), and the thing indicated is the thing compared to (al-mushabbah bihi), the matter fixed in the mind, while the thing compared (al-mushabbah) is what the speech indicates of the external matter. The emphasis (al-mubalagha) is produced only by the mental vagueness (al-ibhām al-dhihni) and by the explanation in His saying ﴿So We tested some of them with others﴾, and this is what everyone knows of the trials, who they are. See "al-Inaya".

(p-2334) Commentary on His, the Exalted, saying:

[54] ﴿And when those who believe in Our signs come to you, say: "Peace be upon you. Your Lord has prescribed for Himself mercy, that whoever of you does evil in ignorance and then repents after it and makes amends, indeed He is Forgiving and Merciful."﴾

His, the Exalted, saying: ﴿And when those who believe in Our signs come to you, say: "Peace be upon you. Your Lord has prescribed for Himself mercy, that whoever of you does evil in ignorance and then repents after it and makes amends, indeed He is Forgiving and Merciful."﴾ A group of the exegetes (mufassirun, those who explain the Qur'an) held that these are the ones whom the polytheists asked to be driven away and distanced, so Allah honoured them with this honour.

Al-Baydawi said: He, the Exalted, described them with belief in the Qur'an and following the proofs, after describing them with persistence in worship, and commanded him to begin them with greeting, or to convey the greeting of Allah, the Exalted, to them, and to give them the good news of the breadth of Allah's mercy and bounty, after the prohibition against driving them away. This is an announcement that they combine the two virtues of knowledge and action, and whoever is like this should be brought near and not driven away, honoured and not humiliated, and given good news from Allah of safety in this world and mercy in the Hereafter. End.

It has passed from Ibn Jarir that it was revealed concerning ʿUmar, may Allah be pleased with him. Al-Firyabi and Ibn Abi Hatim related from Maham, who said: "People came to the Prophet ﷺ and said: 'We have committed great sins,' and he did not answer them with anything, so Allah revealed: 'And when those come to you...' the verse." It is not hidden that the verse encompasses all of that, and perhaps several events share one ruling, so the verse descends as an explanation of all of them. It has been mentioned to us in the introduction of this tafsir, in the discussion of the occasion of revelation (asbab al-nuzul), that the statement of the early scholars, "It was revealed concerning such-and-such," may mean that the event falls under the wording of the verse, since it was revealed after it. So recall this and dwell on its aspects, for it is very important. With knowledge of it the objection of al-Razi, which he established here, is dispelled.

(p-2335) His, the Exalted, saying: ﴿prescribed for Himself mercy﴾ means: made it obligatory, that is, made it obligatory upon His holy Essence, out of His grace, kindness and bounty.

His saying: ﴿that whoever of you does evil...﴾ etc. is a substitution (badal) for ﴿mercy﴾. It has also been read with a kasra on the hamza (إنَّهُ), on the basis that it is an explanation of the mercy by way of a resumed sentence (isti'naf).

His saying: ﴿بِجَهالَةٍ﴾ (bi-jahalah, "in ignorance") is in the position of a circumstantial clause (hal), meaning: he did it while being ignorant. In it there are two meanings:

The first: that he is the doer of the act of the ignorant, because whoever does what leads to harm in its outcome, while knowing that or supposing it, is among the people of foolishness and ignorance, not of wisdom and good judgement. From this is the poet's saying:

"Because she said, on the evening I visited her: 'You acted ignorantly on purpose, and you were not ignorant.'"

The second: that he is ignorant of what is connected to it of harm and injury, and it is the right of the wise not to proceed with anything until he knows its state and manner. Thus in the "Kashshaf" (of al-Zamakhshari).

(p-2336) On the first meaning, jahl (ignorance) means foolishness and recklessness without looking at the consequences, as in the saying:

"So we act ignorantly beyond the ignorance of the ignorant."

The Arabs used to praise themselves with it, so there is no need to supply an object.

On the second meaning, what is intended is ignorance of the harms of what he does.

His, the Exalted, saying: ﴿وأصْلَحَ﴾ (and made amends), that is: the deed, as in His saying: ﴿and does righteous deeds﴾. Imam Ahmad and the two Shaykhs (al-Bukhari and Muslim) related from Abu Hurayrah, who said: The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "When Allah decreed the creation, He wrote in His Book, which is with Him above the Throne: 'Indeed My mercy has overcome My wrath.'"

Note:

Some exegetes related from al-Hakim that he said: The verse indicates the obligation of honouring the believers, (p-2337) and it indicates that it is fitting to bring joy to the believer, because he was commanded to say to them: "He has prescribed for Himself mercy," so that their hearts may be comforted. End.

The discussion on the interpretation of His saying, exalted is He:

[55] ﴿And thus We detail the verses, that the way of the criminals may become clear﴾

﴿And thus We detail the verses﴾, meaning the verses of the Qur'an, describing the obedient and the criminals. The discussion of "thus" (*kadhalika*) has already passed shortly before. ﴿That the way of the criminals may become clear﴾ is read with the verb feminine, *litastabina* (تَسْتَبِينَ), based on the feminine gender of the subject. It was also read in the masculine, *litastabin* (يَسْتَبِينَ), based on the masculine gender of its subject, since *al-sabil* (السَّبِيلَ, "the way") can be either masculine or feminine. This is a coordination with a cause that has been omitted from the stated verb. The causal purpose is not intended to be specifically this one. Rather, the intention is to indicate that it has many benefits, of which the one mentioned is one. Alternatively, it is a cause of an implied verb that refers to what was mentioned, so it is a new (independent) clause, meaning: "And so that their way may become clear, We do what We do of differentiation." It was also read with *al-sabil* in the accusative (السَّبِيلَ), on the basis that the verb is transitive (*muta'addi*), and its *ta'* is for address. That is: "And so that you, O Muhammad (ﷺ), may clarify the way of the criminals, so that you deal with them in what suits them." This was conveyed by Abu al-Su'ud.

Commentary on the interpretation of His words, may He be exalted:

[56] ﴿Say: Indeed, I have been forbidden to worship those whom you invoke besides Allah.﴾ ﴿Say: I will not follow your desires; if I did, I would have strayed, and I would not be among the guided.﴾

﴿Say: Indeed, I have been forbidden to worship those whom you invoke besides Allah.﴾ That is: whom you worship, or whom you name as gods. Then He repeated the command, emphasizing it in order to cut off their hopes, with His words, may He be exalted: ﴿Say: I will not follow your desires﴾, that is, in worshipping the idols and in driving away those who were mentioned.

Then al-Baydawi (d. 685 AH) said: This is a pointing to the cause that necessitates the prohibition, the reason for refraining from following them, a rebuke of their ignorance, a clarification of the source of their error, and that what they are upon is caprice, not guidance. It is also an admonition to whoever seeks the truth, that he should follow the proof and not merely imitate. End of quotation.

(p-2338) ﴿Indeed, I would then have strayed, if I followed your desires, since it would oppose both the divine command and reason together﴾ ﴿and I would not be among the guided﴾, that is, to the truth, if I followed what has been mentioned. And in this there is an implicit allusion that they are likewise.

The Interpretation of His Words, Exalted is He:

[57] ﴿Say: Indeed, I am upon clear evidence from my Lord, and you have denied it. I do not have what you are hastening. The decision is only for Allah. He relates the truth, and He is the best of the deciders.﴾

﴿Say: Indeed, I am upon clear evidence from my Lord﴾ That is: upon insight into the law of Allah which He revealed to me, which cannot be subject to doubt. ﴿And you have denied it﴾ is either a resumed statement or a circumstantial clause, and the pronoun refers to the clear evidence. The masculine form is used in consideration of the intended meaning, namely the revelation, or the Qur'an, or the like. ﴿I do not have what you are hastening﴾ That is: of the punishment.

Abu al-Su'ud said: It is a resumed statement clarifying their error concerning the matter they made the basis for their denial of the clear evidence, which is the non-arrival of the punishment promised in it, which they were hastening by their saying: "When is this promise, if you are truthful?" mockingly, or by way of challenge, according to their claim. That is: what you are hastening of the punishment promised in the Qur'an is not in my authority and power, so that I could bring it and show you its truth; and you make its delay a pretext for denying it. Or its matter is not entrusted to me.

﴿The decision is only for Allah﴾ That is: were it in my hands, I would be the one who decides; but the decision regarding its hastening and delaying belongs only to Allah, and He has decided its delay for the great wisdom He has in it. Yet it is certain to occur, because He: ﴿relates the truth﴾ That is: He makes it clear with a complete clarification. ﴿And He is the best of the deciders﴾ That is: the best judge among His servants.

(p-2339) A subtle point:

It has been read as "yaqḍi al-ḥaqq" (ﯾَقْضِ الحَقَّ) with the ḍād, and "al-ḥaqq" is in the accusative as a verbal noun (maṣdar), since it is an adjective of a deleted verbal noun that took its place; or as an object, by including in "yaqḍī" the sense of "yunfidh" (carries out); or it is transitive from "qaḍā al-dir'a" (he made the coat of mail) when he made it. Al-Hudhali said:

Upon them are two woven coats of mail, which Dawud made, or which the makers of the ample coats (the Tubba') made.

(p-2340) Al-Razi said: Abu 'Amr argued for this reading with His words: "and He is the best of the deciders," saying: "Distinguishing (fasl) occurs in judgment, not in narration (qaṣaṣ)." Abu 'Ali al-Farisi answered, saying: "Qaṣaṣ here means speech, and distinguishing has come in speech. He, Exalted is He, said: ﴿Indeed, it is a decisive word﴾ [al-Tariq: 13], and He said: ﴿Its verses were perfected, then detailed﴾ [Hud: 1], and He said: "We detail the verses." End of quote.

Al-Shihab said: The meaning of "yaqussuhu" is: He makes it clear with a complete clarification, and that is the very same as judgment.

The Interpretation of His Words, the Exalted:

[58] ﴿Say: If I had what you are hastening for, the matter would have been decided between me and you. And Allah knows best the wrongdoers.﴾

﴿Say: If I had what you are hastening for, the matter would have been decided between me and you. And Allah knows best the wrongdoers.﴾ That is: if the punishment you are hastening for were within my power and capacity, by its being entrusted to me from Him, Exalted is He, the matter would have been decided between me and you, by that descending upon you right after your hastening.

In al-'Inayah it is said: "qudiya al-amr" means "it was cut off" (i.e., settled), and its "decreeing" is a metonymy for their destruction.

Abu al-Su'ud said: In the passive construction of the verb there is an indication (of the importance) of specifying the agent, who is Allah, the Exalted, and of magnifying the matter, and of observing good manners, which is not hidden. Therefore, what has been said in its interpretation, "It would have destroyed you swiftly, out of zeal for my Lord and as retribution for your denial of Him, and I would have been quickly rid of you," is far from doing justice to the context.

His words, the Exalted, "And Allah knows best the wrongdoers," are a parenthetical clause confirming what the conditional sentence conveys, namely the negation that the matter of the punishment was entrusted to him, peace and blessings be upon him, which entails the negation of the decreeing of the matter, and it is also a causal explanation for it. The meaning: Allah, the Exalted, knows best the state of the wrongdoers, and that they deserve to be given respite by way of gradual enticement, in order to intensify the punishment; for this reason He did not entrust the matter to me, so He did not decree the matter by hastening the punishment. End.

Note:

Ibn Kathir said: If it is asked: what is the reconciliation between this verse and what is established in the two Sahihs from 'A'ishah, that she said to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, "O Messenger of Allah, has there come upon you a day harder than the day of Uhud?" He said: "I met with much from your people, and the hardest I met from them was on the day of al-'Aqabah, when I presented myself to Ibn 'Abd Yalil ibn 'Abd Kalal, and he did not respond to what I wanted. So I departed, deeply distressed, on my face, and I did not come to myself except at Qarn al-Tha'alib. I raised my head, and behold, a cloud had shaded me. I looked, and in it was Jibril, who called out to me and said: 'Allah, Mighty and Majestic, has heard the words of your people to you and what they replied to you, and He has sent to you the angel of the mountains, so that you may command him with whatever you wish concerning them.' He said: 'The angel of the mountains called out to me, greeted me, and said: "O Muhammad! Allah has heard the words of your people to you, and I am the angel of the mountains. Your Lord has sent me to you so that you may command me with your command. What do you wish? If you wish, I will close the two mountains upon them!"' The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said to him: 'Rather, I hope that Allah will bring forth from their loins those who worship Allah alone and associate nothing with Him.'"

(This is the wording of Muslim.) "He had presented to him their punishment and their annihilation, and he deferred them and asked for them to be given delay, hoping that Allah would bring forth from their loins those who do not associate anything with Him."

The answer, and Allah knows best, is that this verse indicates that if the punishment they seek had been in his hands at the time of their seeking it, he would have inflicted it upon them. As for the hadith, there is nothing in it that they asked him to bring the punishment upon them; rather, the angel of the mountains offered him that, if he wished, he could close the two mountains upon them, which are the two mountains of Makkah flanking it from the south and the north. For this reason he deferred them and asked for leniency for them. End.

**Al-Qasimi's commentary (Mahasin al-Ta'wil) on Surah 6, verse 59:**

Then God, exalted is He, made clear the exclusivity of the unseen matters that are decreed to Him in respect of knowledge, following His explanation that all of them belong exclusively to Him in respect of power, with His saying:

**The discussion on the interpretation of His, exalted is He, saying:**

[59] ﴿With Him are the keys of the unseen. None knows them but Him. He knows what is on the land and in the sea. Not a leaf falls but He knows it, nor a grain in the darknesses of the earth, nor anything fresh or dry, but it is in a clear Book.﴾

﴿With Him are the keys of the unseen﴾: *mafatih* is the plural of *miftah* (with a kasra on the mim), meaning "key." It is also read *mafatih* (with a ya). The unseen matters are likened to great affairs that are secured with locks, and keys are ascribed to them by way of imaginative representation (*takhyil*).

His saying, exalted is He, ﴿None knows them but Him﴾, is an emphasis of what precedes it, and an indication that the intended meaning is exclusivity in respect of knowledge. The meaning is: the punishment you seek to hasten is not within my power, so that I could compel you to bring it about, nor is it known to me so that I could inform you of the time of its descent. Rather, it is among the matters that belong exclusively to Him in power and knowledge, so He sends it down as His will dictates, a will founded upon wisdoms and benefits. This is what Abu al-Su'ud conveyed.

Then, after He made clear His knowledge of the unseen, He drew attention to the observable matters, with their varied kinds and their many individuals, with His saying: ﴿He knows what is on the land and in the sea﴾, of creatures and wonders. Then He went to great lengths to describe the comprehensiveness of His knowledge of the particular details, which are beyond counting, with His, glorified is He, saying: ﴿Not a leaf falls but He knows it, nor a grain in the darknesses of the earth, nor anything fresh or dry, but it is in a clear Book﴾, that is: written down and preserved in the Divine knowledge.

**Notes:**

**The first:** Al-Hakim said: His saying, exalted is He, ﴿With Him are the keys of the unseen﴾ indicates the falsity of the claim of the Imamiyya (the Twelver Shi'a) that the Imam knows some of the unseen. End of quotation.

In *Fath al-Bayan* (by Siddiq Hasan Khan): In this noble verse there is that which refutes the falsehoods of soothsayers (*kuhhan*), astrologers, geomancers and others among those who claim unveiling and inspiration, of matters that are not within their capacity, nor fall under their power, nor does their knowledge encompass them. Islam and its people have been afflicted by wicked folk of these misguided kinds and forsaken types, and they have profited from their lies and falsehoods only through the evil bargain mentioned in the saying of the truthful and the believed (ﷺ): "Whoever goes to a soothsayer or an astrologer has disbelieved in what was sent down to Muhammad."

Ibn Mas'ud said: Your Prophet was given everything except the keys of the unseen.

Ibn 'Abbas said: They are the decrees and the provisions.

Al-Dahhak said: They are the treasuries of the earth and the knowledge of the descent of punishment.

'Ata' said: They are what is hidden from you of reward and punishment.

It has also been said: They are the ends of the terms of life, and the knowledge of the states of the servants, of happiness and wretchedness, and the endings of their deeds. But the word is broader than that. From Ibn 'Umar, that the Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: "The keys of the unseen are five, none knows them but God, exalted is He. No one knows what will happen tomorrow except God. No one knows what is in the wombs except God. No soul knows what it will earn tomorrow. No soul knows in what land it will die. No one knows when the rain will come." Related by al-Bukhari, who has other wordings. In one narration: "And no one knows when the Hour will come except God." End of quotation.

**The second:** It has been read (*wa la habbatun wa la rattbun wa la yabisun*) with the nominative (*raf'*). In this there are two possibilities: that it is a conjunction (*'atf*) upon the position (*mahall*) of "min waraqatin" (of a leaf), or that it is in the nominative as the subject (*mubtada'*), whose predicate is "illa fi kitabin mubin" (but it is in a clear Book), like your saying: "There is no man among them and no woman but in the house." Thus in *al-Kashshaf*.

**The third:** What we have already stated regarding "the clear Book" is that it is the Preserved Tablet (*al-Lawh al-Mahfuz*), which is the one that comes to mind from its unqualified usage wherever it occurs. It has been said: the clear Book is the knowledge of God, exalted is He. The first is more apparent.

Al-Zajjaj said: It is possible that God, may His praise be glorified, recorded the modes of the known things in a Book before He created creation, as He, mighty and majestic is He, said: ﴿No affliction befalls on the earth or in yourselves but it is in a Book before We bring it into being﴾ [al-Hadid: 22]. The benefits of this Book are several:

**One:** God, exalted is He, only recorded these states in the Preserved Tablet so that the angels might witness the penetration of God's knowledge into the known things, and that nothing of what is in the heavens and the earth is hidden from Him. This would be a complete and perfect lesson for the angels entrusted with the Preserved Tablet, because they compare with it what happens on the page of this world, and find it in agreement with it.

**Second:** It may be said that He, exalted is He, mentioned what He mentioned, of the leaf and the grain, as an alert to the responsible beings regarding the matter of reckoning, and as an information that nothing of all that they do in this world escapes Him. For if He does not neglect the states in which there is neither reward nor punishment nor obligation, then how much more so will He not neglect the states that involve reward and punishment.

**Third:** God, exalted is He, knows the states of all existing things, so their alteration contrary to the requirement of that knowledge is impossible, otherwise ignorance would follow. Thus, when He wrote the states of all existing things in that Book in complete detail, their alteration was likewise impossible, otherwise falsehood would follow. So the recording of the totality of states in that Book becomes a complete determinant and a perfect cause for the impossibility of what is late coming early or what is early coming late, as he, may God's blessings be upon him, said: "The pen has dried with what is to be until the Day of Resurrection." End of quotation.

**The fourth:** Ibn Abi Hatim related from Ibn 'Abbas, regarding His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Not a leaf falls but He knows it﴾, that he said: There is no tree on land or sea but that there is an angel entrusted with it, who records what falls from it.

He also related from 'Abd Allah ibn al-Harith, who said: There is no tree on the earth, nor even the size of a needle's eye, but that over it is an entrusted angel who brings God the knowledge of it: its dryness when it dries and its moisture when it is moist. Likewise Ibn Jarir related it.

Ibn Abi Hatim related from Sa'id ibn Jubayr, from Ibn 'Abbas, who said: God created the *nun*, which is the inkwell, and He created the tablets, and He wrote in them the affairs of the world until it ends: whatever is created of created things, or provision, lawful or unlawful, or deed of righteousness or wickedness. And he recited this verse: ﴿Not a leaf falls﴾ to the end of the verse.

The Interpretation of His Words, Exalted is He:

[60] ﴿It is He who takes you back to Himself at night, and knows what you have committed by day. Then He raises you up therein, that a specified term may be fulfilled. Then to Him is your return. Then He will inform you of what you used to do.﴾

﴿It is He who takes you back to Himself at night﴾, that is: He puts you to sleep therein. The term (tawaffi, "taking back" or "causing to die") is used metaphorically for sleep, because of what the two share in the cessation of awareness and discernment, for its basic meaning is the seizing of a thing in its entirety.

﴿And knows what you have committed by day﴾, that is: in it (the day). The specification of night for sleep and day for earning is in accordance with what is customary. ﴿Then He raises you up﴾, that is: He awakens you. The term "raising up" (ba'th) is used without qualification as a complement to "taking back" (tawaffi). ﴿Therein﴾, that is: in the day. ﴿That a specified term may be fulfilled﴾, that is: that the measure of each person's life may be completed.

﴿Then to Him is your return﴾, that is: your return by resurrection after death. ﴿Then He will inform you of what you used to do﴾, that is: in your nights and your days, by recompensing you for it, emphasizing His justice.

Two admonitions:

The first: The apparent address of the verse is general. In al-Kashshaf it is restricted to the disbelievers, on the view that His words "and knows what you have committed by day, then He raises you up" indicate a severe threat that befits only the obstinate deniers, and that the intended meaning is to describe their blameworthy condition at night, just as His words "what you have committed" describe their blameworthy condition by day. The "raising up" is not to be understood as awakening, but as resurrection from the graves. "Therein" is in the sense of "on account of it," like your saying: "For what did you call me?" and he says: "For such-and-such a matter." The meaning is: you lie like carcasses at night, earning sins by day; and He is aware of your deeds, and will raise you from the graves concerning that for which you have cut short your lives, namely sleep at night and the earning of sins by day, so that He may fulfil the appointed term that He set for the resurrection of the dead and their recompense for their deeds. What led him to this is his claim that His words "and knows what you have committed by day" indicate the state of wakefulness and their earning in it, and that the word "then" (thumma) requires the resurrection to be delayed beyond it.

The commentators say: The strain in this is not hidden, and there is no need for it, because His words "and knows what you have committed by day" refer to what was earned during the day preceding that night, and there is no indication in it of awakening from this taking back, and awakening is later than the taking back. Our statement, "He does that taking back so that the appointed span of life may be fulfilled," is an arrangement entirely orderly.

The second: Al-Sharif al-Murtada said in al-Durar wa'l-Ghurar, concerning what occurs in the Qur'an of mention of the return to God, such as "And to God are all matters returned" (2:210 / 57:5 type phrasing): how is it said that they return to Him, when they never left His hand? He answered: In the abode of obligation, some may be heedless, and attribute some of His acts, exalted is He, to others. When the veil is lifted, the ropes of hope in other than Him are cut, and so they return to Him. Or the meaning is that the matters are in His hand without any actual departure and return. So "returned" (raja'a) is in the sense of "became" (sara). The Arabs say: "A calamity returned upon me from so-and-so," meaning it became, and there had been no prior departure. So it is in the sense of arriving at it, as the language attests. Or: in the abode of this world, what belongs to the servants is apparent, like a slave to his master; when the matter reaches the Hereafter, that ceases, and the whole affair returns to God, outwardly and inwardly.

(p-2349) The discussion of the interpretation of His words, may He be exalted:

[61] ﴿And He is the Subjugator over His servants, and He sends over you guardians, until when death comes to one of you, Our messengers take him, and they do not fail [in their duty].﴾

﴿And He is the Subjugator over His servants﴾ Its explanation has already passed: that He is the one who disposes of their affairs, none other than Him, doing with them as He wills. ﴿And He sends over you guardians﴾ That is: angels who guard your deeds and record them, and they are the noble scribes, as in His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And indeed, over you are guardians﴾ [al-Infitar: 10], and His saying: ﴿When the two receivers receive [him]﴾ [Qaf: 17], and so on.

A subtle point:

The wisdom in this is that the accountable person, when he knows that his deeds are recorded against him and displayed before the heads of the witnesses, will be more restrained from sins. And that the servant, when he trusts in the kindness of his master and relies on his pardon and concealment, does not feel as much shame before Him as he feels before his servants who witness him. Related by al-Qadi.

﴿Until when death comes to one of you﴾ That is: its causes and beginnings. ﴿Our messengers take him﴾ That is: angels appointed for this task. ﴿And they do not fail﴾ That is: through negligence or delay. Ibn Kathir said: That is, in preserving the soul of the deceased; rather, they preserve it and leave it wherever Allah, Mighty and Majestic, wills. If he was of the righteous, it is in 'Illiyyin; and if he was of the wicked, it is in Sijjin.

(p-٢٣٥٠)The discussion on the interpretation of His saying, Exalted is He:

[62] ﴿Then they are returned to Allah, their true Master. Unquestionably, judgment belongs to Him, and He is the swiftest of reckoners.﴾

﴿Then they are returned to Allah, their true Master﴾: that is, the One who manages their affairs. And *al-Haqq* (the True): the Just, who judges only with truth. Ibn Kathir said: the pronoun refers to the angels, or to the creatures indicated by *aḥad* (one of you). The singular comes first and the plural last, because the taking of souls happens individually while the return happens collectively. That is: they are returned after the resurrection, and He judges among them with His justice, as He said: ﴿Say: Indeed, the former and the latter﴾ [al-Waqi'ah: 49] ﴿will surely be gathered to the appointed time of a known day﴾ [al-Waqi'ah: 50]. And He said: ﴿And We gathered them, and We left none of them behind﴾ [al-Kahf: 47], up to His saying: ﴿And your Lord does not wrong anyone﴾ [al-Kahf: 49]. For this reason He said: ﴿their true Master﴾.

﴿Unquestionably, judgment belongs to Him﴾ on that Day, when no one else has any judgment. ﴿And He is the swiftest of reckoners﴾: He reckons the creatures in the swiftest time.

Benefits:

The first: Ibn Kathir said: We mention here the hadith which Imam Ahmad narrated from Sa'id ibn Yasar, from Abu Hurayrah, may Allah be pleased with him, from the Prophet (ﷺ), that he said: "Indeed, the dead person is attended by the angels. (p-٢٣٥١) If he is a righteous man, they say: 'Come forth, O good soul, that was in the good body. Come forth praiseworthy, and rejoice in rest, sweet fragrance, and a Lord who is not angry.' This continues to be said until it departs. Then it is ascended to the heaven, and its opening is requested for it, and it is asked: 'Who is this?' It is said: 'So-and-so.' They say: 'Welcome to the good soul that was in the good body. Enter praiseworthy, and rejoice in rest, sweet fragrance, and a Lord who is not angry.' This continues to be said to it until it is brought to the heaven in which Allah, Mighty and Majestic, is. And if he is an evil man, they say: 'Come forth, O wicked soul, that was in the wicked body. Come forth blameworthy, and rejoice in boiling water, and dark, cold liquid, and other punishments of their kind.' This continues until it departs. Then it is ascended to the heaven, and its opening is requested, and it is asked: 'Who is this?' It is said: 'So-and-so!' It is said: 'No welcome to the wicked soul that was in the wicked body. Return blameworthy, for the gates of heaven will not be opened for you.' So it is sent down from the heaven, then it goes to the grave. The righteous man sits up, and he is told what was said in the first hadith, and the evil man sits up, and he is told what was said in the first hadith."" Al-Hafiz Ibn Kathir said: This is a gharib (rare) hadith.

The second: Some of the people of kalam (theological discourse) said: For each of these senses there is a spirit which is taken at sleep and then returned to it when sleep departs. As for the spirit by which the soul lives, it is not taken except at the end of the term. What is meant by the spirits are the meanings and faculties which subsist in the senses, and by which hearing, sight, grasping, walking and smelling occur. The meaning of "then He raises you up in it" is: He awakens you and returns to you the spirits of the senses. Thus it is taken as evidence against those who deny resurrection, for by sleep the spirits of these senses depart, then He returns them to them. Likewise He gives life to souls after their death. Narrated by al-Nasafi.

The third: Al-Khazin said: If you say: Allah said in one verse: ﴿Allah takes the souls at the time of their death﴾ [az-Zumar: 42], (p-٢٣٥٢) and He said in another verse: ﴿Say: The angel of death who has been entrusted with you will take you﴾ [as-Sajdah: 11], and He said here: ﴿Our messengers take him﴾ [al-An'am: 61]. How are these verses reconciled?

I say: The way of reconciliation is that the one who truly takes (the soul) is Allah, Exalted is He. When the term of the servant arrives, Allah commands the angel of death to seize his spirit, and the angel of death has assistants among the angels, whom he commands to draw the spirit of that servant from his body. When it reaches the throat, the angel of death himself takes hold of it, and thus the reconciliation is achieved.
