Mujahid said: The earth was made for the angel of death like a basin; he takes from wherever he wills, and he was given assistants who draw out the souls, then he takes them from them. End of quotation.

Then Allah, Exalted is He, commanded that the polytheists be silenced regarding the failure of their partners to do what they claimed for them, by saying that they single out the Truth, Exalted is He, for turning to Him in times of hardship, in His saying:

The discussion on the interpretation of His saying, exalted is He:

[63] ﴿Say, "Who delivers you from the darknesses of the land and the sea, calling upon Him humbly and secretly, [saying], 'If He should deliver us from this, we will surely be among the grateful.'"﴾

﴿Say, "Who delivers you from the darknesses of the land"﴾ i.e., its hardships, such as the fear of an enemy and losing the way. ﴿And the sea﴾, such as the fear of drowning, losing the way, and the stilling of the wind. Darkness is used metaphorically for hardship, because they share in terror, the blinding of sight, and the bewilderment of minds. It is said of a severe day, "a dark day" and "a day full of stars," meaning its darkness intensified until it became like night, and the stars appeared in it.

﴿Calling upon Him humbly﴾ i.e., submissively toward Him, realizing servitude. ﴿And secretly﴾ with the kha' vowelled with a damma (خُفْيَةً), and it has been read with a kasra (خِفْيَةً). I.e., privately, realizing sincerity (ikhlas, sincere devotion). ﴿If He should deliver us﴾ is a circumstantial clause (ḥāl, حالٌ) from the subject, with the verb "saying" implied: i.e., saying, pledging thankfulness, "If You deliver us..." ﴿from this﴾ i.e., the hardship expressed by "darknesses." ﴿We will surely be among the grateful﴾ i.e., to You, believing that You are the One specially deserving of fine praise.

The Interpretation of His Words, Exalted is He:

[64] ﴿Say: "It is Allah who delivers you from them and from every distress; yet you still associate partners with Him."﴾

Then Allah, Exalted is He, commanded him to give this answer, to draw attention to its being evident and certain to them, or as a humiliation of them, since they do not heed His address. His words ﴿Say: "It is Allah who delivers you from them and from every distress"﴾ mean: without the intercession of anyone or any helper. ﴿Yet you still associate partners with Him﴾ means: even after you witness the deliverance from them, which was promised, with a firm oath, to be met with gratitude, you associate partners with Him in worship and in praise, [ascribing to] others [what belongs to Him alone]. You attribute the deliverance that came after you singled Him out in supplication to the intercession of an associate; thus you have put shirk in the place of gratitude.

Points of Caution:

First: What we have already mentioned, that the "darknesses of the land and the sea" are a metaphor for their fears and terrors, is what the verifying scholars have said.

Al-Razi said: Some of them took it literally, saying: As for the darknesses of the sea, they are the gathering of the darkness of the night, the darkness of the sea, and the darkness of the clouds, to which are added the fierce winds and the towering waves, so that they do not know how to be saved and the fear grows great. As for the darknesses of the land, they are the darkness of the night and the darkness of the clouds, together with the intense fear of the attack of enemies and the intense fear of not finding the way of right guidance. The point is that when these causes that necessitate intense fear come together, a person returns only to Allah, Exalted is He. This return happens outwardly and inwardly, because in this state a person's sincerity in the presence of Allah, Exalted is He, becomes great, and his hope is severed from everything other than Allah, Exalted is He. This is what is meant by His words: ﴿humbly and secretly﴾. Thus Allah, Exalted is He, makes clear that when sound natural disposition and original creation witness, in this state, that there is no refuge but Allah and no reliance except on the bounty of Allah, this sincerity ought to remain in all states and times. But it is not so: after a person attains safety and deliverance, he attributes that safety to causes and falls into shirk. Among the exegetes are some who say: the purpose of this verse is to criticize the divinity of idols and images.

Then al-Razi, may Allah have mercy on him, said, and I say: attachment to anything other than Allah in the way of worship comes close to being attachment to an idol; for this reason the people of verification call it hidden shirk. End.

Second: Some exegetes said: His words, Exalted is He, ﴿calling upon Him humbly and secretly﴾ indicate that supplication in secret is more excellent. It was said: The Prophet ﷺ used to supplicate aloud only to teach others. End.

This is based on the view that His words "humbly" mean "in submission," not "aloud." Many exegetes held that the meaning is both aloud and in secret, and this is probably the correct view, for direct observation supports it: one who is severely afflicted, whose way to deliverance has been darkened, cannot restrain himself to supplicating in secret alone. And Allah knows best.

In al-Qamus and its commentary: "Tadarra'a ila Allah" means: entreat and humble yourself to Allah, Exalted is He. It was said: show ḍaraʿa, which is the intensity of poverty and need before Allah, Exalted is He. From this is His words, Exalted is He, ﴿humbly and secretly﴾, meaning: manifesting ḍaraʿa and the reality of humility. End.

Third: The meaning of "distress" (karb) encompasses what preceded, and there is no objection to generalizing after specifying, given how frequently this occurs. Or it means the psychological afflictions that befall a person, which are countless, such as illnesses and sicknesses, and what has been said, that the first refers to a specific distress, or that the first is a blessing of removal and this is a blessing of prevention, and that it is of the type of (wearing a sword and a spear) [a figure of speech], is far-fetched with no need for it. Thus [states] the "al-Ināya."

Fourth: The verb "you associate partners" (tushrikun) was placed in the position of "you do not associate partners" (la tushrikun), which is what the apparent sense would call for, to fit His words ﴿we will surely be among the grateful﴾ [al-An'am: 63]. This is because their association implies that their worship and their thankfulness are invalid, since thankfulness is itself worship; rather, it negates them, because they are not counted in His presence, for tawhid is the foundation of the matter and the basis of worship. So He placed it in that position as a rebuke for them, for failing to keep the covenant. He did not mention its object, to treat it as intransitive, drawing attention to how improbable shirk itself is. Thus [states] the "al-Ināya."

**On the interpretation of His words, may He be exalted:**

[65] ﴿Say: "He is the One able to send upon you a punishment from above you or from beneath your feet, or to confuse you into factions and make you taste the violence of one another." Observe how We vary the signs, that they may understand.﴾

﴿Say: "He is the One able to send upon you a punishment from above you﴾ Al-Mahayimi said: That is, say to the polytheists, after the deliverance promised in it for gratitude: You associated partners with Him only because you feel safe from hardships, but there is no ground for feeling safe from them, since the source of fear remains, namely the divine power over all kinds of hardship from every direction. For He is able to send a punishment greater than that hardship from above you, such as a rain of fire or stones, or the falling of the sky.

﴿or from beneath your feet﴾ such as being swallowed by the earth or a flood. ﴿or to confuse you into factions﴾ that is, to mix you into groups in a confusion of disorder, so that you become divided and at odds in fighting, by strengthening your enemies. ﴿and make you taste the violence﴾ that is, the severity ﴿of one another﴾ meaning: He sets some of you upon others to kill and torment them.

(p-2356) ﴿Observe how We vary the signs﴾ that is, We turn them from one kind to another. ﴿that they may understand﴾ that is, that they may comprehend and take warning, and so cease their disbelief and obstinacy.

**Two notes:**

**The first:** Al-Bukhari related from Jabir, may Allah be pleased with him, who said: "When this verse was revealed, ﴿Say: 'He is the One able to send upon you a punishment from above you﴾, the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: 'I seek refuge in Your Face!' ﴿or from beneath your feet﴾, he said: 'I seek refuge in Your Face!' ﴿or to confuse you into factions and make you taste the violence of one another﴾, he said: 'This is easier,' or 'lighter.'"

The hafiz Ibn Hajar said: Ibn Mardawayh has related, from the hadith of Ibn Abbas, something that explains the hadith of Jabir. Its wording is: from the Prophet (ﷺ), who said: "I asked Allah to lift from my community four things. He lifted two of them and refused to lift two. I asked Allah to lift from them the stoning from the sky and the swallowing from the earth, and that He not confuse them into factions or make some of them taste the violence of others. Allah lifted the swallowing and the stoning, and refused to lift the other two." From this narration, by His words ﴿from above you or from beneath your feet﴾, the meaning is drawn, and it is supported by His words, may He be exalted: ﴿Do you feel secure that He will not cause the side of the land to swallow you, or send against you a storm of stones?﴾ [al-Isra: 68].

Imam Muslim related from Sa'd ibn Abi Waqqas that: "He once came with the Prophet (ﷺ) from al-Aliyah, and when he passed the mosque of Bani Mu'awiyah, he entered and prayed two rak'ahs in it. We prayed with him, and he supplicated his Lord at length. Then he turned to us and said: 'I asked my Lord for three things, and He gave me two and denied me one. I asked my Lord that He not destroy my community by famine, and He gave it to me. I asked Him that He not destroy my community by drowning, and He gave it to me. I asked my Lord that He not make their violence among themselves, and He denied it to me.'"

Imam Ahmad related a similar report from the hadith of Abu Basrah, but he said, instead of the matter of destruction: "that He not gather them upon misguidance." Al-Tabari likewise related it from a mursal report of al-Hasan.

Al-Khafaji said: If you say: How were the two supplications answered, when there will be a swallowing in the East and a swallowing in the Arabian Peninsula? That is, as related by al-Tirmidhi and others? I say: What was prevented is a total swallowing that uproots them. As for the non-answering of His request concerning their violence, it is due to sins on their part, and because after the Prophet (ﷺ) conveyed to them and advised them, they did not act upon his words. End of quotation.

Ahmad and al-Tirmidhi have related from the hadith of Sa'd ibn Abi Waqqas, who said: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) was asked about this verse, ﴿Say: 'He is the One able﴾ and so on. He said: 'Indeed, it will happen, but its interpretation has not yet come.'" The hafiz Ibn Hajar said: This may be understood as not contradicting the hadith of Jabir, in that what is meant by its interpretation (p-2358) is what pertains to trials and the like. End of quotation. That is, the matters to which the verse will apply, which have not yet befallen the Muslims. So his saying "it will happen" means: among the Muslims, not that it is addressed to them, nor that it was revealed concerning them, as has been wrongly supposed, since the context and the preceding and following verses refute that, and the completion of the verse, as is not hidden, will be further explained by us.

**The second:** What is related from Ibn Abbas, that he used to say concerning His words, may He be exalted, ﴿a punishment from above you﴾: it means the wicked leaders, and ﴿from beneath your feet﴾ means the wicked servants. This was related by Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim. If it is authentically transmitted from him, his meaning is that the wording of the verse can apply to that, because punishment is everything that is bitter to the soul and grievous to it. It is not that this is the intended meaning of the verse, because it departs from the position of awe in the severe warning, and because the implication of that meaning is not evident from the essence of the wording, and because it does not accord with the parallels of the verse in this theme, as is not hidden.

It appears that the early generations (al-Salaf) would recite some verses in certain circumstances, indicating that their meaning resembles those events, not that they were revealed concerning those events. Among this is the saying of Ubayy ibn Ka'b, who said concerning this verse: "They are four characteristics, all of which will occur. Two of them have come after the death of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) by twenty-five years: being confused into factions, and tasting the violence of one another. Two remain that must come: the stoning and the swallowing." Related by Imam Ahmad and others. This report has been criticized on the ground that Ubayy did not live to the year twenty-five after the Prophetic death, and that the restriction to that date seems to be a statement of Abu al-Aliyah, transmitted from him. In sum, the early generations citing verses for some matters, for the indication mentioned, is not to be denied. Understand this, for it will benefit you in many places.

The discussion on the interpretation of His saying, exalted is He:

[66] ﴿Your people have denied it, though it is the truth. Say: I am not a guardian over you.﴾

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Your people have denied it﴾, i.e., the Glorious Qur'an. ﴿Though it is the truth﴾, i.e., the Book that is true in everything it states. ﴿Say: I am not a guardian over you﴾, i.e., your affair has not been entrusted to me, so that I could prevent you from denying it or compel you to believe. I am only a warner, and I have conveyed (the message). Some of them returned the pronoun in (it) to the punishment, i.e., your obstinate people denied the promised punishment, and it is certainly going to befall them.

The discussion on the interpretation of His saying, exalted is He:

[67] ﴿For every news there is a fixed time, and you will surely know.﴾

﴿For every news there is a fixed time﴾ means: for every great report there is a time of settling and becoming established, whether it proves true or false. ﴿And you will surely know﴾ means: the final resting place of this news and its outcome, and that the ultimate consequence belongs to it, as He, exalted is He, said: ﴿And you will surely know its news after a while﴾ [Sad: 88].

The discussion on the interpretation of His saying, exalted is He:

[68] ﴿When you see those who engage in vain talk about Our signs, turn away from them until they engage in a different discourse. And if Satan causes you to forget, then do not sit after the reminder with the wrongdoing people.﴾

﴿When you see those who engage in vain talk﴾, that is, with slander and mockery, ﴿about Our signs﴾, that is, those attributed to the station of Our greatness, which deserve to be held in honour in a manner befitting Our greatness. The relative clause is a metonymy for the polytheists of Mecca, for this was their habit. ﴿Then turn away from them﴾, that is, do not sit with them, and get up away from them. ﴿Until they engage in a different discourse﴾, that is, until they begin speaking about something other than what they were engaged in, namely their vain talk about Our signs.

(p-2360) ﴿And if Satan causes you to forget﴾ by distracting you so that you forget the prohibition against sitting with them, ﴿then do not sit after the reminder with the wrongdoing people﴾. That is: if Satan causes you to forget and you sit with them, you will not be held accountable for it; but once you recall the prohibition, do not sit with them, because they are wrongdoers through slandering the miraculous speech, out of obstinacy.

In a hadith: "Indeed Allah has overlooked for my community error, forgetfulness, and what they have been coerced into." Narrated by al-Tabarani from Thawban, traced to the Prophet (ﷺ). Its chain is sound. This verse is the one alluded to in His saying: ﴿He has already revealed to you in the Book that when you hear the signs of Allah being rejected and mocked, do not sit with them until they engage in a different discourse; otherwise, you would be like them﴾ [al-Nisa: 140]. This is because being present at an evil while being able to distance oneself from it amounts to sharing in the wrongdoing of its perpetrator.

Benefits:

Al-Suyuti said in al-Iklil: This verse makes it obligatory to avoid the gatherings of the heretics (mulhidun) and of those who indulge in idle talk. It is also used as evidence that the forgetful person is not legally accountable, and that when he remembers, legal responsibility returns to him, so he is excused for what he committed while forgetful. Many rulings concerning acts of worship and conditional oaths fall under this principle. End of quotation.

Al-Razi said: Among the Hashwiyyah (literalist extremists) are those who used this verse to prohibit reasoning and debate about the Essence of Allah and His attributes. They said: this is "plunging" (khawd) into the signs of Allah, and plunging into the signs of Allah is forbidden, as this verse shows.

The answer to this: the "plunging" meant in the verse is the beginning of slander and mockery. Thus this argument falls. And Allah knows best.

(p-2361) One of the commentators of the Zaydiyyah said, and the fruits of the verse are rulings:

The first: it is obligatory to turn away from the gatherings of those who mock the signs of Allah, His proofs, or His messengers, and not to sit with them, because sitting with them shows a lack of disapproval. This is because the obligation applies to us and to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ). Turning away and refraining from sitting with them is obligatory only when there is no hope of their accepting the message. When hope of them is cut off, there is no benefit in calling them. It is also obligatory to rise from their gatherings when one knows that rising will be a cause for them to stop their vain talk, and that they are doing it only to provoke the one who stays, since his staying would give the impression of not disapproving.

The second ruling: it is permissible to sit with the disbelievers so long as no vain talk takes place, since we have only been commanded to turn away when they engage in it. Also, Allah, exalted is He, said: ﴿until they engage in a different discourse﴾. Al-Hakim said: The verse also indicates the prohibition of sitting with oppressors and sinners when they openly commit evils, and it shows that entering upon them for a purpose is permissible, as it is permissible for the purpose of admonition. The verse also indicates the obligation of disapproval, since turning away is a form of disapproval. He said: It also shows that taqiyyah (concealing one's beliefs out of fear) by prophets and imams, by displaying what is evil, is not permitted, contrary to the Imamiyyah; and it shows that forgetfulness is permissible for the prophets.

The third ruling: the forgetful person is lifted of blame. If it is said: forgetfulness is the act of Allah, so why is it attributed to Satan? The answer: the cause comes from Satan, namely whispering and turning away from remembrance, so it is attributed to him for that reason, just as one who throws another into fire, and the latter dies, is said to be the killer, even though burning is the act of Allah. And there is disagreement about what forgetfulness is. Al-Hakim said: it is a meaning that Allah creates in the heart. Abu Hashim and his followers said: it is not a meaning, but rather the disappearance of the necessary knowledge that is customarily present. End of quotation.

(p-2362) The discussion of the interpretation of His saying, Exalted is He:

[69] ﴿And there is nothing upon those who fear God for their reckoning, of anything, but a reminder, that they may fear God.﴾

﴿And there is nothing upon those who fear God for their reckoning, of anything﴾ That is: nothing is incumbent upon the God-fearing who sit with them of the accountability for what they engage in of their plunging (into such talk). ﴿But a reminder﴾ That is: rather, they were commanded to turn away from them, so that it would be a reminder for the weak among the Muslims, lest anything of the slanders of the mockers fall into their hearts. ﴿That they may fear God﴾ That is: it reaches the degree of guarding against their doubts, by sitting with its scholars instead of them.

Two cautions:

The first: what we have mentioned regarding the meaning of the verse is what al-Mahayimi (may God have mercy on him) established. It has been said that the meaning is: rather, it is incumbent upon the God-fearing to admonish them with a reminder when they hear them plunging, by standing up away from them, showing their disapproval of them, and advising them, so that they may refrain from plunging out of shame or out of dislike for offending them, and so they do not return to it. They also allowed that the pronoun refers to "those who fear God," i.e., they remind them, hoping that they will remain firm in their piety or increase it. End of quotation.

What we have mentioned is more solid and more correct.

Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Sa'id ibn Jubayr, who said regarding the verse: That is: there is nothing upon you if they plunge into the verses of God when you do that, i.e., when you avoid them and turn away from them. Accordingly, the relative pronoun is a metonymy for the Prophet (ﷺ), turned to in this manner as a mark of honor and dignity.

The second: al-Suyuti said in al-Iklil: It may be cited from His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿And there is nothing upon those who fear God﴾ etc., as evidence that whoever sits with the people of evil, while not pleased with their deed, bears no sin. But the verse of al-Nisa' indicates that he is sinful, as long as he does not part from them, since He said: "Indeed, you would then be like them." That is: (p-2363) if you sit, you are like them in sin. That verse is later, so it is possible that it abrogates this one, as some people, including al-Suddi, held.

I say: What is negated in the verse is the affliction of some of the punishment of the plungers, and the sin of their disbelief, falling upon their God-fearing companions. This does not contradict the affliction of the harm of sitting with them considered by itself, which is what the verse of al-Nisa' conveys. The likeness, then, is in general sinfulness, even though its specific instances differ between the two; for no one holds that merely sitting with them is apostasy and disbelief. Yes! If it were said that the likeness is to be understood as applying when there is approval of their conduct of sitting with them, then there would be no difficulty at all. In sum, the evidence drawn by al-Iklil is weak, which is why he expressed it with (qad, "it may be"), and the claim of abrogation is weaker still. So reflect!

Commentary of al-Qasimi (Mahasin al-Ta'wil) on surah 6, verse 70:

The discussion of His saying, may He be exalted:

[70] ﴿And leave those who have taken their religion as amusement and play, and whom the worldly life has deceived. And remind [them] thereby, lest a soul be given up to destruction for what it has earned. It will have, besides Allah, no protector and no intercessor. And if it should offer every compensation, it would not be accepted from it. Those are the ones who have been given up to destruction for what they earned. For them is a drink of scalding water and a painful punishment because they used to disbelieve.﴾

﴿And leave those who have taken their religion﴾, i.e., that which they were charged with and called to, which is the religion of Islam, ﴿as amusement and play﴾, in that they mocked it and ridiculed it. ﴿And the worldly life has deceived them﴾, in that they were content with it and claimed that there is no life after it, ever, and that happiness lies in its pleasures. That is: turn away from them, leave them, do not care about their denial, and give them respite for a little while, for they are headed toward a great punishment. ﴿And remind [them] thereby﴾, i.e., remind the people by this Qur'an, ﴿lest a soul be given up to destruction for what it has earned﴾, i.e., for fear that it be delivered to ruin and held in pledge for the evil of its earnings and its deception through denying the Hereafter. It is said: abslahu li-kadha means he exposed him to it and pledged him, or he delivered him to perdition.
﴿It will have, besides Allah, no protector﴾ who would defend it by force, ﴿and no intercessor﴾ who would ward off [punishment] from it by request.

﴿And if it should offer every compensation, it would not be accepted from it﴾, i.e., even if it were to ransom itself with every kind of ransom, matching the punishment, it would not be accepted from it, because they are too far from the station of ransom. And al-'adl (the equivalent) is the ransom, because the one who ransoms equalizes the ransomed with its like.

﴿Those﴾ refers to those who took their religion as amusement and play: ﴿are the ones who have been given up to destruction﴾, i.e., delivered to ruin, such that nothing can oppose it, ﴿for what they earned﴾ through this deception, including denial of the Hereafter alongside it, and immersion in forbidden desires. ﴿For them is a drink of scalding water﴾, i.e., water boiling, which churns in their bellies and by which their intestines are cut to pieces, ﴿and a painful punishment﴾, i.e., with a fire that blazes upon their bodies, ﴿because they used to disbelieve﴾, i.e., because of their disbelief.

The discussion on the interpretation of His saying, exalted is He:

[71] ﴿Say, "Shall we call upon, besides Allah, that which can neither benefit us nor harm us, and be turned back on our heels after Allah has guided us, like one whom the devils have lured away in the earth, bewildered, while he has companions who call him to guidance, saying, 'Come to us.'" Say, "Indeed, the guidance of Allah is the [true] guidance, and we have been commanded to submit to the Lord of the worlds."﴾

﴿Say, "Shall we call upon, besides Allah, that which can neither benefit us nor harm us"﴾ That is: shall we worship, besides Him, that which has no power to benefit us if we call upon it, nor to harm us if we abandon it. ﴿And be turned back on our heels﴾ is a conjunction (ʿatf) with "shall we call upon" and falls under the same denial and negation. That is: and be turned back to shirk. Expressing it as being turned back on one's heels serves to intensify its ugliness by depicting it in the form of something that is a sign of ugliness, and it also indicates that shirk is a state that has been left behind and cast behind the back. This is what Abu al-Su'ud stated.

﴿After Allah has guided us﴾ That is, to Islam and monotheism, and has rescued us from worshipping idols, so that we would become like one who persists in misguidance. Rather, ﴿like one whom the devils have lured away﴾, that is, whom the rebellious jinn have led away from the clear path, ﴿in the earth﴾, the desolate, deadly wasteland, ﴿bewildered﴾, that is, wandering astray from the main road, not knowing what to do. ﴿He has﴾, that is, for this one who has been lured away, ﴿companions﴾, that is, a group of travelling companions, ﴿who call him to guidance﴾, that is, to the straight path, ﴿saying, "Come to us"﴾, with the verb "saying" understood, that is, they say: "Come to us." Yet he has trod the wilderness, following the devils, neither answering them nor coming to them. Thus the state of one who has been freed from shirk and then returned to it is likened to the state of one whom the rebellious devils have led into a desert after he had been on the right road, and who does not know the destination toward which he is heading, even though there are companions calling him to guide him, while he does not hear them. ﴿Say, "Indeed, the guidance of Allah"﴾, that is, that with which He sent His messengers, ﴿is the [true] guidance﴾, that is, and beyond it there is only error and deviation. ﴿And we have been commanded to submit to the Lord of the worlds.﴾

The discussion of the Exalted's saying:

[72] "And that you establish prayer and fear Him. And it is He to whom you will be gathered."

"And that you establish prayer and fear Him" — i.e., in opposing His command. "And that you establish" is a conjunction (ʿatf) upon "li-nuslima" (so that we may submit). Its meaning is "that we submit." Thus the lam in it is a redundant lam (radifa li-an), or it is a conjunction upon it; the lam is causal (taʿlīliyya), i.e., for submission and for establishing prayer. Regarding the occurrence of "establish prayer" reported in its own wording, and the occurrence of "we submit" reported in its meaning, there is the possibility that the Prophet (ﷺ) related the words of God in their meaning, not their exact wording. See "al-Intisaf" (of Ibn al-Munayyir).

Note:

In singling out prayer for mention from among the kinds of legal obligations, and in conjoining it to the command to submit and pairing it with the command to be mindful of God, there is evidence of the magnification of its matter and the greatness of its station. This was mentioned by some of the Zaydiyya.

"And it is He to whom you will be gathered."

(p-2366) The discussion of the interpretation of His saying, exalted is He:

[73] ﴿And it is He who created the heavens and the earth in truth. And the day He says, "Be," and it is, His word is the truth. And to Him belongs dominion on the day the Horn is blown. Knower of the unseen and the witnessed. And He is the Wise, the Acquainted.﴾

﴿And it is He who created the heavens and the earth in truth﴾ i.e., with wisdom, like His saying: ﴿And We did not create the heaven and earth and that between them in vain﴾ [Sad: 27].

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And the day He says, "Be," and it is, His word is the truth﴾ is a demonstration of His power, exalted is He, to resurrect them, by the fact that His will does not fall short of His command, and that His word is the one that takes effect and is realized. By "the word" is meant the word "Be," either literally or figuratively. So "His word is the truth" is a subject and predicate, and "the day" is an adverbial complement of the content of this clause, like His saying: ﴿His command, when He intends a thing, is only that He says to it, "Be," and it is﴾ [Ya-Sin: 82].

It seems that His saying, exalted is He, ﴿And it is He who created the heavens﴾ etc., following His saying ﴿And it is He to whom you will be gathered﴾ [al-An'am: 72], was brought for the argument concerning His power over the resurrection, refuting those among the polytheists who denied it, and the context concerns them. The verse is similar to His saying: ﴿Is not He who created the heavens and the earth able to create the likes of them? Yes, and He is the Knowing Creator﴾ [Ya-Sin: 81], and ﴿His command, when He intends a thing﴾ [Ya-Sin: 82].

It is not hidden that by bringing to mind the Qur'anic parallels, the realities become clear. The exegetes have expanded here on the i'rab (grammatical analysis) of this clause, enumerating many aspects among which the apparent meaning was lost—and you already know it, so be keen upon it.

(p-2367) ﴿And to Him belongs dominion on the day the Horn is blown﴾ i.e., He must necessarily act toward the obedient and the disobedient as kings act toward those who obey or disobey them. "The day" is an adverbial complement of His saying "and to Him belongs dominion"—so said Abu al-Su'ud. The restriction of the possession of dominion to Him, exalted is He, on that day, despite the general restriction to Him at all times, is for the sake of the clear manifestation of that, with the severing of the figurative ties existing in the world, which make figurative ownership valid in the clause, like His saying: ﴿Whose is the dominion today? It is for Allah, the One, the Subduer﴾ [Ghafir: 16], and His saying: ﴿The dominion that day is true, for the Most Merciful﴾ [al-Furqan: 26].

Some have claimed that "the Horn" (al-Suwar) here is the plural of "sura" (form), i.e., the day when it is blown into them and they come to life. Ibn Kathir said: The correct view is that "al-Suwar" means the horn into which Israfil, peace be upon him, will blow. Likewise Ibn Jarir said: What we hold to be correct is what the reports from the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) have made widely known, that he said: "Indeed Israfil has taken the Horn into his mouth and bent his forehead, awaiting when he will be commanded so that he may blow."

Imam Ahmad narrated from Abdullah ibn Amr, who said: "A Bedouin asked the Prophet (ﷺ) about the Horn?" (p-2368) He said: "It is a horn into which one blows." It was also narrated by Abu Dawud, al-Tirmidhi and al-Hakim, from him as well.

﴿Knower of the unseen and the witnessed﴾ i.e., He is the Knower of both. ﴿And He is the Wise, the Acquainted﴾ [al-An'am: 18], the Possessor of wisdom in all His acts, and of knowledge of both manifest and hidden matters.

Then Allah the Exalted commanded His Prophet (ﷺ) to mention to those who take their religion as mockery and play the denial of Abraham, peace be upon him, the one they claim to follow and take pride in, against his father over the latter's polytheism, in His words, glorified is He:

The discussion on the interpretation of His words, exalted is He:

[74] ﴿And when Abraham said to his father Āzar, "Do you take idols as gods? Indeed, I see you and your people in manifest error."﴾

﴿And when Abraham said to his father Āzar, "Do you take idols,"﴾ that is, figures made by hands, ﴿as gods? Indeed, I see you and your people in manifest error.﴾ That is, in believing in their divinity, or in their attributing to themselves His attributes, or in their deserving worship. This is because divinity belongs to necessary existence in itself, whereas they are contingent and made. How could they possess His attributes when they are incapable of benefit and harm, devoid of life, hearing and sight? Worship is the utmost of humility, so one who is not free of these defects of lowliness does not deserve it. It is only deserved by one who is at the utmost height. This was stated by al-Mahayimi.

Notes (tanbihat):

First: It was recited as "Āzar" with a fatha, as an explanatory apposition (ʿatf bayān) to His words "to his father," and with a damma, as a vocative (nidāʾ).

Second: The verse is a proof against the Shiʿah (a sect that holds the Imamate of ʿAlī and his descendants) in their claim that none of the fathers of the prophets was an unbeliever, and that Āzar was Abraham's paternal uncle, not his father, as al-Razi expounded here. This is because the primary sense of a term in its unqualified use is its literal meaning, and such a matter cannot be asserted with certainty without transmission.

(p-2369) Third: One of the commentators of the Zaydiyyah (a Shiʿi school named after Zayd ibn ʿAlī) said: The verse indicates the invalidity of the view of the Imamiyyah (the Twelver Shiʿah) that the Imam cannot have an unbelieving father, for if a prophet may have a father and a wife who are both unbelievers, then the Imam is more entitled to this.

The speech of Abraham, peace be upon him, contains a general mention of the rational argument against the view of the idol-worshippers, by his denying that they be taken as gods, and they are what they are in their incapacity. It has come in detail in Surah Maryam, in His words: ﴿And mention in the Book Abraham. Indeed, he was a man of truth and a prophet.﴾ [Maryam: 41] ﴿When he said to his father, "O my father, why do you worship that which does not hear and does not see and does not avail you at all?"﴾ [Maryam: 42] ﴿"O my father, indeed there has come to me of knowledge what has not come to you, so follow me; I will guide you to a straight path."﴾ [Maryam: 43] ﴿"O my father, do not worship Satan. Indeed, Satan has ever been disobedient to the Most Merciful."﴾ [Maryam: 44] ﴿"O my father, indeed I fear that a punishment from the Most Merciful will touch you, so you would be a companion to Satan."﴾ [Maryam: 45] ﴿[The father] said, "Do you turn away from my gods, O Abraham? If you do not desist, I will surely stone you, so leave me alone a long time."﴾ [Maryam: 46] and the verses.

Ibn Kathir said: It is established in the Sahih, from Abu Hurayrah, from the Prophet (ﷺ), who said: "Abraham will meet his father Āzar on the Day of Resurrection, and on Āzar's face will be dust and darkness. Abraham will say, 'Did I not tell you, "Do not disobey me"?' His father will say, 'Today I will not disobey you.' Abraham will say, 'O Lord! You promised me that You would not disgrace me on the Day they are resurrected. What disgrace is greater than my father, the farthest away?' Allah the Exalted will say, 'Indeed I have forbidden Paradise to the disbelievers.' Then it will be said, 'O Abraham! Look beneath your feet.' He will look, and behold, there is a dhīkh (a term here for a filthy, mud-smeared creature) smeared with filth, which will be seized by its legs and thrown into the Fire."

Fourth: One of the commentators of the Zaydiyyah said: The fruit of the verse is the indication of the obligation of sincere advice in religion, especially to relatives, for whoever is closer has greater importance. For this reason the Exalted said: ﴿And warn your closest kindred﴾ [al-Shuʿarāʾ: 214], and He said: ﴿Protect yourselves and your families from a Fire﴾ [al-Tahrim: 6]. He (ﷺ) said: "Begin with yourself, then with those you support." For this reason the Prophet (ﷺ) began with ʿAlī, Khadijah and Zayd, who were with him in the house, and they believed and were first. Then with the rest of Quraysh, then with the Arabs, then with the mawālī (freed slaves and non-Arab clients). Abraham began with his father, then with his people. This verse also indicates that sincere advice in religion, and rebuke and reproach for its sake, is not disobedience to parents, like emigration. Thus it is in al-Tahdhib. End.

Commentary of al-Qasimi (Mahasin al-Ta'wil) on surah 6, verse 75:

(p-2371) The discussion of the interpretation of His saying, the Exalted:

[75] ﴿And thus did We show Abraham the dominion (malakut) of the heavens and the earth, that he might be among the certain (in faith).﴾

﴿And thus did We show Abraham the dominion (malakut) of the heavens and the earth﴾ That is: We made him aware of their realities, and We made him perceive, through their indication, the affairs of Him, Mighty and Majestic, insofar as they, with all that is in them, are both nurtured and owned by Him, Exalted. The word malakut is a verbal noun on the pattern of intensification, like rahabut and jabarut, and its meaning is: the great dominion and the overpowering sovereignty. It has also been said: its malakut is its wonders and marvels. We have already discussed the word "thus" (wa-kadhalika) shortly before, at His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And thus did We test﴾ [al-An'am: 53], and that the preference of al-Zamakhshari is that it is a reference to the verbal noun of what follows it, with the kaf being superfluous, and the sense being: that showing and the wondrous making-to-see, We showed him and We made him see. Thus he renewed the covenant with him.

﴿and that he might be among the certain (in faith)﴾ is a conjunction over a deleted cause that was not specified, to indicate that this showing has many benefits, of which the one mentioned is among them.

Al-Mahayimi said regarding the verse: ﴿And thus did We show Abraham the dominion of the heavens and the earth﴾ so that he would know that nothing of the spiritual beings of the spheres, the stars, the shaykhs and the devils is fit for divinity; and that he might be among those certain of the Oneness through reasoning with the many proofs. It has also been said: "that he might be" is a cause for an implied matter which is an expression of what was mentioned. That is: that he might be among those certain of the Oneness, We did what We did of showing and making-to-see the signs of the heavens and the earth.

Subtleties:

The first: al-Razi said: Here there is a rational subtlety, namely that the light of God's majesty is shining, not cut off nor ever removed at all, and human souls are not deprived of those lights except because of a veil, and that veil is nothing but occupation with other than God, the Exalted. So when the matter is such, then to the degree that veil is removed, this manifestation occurs. Thus the saying of Abraham, peace be upon him: "Do you take idols as gods?" is an indication of condemning occupation with the worship of other than God, the Exalted; for everything other than God is a veil from God, the Exalted. So when that veil was removed, inevitably the dominion of the heavens was manifested to him completely. So His saying: ﴿And thus did We show Abraham the dominion of the heavens﴾ means: after the cessation of occupation with other than God, there came to him a light in which the majesty of God, the Exalted, was manifested; so "thus" was the source of this noble spiritual benefit.

The second: al-Razi said: certainty (yaqin) is an expression for knowledge that arises after the removal of doubt by means of reflection. For this reason the knowledge of God, the Exalted, is not described as certainty, because His knowledge is not preceded by doubt and is not derived from thought and reflection. Know that a person, at the first of what he reasons with, his heart does not fail to be free of doubt and suspicion in some respects; so when the proofs multiply and agree and correspond, they become a cause for the attainment of certainty. This is for several reasons:

The first: each one of those proofs produces a kind of impression and strength, so the strength keeps increasing until it reaches firm conviction.

The second: the multiplication of acts is a cause for the attainment of a habit. So the repetition of reasoning with various proofs toward one single object runs like the repetition of one lesson. Just as much repetition yields a firm memorization that does not depart from the heart, so too here.

The third: the heart, at the time of reasoning, was very dark; when the belief derived from the first proof took hold in it, the light of that reasoning mingled with the darkness of the other qualities present in the heart, so a state arose in it resembling the state mixed of light and darkness. When the second reasoning occurs, its light mingles with the first state, so the brightness and radiance become more complete. Just as the sun, when it draws near the eastern horizon, its light appears at first, which is the dawn, so the first reasoning is like the dawn. Then, just as the dawn keeps increasing as the sun draws nearer to the zenith, and when it reaches the zenith the full light arises, so too the servant: whenever his contemplation of the levels of God's creatures is greater, the rising of the light of knowledge and Oneness becomes clearer. Yet the difference between the sun of knowledge and the sun of the world is that the sun of the physical world has a determined limit in its rising and ascent, beyond which it cannot ascend further. But the sun of knowledge, reason and Oneness has no end to its ascent, and no limit to its increase. So His saying: ﴿And thus did We show Abraham the dominion of the heavens and the earth﴾ is an indication of the levels of proofs and evidences. And His saying: ﴿that he might be among the certain﴾ is an indication of the degrees of the lights of manifestation and the rising of the sun of knowledge and Oneness. End.

The third: He, the Exalted, mentioned the showing in this verse in summary, then detailed it with His saying:

**On the interpretation of His words, may He be exalted:**

[76] ﴿So when the night covered him, he saw a star. He said, "This is my lord." But when it set, he said, "I do not love those that set."﴾

﴿So when the night covered him, he saw a star. He said, "This is my lord."﴾ Al-Mahayimi said: When Ibrahim, peace be upon him, saw the *malakut* (the unseen realm of dominion), and became certain that none of it was fit for divinity, he intended to refute his people in their belief in its divinity, on the ground of its baseness, since its actions depend on bodies that have the lowliness of setting, even though they are celestial. Likewise (he refuted them) in their belief in the divinity of those bodies, just as he refuted them in their belief in the divinity of idols. So (his argument) would become manifest, like the stars that they used to worship. End of quotation.

In summary, the verse explains the manner of his reasoning, peace be upon him, and his arrival at the rank of certainty.

The meaning of "covered him" (*jpast 'alayhi al-layl*) is: it concealed him with its darkness. As for "the star" (*al-kawkab*), it is said to be Venus, and it is said to be Jupiter.

I say: *al-kawkab* (الكوكب), linguistically, is a star (*al-najm*). Al-Zubaydi said in his *Sharh al-Qamus*: Its being a proper name by dominance for Venus is not to be relied upon; rather, the word is *al-kawkabah*, with the *ha'*. End of quotation.

Al-Zamakhshari said: His father and his people used to worship idols, the sun, the moon, and the stars. He wanted to alert them to the error in their religion, and to guide them to the path of reflection and inference, and to make them understand that correct reflection leads to the conclusion that none of these can be a god, because of the evidence of origination (*hudūth*) in them, and that behind them there is an originator who originated them, a maker who made them, and a manager who directed their rising, their setting, their movement, their course, and all their conditions. Ibrahim's saying to his people, "This is my lord," was a loosening of the reins with them, by showing agreement with them at first, and then nullifying their claim through inference, because that is closer to bringing the opponent back. Al-Zamakhshari said: Ibrahim's saying that is the saying of one who is fair to his opponent, while knowing that he is in error, recounting his words as they are, without being partisan to his own school, because that is more conducive to the truth and more effective in avoiding dispute. Then he turns against it after recounting it, and refutes it with proof.

﴿But when it set﴾, that is, disappeared: ﴿he said, "I do not love those that set."﴾ That is, I do not love to worship whoever is like this, for setting is a baseness that contradicts divinity. Rather, it prevents one from inclining toward its companion, let alone taking it as a god or an object of worship, let alone what depends on it.

On the interpretation of His saying, exalted is He:

[77] ﴿So when he saw the moon rising, he said: "This is my Lord." But when it set, he said: "Unless my Lord guides me, I will surely be among the people who go astray."﴾

﴿So when he saw the moon rising﴾, i.e., appearing and spreading its light. ﴿He said: "This is my Lord,"﴾ in the manner previously described. ﴿But when it set, he said: "Unless my Lord guides me, I will surely be among the people who go astray."﴾ For what he had seen is not fitting for divinity, because of its lowliness through its disappearance.

Al-Zamakhshari said: In it is an admonition to his people that whoever takes the moon as a god, and it is like the stars in setting, is astray. And that guidance to the truth is by the success and subtle kindness of God, exalted is He.

In al-Intisaf (by Ibn al-Munayyir): The allusion to their error the second time is clearer and stronger than his earlier statement: "I do not love those that set." He only progressed to that because the opponents had already established against him a proof by the first argument, so they became accustomed to having their belief criticised. Had this been said at first, they might have recoiled and not listened to the argument. He did not allude to their being in error until after he was confident of their attentiveness to the full purport and their listening to the end. The evidence for this is that in the third round he progressed to an explicit declaration of disavowal of them and a rebuke that they were in polytheism, once the establishing of the proof was complete and the truth had become manifest and reached the utmost clarity of the intended aim, as God, exalted is He, said:

The discussion of the Lord's words (Exalted is He):

[78] ﴿So when he saw the sun rising, he said, "This is my lord; this is greater." But when it set, he said, "O my people, indeed I am free from what you associate [with Allah].﴾

﴿So when he saw the sun rising, he said, "This is my lord"﴾ is in the same manner as what preceded. The use of the demonstrative in the masculine ("This") is either to match the masculine predicate (khabar), or because he intended: "This rising one," or "the one I see," or to protect the Lord from the suspicion of femininity, in order to draw them on (li-yastadrijahum). For had he belittled [the sun] in any way, that would have been a cause for them not to lend him an ear. Al-Mahayimi restricted himself to the last reason, saying: "He did not make it feminine, lest the lack of femininity contradict its greatness, even if only figuratively; and although it is in reality feminine, he did not use the feminine form verbally, because he intended by that first to assist his opponent."

And His saying: ﴿This is greater﴾ means: greatest of the heavenly bodies in size and strongest in power, so it is more deserving of divinity. In it is an emphasis on what he (peace be upon him) intended of showing fairness, together with a hidden indication of the corruption of their religion from another angle, by clarifying that the greater is more worthy of lordship than the lesser.

(p-2376) ﴿But when it set, he said﴾ proclaiming the truth: ﴿"O my people, indeed I am free from what you associate [with Allah]."﴾ That is: from the created bodies that change from one state to another, or from your associating [partners with Allah].

The Interpretation of His Words, the Exalted:

[79] ﴿Indeed, I have turned my face toward He who created the heavens and the earth, inclining (ḥanīf) and I am not of those who associate others with Allah.﴾

﴿Indeed, I have turned my face﴾ means: I have turned my heart and my spirit in love and worship; rather, I have made it submissive. ﴿toward He who created the heavens and the earth, inclining﴾ means: turning away from the false religions and the deviant beliefs. ﴿and I am not of those who associate others with Allah.﴾

On this point there are several discussions (mabāḥith):

The first: The exegetes have elaborated at length on His words: "This is my Lord."

Some said that the one who spoke these words was Āzar, and that when he said this, Ibrāhīm replied: "I do not love those that set."

It was also said that it was Ibrāhīm himself, and that this occurred in his childhood, before his reflection on the knowledge of Allah had become firm, based on His words: ﴿If my Lord does not guide me...﴾ (Al-An'ām: 77) "my Lord..." etc.

It was also said that it occurred after he reached maturity and was honored with prophethood, but that he intended it as a rhetorical question of denial, rebuking his people, and omitted the interrogative particle; many similar examples exist.

It was also said that it is by implying a verb of speech, meaning: "They say, this is my Lord," and the omission of the verb of speech is common.

It was also said that the meaning is "in your assumption and your belief," and it was said that it is a statement made in mockery... along with other sayings.

The purpose of all this is to clear his station, peace be upon him, from doubt and perplexity, and from believing that such things are lordly, since that contradicts infallibility (ʿiṣmah).

[p-2377] I say: This is accepted without doubt. But the most correct of all of this is what we previously stated first: that his words "This is my Lord" are from the method of employing fairness with opponents, by way of stipulation: it is the introduction of a premise in an argument which he does not himself believe, because it is accepted by the other party, in order to bind him to it. This is the terminology of the people of disputation (jadal). Al-Zamakhsharī restricted himself to this unique view.

Al-Nāṣir said in al-Intiṣāf: "This is the only valid interpretation." It has been reported in the hadith about intercession that the people will come to Ibrāhīm, peace be upon him, asking him for intercession, and he will say: "Myself! Myself!" and he will mention his three lies, and say: "I am not fit for it," meaning his saying to Sarah: "She is my sister," and by it he meant in Islam; and his saying: "I am sick," and by it he meant his concern over his people and their polytheism, which a believer finds distressing; and his saying: "Rather, it was their chief who did it," for which several indirect interpretations have been given. So when he, may the blessings and peace of Allah be upon him, counted these words against himself, knowing that he will not be held accountable for them, this shows that they were the greatest of what came from him. If the matter were as is said, that this statement is related from him as his own opinion about himself, then it would be even more fitting for him to count it as the greatest, since then it would be a doubt, indeed a certainty. Moreover, the correct view is that prophets are protected from such things before prophethood. End of quote.

Ibn Kathīr said: The exegetes differed on this point: Is this a station of reflection (naẓar) or of debate (munāẓarah)? Ibn Jarīr narrated through ʿAlī ibn Abī Ṭalḥah from Ibn ʿAbbās what implies that it is a station of reflection, and Ibn Jarīr preferred it, citing as evidence His words: "If my Lord does not guide me..." etc. Muḥammad ibn Isḥāq said: He said that when he came out of the cave in which his mother had given birth to him, when she feared for him from Nimrod ibn Kanʿān, for he had been informed of the existence of a child who would cause the loss of his kingdom at his hands, so he ordered the slaughter of the boys that year. When Ibrāhīm's mother became pregnant with him and her time of delivery came, she went to a cave outside the town, gave birth to Ibrāhīm there, and left him there. He mentioned matters of extraordinary occurrences, as others among the exegetes also mentioned. Then Ibn Kathīr said: The truth is that Ibrāhīm, peace be upon him, in this station was debating with his people, clarifying to them the falsehood of what they were upon of worshipping temples and idols. In the first station with his father, he made clear their error in worshipping earthly idols, which are in the form of the heavenly angels, so that they would intercede for them with the Great Creator, whom they consider too insignificant to be worshipped themselves; rather they seek nearness to Him through worshipping His angels, so that they might intercede for them with Him regarding provision and other things they need. And in this station he made clear their error and misguidance in worshipping the temples, which are the seven wandering stars. The most luminous and the most honored of them in their view are the Sun, then the Moon, then Venus. So he first made clear, may the blessings and peace of Allah be upon him, that this Venus is not fit for divinity, for it is subjected and determined by a specific motion from which it does not deviate, and it does not control itself in any action; rather it is a body among bodies, which Allah created luminous for His great wisdoms, rising from the east, then moving between it and the west, until it disappears from sight there, then appears again on the following night in the same manner. And this is not fit for divinity. Then he made the same point about the Moon as he made about the star, and then about the Sun likewise. When divinity was denied from these three bodies, which are the brightest things upon which eyes fall, and this was established by a decisive proof, he disassociated himself from their worship and allegiance, and declared that he worships their Creator and Subjugator.

Then Ibn Kathīr said: How could it be permissible for him to be a reflector in this station, when Allah said about him: ﴿And We had given Ibrāhīm his right guidance before, and We were knowing of him﴾ (Al-Anbiyāʾ: 51), ﴿when he said to his father and his people, "What are these statues to which you are devoted?"﴾ (Al-Anbiyāʾ: 52). And He, exalted, said: ﴿Indeed, Ibrāhīm was a nation, devoutly obedient to Allah, inclining (ḥanīf), and he was not of those who associate others with Him﴾ (Al-Naḥl: 120), ﴿grateful for His favors. He chose him and guided him to a straight path﴾ (Al-Naḥl: 121).

[p-2379] It is established in the two Ṣaḥīḥs from Abū Hurayrah, from the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, that he said: "Every child is born upon the fiṭrah (natural disposition)."

In Ṣaḥīḥ Muslim, from ʿIyāḍ ibn Ḥimār, that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "Allah, the Exalted, said: Indeed I created My servants inclining (ḥunafāʾ)." And He, exalted, said: ﴿The nature (fiṭrah) of Allah upon which He created mankind; there is no altering of the creation of Allah﴾ (Al-Rūm: 30). And He, exalted, said: ﴿And when your Lord took from the Children of Adam, from their loins, their descendants, and made them testify concerning themselves, "Am I not your Lord?" They said, "Yes"﴾ (Al-Aʿrāf: 172). Its meaning, according to one of the two opinions, is like His saying: ﴿the nature of Allah upon which He created mankind﴾ (Al-Rūm: 30). So if this is the case concerning all of creation, how could Ibrāhīm the Friend [of Allah] [p-2380] whom Allah made ﴿a nation, devoutly obedient to Allah, inclining, and not of those who associate others with Him﴾ be a reflector in this station? Rather, he is the most deserving of people, after the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, of the sound nature and the upright disposition, without doubt or uncertainty.

What further supports that he was debating his people about the polytheism they were in, and not reflecting, is His saying: ﴿And his people argued with him﴾ (Al-Anʿām: 80), the verse that follows. End of quote.

Among those who excelled in this noble topic, and who made clear that Ibrāhīm, peace be upon him, was debating his people, is the scholar al-Shahrastānī in his book al-Milal wa al-Niḥal. We quote him here in support of this important discussion, and to acquaint the reader with the belief of his people and what drove them to it, for it contains benefits.

He, may Allah have mercy on him, said under the heading "The People of Temples and Figures": These are among the sects of the Ṣābiʾah (those who are zealous for the spiritual beings). We have included their doctrine in the debates in general, and we mention it here in detail:

Know that the people of spirituality, when they realized that a human must have an intermediary, and that the intermediary must be seen so that one may turn to it for nearness and benefit from it, they resorted to the temples, which are the seven wandering stars. First, they learned their houses and dwellings; second, their risings and settings; third, their connections in forms of agreement and disagreement, arranged according to their natures; fourth, they divided the days, nights and hours among them; fifth, they assigned to them the forms, persons, regions and cities. They made seals, learned incantations and invocations, and assigned to the day of Saturn, for example, Saturday, observing its first hour in it, and sealed themselves with its ring made according to its image and description, wore its special garments, fumigated with its special incense, invoked its special supplications, and asked from it their needs, the need that is sought from Saturn according to its specific actions and effects.

Likewise, the removal of the need that belongs to Jupiter on its day and hour, and all the additions which (p-2381) we mentioned relating to it. Likewise all other needs directed to the stars. They called them: lords, gods, while Allah, exalted, is the Lord of lords and God of gods. Some of them made the Sun the God of gods and Lord of lords. They drew near to the temples, seeking nearness to the spiritual beings, that is, the angels, and drew near to the spiritual beings, seeking nearness to the Originator, exalted, believing that for every spiritual being there is a temple, and for every temple a sphere. So the temples are the bodies of the spiritual beings, and their relation to the spiritual beings is like the relation of our bodies to our souls. They are the living ones who speak by the life of the spiritual beings, and these are their lords and governors, who manage their bodies, direct and move them, just as our bodies are managed. Without doubt, whoever draws near to a person has drawn near to his soul. Then they extracted from the wonderful stratagems arranged on the operation of the stars what amazed people. These talismans mentioned in books, magic, soothsaying, sealing, incantation, rings and images, are all from their sciences.

Commentary of al-Qasimi (Mahasin al-Ta'wil) on surah 6, verse 79 (part 2 of 2):

As for the adherents of the *ashkhas* (images), they said: "If there must be an intermediary through whom one seeks nearness, and an intercessor to whom one appeals, and the spiritual beings (*al-ruhaniyyat*, the spiritual intelligences) are indeed the means, yet since we do not see them with our eyes, nor address them with our tongues, nearness to them cannot be realized except through their *hayakil* (temples, the bodies assigned to them). But the *hayakil* are visible at one time and not visible at another, because they have rising and setting, and appearance by night and concealment by day. Thus nearness to them and turning toward them is not made pure for us. Therefore we must have figures and individual images that exist, stand, and are set up before our eyes, so that we may devote ourselves to them and seek nearness through them to the *hayakil*, and draw near through the *hayakil* to the spiritual beings, and draw near through the spiritual beings to God Most High. So we worship them so that they may bring us near to God in closeness."

So they made idols as images in the likeness of the seven *hayakil*, each image corresponding to one temple. They observed in this the essence of the temple, meaning the substance specific to it, of iron or other material, and they shaped it in its form, in the posture from which its actions proceed. They also observed the time, the hour, the moment, the degree, the minute, and all the astral relations, of a favorable connection that affects the success of the requests sought from it. They drew near to it on its day and at its hour, fumigated with its specific incense, put on its ring, wore its garments, humbly prayed with its supplications, and performed its invocations (*aza'im*), and they asked it for their needs. They would say: "Their needs were fulfilled after observing all these relations." This is what the revelation described when it said that they were worshippers of the stars and of idols. The adherents of the temples are the worshippers of the stars, since they affirmed their divinity, as we have explained. The adherents of the images are the worshippers of idols, since they named them gods in opposition to the heavenly gods of those others, and said: "These are our intercessors with God."

The Friend (al-Khalil, Abraham), peace be upon him, debated these two groups. He began by refuting the doctrine of the adherents of the images, and this is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And that was Our argument which We gave Abraham against his people. We raise by degrees whom We will. Indeed your Lord is Wise and Knowing.﴾ [al-An'am: 83] That argument was that he refuted them by speech with His saying: ﴿Do you worship what you carve?﴾ [al-Saffat: 95] ﴿And God created you and what you make.﴾ [al-Saffat: 96]

Since his father Azar was the most knowledgeable of his people in the work of images and idols, and in observing the astral relations in them to the fullest extent, and for this reason they used to buy idols from him and from no one else, most of the arguments were with him and the strongest obligations were upon him: ﴿And when Abraham said to his father Azar, "Do you take idols as gods? Indeed I see you and your people in manifest error."﴾ [al-An'am: 74] And He said: ﴿When he said to his father, "O my father, why do you worship what does not hear nor see and does not avail you at all?"﴾ [Maryam: 42] (meaning): because you exerted every effort, and employed all knowledge, until you made idols in correspondence with the heavenly bodies. Yet your scientific and practical power did not reach the point of giving them hearing and sight, nor that they could avail you, harm, or benefit. Indeed, by your nature and creation you are higher in rank than they, for you were created hearing, seeing, harming, and benefiting, while the heavenly influences are more manifest in you than in this thing made with effort and fashioned with artifice. Alas, what a bewilderment, that the thing made by your hands became a god for you, while the maker is nobler than the made! "O my father, do not worship Satan. Indeed Satan..." ﴿O my father, indeed there has come to me of knowledge what has not come to you, so follow me, and I will guide you to a straight path.﴾ [Maryam: 43] ﴿He said, "Do you turn away from my gods, O Abraham?"﴾ [Maryam: 46] So he did not accept his verbal argument. Then, peace be upon him, he turned to refutation by action, and made them into fragments, except their chief: ﴿They said, "Who has done this to our gods? Indeed he is among the wrongdoers."﴾ [al-Anbiya': 59] ﴿He said, "Rather, their chief has done it, so ask them, if they can speak."﴾ [al-Anbiya': 63] ﴿So they returned to themselves and said, "Indeed you are the wrongdoers."﴾ [al-Anbiya': 64] ﴿Then they were overturned upon their heads: "You have certainly known that these do not speak."﴾ [al-Anbiya': 65] Thus he silenced them by action, when he attributed the act to their chief, just as he silenced them by speech, when he attributed the act to them. All of this was by way of imposing obligation upon them. Otherwise, the Friend was never a liar.

Then he turned to refuting the doctrines of the adherents of the temples, as God Most High showed him the argument against his people. He said: ﴿And thus did We show Abraham the dominion of the heavens and the earth, that he might be among the certain.﴾ [al-An'am: 75] So He let him see the dominion of the two worlds and the two realms, honoring him above the spiritual beings and their temples, favoring the doctrine of the *hunafa'* (the upright monotheists) over the doctrine of the Sabians, and establishing that perfection belongs to men. Then he turned to nullifying the doctrine of the adherents of the temples: ﴿So when the night covered him, he saw a star and said, "This is my lord."﴾ [al-An'am: 76] This was on the scale of imposing obligation upon the adherents of the idols, "Rather, their chief has done it." Otherwise, the Friend was not a liar in this statement, nor an associator in that gesture. Then he argued from setting, cessation, change, and transition, that it is not fitting to be a lord and god, for the eternal God does not change, and whatever changes needs a changer. This applies if you believe it to be an eternal lord and a timeless god, and also if you believe it to be an intermediary, a *qibla* (direction of worship), an intercessor, and a means. Setting and cessation also remove it from perfection. For this reason (p-2384), he argued against it by its rising, though rising is closer to having come into being than setting is. They had only moved to the images because of the bewilderment that overtook them through setting, so the Friend, peace be upon him, came to them from the very point of their bewilderment, and argued against them with what they acknowledged as correct, and this is more eloquent in argumentation. Then: ﴿So when he saw the moon rising, he said, "This is my lord." But when it set, he said, "If my Lord does not guide me, I will surely be among the misguided people."﴾ [al-An'am: 77] How strange! How can one who does not know a lord say: ﴿If my Lord does not guide me, I will surely be among the misguided people﴾? Seeing guidance from the Lord, exalted is He, is the ultimate goal of monotheism and the final end of knowledge. How can the one who has arrived at the goal and the end be on the stages of the beginning? Leave all of this behind the mountain of Qaf, and return with us to what is healing and sufficient. For agreement in expression, by way of imposing obligation upon the opponent, is among the most eloquent proofs and the clearest methods. For this reason he said: ﴿So when he saw the sun rising, he said, "This is my lord; this is greater."﴾ [al-An'am: 78] Because the people believed that the sun is the king of the sphere, and the lord of lords from whom they draw lights and receive effects. ﴿But when it set, he said, "O my people, indeed I am free of what you associate."﴾ [al-An'am: 78] ﴿Indeed I have turned my face toward He who originated the heavens and the earth, inclining, and I am not of those who associate.﴾ This established the doctrine of the *hunafa'* and nullified the doctrine of the Sabians, and made clear that *al-fitra* (the primordial nature) is the *hanifiyya* (upright monotheism), that purity lies in it, that the testimony to tawhid (oneness of God) is confined to it, and that the prophets and messengers were sent to establish and affirm it, and that the beginning and the end, the origin and the perfection, are bound to summarizing and clarifying it. This is the upright religion, the straight path, the clear method, and the evident way.

The words of al-Shahrastani, may God Most High have mercy on him, have ended. I have transmitted his speech in full, because, as it is said:

*"Indeed, the beauties of a thing are not all beautiful."* (Wait, correct rendering:) *"And what are the beauties of a thing if all of it is not beautiful?"*

He, may God have mercy on him, presented the discussion of the Sabians of the spiritual beings first, and followed it with a wonderful debate that took place between them and the *hunafa'*, which great benefit is gained by reviewing.

May God reward him with good.

(p-2385) Second: It becomes clear from what al-Shahrastani mentioned that the secret of the Friend's, peace be upon him, argument by setting rather than rising, although each of them is incompatible with the deserving of its subject to lordship, is that it came to them from the very point of their bewilderment, as an imposition of obligation upon them by what they acknowledge as correct.

Abu al-Su'ud said: "Since rising is a state that necessitates the appearance of effects and judgments, and is suitable for a vague notion of deserving in general, he turned from it to setting, because it is a state that requires the obliteration of effects and the nullification of judgments, which clearly contradict the aforementioned deserving, a contradiction that every stubborn obstinate denier would almost acknowledge." End of quote. This is subtle, but the first is more solid.

Third: If it were said that setting, since it prevents its subject from deserving the attribute of lordship as we have mentioned, and this has been established for the greatest of the stars (namely the sun), then it necessarily follows that it is established for what is below it by greater necessity. Why then did he not limit himself to the setting of the sun, for the sake of brevity and conciseness? It is answered: taking from the lower to the higher in sequence has a kind of effect in affirmation, explanation, and emphasis that cannot be obtained otherwise, so directing the argument in this manner is preferable. This was stated by al-Razi.

Fourth: Al-Razi said: This verse indicates that religion must be founded on proof, not on blind imitation (*taqlid*), for otherwise this argument would have no benefit at all.

**The interpretation of His saying, exalted is He:**

﴿And his people argued with him. He said: "Do you argue with me concerning God, when He has guided me? I do not fear what you associate with Him, unless my Lord wills something. My Lord encompasses all things in knowledge. Will you not then take heed?"﴾

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And his people argued with him﴾, meaning they disputed with him, seeking to overcome him with argument regarding what he had adopted of the Oneness of God (tawhid) and the negation of partners from Him. They did this at times with corrupt proofs rooted in the depths of blind imitation (taqlid), and at other times through intimidation. The response to each of these has already been indicated. ﴿He said: "Do you argue with me concerning God, when He has guided me?"﴾ meaning: Do you dispute with me about His Oneness, when He has guided me to establish proofs and remove doubts, to show that nothing other than Him is divine? (p. 2386) It is established that the others are deficient in their very essences, so their perfections come from something else, and there is no divinity for the one who is deficient in himself, because his perfection cannot be absolute. The word ﴿تُحاجُّونِّي﴾ (tuhājjūnnī) is read with the nūn of the plural assimilated into the nūn of protection (nūn al-wiqāyah), and it is also read with the first of the two nūns deleted.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿and I do not fear what you associate with Him﴾, meaning: I do not fear your objects of worship, because they are inanimate objects that neither harm nor benefit by themselves. This is a response to what they threatened him with during the argument, namely that harm would befall him from their idols, as when the people of Hud said to him, peace be upon him: "We say nothing except that some of our gods have struck you with evil" (Hud 11:54). Their intimidation is implied, even though no mention of it preceded, from His saying "and I do not fear".

Ibn Kathir said: That is, among the evidence for the falsity of your claim is that these objects of worship do not affect anything, and I do not fear them or heed them. So if they have any scheming power, then scheme against me with them and do not give me respite. End of quotation.

﴿unless my Lord wills something﴾, meaning: unless He wills harm to befall me from their direction. That comes only from Him, exalted is He, without the objects of worship having any involvement in it at all.

In al-Intisaf: The ultimate extent of Abraham's fear of them, which he made contingent upon the will of God, exalted is He, was a fear of harm from them through the power of God, not from them themselves. It is as though, in reality, he feared none but God, because the fear he attributed to them is contingent upon the will and power of God, and it is like fear of them. And God knows best.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿My Lord encompasses all things in knowledge﴾ appears to be the reason for the exception, meaning: He has encompassed all things in knowledge. So it is not far-fetched that His knowledge includes sending down the harm I fear from their direction, like His stoning [of the wrongdoers] with stones, for when something is referred to the knowledge of God, it implies the possibility of its occurrence. In placing the explicit name in the position of the pronoun, together with mention of the title of Lordship, there is a declaration by him, peace be upon him, of his submission to the judgment of Him, glory be to Him and exalted is He, a surrender to His command, and an acknowledgment that he is under His dominion and lordship.

(p. 2387) Al-Mahayimi made that the reason for an omitted counter-statement, which he knew from the context, when he said regarding the verse: "And I do not fear harm to myself from the influence of what you associate with Him, unless my Lord wills to give them some influence. But He does not will this regarding me, because: My Lord encompasses all things in knowledge. So it is known that if He created influence in them by which they harm whomever He sends to call to His Oneness, he would be veiled." End of quotation. The first view is closer.

﴿Will you not then take heed?﴾ meaning: Will you not consider that these objects of worship are inanimate, that they neither harm nor benefit, and that the One who benefits and harms is the One who created the heavens and the earth?

The Explanation of His Words, Exalted is He:

[81] ﴿And how should I fear what you associate with Him, when you do not fear that you have associated with Allah that for which He has sent down to you no authority? So which of the two parties is more deserving of security, if you should know?﴾

﴿And how should I fear what you associate﴾ i.e., your objects of worship, which are safe from being feared. ﴿But you do not fear that you have associated with Allah that for which He has sent down to you no authority﴾ i.e., by associating it with Him: ﴿authority﴾ i.e., proof. For associating partners with Allah cannot have any proof behind it. The meaning is: What is the matter with you that you denounce me for feeling secure in a place of security, while you do not denounce yourselves for feeling secure in a place of the greatest and most terrifying dangers? ﴿So which of the two parties﴾ i.e., the party of the monotheists and the party of the polytheists ﴿is more deserving of security﴾ i.e., from being harmed ﴿if you should know﴾ i.e., what deserves to be feared. Or is it: "Which of them is more deserving of security, or [which is more deserving] of the people of knowledge?" The answer to the conditional clause is omitted, i.e., "then inform me."

The commentary then explains who is granted security, in answer to the question Abraham (peace be upon him) raised in his words:

The Discourse on the Interpretation of His Exalted Words:

[82] ﴿Those who believe and do not mix their belief with wrongdoing, those are the ones who will have security, and they are guided.﴾

﴿Those who believe and do not mix their belief with wrongdoing﴾ means: with shirk (associating partners with God), as the polytheists do. They claim that they believe in God, Mighty and Majestic, and that their worship of the idols is a completion of their faith and its rulings, because it is for the sake of drawing near to God and for intercession, as they said: "We only worship them so that they may bring us near to God in closeness." This is the meaning of confusion (al-labs), as Abu al-Su'ud stated, and more on this will come later.

﴿Those are the ones who will have security﴾ on the Day of Resurrection. ﴿And they are guided﴾, that is, to the truth, while everyone other than them is in error.

Al-Bukhari, Muslim and others narrated from Abdullah (ibn Mas'ud) who said: "When the verse ﴿and do not mix their belief with wrongdoing﴾ was revealed, his companions said: 'And which of us has not wronged himself?' Then the verse was revealed: ﴿Indeed, shirk is a great wrong﴾ [Luqman: 13]." This is the wording of al-Bukhari's narration.

The wording of Imam Ahmad's narration from Abdullah is: "When this verse was revealed: ﴿Those who believe and do not mix their belief with wrongdoing﴾, it weighed heavily on the people, and they said: 'O Messenger of God! Which of us does not wrong himself?' He said: 'It is not what you mean.
