Have you not heard what the righteous servant said: ﴿O my son, do not associate anything with God; indeed, shirk is a great wrong﴾? It is only shirk.'"

I say: this narration clarifies the earlier narration of al-Bukhari, namely the statement of Ibn Mas'ud: "Then it was revealed: Indeed, shirk..." etc., in that the word "revelation" (nuzul) here is meant as the explanation of the verse, not its occasion of revelation (sabab al-nuzul). This is a precise technical usage of the Companions and the Successors (al-tabi'un), and one must be attentive to it. We have already pointed this out in the introduction, so return to it.

Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Abdullah, traced to the Prophet (ﷺ): "'And do not mix their belief with wrongdoing': he said, 'with shirk.'"

He said: It has also been narrated from Abu Bakr, Umar, Ubayy ibn Ka'b, Huthayfah, Ibn Abbas, Ibn Umar, Amr ibn Shurahbil, Abu Abd al-Rahman al-Sulami, Mujahid, Ikrimah, al-Nakha'i, al-Dahhak, Qatadah, al-Suddi, and others, something similar to this. Ibn Kathir transmitted it. In sum, no dissent is known among the Companions and the Successors regarding the interpretation of "wrongdoing" (al-zulm) here as shirk, adhering to the authentic hadith on this, which explains the Qur'anic parallels, some of which clarify what is ambiguous in others. Recognizing this principle from such a hadith uncovers many confusions. If it is said: "From His saying, ﴿Indeed, shirk is a great wrong﴾ [Luqman: 13], it does not follow that other than shirk cannot be wrongdoing," the answer is: the tanwin in "wrongdoing" (bi-zulmin) is for magnification, as if it were said: "They did not mix their belief with a great wrong." And since it has become clear that shirk is a great wrong, it is known that what is meant is: "They did not mix their belief with shirk," or that what comes first to mind from the unqualified term is its most complete instance. Thus said al-Inayah.

Al-Razi said: The evidence that this is what is meant is that this whole story from beginning to end came only to deny partners, rivals and equals to God, and there is no mention in it of acts of obedience or worship. Therefore it is necessary to understand "wrongdoing" here in that sense.

Note:

Since it is known that the Truthful, the one whose truthfulness is affirmed (ﷺ), explained the verse in the manner already mentioned, one should hold firmly to it with the molars. As for what al-Zamakhshari uttered in his interpretation of the verse, namely: "That is, they did not mix their faith with disobedience that makes them corrupt (fasiq), and he refused to interpret wrongdoing as disbelief," and [he objected to] the word "confusion" (al-labs), because mixing belief with shirk, i.e., combining it with it, is unimaginable, since they are opposites that cannot coexist according to his claim, this is refuted: it can indeed be mixed with it. For if by belief is meant mere assent, whether by the tongue or otherwise, it is evident that it can coexist with shirk, as with the hypocrite. Likewise, if by belief is meant the assent of the heart, it is possible for one to assent to the existence of the Creator without assenting to His oneness, as in His saying, ﴿And most of them do not believe in God except that they are associators﴾ [Yusuf: 106], which was pointed out earlier. And if it is meant as assent to everything that must be assented to, such that one exits disbelief, then mixing belief with shirk does not require combining the two in such a way that one is truly described as both a believer and a polytheist. Rather, it means covering it with disbelief and making it subdued and extinguished, or being characterized by belief, then disbelief, then belief, then disbelief repeatedly. And even granting what has been mentioned, restricting security to non-sinners does not necessitate that sinners are certainly punished, but rather that they are fearful of that, anticipating it as a possibility, with the likelihood of its occurrence being dominant. Thus said the commentary on al-Kashshaf.

In al-Intisaf: Al-Zamakhshari only aims by this to bring the verse into line with his doctrine concerning the obligation of the threat against sinners, and that they have no share in security, like the disbelievers. He makes this verse imply that security is restricted to those who combine the two matters: belief and freedom from sins. We grant that, but it does not follow that the fear that befalls sinners is the same fear that befalls disbelievers, because sinful believers fear only a temporary punishment, and they are secure from eternity in it. As for the disbelievers, they are not secure in any way. End.

As for the statement of the Mu'tazilah: the hadith of Abdullah mentioned above, if it is authentic, is a solitary report (khabar al-wahid), against a decisive proof, and such a thing is not acted upon. The answer is: it is indeed authentic beyond doubt, since al-Bukhari and Muslim (the two Shaykhs) included it.

"And when the river of God comes, the river of Ma'qil is nullified."

Their statement "against a decisive proof" is a great slander. How strange are these people, who set the authentic Sunnah against the dregs of opinion, and were not ashamed before God and His Messenger in this opposition. Where do their minds go, toward the truth or toward falsehood? But as Ibn Sahl said:

"How wasted is proof in the presence of the blind follower."

Furthermore, Ibn Mardawayh narrated from Sa'id ibn Jubayr, from Ibn Abbas, who said: "We were with the Messenger of God (ﷺ) on a journey he was making, when a Bedouin met him and said: 'O Messenger of God! By the One who sent you with the truth! I have left my lands, my people and my wealth, to be guided by your guidance and to take from your words. I have not reached you until I have no food except from the greens of the earth, so present (Islam) to me.' The Messenger of God (ﷺ) presented it to him, and he accepted. We crowded around him, and the hoof of his camel entered a rats' hole, so the Bedouin fell and his neck was broken. The Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: 'He spoke truly! By the One who sent me with the truth! He left his lands, his people and his wealth to be guided by my guidance and to take from my words, and he did not reach me until he had no food except from the greens of the earth. Have you heard of one who did a little and was rewarded much? This is one of them! Have you heard of: ﴿Those who believe and do not mix their belief with wrongdoing, those are the ones who will have security, and they are guided﴾? Indeed, this is one of them.' In another wording he said: 'This one did a little and was rewarded much.'"

Imam Ahmad narrated something similar from Jarir ibn Abdullah at length, and in it is the explanation of his words "present (Islam) to me." Its wording is: "What is faith?" He said: "That you testify that there is no god but God, and that Muhammad is the Messenger of God, that you establish prayer, pay zakat, fast Ramadan, and make pilgrimage to the House." He said: "I have affirmed it."

(p-2392) The discussion on the interpretation of His words, exalted is He:

[83] ﴿And that was Our argument, which We gave to Abraham against his people. We raise in degrees whom We will. Indeed, your Lord is All-Wise, All-Knowing.﴾

His words, exalted is He: ﴿And that﴾ means: the proofs indicated in His words, "Do you take idols as gods?" up to here. ﴿Our argument﴾ means: it cannot be refuted. ﴿We gave it to Abraham﴾ means: We guided him to it and taught it to him without any intermediary teacher. ﴿Against his people﴾ is connected to "Our argument" if "that" is taken as the predicate (khabar, the predicate of the subject), and to a deleted element if it is taken as an apposition (badal, a noun that repeats and clarifies the preceding noun). That is, "We gave it as a proof and evidence against his numerous people, so that he alone would prevail."

﴿We raise in degrees whom We will﴾ means: in knowledge and wisdom. It is also read with tanwin (التَّنْوِين, the nunation, the added "n" sound at the end of a noun). ﴿Indeed, your Lord is All-Wise﴾ in His raising and lowering. ﴿All-Knowing﴾ of the state of the one whom He raises and of his readiness for it.

Commentary of al-Qasimi (Mahasin al-Ta'wil) on surah 6, verses 84–86:

The discussion of the interpretation of His saying, Exalted is He:

[84] ﴿And We gave him Isaac and Jacob; each We guided, and Noah We guided before, and among his descendants David and Solomon and Job and Joseph and Moses and Aaron. Thus do We reward the good-doers.﴾

[85] ﴿And Zechariah and John and Jesus and Elias; each was of the righteous.﴾ [al-An'am: 85]

[86] ﴿And Ishmael and Elisha and Jonah and Lot; and each We preferred over the worlds.﴾ [al-An'am: 86]

﴿And We gave him﴾ means: to Abraham, as a replacement for his people when he withdrew from them and from what they worshipped. ﴿Isaac and Jacob﴾ means: a son, and a grandson, so that his eye would be comforted by the continuation of his lineage. ﴿Each We guided﴾ means: each of them We guided with the great guidance, by their joining their father in prophethood, as He, Exalted is He, said: ﴿So when he withdrew from them and what they worshipped besides Allah, We gave him Isaac and Jacob, and each We made a prophet﴾ [Maryam: 49].

(p-2393) Ibn Kathir said: He, Exalted is He, mentions that He gave Abraham Isaac, after he had grown old and he and his wife Sarah had despaired of children. The angels came to him while they were going to the people of Lot, and they gave him the good news of Isaac. The woman was amazed at this: ﴿She said, "Woe to me! Shall I give birth while I am an old woman and this is my husband, an old man? Indeed, this is an astonishing thing!"﴾ [Hud: 72] ﴿They said, "Are you amazed at the decree of Allah? The mercy of Allah and His blessings be upon you, people of the house. Indeed, He is Praiseworthy and Glorious."﴾ [Hud: 73] So they gave them the good news, and she was amazed. They gave them the good news, along with his existence, of his prophethood and that he would have offspring and descendants, as He, Exalted is He, said: ﴿And We gave him the good news of Isaac, a prophet from among the righteous﴾ [al-Saffat: 112]. This is more complete in the good news and greater in blessing. And He said: ﴿So We gave her the good news of Isaac and, after Isaac, Jacob﴾ [Hud: 71], meaning: a child will be born to this newborn during your lifetimes, so that your eyes will be comforted by him just as they were comforted by his father. Indeed, joy at a grandchild is intense, for the continuation of the lineage and descendants. Since the child of an old man and an old woman might be thought to have no descendants because of his weakness, the good news was given of him and of a son named Jacob, in whose name is derived the notion of lineage and offspring. This recompense was for Abraham, peace be upon him, when he withdrew from his people and left them, distanced himself from them, and migrated from their lands, going to worship Allah on the earth. So Allah, Mighty and Majestic, compensated him for his people and kin with righteous children from his own loins, upon his religion, so that his eye would be comforted by them, as He, Exalted is He, said: ﴿So when he withdrew from them and what they worshipped﴾ [Maryam: 49], the verse...

﴿And Noah We guided before﴾ means: before him; We guided him as We guided him. He counted his guidance as a blessing upon Abraham, insofar as he was his father, and the nobility of the father extends to the son.

(p-2394) Ibn Kathir said: Each of them has a great distinction. As for Noah, peace be upon him, when Allah drowned the people of the earth, except those who believed in him, who were those who accompanied him in the ark, Allah made his descendants the ones who remained, so all of mankind is from his descendants. As for the Friend (Khalil) Abraham, peace be upon him, Allah, Mighty and Majestic, did not send any prophet after him except from his descendants, as He, Exalted is He, said: ﴿And We placed in his descendants prophethood and the Book﴾ [al-'Ankabut: 27], the verse... And He, Exalted is He, said: ﴿And We had certainly sent Noah and Abraham and placed in their descendants prophethood and the Book﴾ [al-Hadid: 26]. And He, Exalted is He, said: ﴿Those are the ones upon whom Allah bestowed favor from among the prophets, of the descendants of Adam and of those We carried with Noah, and of the descendants of Abraham and Israel, and of those We guided and chose. When the verses of the Most Merciful were recited to them, they fell in prostration and weeping﴾ [Maryam: 58].

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And among his descendants﴾: the pronoun refers to Abraham or to Noah, as will come. ﴿David﴾ is coordinated with "Noah," meaning: and We guided David and Solomon and Job and Joseph and Moses and Aaron, and thus do We reward the good-doers.

﴿And Zechariah and John and Jesus and Elias; each was of the righteous﴾ [al-An'am: 85]

﴿And Ishmael and Elisha and Jonah and Lot; and each We preferred over the worlds﴾ [al-An'am: 86]

Know that the purpose of these verses, and of what precedes them and what follows them, is to enumerate the kinds of Allah's blessings upon Abraham, peace be upon him, as recompense for his withdrawing from his people and what they worshipped, and his standing up to support monotheism and refute polytheism. So He, Exalted is He, first mentioned the raising of his rank by giving him the proof against his people and singling him out with it; then He made him honored in this world, in lineage and ancestry, root and branch, because he was descended from Noah, the first of the messengers, a general messengership (p-2395), and was granted the pure descendants, the prophets of mankind. Therefore, most scholars held that the pronoun in "and among his descendants" refers to Abraham, because the flow of the verse is to explain his great affairs, as if it were said: "We did not cease raising his ranks after that, when We guided from among his descendants David..." etc. So he is the one intended by mention in these verses. Noah, peace be upon him, was mentioned because Abraham being among his offspring is one of the causes of his elevation, as has preceded. The aim is to confront those polytheists who trace their lineage to him.

[86] ﴿And Ishmael and Elisha and Jonah and Lot; and each We preferred over the worlds.﴾ [al-An'am: 86]

The angels came to him while they were going to the people of Lot, and they gave him the good news of Isaac. The woman was amazed at this: ﴿She said, "Woe to me! Shall I give birth while I am an old woman and this is my husband, an old man? Indeed, this is an astonishing thing!"﴾ [Hud: 72] ﴿They said, "Are you amazed at the decree of Allah? The mercy of Allah and His blessings be upon you, people of the house. Indeed, He is Praiseworthy and Glorious."﴾ [Hud: 73] So they gave them the good news, and she was amazed. So he named him "son," which indicates his entry among the sons. Others said: This is a figurative usage. End.

In al-'Inayah: It was objected to the argument from the inclusion of the sons of a daughter in "descendants" in this verse, that Jesus, peace be upon him, has no father to turn his ascription to the mother into an ascription to himself, so the analogy of others to him does not hold. The matter is disputed, and the one who holds it argued with this verse and the verse of mubahala, where the Prophet ﷺ called al-Hasan and al-Husayn, may Allah be pleased with them both, after it was revealed: "Let us call our sons and your sons" — if we do not say that this is among his special privileges, ﷺ. End.

Second: Ismail, peace be upon him, was not mentioned together with Isaac, but his mention was postponed after him, because the intended mention here is the prophets of the Children of Israel, all of whom are sons of Isaac and Jacob. As for Ismail, none of the prophets came out of his loins except its seal and most excellent, ﷺ. The context does not require mentioning him ﷺ, because he was commanded to argue against the Arabs regarding the negation of polytheism: that when Abraham left his people and what they worshipped for the worship of Allah alone, Allah granted him great blessings in religion and in this world, among them that He gave him children who were prophets. When the one arguing with them is the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, he is not mentioned in this context. For this reason Ismail was not mentioned with Isaac. Al-Razi conveyed this.

Third: Know that He, Exalted is He, mentioned here eighteen prophets, peace be upon them, without order, neither by time nor by merit, because the conjunction "wa" does not imply order. But there is a subtle point in this ordering: Allah, Exalted is He, specified each group of the prophets, peace be upon them, with a kind of honor and excellence. He first mentioned Noah, Abraham, Isaac and Jacob, because they are the roots (usul) of the prophets, and all their lineages return to them. Then among the considered ranks, after prophethood, is kingship, power and authority, and Allah gave David and Solomon a abundant share of that. Among the ranks is patience at the descent of trials, tribulations and hardships, and Allah specified Job, peace be upon him, with this. Then He coordinated with these two ranks one who combined both, Joseph, peace be upon him, for he was patient under trial and hardship until Allah gave him the kingdom of Egypt along with prophethood. Then among the considered ranks in the preference of the prophets, peace be upon them, is the abundance of miracles and the strength of proofs, and Allah specified Moses and Aaron with a large share of that. Then among the considered ranks is asceticism in this world and turning away from it, and Allah specified Zechariah, John, Jesus and Elias, peace be upon them, with that, and for this reason He described them as "of the righteous." Then Allah mentioned, after these prophets, those for whom no followers or law remained: Ismail, Elisha, Jonah and Lot. If we consider this subtle point in this manner, this ordering is among the finest things mentioned, and Allah knows best His intent and the secrets of His Book. (Conveyed by al-Khazin, and its source is al-Razi.)

Fourth: One who holds that the prophets are better than the angels has used His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿and each We preferred over the worlds﴾ [al-An'am: 86], because "al-'alam" (the worlds) is a term for every existent other than Allah, Exalted is He, and so it includes the angel.

Fifth: The point of mentioning "guidance" in His saying ﴿each We guided﴾ is the enumeration of blessings upon Abraham, peace be upon him, through the nobility of roots and branches, as we have previously stated, and a child is not counted as a blessing unless he is guided.

Sixth: Al-Suyuti said in "al-Iklil": One who denies that fronting (taqdim) indicates restriction (hasr) has used His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿each We guided, and Noah We guided﴾.

Commentary of al-Qasimi (Mahasin al-Ta'wil) on surah 6, verse 87:

(p-2399) The discussion on the interpretation of His saying, exalted is He:

[87] ﴿And of their fathers and their offspring and their brothers; and We chose them and guided them to a straight path.﴾

﴿And of their fathers and their offspring and their brothers﴾ is a conjunction (ʿatf) upon "each of them" (kullan) or upon "Noah" (nuhan), meaning: We preferred each of them, and We preferred some of their fathers; or, We guided from among their fathers and those with them to the pure religion (al-din al-khalis) many groups, so the object is omitted. ﴿And We chose them and guided them to a straight path﴾, meaning in beliefs, morals, and deeds. Thus these virtues were also granted to them, and they joined Abraham, so the elevation of his ranks increased.

The discourse on the interpretation of His saying, exalted is He:

[88] ﴿That is the guidance of Allah; He guides therewith whom He wills of His servants. And had they associated (partners with Allah, shirk), what they used to do would have been nullified for them.﴾

﴿That is the guidance of Allah﴾ refers to that which they adhered to. ﴿He guides therewith whom He wills of His servants. And had they associated﴾ i.e., these (people), despite their greatness: ﴿what they used to do would have been nullified for them﴾ of the deeds that were pleasing. So how about those other than them?

Ibn Kathir said: In it is an intensification of the matter of shirk, a severe warning concerning its gravity, and a magnification of the seriousness of being involved in it, like His saying: ﴿And it has certainly been revealed to you and to those before you: If you should associate others with Allah, your work would surely be nullified﴾ [al-Zumar: 65]. And this is a conditional, and a conditional does not imply the possibility of occurrence, like His saying: ﴿Say, "If the Most Merciful had a son, then I would be the first of the worshippers."﴾ [al-Zukhruf: 81], and like His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Had We intended to take a diversion, We would have taken it from Our presence, if We were to be doing [so].﴾ [al-Anbiya: 17]

(p-2400) And like His saying: ﴿Had Allah intended to take a son, He would have chosen from what He creates what He wills. Glorified is He; He is Allah, the One, the Subduer.﴾ [al-Zumar: 4]

**On the interpretation of His words, may He be exalted:**

[89] ﴿Those are the ones to whom We gave the Book, and judgment, and prophethood. If these disbelieve in them, We have entrusted them to a people who are not disbelievers in them.﴾

﴿Those﴾ refers to the eighteen prophets mentioned, and those joined with them, in respect of their being characterized by the guidance and other qualities that were mentioned. ﴿To whom We gave the Book﴾, meaning the category of Book, which is realized in any single one of the heavenly books. By ﴿giving﴾ (ītā') is meant complete comprehension of what it contains of realities, and enablement to grasp its grand and subtle matters. This is more general than whether it occurs by direct revelation at the outset, or by inheritance after it. For not every one of those mentioned received a specific book revealed to him. This is the view of Abu al-Su'ud.

﴿And judgment﴾, meaning wisdom, or the deciding of matters according to what truth and correctness require. ﴿And prophethood﴾. Al-Baydawi and Abu al-Su'ud said: meaning messengership. Al-Khafaji said: although prophethood is more general, what is meant by it here is that which includes messengership, because those mentioned are messengers. End of quotation.

﴿If these disbelieve in them﴾, meaning in these three, ﴿these﴾, meaning the Quraysh. Through their disbelief in the Messenger of God (ﷺ) and in what was revealed to him of the Qur'an, they disbelieve in all that confirms it. ﴿Then We have entrusted them﴾, meaning We have granted success to belief in them, ﴿to a people who are not disbelievers in them﴾. These are the prophets, peace be upon them, those mentioned, and their followers. Or they are the companions of the Prophet (ﷺ), which is the more apparent view, set against the disbelieving Quraysh. That is, their belief is sufficient without the belief of the unbelievers in them. In the metaphorical expression of granting them success in believing in them, through entrustment (tawkīl), whose root meaning is the safekeeping of a thing and attending to it, there is an indication of the magnificence and exaltedness of these matters, and that they ought to be valued in a manner befitting the trust placed in them and the covenant of safekeeping.

Al-Razi said: this verse indicates that God, exalted is He, will support His Prophet, strengthen his religion, and make it dominant over everyone who opposes him, victorious over everyone who contends with him. And this which God, exalted is He, reported has indeed occurred in this place. Thus it operates as a report of the unseen, and so it is a miracle.

The Discussion on the Interpretation of His Words, Exalted is He:

[90] ﴿Those are the ones whom Allah guided, so follow their guidance.﴾ Say: ﴿I do not ask of you any payment for it. It is not but a reminder to the worlds.﴾

﴿Those﴾ refers to the prophets mentioned. ﴿Whom Allah guided﴾, i.e., to the straight path. ﴿So follow their guidance﴾, i.e., follow their way in faith in Allah and His Oneness, the praiseworthy character, the pleasing deeds, and the lofty attributes; act.

Remarks:

The first: Whoever said that the law of those before us is law for us, so long as no abrogating text has come, cited this verse as evidence.

The second: Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him, cited this verse as evidence for the recommendation of prostration in (Sad), because Dawud, upon him be peace, prostrated for it. Al-Bukhari and others narrated it, and the wording of al-Bukhari is: from al-'Awwam, who said: "I asked Mujahid about the prostration in (Sad). He said: I asked Ibn 'Abbas: From where did you prostrate? He said: Do you not recite: ﴿And from his offspring, Dawud and Sulayman﴾ [al-An'am: 84] ﴿Those are the ones whom Allah guided, so follow their guidance﴾. So Dawud was among those whom your Prophet ﷺ was commanded to follow, and Dawud prostrated for it, and the Messenger of Allah ﷺ prostrated for it." 

The third: Al-Razi said: The scholars have argued from this verse that our Messenger ﷺ is more excellent than all the prophets, upon them be prayer and peace. Its explanation: We have shown that the qualities of perfection and the attribute of nobility were scattered among all of them. Dawud and Sulayman were among those who gave thanks for blessings; Ayyub was among those who were patient in trial; Yusuf combined both of these states; Musa, upon him be peace, was the possessor of the strong, dominating law and the manifest miracles; Zakariyya, Yahya, 'Isa and Ilyas were possessors of asceticism; Isma'il was possessor of truthfulness; Yunus was possessor of supplication. Thus it is established that He, Exalted, mentioned each of these prophets because the predominant trait in him was a specific quality of praise and nobility. Then, when He mentioned them all, He commanded our Prophet ﷺ to follow all of them together, as if he was commanded to gather from the qualities of servitude and obedience all the attributes that were scattered among all of them. He is protected from opposing what he was commanded, so it is established that in him was gathered all the perfection that was scattered among them, and it is established that he is the most excellent of them. This is a good deduction.

The fourth: "﴿اقْتَدِهْ﴾" (iqtadih) is read with the ha' silent and retained when pausing, not when continuing. On this reading it is the ha' of pause (ha' as-sakt). Some retain it in continuation as well, because it resembles the ha' of the pronoun. Some read it with a kasra, and there are two views on this:

One: it is also the ha' of pause, made similar to the pronoun ha'; but this is not sound.

The second: it is the ha' of the pronoun referring to the verbal noun; i.e., follow the following (al-iqtida'). A similar example is the line of poetry:

"This is Suraqa, reciting the Qur'an to him; and a man, when bribes are offered, if a wolf meets him..."

Here the ha' is the pronoun of the study (ad-ars), not an object, because (yadrus) has already transitively taken (al-Qur'an). It was said: whoever makes the ha' silent takes it as the ha' of the pronoun, treating continuation as pause. This was stated by Abu al-Baqa'.

As for al-Wahidi's statement: those who retained the ha' aimed to agree with the written codex, since the ha' is written; so they disliked contradicting the script in both pause and continuation, then they retained it. Al-Khafaji said: this is something not fit to mention, because it implies that reading without transmission is imitation of the script. Whoever said it has erred.

"Say: I do not ask of you any payment for it," i.e., for the Qur'an or for conveying it, since the context indicates both, even though neither is explicitly mentioned. "It is not but a reminder to the worlds," i.e., an admonition and reminder to them, so that they may be guided from blindness to guidance.

Remarks:

The first: This indicates that he ﷺ was sent to all creation, of jinn and humankind, and that his call has encompassed all creatures.

The second: Al-Khafaji said: It has been said that the verse indicates that taking payment for teaching and for conveying rulings is permissible. He said: The jurists have discussion on this. End.

Some commentators from the Zaydi school reversed this, saying: In this there is an indication that it is not permissible to take payment for teaching the sciences, because that falls under the category of conveying the message. End.

I say: The verse negates his ﷺ asking them for payment, so that the compliance would not be burdensome for them. As for deriving permissibility or prohibition from it, there is obscurity. The one who holds the first view says: the meaning is: I do not ask you for a fee out of abstinence, even though it would be lawful for me to take it. The one who holds the second says: I do not ask you for payment because I have been forbidden from that.

Ibn al-Qayyim said: As for a gift to the mufti, there is detail: if it is not because of the fatwa, such as one who customarily gives gifts to him, or one who does not know he is a mufti, then there is no harm in accepting it, and it is better to reciprocate. If it is because of the fatwa, then if it is a means to having him issue a ruling he would not give others who do not give him gifts, it is not permissible for him to accept the gift, because it resembles an exchange for the fatwa. As for taking provision from the public treasury, if he is in need of it, it is permissible. If he is independent of it, there are two views on this; this is a disputed case between the collector of zakat and the guardian of the orphan. Whoever equates him with the zakat collector says: the benefit in it is general, so he may take. Whoever equates him with the guardian of the orphan forbids him from taking. The ruling of the judge in this matter is the ruling of the mufti, and indeed the judge is more deserving of prohibition. As for taking a wage, it is not permissible, because issuing a fatwa is a position of conveying from Allah and His Messenger, so it is not permissible to exchange for it, just as if one said: I will not teach you Islam, ablution and prayer except for a wage; or if asked about what is lawful or unlawful, said to the questioner: I will not answer you about it except for a wage; this is definitely forbidden, and he must return the compensation and not own it. End.

In the hadith of 'Abd al-Rahman ibn Shibl from the Prophet ﷺ, he said: "Recite the Qur'an, but do not exaggerate in it, do not neglect it, do not eat by it, and do not make much worldly gain by it." Imam Ahmad narrated it with reporters of the sound collections. It was also narrated by al-Bazzar, and it has supporting reports.

Ahmad and al-Tirmidhi, who graded it sound, narrated from 'Imran ibn Husayn that the Prophet ﷺ said: "Whoever recites the Qur'an, let him ask Allah, Blessed and Exalted, by it, for there will come a people who recite the Qur'an and ask people by it." Ibn Majah and al-Bayhaqi narrated from Ubayy ibn Ka'b who said: "I taught a man the Qur'an and he gave me a bow as a gift. I mentioned that to the Prophet ﷺ and he said: If you take it, you have taken a bow of fire."

There are other hadiths, and from them it has been derived that taking payment for teaching is prohibited.

As for taking payment for recitation, in the two Sahihs from 'Abd Allah ibn Mas'ud, in the story of the stung man, the Prophet ﷺ said: "The most deserving of what you take a wage for is the Book of Allah. You have succeeded; divide it, and set aside a share for me with you."

Allama al-Shawkani said: The hadith "the most deserving of what you take a wage for" is general and applies to teaching, taking payment for recitation when one is asked for it, taking payment for ruqyah, taking what is given to a reciter as a gift because of his being a reciter, and the like. The general wording is specified regarding the teaching of the one obligated, and what remains outside it stays within the general. Some individual instances of the general have specific evidences showing their permissibility, just as the general indicates it. Among those instances are taking payment for ruqyah and teaching a woman in exchange for her dowry. He said: This is how the matter should be clarified here, and resorting to preference is a sign of narrowness of outlook, that is, because one resorts to it only when reconciliation is impossible, and here reconciliation is possible, so it is the more deserving. And Allah is the Granter of success.

(p-2407)

**Commentary on His words, exalted is He (6:91):**

When Exalted God had explained the great status of the Glorious Qur'an, and that it is a great blessing upon all the worlds, He followed this with a statement of their disbelief in it, in a manner that extended to disbelief in all the revealed Books. So Glorified is He said:

(p-2407) The discussion on the interpretation of His words, exalted is He:

[91] ﴿They did not measure God with His true measure when they said, "God has not sent down anything upon any human being." Say, "Who sent down the Book that Moses brought, a light and guidance for people, which you make into scattered pages, displaying some and concealing much? And you were taught what neither you nor your fathers knew." Say, "God," then leave them in their idle talk, playing.﴾

﴿They did not measure God with His true measure﴾: that is, they did not magnify Him as He deserves to be magnified. The word *ḥaqq* (true, due) is in the accusative as a verbal noun (*maṣdar*). In origin it is an adjective of the verbal noun, meaning "His measure, the true one." When it was made a construct with its modified noun, it took the case that its noun would have taken. ﴿when they said, "God has not sent down anything upon any human being"﴾: that is, when they dared to utter this monstrous statement. This was from them an exaggeration in denying the sending down of the Qur'an to the Messenger of God (ﷺ). Therefore they were confronted with what they had no way at all to deny, since it was said, in reply to their general negation, by affirming a particular proposition that is self-evident in acceptance:

﴿Say, "Who sent down the Book that Moses brought, a light"﴾: *nūran* is a state (*ḥāl*) either from the pronoun in *bihi* (with it) or from *al-kitāb* (the Book). ﴿and guidance for people﴾: that is, a radiance from the darkness of ignorance, and an exposition that distinguishes truth from falsehood. ﴿which you make into scattered pages, displaying some﴾: they divide it into sheets, displaying to the people those they select from it. That is: how then can the sending down of something be denied, when this sent-down Book is manifest to sight? The shift from the Torah to mentioning "the Book" and its description, and the situation after it, serves to increase the rebuke, intensify the censure, and silence them completely. ﴿and concealing much﴾: this is coordinated with *tubdūnahā* (displaying some), and the returning pronoun is omitted, meaning "much of it." Or it is an independent sentence with no place in the grammatical analysis (*i'rāb*), meaning "and they conceal much." That is: nevertheless, the rebuke suffices by what they display, which they acknowledge to be true. In this there is a reproach against the People of the Book (*ahl al-kitāb*) for their evil conduct mentioned, since they intend by concealing much of it nothing but altering the religion.

﴿And you were taught﴾: that is, through the tongue of Muhammad (ﷺ): ﴿what neither you nor your fathers knew﴾ of the knowledge (p-2408) which no one doubts is a divine revelation. ﴿Say, "God"﴾: that is, God sent it down, or God sent it down. He commanded him to answer on their behalf, indicating that the answer is determined and that no other can be given, and alerting that they have been stunned, to the point that they are unable to answer.

﴿Then﴾: after the delivery and the establishment of proof: ﴿leave them in their idle talk﴾: that is, in their falsehood. ﴿playing﴾: that is, they act as one who plays, which brings them no benefit and averts no harm from them, while wasting time.

**Note:**

There are two opinions concerning this verse.

The first: it was revealed in Mecca in accordance with the surah, and those who said it were the polytheists, and the rebuke concerns their being made to acknowledge the sending down of the Torah, because it was among the well-known and widely spread matters among them. This is the apparent meaning.

Ibn Kathir said: Ibn 'Abbas, Mujahid and Abd ibn Kathir said: this verse was revealed concerning the Quraysh, and Ibn Jarir chose this view. Ibn Kathir said: and this is the most sound, because the Jews do not deny the sending down of Books from heaven, whereas the disbelievers of the Quraysh denied the prophethood of the Prophet (ﷺ), because he was a human being, as He, exalted is He, said: ﴿Was it a wonder for the people that We revealed to a man from among them, "Warn the people"?﴾ [Yunus: 2], and as His words: ﴿And nothing prevented the people from believing when guidance came to them, except that they said, "Has God sent a human as a messenger?"﴾ [al-Isra': 94]. Likewise they said here: ﴿"God has not sent down anything upon any human being"﴾. So they were made to acknowledge the sending down of (p-2409) the Book that Moses brought, which is the Torah, which they and everyone knew that God sent down to Moses, as a refutation of their statement and a confrontation with their obstinacy. It is well known what existed between the Quraysh and the Jews of Medina of acquaintance, and the Quraysh's acceptance that they were People of the Book, and that they were more knowledgeable than them because of it. This necessitates their acknowledgment of the truth of the Torah and that it was sent down from Him, exalted is He. According to this view, the reading with the third-person verb (*yā'* at the beginning) is evident. And according to the reading with the second-person address, it is a shift (*iltifāt*) from addressing one people to addressing another people. This is a shift considered by men of letters (*udabā'*), as al-Khafaji related. It is treated as a transition from addressing them to addressing the Jewish people, as an implicit rebuke to them that their denial of God's sending down is of the same kind as the conduct of these people regarding the Torah, in falsehood and in not ascribing it to any proof. Then the claim that the address in *ullimtum* (you were taught) is to the believers of Quraysh is not required by the context or the preceding discourse, and it dismantles the sublime composition, like the claim that it is a parenthetical clause (*i'tirāḍ*) of favour upon the Prophet (ﷺ) and his followers for guiding them to argue in the best manner. Rather, the address in it is like its predecessor, and what is meant by teaching them, while they are polytheists, is what they hear and receive from the Prophet (ﷺ) and his Companions, of the choicest revelations and benefits, which no one doubts is a revelation, as we have clarified before.

The second opinion: this verse was revealed in Medina. It is not an objection that this surah is Meccan, while the disputations with the Jews took place in Medina, because many Meccan surahs had Medinan verses attached to them. In that case, their saying "this surah is Meccan" means: except what is excepted from what was attached to it, as al-Suyuti clarified in *al-Itqan* and cited evidence for it. We have already pointed to this at the beginning of this surah, so remember!

Then those who hold that it is Medinan are of different views: some said it was revealed concerning a group of Jews, or concerning Phinehas (Fanhas), or concerning Malik ibn al-Sayf. Ibn Jarir related through the route of Ibn Abi Talha from Ibn 'Abbas, who said: The Jews said, "By God, God has not sent down any Book from heaven," so this was revealed.

(p-2410) Ibn Abi Hatim related from Sa'id ibn Jubayr, as a *mursal* report, who said: "A man of the Jews called Malik ibn al-Sayf came, and disputed with the Prophet (ﷺ). The Prophet (ﷺ) said to him: 'I adjure you by He who sent down the Torah to Moses: do you find in the Torah that God hates the fat rabbi?' — and he was a fat rabbi. He became angry and said: 'God has not sent down anything upon any human being!' His companions said to him: 'Woe to you! Not even upon Moses?' So God sent down: ﴿They did not measure God with His true measure﴾, the verse." Al-Baghawi said: In the story, when the Jews heard that statement from him, they reproached him and said: "Did not God send down the Torah to Moses? Why did you say, 'God has not sent down anything'?" Malik ibn al-Sayf said: "Muhammad made me angry, so I said that!" They said to him: "And when you become angry, you say about God other than the truth!" So they removed him from the rabbinate. After establishing this, there is no meaning in the objection of some that Malik ibn al-Sayf was proud of being a Jew, openly displaying it, and with this view it is absolutely impossible for him to say, "God has not sent down anything upon any human being," because it is clear that he said that in anger, and anger had taken from him its full effect, out of obstinacy and arrogance, as a means to repel what he wanted. Folly may reach its owner to the point that he disowns his own creed and belief, in order to enrage his opponent on his claim. Slips of the tongue regarding the Lord, exalted and sanctified is He, are not excusable, and therefore He, exalted is He, showed the ignorance of that speaker by His words: ﴿They did not measure God with His true measure﴾.

Al-'Allama al-Biqa'i said: Because whoever ascribes to a king of complete sovereignty that he did not disseminate his commands among his subjects, so that they would do what pleases him and avoid what displeases him, has ascribed to him a great deficiency. How much more so when that ascription is a lie? It was attributed to all of them, though only some of them said it, because they did not reply to its speaker and did not swiftly restrain him (p-2411) by force, as an expression of the gravity of the matter and a clarification that everyone who hears of a sign from the signs of God must strive towards it and learn its affairs; whoever disparages it is restrained by whatever power reaches him. He said, referring to the Jews who made that statement, binding them to acknowledge the lie or to be equal to the unlettered (*ummiyyūn*) in clinging to desire without a book, rebuking them, censuring their evil ignorance, their great audacity, their severe impudence and their lack of shame: ﴿Say, "Who sent down the Book that Moses brought?"﴾. That is: say to these fools who dared to utter this statement, without considering its consequences and what follows from it, as a rebuke to them and a confrontation with the monstrous nature of their ignorance: "Who sent down the Book that Moses brought, whose law you claim to hold to? You make it into scattered pages, so that you can use them to conceal what you wish, displaying some to the people," that is, showing them to the people, "and concealing much," that is, of it, which you intend by it to alter the religion. This is according to the reading with the second-person verb. According to the reading with the third-person verb, it is an *iltifāt* indicating intense anger, pointing out that what they said is deserving of being ashamed to mention, let alone to do. His words: ﴿And you were taught﴾: that is, O Jews, through the Book that was sent down to Moses: ﴿what neither you nor your fathers knew﴾: that is, O Jews of this era; ﴿nor your fathers﴾: that is, the ancients. End of al-Biqa'i's words, may God have mercy on him. Concerning his words "And it was attributed to all of them…" and what follows, there is room for objection, because the ascription was not to them, since they were not pleased with it, as the preceding story indicates the opposite. Al-Biqa'i, may God have mercy on him, has another view on the verse. He said: It is possible that it is Meccan, and that their saying this was when the Quraysh sent to them to ask them about him (ﷺ) concerning the matter of his prophethood, so they were argued against by the sending of Moses, peace be upon him, and the sending down of the Torah to him. End. This is close and very persuasive.

In sum, the noble verse is consistent with the aspects mentioned, and it can be applied in interpretation, as we have explained in each case, as a revelation with no trace of any difficulty. Al-Razi found its interpretation difficult and began to raise questions that are of no weight after examining what we have explained. Praise be to God who guided us to this.

**Subtleties:**

The first: Abu al-Su'ud, may God have mercy on him, said: The purpose of the verse is not merely to compel them to acknowledge the sending down of the Torah alone, but the sending down of the Qur'an as well; for acknowledging the sending down of the Torah necessarily entails acknowledging the sending down of the Qur'an with certainty, because it contains clear witnesses to it.

The second: He also said, regarding God's words ﴿you make it into *qarāṭīs*﴾: that is, you place it into cut-up sheets and separated leaves, with the preposition omitted, on the basis of treating *qarāṭīs* as an indefinite adverb of place (*ẓarf mubham*), or you make it the cut-up sheets themselves. In this there is an additional rebuke for their evil conduct, as if they had removed it from the category of Book and treated it as blank sheets free of writing.

The third: God's words ﴿displaying some and concealing much﴾ indicate that it is not permissible to conceal religious knowledge from one who would be guided by it. This was said by some of the Zaydiyya (Zaydis).

The Commentary of al-Qasimi (Mahasin al-Ta'wil) on surah 6, verse 92:

When Allah, exalted is He, nullified their outrageous statement by establishing the revelation of the Torah, He clarified the sending down of what confirms it, with His saying:

The discussion on the interpretation of His saying, exalted is He:

[92] ﴿And this is a Book which We have revealed, blessed, confirming that which was before it, and that you may warn the Mother of Cities (Makkah) and those around it. And those who believe in the Hereafter believe in it, and they are over their prayers ever attentive.﴾

﴿And this﴾ means: the Qur'an. ﴿is a Book which We have revealed, blessed﴾ i.e., abundant in benefits and advantages, because it includes the benefits of both abodes, the sciences of the first and the last, and benefits that are without end.

Al-Razi said: Sciences are either theoretical or practical. The first is the most noble of them, and the most complete of them is knowledge of the essence of Allah, His attributes, His acts, His rulings, and His names. You will not find these sciences more complete or more noble than what you find in this Book.

As for the second: what is sought is either the deeds of the limbs or the deeds of the hearts, and this is called the purification of character and the purifying of the soul. You will not find these two sciences like what you find in this Book. Then the way of Allah, exalted is He, has been that whoever seeks it and holds fast to it, he attains the honour of this world and the felicity of the Hereafter. End. Al-Khafaji said: This has been witnessed in every age.

﴿confirming that which was before it﴾ i.e., of the Torah or of the books that were sent down before it, in establishing the Oneness of Allah, commanding it, negating association with Him, and forbidding it. And in all the foundations of the laws that are not abrogated.

﴿and that you may warn the Mother of Cities﴾ means: Makkah. It was so named because it is the place of the first House set up for mankind, and because it is the qibla and place of pilgrimage for the people of all the towns, and because it is the greatest of the towns in standing, while the others follow it as a branch follows its root. In mentioning it by this name, which indicates what has been mentioned, there is an indication that warning its people entails warning the people of the earth entirely. ﴿And those around it﴾ from the far regions of the earth, east and west. As He said in another verse: ﴿That I may warn you thereby and whomever it reaches﴾ [al-An'am: 19], and His saying: ﴿Say: O mankind, indeed I am the Messenger of Allah to you all﴾ [al-A'raf: 158], and He said: ﴿Blessed is He who sent down the Criterion upon His servant that he may be a warner to the worlds﴾ [al-Furqan: 1], and Allah, exalted is He, said: ﴿And say to those who were given the Scripture and to the unlettered, "Have you submitted?" If they submit, then they have been guided; but if they turn away, then upon you is only the notification. And Allah is Seeing of [His] servants﴾ [Al 'Imran: 20].

(p-2414) It is established in the two Sahihs that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "I have been given five things which none before me was given. Among them: every prophet used to be sent to his own people specifically, and I have been sent to mankind generally."

﴿And those who believe in the Hereafter believe in it, and they are over their prayers ever attentive.﴾ For whoever believes in the Hereafter fears the consequence, and fear does not cease to carry him to reflection and contemplation, until he believes in the Prophet and the Book (and the pronoun may refer to either) and attends to the prayer. What is meant by it is either obedience, metaphorically, or its literal sense, and it is singled out because it is the noblest of acts of worship after faith and the greatest in importance.

Al-Razi said: Do you not see that the name of faith was applied to none of the outward acts of worship except to the prayer, as He, exalted is He, said: ﴿And Allah would not let your faith go to waste. Indeed, Allah is Kind and Merciful to the people﴾ [al-Baqarah: 143], (p-2415) i.e., your prayer. And the name of disbelief was applied to none of the sins except to abandoning the prayer. He, upon whom be blessings and peace, said: "Whoever deliberately abandons the prayer has disbelieved." So when the prayer was singled out with this kind of honour, it is no wonder that Allah singled it out for mention in this place. End.

I say: The aforementioned hadith was narrated by al-Tabarani in his al-Mu'jam al-Awsat from Anas, and it was graded sahih. Its completion is: "then he has disbelieved openly," as in al-Jami' al-Saghir.

Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Masruq, who said regarding this verse: i.e., they guard its appointed times.

The discussion of His saying, Exalted is He:

﴿And who is more unjust than one who invents a lie against Allah, or says, "It has been revealed to me," when nothing has been revealed to him, or who says, "I will reveal the like of what Allah has revealed"? If only you could see when the wrongdoers are in the agonies of death and the angels extend their hands, [saying], "Discharge your souls! Today you will be recompensed with the punishment of humiliation for what you used to say about Allah other than the truth and for being arrogant toward His signs."﴾

﴿And who is more unjust than one who invents a lie against Allah﴾, i.e., fabricates falsehood, by attributing to Him partners or a son, or by ruling on what is lawful and unlawful, like 'Amr ibn Luhayy (a pre-Islamic figure who introduced idolatrous practices) and his likes, who made his own word the word of Allah.

﴿or says, "It has been revealed to me," when nothing has been revealed to him﴾, i.e., one who falsely claims prophethood. This is more severe than fabrication in the claim to prophethood.

Al-Biqa'i (a Qur'an commentator) said: This is a general threat, in the manner of the beautiful Qur'an, encompassing everyone who is characterized by any of these, such as Musaylima (the false prophet of Yamama), al-Aswad al-Ansi (another false claimant to prophethood), and others. Then he said: I saw in the book "Ghayat al-Maqsud fi al-Radd 'ala al-Nasara wa al-Yahud" (The Aim of the Intent in Refuting the Christians and Jews) by Ibn Yahya al-Maghribi, who was among their scholars around the year 560, and then Allah guided him to Islam, and he exposed their scandals: that the rabbis among them claimed that Allah reveals to all of them several times each day. Then he said: The rabbis, who are the most numerous of them, claim that Allah speaks to them concerning every matter with what is correct, and this group is the most hostile of the Jews toward other nations. End of quote.

﴿and who says, "I will reveal the like of what Allah has revealed"﴾, i.e., one who claims that he can produce the equivalent of the revelation of Allah by fabricating speech, such as al-Nadr ibn al-Harith. This is like His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿When Our signs are recited to them, they say, "We have indeed heard. If we wished, we could say the like of this"﴾ (al-Anfal: 31).

Al-Mahayimi said: That is, one who denies the inimitability (i'jaz, the miraculous unmatchability of the Qur'an) of the Qur'an, to the point of saying, "I will reveal the like of what Allah has revealed," even though he knows its inimitability. It is as if he claimed for himself the power of Allah, and as if he claimed divinity for himself. Whoever believes in the Hereafter does not dare to commit these forms of wrongdoing, knowing what awaits the wrongdoers therein, which is explained by His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿If only you could see when the wrongdoers are in the agonies of death﴾, i.e., its hardships, its convulsions, and its distresses, ﴿and the angels extend their hands﴾, i.e., to strike and punish, like His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿If only you could see when the angels take the souls of those who disbelieved, striking their faces and their backs﴾ (al-Anfal: 50).

﴿Discharge your souls!﴾, i.e., saying to them: Bring out to us your spirits from your bodies, as harshness, rebuke, and reproach toward them. Some have inclined to the view that what is mentioned is a figurative expression (majaz, figurative language) of representation (tamthil): the action of the angels in seizing their spirits is likened to the action of a creditor who extends his hand to one owed a debt, and rebukes him in collecting his right without giving respite. In al-Kashshaf (al-Zamakhshari's commentary), it is said that it is a metonymy (kinayah) for that, and there is no literal extending nor literal speech. Al-Nasir (Ibn al-Munir) said in al-Intisaf: There is no need for that. The apparent meaning is that they actually do these things with them, in the forms described. And when it is possible to remain with the literal meaning, there is no departure from it. End of quote.

Ibn Kathir (the hadith scholar and exegete) said: When the disbeliever is at the point of death, the angels bring him tidings of punishment, chains, shackles, the blazing fire, boiling water, and the wrath of the Most Merciful. His soul then scatters through his body, rebels, and refuses to leave. So the angels strike them until their spirits come out of their bodies, saying to them: ﴿Discharge your souls!﴾ End of quote.

I say: Among what supports the literal interpretation is the verse ﴿If only you could see when﴾ (al-Anfal: 50) mentioned above, for it is explicit. And observing the Qur'anic parallels is the greatest means of benefit in the field of interpretation (ta'wil).

Al-Suyuti (the Egyptian scholar) said in al-Iklil: In this verse is the condition of the disbeliever at the time of seizure and the punishment of the grave. Muhammad ibn Qays used it as evidence that the Angel of Death has helpers from among the angels. Ibn Abi Hatim narrated it.

﴿Today﴾, i.e., the time of causing death, or the extended period from death to an endless end, ﴿you will be recompensed with the punishment of humiliation﴾, i.e., severe disgrace, ﴿for what you used to say about Allah other than the truth﴾, such as distortion and the false claim to prophethood. This is audacity toward Allah, containing contempt for Him, as al-Mahayimi said, ﴿and for being arrogant toward His signs﴾, to the point that some of you said: "I will reveal the like of what Allah has revealed."

**The commentary on His words, Exalted is He:**

[94] ﴿And you have certainly come to Us alone, as We created you the first time, and you have left behind what We bestowed upon you, behind your backs. And We do not see with you your intercessors (shufa'a') whom you claimed were partners in regard to you. Your ties have certainly been severed, and what you used to claim has strayed from you.﴾

﴿And you have certainly come to Us﴾, i.e., for the reckoning and the recompense. ﴿Alone﴾ (furada), i.e., separated from wealth and children, and from what you accumulated in this world; or separated from the helpers and the idols that you claimed were your intercessors. *Furada* is the plural of *farid*, like *asir* and *asara* (prisoner and prisoners).

(p-2418) ﴿As We created you the first time﴾, i.e., resembling the beginning of your creation: barefoot, naked, and uncircumcised (*ghurlan*, meaning *qulfan*).

Al-Shaykhan (al-Bukhari and Muslim) narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, who said: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) stood up to give an admonition and said: 'O people! You will be gathered before Allah barefoot, naked, and uncircumcised.' ﴿As We began the first creation, We will repeat it; a promise upon Us; indeed We are ever doers﴾ (Al-Anbiya: 104)."

They also narrated from 'A'isha, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "You will be gathered barefoot, naked, and uncircumcised." 'A'isha said: "I said: 'O Messenger of Allah! Men and women all together, looking at one another?!' He said: 'The matter is too grave for that to concern them.'"

Al-Tabari narrated with his chain from 'A'isha that she recited the saying of Allah, Mighty and Majestic: ﴿And you have certainly come to Us alone, as We created you the first time﴾, and said: "O Messenger of Allah! Alas for shame! Men and women will be gathered (p-2419) altogether, looking at one another's private parts!" The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: ﴿For every one of them that Day is a matter that will occupy him﴾ (Abasa: 37). Men will not look at women, nor women at men; each will be preoccupied with himself."

﴿And you have left behind what We bestowed upon you﴾, i.e., what We favored you with in this world, with which you were preoccupied away from the Hereafter, of wealth, children, servants, and attendants. ﴿Behind your backs﴾, i.e., in this world, and you did not carry from it even a speck. This is a metaphor for their not having spent it on what would benefit them in the Hereafter.

It is established in the Sahih that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "The son of Adam says: 'My wealth! My wealth!' Do you have from your wealth anything except what you ate and consumed, or what you wore and wore out, or what you gave in charity and sent forward?" He added in another narration: "Whatever is other than that will go away, and he will leave it for people."

﴿And We do not see with you your intercessors whom you claimed were partners in regard to you﴾, i.e., partners of Allah in lordship (*rububiyya*) and in the entitlement to worship.

﴿Your ties have certainly been severed﴾. It is read with a *raf'* (nominative vowel). That is, it encompassed you; for *al-bayn* is among the words with contrary meanings (*al-addad*), used both for connection and for separation. It is also read with a *nasb* (accusative vowel), with an implied subject because of what precedes it, meaning: the matter has been severed, or the partnership, or your connection between you. Or it is read as a substitute for its qualifier. The original is: ﴿Your ties have certainly been severed﴾ (*la-qad taqatta'a ma baynakum*), and it has been read so. That is: what was between you of causes and connections has been severed.

﴿And what you used to claim has strayed from you﴾, i.e., what you claimed of hope in the rivals and idols has departed from you, like His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿When those who were followed disown those who followed, and they see the punishment, and their ties are cut off﴾ (Al-Baqara: 166); ﴿And those who followed said: "If only we had another return, we would disown them as they have disowned us." Thus Allah will show them their deeds as regrets upon them, and they will not exit from the Fire﴾ (Al-Baqara: 167). And He, Exalted is He, said: ﴿So when the Trumpet is blown, there will be no kinship among them that Day, nor will they ask one another﴾ (Al-Mu'minun: 101); ﴿And he said: "You have only taken idols besides Allah out of affection among yourselves in the life of this world; then on the Day of Resurrection, some of you will disbelieve in others and some of you will curse others"﴾ (Al-'Ankabut: 25). The verses on this are very numerous.

The Discourse on the Interpretation of His Words, Exalted is He:

[95] ﴿Indeed, Allah is the Splitter of the grain and the date-pit. He brings the living out of the dead and brings the dead out of the living. That is Allah; so how are you deluded away?﴾

﴿Indeed, Allah is the Splitter of the grain and the date-pit﴾ begins a discussion of some of His originated creations that demonstrate the perfection of His power, knowledge and wisdom, following the establishment of the matter of His oneness, Exalted is He. This is to draw attention to the fact that the greatest objective is knowledge of Him, glorified and exalted is He, with all His attributes and acts, and that He is the Originator of things and their Creator. Whoever is so is the one deserving of worship, not these idols which they used to worship, and it also clarifies the error of the polytheism in which they were. The meaning is: the one who deserves worship to the exclusion of others is Allah, who splits the grain from the plant and the pit from the date palm.

Regarding the meaning of (fāliq) (Splitter), there are two views:

The first: it means "creator" (khāliq). This is the view of Ibn ʿAbbas in the narration of al-ʿAwfi from him, and it was also held by al-Ḍaḥḥāk and Muqātil. Al-Wāḥidī said: they took (fāliq) in the sense of (fāṭir) (Originator). Al-Ṭabarī rejected this and said: it is not known in the speech of the Arabs that (faláqa Allāhu al-shayʾ) (God split the thing) means "created." Al-Azharī related from al-Zajjāj its permissibility, and so did al-Majd in al-Qāmūs.

Al-Rāzī said: (al-faṭr) is splitting, and so is (al-falaq). Before a thing entered existence, it was purely non-existent, a pure negation. The intellect conceives of non-existence as an unbroken darkness with no opening, no cleaving and no splitting. When the existent Originator brings it out from non-existence into existence, it is as if, in imagination and supposition, He split that non-existence and cleaved it, and brought the occurrence out of that split. So this interpretation does not preclude taking the Splitter to mean the Bringer into being and the Originator.

The second view, which is the view of most scholars, is that splitting (falq) is cleaving (shaqq). Regarding its meaning there are two opinions:

The first, related from Ibn ʿAbbas, who said: He splits the grain away from the ear of grain, and the pit away from the date palm. This is the view of al-Ḥasan, al-Suddī and Ibn Zayd. Al-Zajjāj said: He splits the dry grain and the pit from the dry husk, and then brings forth from them green leaves.

The second opinion, which is the view of Mujāhid, is that it refers to the two halves that are in the grain and the pit.

This was deemed weak, because it does not indicate the perfection of power.

(al-ḥabb) (grain) is that which has no pit, such as wheat, barley and rice.

(al-nawā) (pits) is the plural of (nawāh) (pit), which is what is found inside the fruit, like the pits of dates, peaches and others.

The Imam al-Rāzī said: Knowing this, we say: when a grain or pit is placed in moist earth and a period of time passes, Allah, exalted is He, causes in that grain or pit a split at its top and another split at its bottom. The first split yields the tree that rises into the air, and the second yields the tree that descends into the earth, known as the roots of the tree. That grain or pit becomes the means by which the rising tree in the air is connected to the descending tree in the earth. Then there are here some wonders:

The first: if the nature of the tree required descent into the depths of the earth, how did the rising tree in the air come forth from it? And if its nature required rising into the air, how did the descending tree in the earth come forth from it? Since two trees came forth from it, while sense and reason witness that the nature of one of the two trees is contrary to the nature of the other, we know that this is not by the requirement of nature and property, but by the requirement of origination, creation, fashioning and invention.

The second: the interior of the earth is a dense, solid body, through which a strong needle cannot pass and into which a sharp, strong knife cannot sink. Yet we observe the tips of those roots in extreme fineness and delicacy, such that if a person rubs them with his finger with the slightest force, they turn into water. Then, with all their extreme delicacy, they are capable of penetrating that hard earth and sinking into the interiors of those dense bodies. The acquisition of these strong powers by these weak bodies, which are in extreme delicacy, must be by the decree of the Mighty, the Wise.

The third: from that pit there grows a tree, and in that tree there arise various natures. The bark of the wood has a particular nature, and inside that bark is the body of the wood, and in that wood is a soft, weak substance resembling carded wool. Then from the trunk of the tree its branches grow, and on the branches leaves appear first, then blossoms and flowers second, then fruit third. Then the fruit may acquire four types of skin, like the walnut: its outermost skin is that green one, beneath it is the skin resembling wood, beneath that is the skin that is like a thin membrane surrounding the kernel, and beneath that is the kernel. The kernel contains a dense body, which is also like a skin, and a subtle body, which is the oil, and this is the primary objective. Thus these bodies, differing in their natures, attributes, colours, shapes and flavours, come into being, despite the equal influence of the natures, the stars, the four seasons and the four elements. This indicates that they came into being only by the management of the Wise, the Merciful, the Chooser, the Capable, and not by the management of natures and elements.

The fourth: you find the four natures present in a single fruit. The citron: its peel is hot and dry, its flesh cold and moist, its juice cold and dry, and its seed hot and dry. Likewise the grape: its skin and its seeds are cold and dry, while its water and flesh are hot and moist. Thus the emergence of these opposing natures and contrary properties from one single grain must be by the bringing into being of the Chooser, the Agent.

The fifth: you find fruits differing. Some have the kernel inside and the shell outside, as in the walnut and the almond. Some have the desired fruit outside, and the wood inside, like the peach and the apricot. Some have a pit that has a kernel, as in the pits of the apricot and the peach. Some have no kernel, as in the date pit. Some fruits have no inner or outer skin, but are entirely edible, like the fig. These are differing conditions among these fruits. Likewise these grains differ in shapes and forms: the shape of wheat is like a half-circle, the shape of barley is like two cones joined at their bases, the shape of lentil is like a circle, and the shape of chickpea is in another manner. These differing shapes must be for secrets and wisdoms, which the Creator knew that their composition could not be perfected except in that shape. Also, the Creator, exalted is He, has deposited in each kind of grain another property and another benefit. Also, one fruit may be food for one animal and poison for another. Thus the difference of these attributes, shapes and conditions, with the unity of natures and the influences of the stars, indicates that all of them came into being only by the fashioning of the Chooser, the Wise Agent.

The sixth: if you take a single leaf from the leaves of the tree, you will find a single straight line in its middle, which in relation to that leaf is like the spinal cord in relation to the human body. Just as many nerves branch from the spinal cord, to the right and the left, in the human body, and then from each branch further branches continue to divide and become finer until they escape the senses and sight because of their smallness, so in that leaf, from that great median line, separate lines branch off, and from each of them other different lines, finer than the first, branch off, and this pattern continues until those lines escape sense and sight. The Exalted Creator did this so that the attractive powers embedded in the body of that leaf are strong enough to draw the subtle earthly parts into those narrow channels. When you have comprehended the Creator's care in producing that single leaf, you know that His care in fashioning the whole tree is more perfect, and you know that His care in forming all plant life is more perfect. Then, when you know that He, exalted is He, created the whole of plant life for the benefit of animals, you know that His care in creating animals is more perfect. And when you know that the purpose of creating all animals is man, you know that His care in creating man is more perfect. Then He, exalted is He, created plants and animals in this world to be food and medicine for man according to his body, and the purpose of creating man is knowledge, love and service, as He, exalted is He, said: "I did not create the jinn and mankind except that they should worship Me" (al-Dhāriyāt 51:56). So look, O wretched one, with the eye of your head at that single leaf of that tree, know the nature of those veins and fibres in it, then move from one level to what is above it, until you know that the final purpose of them is the attainment of knowledge and love in human souls. Then a door of unveilings without end will open for you, and it will become clear to you that the kinds of Allah's blessings upon you are without limit, as He said: ﴿And if you were to count the favour of Allah, you could not enumerate it﴾ [al-Naḥl: 18]. All of this has only become apparent from the manner of the creation of that leaf from the grain and the pit. This is a brief statement in the interpretation of His words, exalted is He: ﴿Indeed, Allah is the Splitter of the grain and the date-pit﴾. Whoever comprehends it will be enabled to divide and diversify these matters without end. We ask Allah for success and guidance. The words of al-Rāzī end, may God Exalted have mercy on him.

﴿He brings the living out of the dead﴾, like the animal out of the sperm-drop, and the fresh, tender plant out of the dry grain. ﴿And brings the dead out of the living﴾, like the sperm-drop and the grain from the living, such as animals and plants.

﴿That is Allah﴾, that is, the Splitter of the grain and the pit, the One who brings the living out of the dead and the reverse, is Allah, the Capable, the One of great majesty, the one alone deserving of worship.

﴿So how are you deluded away?﴾ That is: how are you turned away from Him toward other than Him?

Al-Rāzī said: The purpose of this is that the living and the dead are opposites, mutually contradictory. The emergence of like from like might suggest that it is by nature and property, but the emergence of opposite from opposite is impossible by nature and property. Rather, it must be by the decree of the Wise Decreer and the All-Knowing Manager.

A note:
Al-Zamakhsharī and those who followed him held that the words of Allah, exalted is He, ﴿and brings the dead out of the living﴾ are coordinated with ﴿Splitter﴾ and not with ﴿brings the living out of the dead﴾, because it explains the Splitter of the grain and the pit. This does not suit explanation, even though it is valid to coordinate an active participle with a verb and vice versa, as in His saying: "those spreading their wings and folding them." The correct view is that it is coordinated with "brings the living out of the dead," and its inclusion of additional meaning does not harm its being an explanation. Just as "brings the dead out of the living" is an explanation while including animals and plants. Within it there is the rhetorical device of tabdīl (substitution, a figure of speech in which one term is replaced by a more precise one), as in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿He causes the night to enter into the day and causes the day to enter into the night﴾ [al-Ḥadīd: 6].

[p. 2421] [p. 2422] [p. 2423] [p. 2424] [p. 2425]

(p-٢٤٢٦) Ibn al-Munir said in *al-Intisaf*: All of these have appeared frequently in the verb form, as in His words: ﴿He brings forth the living from the dead and brings forth the dead from the living, and He brings the earth to life after its death. Thus you will be brought forth﴾ [al-Rum: 19], and His words: ﴿Or who controls hearing and sight, and who brings forth the living from the dead and brings forth the dead from the living?﴾ [Yunus: 31]. So the conjoining of one of the two categories to the other, frequently, is evidence that they are twins, linked together, and that separates it from this verse of al-An'am, where it is brought back to ﴿Cleaver of the grain and the date-stone﴾. The correct view, and God knows best, is to say: the original form was that it came in the form of the active participle (*ism al-fa'il*, the agent noun), like its counterparts among the attributes mentioned in this verse, in His words: ﴿Cleaver of the grain﴾ and ﴿Cleaver of the daybreak﴾ [al-An'am: 96], and ﴿and He made the night﴾ [al-An'am: 96], and ﴿and Bringer-forth of the dead from the living﴾. Except that He shifted from the active participle to the imperfect verb (*al-fi'l al-mudari'*, the present-tense verb) in this attribute alone, which is His words: ﴿He brings forth the living from the dead﴾, intending to depict the bringing forth of the living from the dead and to make it present in the mind of the listener. This depiction and this making present is only fully achieved by the imperfect verb in its performance, not by the active participle (p-٢٤٢٧) or the perfect verb. The illustration of this has already passed, with His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Do you not see that God sends down water from the sky, and so the earth becomes green?﴾ [al-Hajj: 63]. He shifted from the perfect verb, which would correspond to His words "sent down" (*anzala*), for this meaning. Among its examples is what is in the verse:

*Indeed I have met the ghoul, as it runs through a wilderness flat as a page,*
*So I struck it without faltering, and it fell prone upon its hands and its chest.*

(p-٢٤٢٨) He shifted to the imperfect verb, intending to depict his bravery and to make it present in the mind of the listener. Among its examples: ﴿Indeed We subjected the mountains to glorify with him at evening and at sunrise﴾ [Sad: 18], ﴿and the birds gathered together﴾ [Sad: 19]. He shifted from "glorifying" (*musabbihat*, the active participle form), though it corresponds to "gathered together" (*mahshurah*), for this reason, and God knows best. Then, this purpose only comes where the concern with it is stronger. There is no doubt that the bringing forth of the living from the dead is more evident as a display of power than its reverse. It is also the first of the two states, and observation begins with it. Then the other category, which is the bringing forth of the dead from the living, is separated from it. So the first is more worthy of being confirmed and emphasized in the soul, and for this reason it always precedes the other category in mention, in accordance with their order in reality. What facilitated and made beautiful the conjoining of the noun to the verb is that the active participle carries the meaning of the imperfect verb, so each of the two may be understood in terms of the other, and there is no fault in conjoining one to the other, and God knows best. End of quotation.

The Interpretation of His Words, Exalted is He:

[96] ﴿He is the Splitter of the daybreak; and He made the night for rest, and the sun and the moon for reckoning. That is the decree of the Mighty, the Knowing.﴾

His words, exalted is He, ﴿Splitter of the daybreak﴾, are another predicate of (inna) [indeed], or of an omitted subject. And (al-isbah) is a verbal noun (masdar) by which the morning (al-subh) is named. Imru' al-Qays said:

"Unquestionably, O long night, will you not clear away with a dawn? Yet the dawn in you is no better."

That is: He splits it [the night] from the darkness of the night. ﴿And He made the night for rest﴾, i.e., He made the darkness something to be rested in and to find tranquility in, as relief from the fatigue of the day. Or, the creatures dwell in it, i.e., they settle down and become still (from al-sukun, stillness). The latter is the more apparent, due to His words, "that you may rest therein." It was also read as (wa-ja'ilu al-layl) [and the Maker of the night].

﴿And the sun and the moon for reckoning﴾, i.e., in varying orbits, so that by them the times may be reckoned, to which worship and transactions are tied, as He mentioned in Surah Yunus in His words: ﴿It is He who made the sun a radiance and the moon a light and measured for it stations that you may know the number of years and the reckoning﴾ [Yunus: 5].

﴿That﴾, i.e., the running by precise reckoning, ﴿is the decree of the Mighty, the Knowing﴾, i.e., the One Dominant over His command, the Knowing of the management of both and of observing wisdom in their affairs.

Remarks:

The first: al-Razi said: His words, exalted is He, ﴿Splitter of the daybreak﴾ [and so on], are another type of proof of the existence of the Creator, His knowledge, His power and His wisdom. The previous type was drawn from the states of plants and animals, while the type mentioned in this verse is drawn from celestial states. This is because splitting the darkness of night with the light of dawn is greater in the perfection of power than splitting the grain and the date-stone to produce plants and trees, and because it is known necessarily that celestial states are greater in hearts and more striking than earthly states. He then established the proof from many aspects, and excelled, may God have mercy on him.

The second: It was read (al-asbah) with an open hamza, as a plural of subh, like qufl and aqfal.

The third: In "al-Bahr al-Kabir": the legal year is lunar, not solar; the solar year is something that arose in the registers of land tax. The reckoning is attributed to the two in the verse because by the rising and setting of the sun the number of days is known, of which months and years are composed; from here it entered... [end of quotation].

The fourth: The Hafiz Ibn Kathir, may God have mercy on him, said: Often, when God the Exalted mentions the creation of night and day, the sun and the moon, He concludes the statement with might and knowledge, as He mentioned in this verse, and as in His words: ﴿And a sign for them is the night; We strip from it the day, and behold, they are in darkness﴾ [Ya-Sin: 37], ﴿And the sun runs toward its resting place; that is the decree of the Mighty, the Knowing﴾ [Ya-Sin: 38].
