And when He mentioned the creation of the heavens and the earth and what is in them at the beginning of Surah Ha-Mim al-Sajdah, He said: ﴿And We adorned the nearest heaven with lamps and as a protection; that is the decree of the Mighty, the Knowing﴾ [Fussilat: 12]. [End of quotation.]

In "al-'Izzah" [might] there is the sense of subjugation, i.e., He who subdued them by making them subservient, so that nothing is accomplished for them except what is intended for them, as He said: ﴿And the sun and the moon and the stars are subjected by His command﴾ [al-A'raf: 54]. It also carries the meaning of complete power.

Al-Razi said: "the Mighty" indicates the perfection of His power, and "the Knowing" indicates the perfection of His knowledge. Its meaning is that the determination of the bodies of the celestial spheres with their specific attributes, their defined constitutions, and their movements measured by specific quantities in slowness and speed, cannot be achieved except by a perfect power connected to all possibilities, and a knowledge penetrating all that is known, universal and particular. This is a declaration that the occurrence of these states and attributes is not by nature or inherent property, but by the specification of a free-choosing agent. And God knows best.

The fifth: Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted from Ibn Abbas, regarding His words, exalted is He, ﴿for reckoning﴾, that he said: it means the number of days, months and years. Qatadah said: they revolve in a reckoning. As-Suyuti said: the verse is therefore a foundation for reckoning and timekeeping. [End.]

Commentary of al-Qasimi (Mahasin al-Ta'wil) on surah 6, verse 97:

Then the Exalted explained His blessing in the stars, following His explanation of His blessing in the two luminaries (al-nayyirayn), to make known the perfection of His power, wisdom and mercy, by His saying, glorified is He:

The discussion on the interpretation (ta'wil) of His saying, exalted is He:

[97] ﴿And it is He who placed for you the stars that you may be guided by them in the darknesses of the land and the sea. We have detailed the signs for a people who know.﴾

﴿And it is He who placed for you the stars that you may be guided by them in the darknesses of the land and the sea﴾ That is: in the darknesses of the night, on the routes of the land and the sea. ﴿We have detailed the signs﴾ That is: We have made the signs clear, as evidence of His power, His wisdom, and the Last Day. ﴿for a people who know﴾ That is: the manner of deriving proof from them. They were created for reasoning (istidlal) that is affected by acting upon what it requires, namely reasoning by them toward knowledge of the Wise Creator, the perfection of His power and knowledge, and His right to be worshipped alone.

Two cautions (tanbihan)

The first: In other than this surah, the Exalted mentioned that these stars are an adornment of the heaven and a means of stoning the devils. One of the early scholars (al-salaf) said: Whoever believes about these stars anything other than three things has erred and lied against God, glorified is He: that God made them an adornment of the heaven, missiles against the devils, and a means of guidance in the darknesses of the land and the sea. Ibn Kathir transmitted this.

I say: His intent is a belief contrary to the sound creed, not the belief that there are other wisdoms and secrets in them beyond these three, since the benefits of created things are not limited. Mentioning one wisdom in a created thing does not negate what lies beyond it, so understand.

The second: al-Suyuti said in al-Iklil: this verse is a foundation for timekeeping (al-miqat) and the proofs of rational matters (adillat al-'aqliyyat),

The Most High then explained another kind of His blessings and proofs of His overwhelming power, by His saying:

The discussion on the interpretation of His saying, the Most High:

[98] ﴿And it is He who produced you from a single soul, and [for you is] a place of settlement and a place of storage. We have detailed the signs for a people who understand﴾

﴿And it is He who produced you from a single soul﴾ meaning: Adam, peace be upon him. ﴿A place of settlement and a place of storage﴾ It is read as "mustaqarr" with a fatḥah and with a kasrah on the qāf, but "mustawda'" is read only with a fatḥah on the dāl. On the first reading, both may be verbal nouns (maṣdar), meaning: for you is settlement and deposit; or they may be nouns of place (ism makān), meaning: a place of settlement and a place of deposit. Settlement may be in the loins (aṣlāb), or upon the earth, due to His saying, the Most High: ﴿And for you on the earth is a place of settlement and provision for a time﴾ [al-A'raf: 24], or in the wombs, due to His saying, the Most High: ﴿And We cause to settle in the wombs﴾ [al-Hajj: 5]. Or storage is in the wombs, so the loins are made the settling place of the drop (nuṭfah) and the womb its place of storage, because it is produced in the loins, not from another person, and in the womb from the father's side; so it resembles a deposit, as if the man had deposited with it what was with him. Or [the meaning is]: in the loins, or under the earth, or above it, for it is upon it; or it is placed in them so that it will come out from them once more, as in the saying:

"Wealth and family are but deposits, and deposits must one day be returned."

Al-Razi transmitted from al-Asamm that the mustaqarr is whoever was created from the first soul, entered the world and settled in it, and the mustawda' is the one not yet created who will be created. Al-Isfahani made the mustaqarr a metaphor for the male and the mustawda' a metaphor for the female. He said: He expressed the male by "mustaqarr" because the drop is only generated in his loins and only settles there; and He expressed the female by "mustawda'" because her womb resembles a storage place for that drop. And God knows best.

And according to the reading "mustaqirr" with a kasrah on the qāf, it is an active participle (ism fā'il), meaning: among you is one who settles, and among you is one who is stored; the reason the first is known and the second unknown is that settlement proceeds from us, not storage.

Al-Razi said: The intent of the verse is that people were only generated from one person, Adam, peace be upon him, then they differed in settlement and storage according to the aspects mentioned. So we say: human persons are equal in corporeality and differ in the attributes by which the distinction in settlement and storage occurs. The difference in those attributes necessarily has a cause and an agent, and the cause is not corporeality and its necessary properties, for otherwise the occurrence of difference in attributes would be impossible; so the cause must be the free, wise Agent. A parallel to this verse in indicating this is His saying, the Most High: ﴿And the difference of your tongues and your colours﴾ [al-Rum: 22].

﴿We have detailed the signs for a people who understand﴾ Al-Zamakhshari said: If you ask: why was "ya'lamun" (know) said with the mention of the stars, and "yafqahun" (understand) with the mention of the creation of the children of Adam? I say: the creation of mankind from a single soul, and their being turned among varied states, is more subtle and finer in craftsmanship and governance. So the mention of fiqh, which is the use of acumen and close examination, corresponds to it. End of quote. This is based on the view that fiqh is intense understanding and acuteness; but whoever says it is understanding in general, and not more eloquent than 'ilm (knowledge), says it is a variation, to avoid the appearance of repetition.

Al-Nasir said in "al-Intisaf": Al-Zamakhshari's answer is artificial, for otherwise this difference is not realised, and there is no way to the reality.

He said: The verification is that when it was intended to separate the two by a closing phrase, to draw attention to the independence of each of them with respect to the purpose of the argument, it was disliked to separate them by two closing phrases equal in wording, because of the repetition in that; so it turned to a different closing phrase, for embellishing the composition and harmony in eloquence. And there is another possibility (p-2435) in singling out the first with knowledge and the second with fiqh: since the purpose was an allusion to those who do not reflect on the signs of God and do not take lesson from His creatures, and the signs mentioned first were external to the observers' selves and separate from them (the stars, looking at them, and knowledge of the divine wisdom in their governance are a matter external to the observer's self), whereas considering the creation of them from a single soul and their turning through varied stages and differing states does not go beyond the self of the observer. When this is established: the human's ignorance of himself and his states, and not looking into them and reflecting upon them, is more shameful than his ignorance of external matters such as the stars, the spheres, and the measures of their courses and changes. Since fiqh is the lowest rank of knowledge, being an expression for understanding, it was negated from the more shameful of the two kinds of ignorance, namely those who do not perceive within themselves; and negating the lower is more shameful than negating the higher in rank, so it was specified for the worse of the two groups in condition. "Yafqahun" here is the present tense of faqiha al-shay' (with a kasrah on the qāf) when one understands it, even with the least understanding. It is not from faquha (with a ḍammah on the qāf), for that is a high rank, and its meaning is "became a faqih" (jurist) — said by al-Harawi in the context of arguing that fiqh is lower than 'ilm. In the hadith of Salman, that he said when a woman asked him: "faqihat" (she understood), meaning she understood, as one who marvels at the woman's understanding of him. And when it is said: "So-and-so does not understand anything," it is more blameworthy in custom than the saying: "So-and-so does not know anything." It seems that the meaning of your saying "he does not understand anything" is that he lacks the capacity for understanding, even if he understands. As for your saying "he does not know anything," its extent is only the negation of his attaining knowledge, and he may have the capacity for understanding and knowledge, if he were to know. What indicates that one who abandons reflection upon himself is more ignorant and in a worse state than one who abandons reflection upon others is His saying, the Most High: ﴿And in the earth are signs for the certain [of faith]﴾ [al-Dhariyat: 20] ﴿And in yourselves; will you not then see?﴾ [al-Dhariyat: 21]. He specified seeing into the self (p-2436) after it had been included among the signs in the earth, and He denounced those who do not look into themselves with a fresh denunciation. And our statement, within the course of this discussion, that "He negated knowledge from one of the two groups and negated fiqh from the other" is meant by way of allusion, in that He specified knowledge with the detailed signs and understanding of them with a people. This indicates that other people have neither knowledge nor fiqh—and God is the Granter of success. So ponder this section, though it runs somewhat long, for looking into beauty is not tiresome. End of quote. This is among the fine points of inquiry into the Mighty Book, and the display of its beauties and subtleties.

Then Allah, exalted is He, demonstrated a great proof of the perfection of His power and another favour from the magnitude of His bounty, by His saying:

The discussion on the interpretation of His saying, exalted is He:

[99] ﴿It is He who sends down water from the sky, and We bring forth by it the growth of every thing; then We bring forth from it green (growth), from which We bring forth clustered grain; and from the palm tree, from its spathe, hang clusters near at hand, and gardens of grapes, and olives and pomegranates, similar and dissimilar. Look at their fruit when it bears fruit, and at its ripening. Indeed, in that are signs for a people who believe.﴾

﴿It is He who sends down water from the sky﴾: that is, from the clouds. This is based on His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Have you considered the water which you drink? Is it you who bring it down from the cloud, or are We the One who brings it down?﴾ [al-Waqi'a: 68–69]. The cloud is called "sky" (sama') because the Arabs call everything that is high a sky.

﴿And We bring forth by it﴾: the shift to the first-person plural (iltifat, a shift of grammatical person) displays the complete care for the matter for which the water was sent down. That is: We bring forth, by Our might, with that water despite its unity, ﴿the growth of every thing﴾, that is, every kind of plant and fruit, differing in taste and colour, as in His saying: ﴿Watered with one water, yet We make some of them excel others in fruit﴾ [al-Ra'd: 4].

﴿Then We bring forth from it﴾: that is, from the plant, meaning its roots. ﴿Green﴾: that is, something tender and green. It is said: akhdar and khadir, like a'war and 'awir. It is what branches out from the root of the plant emerging from the seed. ﴿From which We bring forth﴾ is a qualifier of (khadiran). The present tense is used to make the scene present to the mind, because of its strangeness. That is: We bring forth from that green (growth) ﴿clustered grain﴾, that is, grain piled one upon another, like the ears of wheat, barley and rice.

Al-Razi said: Above the ear there form fine, sharp bodies, as though they were needles, and their purpose in being created is to prevent birds from picking up those clustered grains.

Then Allah, exalted is He, explained what arises from the date-stone among trees, after explaining what arises from the grain among plants, by His saying, glorified is He: ﴿And from the palm tree, from its spathe, hang clusters near at hand﴾. Al-tal‘ (spathe) is the first thing that appears of the palm's fruit, like sheaths, in which is the 'idhq (stalk). When its sheaths are split open, it is called 'idhq (with a kasra on the ‘ayn and a sukun on the dhal) – and it is the qinw, that is, the 'ur-juwn (the stalk), together with the strands it contains; its plural is qinwan (with the qaf having three vowel forms), and both the singular and dual forms are the same, differing only in i‘rab (grammatical inflection).

Al-Zamakhshari said: qinwan is in the nominative as the subject (mubtada'), and (min al-nakhl) is its predicate, and (min tal‘ihā) is a substitute (badal) for it, as if it were said: and from the spathe of the palm there is a stalk (qinwan). End of quote. It is also permissible that (min al-nakhl) be a coordinated element (ʿatf) on (minhu), and what follows it be a subject and predicate; that is: And We bring forth from the palm tree palms, from whose spathe are clusters near at hand, that is, dense, close to one another, or near to the reach. Only this was mentioned (p-2438) because it implies its opposite, namely the distant ones, as in His saying: ﴿Garments that protect you from the heat﴾ [al-Nahl: 81]; and to increase the blessing in it.

﴿And gardens of grapes﴾ is coordinated (ʿatf) upon (nabata kulli shay'): that is, and We brought forth by it gardens; or upon (khadiran).

Al-Tibi said: The more evident view is that it is coordinated upon (ḥabban), because His saying (nabata kulli shay') is a detail, since it includes every kind of growing thing, as if He had said: We brought forth by the growing things the growth of every thing, producing every kind of growing thing. The growing things are grain, date-stones and the like. His saying (fa-akhrajnā minhu khaḍiran), etc., is a detail of that growth; that is, We brought forth from it green growth by means of the water, so it is a substitute (badal) for the first (fa-akhrajnā), a substitute of inclusion (badal al-ishtimal). From here the details arise: some produce ears with abundant grains, some produce stalks hanging near at hand, and some produce gardens, trellised and untrellised… etc.

﴿And the olive and the pomegranate﴾: the coordination in it is as previously stated. ﴿Similar and dissimilar﴾ is a circumstantial clause (hal) from (al-zaytun), and it suffices with it instead of the circumstance of what follows it. Or it is from (al-rummān) because of its proximity; and the omitted is the circumstance of the first.

Al-Zamakhshari said: It is said: the two things were similar (ishtabaha) and resembled one another (tashabaha), as you say: they were equal and matched (istawayā and tasawayā). The iftiʿal and tafāʿul forms frequently share meaning. It was also read: (mutashābihan wa-ghayra mutashābihin). The meaning is: some of it is similar, and some of it is dissimilar, in form, quantity, colour and taste, and other attributes which indicate the perfection of the power of its Maker and the wisdom of its Originator and Creator.

﴿Look at their fruit when it bears fruit﴾: that is, the fruit of each of these, when it brings forth its fruit, how it is small and weak, so that one can hardly benefit from it. ﴿And at its ripening﴾: that is, and at the state of its ripening and maturity, how it becomes something gathering benefits and delights. That is: look at that with the look of consideration, insight and inference, to (see) the power of the One who measures it, manages it and transfers it, in accordance with mercy and wisdom, from state to state; for in it are great signs indicating that.

As He said: (p-2439) ﴿Indeed, in that are signs for a people who believe﴾: that is, who affirm that He who brought forth this plant and these fruits is the one deserving of worship to the exclusion of all else, or that He is capable of giving life to the dead and resurrecting them. Some of them said: The people used to deny the resurrection, so He argued against them by the transformation of what He created and its transfer from state to state, which is what they know with certainty and witness of the revival of the earth after its death, and the bringing forth of kinds of plants and fruits from it, and that none can do that except Allah, exalted is He. So He made clear that He is likewise able to bring them into existence from their souls and bodies, and to resurrect them by sending rain from the sky, then the growth of bodies like plants, then making them green with life, then shaping their deeds into many forms, adding further matters and branching them out, and giving foods similar in appearance but dissimilar in pleasure, as a reward for them. And Allah knows best.

A subtle point:

Al-Razi said: Know that He, exalted is He, mentioned here four kinds of trees: the palm, the grape, the olive and the pomegranate. He placed grain before trees because grain is sustenance, while the fruits of trees are fruit, and sustenance takes precedence over fruit. The palm was placed before the rest of the fruits because dates function as a staple food for the Arabs, and because the philosophers explained that between it and animals there is a resemblance in many properties, such that this resemblance is not found in other kinds of plants. For this reason the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "For it was created from the remainder of the clay of Adam." The grape was mentioned after the palm because the grape is the most noble of the kinds of fruit; this is because from the first moment it appears it becomes beneficial until the final state. First there appear on the vine fine green threads of sour taste yet pleasant to eat, and from it one can make cooked dishes. Then after that appears the unripe grape (hisrim), which is a noble food for the healthy and the sick, and unripe grape is made into pleasant-tasting drinks beneficial for those with bile disorders, and a cooked dish can be made from it, so it is as though it were the most delicious of sour dishes. Then when the grape is complete it is the most delicious and most desirable of fruits; and hanging grapes can be preserved for a year or less or more (p-2440), and it is in reality the most delicious of stored fruits. Then there remain from it kinds of foodstuffs: raisins, grape-syrup (dibs) and vinegar, and the benefits of these cannot be mentioned except in volumes. The best part of the grape is its seeds, and physicians make from them (jawarshanat, digestive electuaries) of great benefit to the weak, moist stomach. Thus it is established that the grape is, as it were, the sultan of fruits.

As for the olive, it is also very beneficial, for it can be eaten as it is, and much oil separates from it, of great benefit in eating and in all other uses.

As for the pomegranate, its condition is extremely wondrous; for it is a body composed of four parts: its rind, its pith, its seeds and its juice. As for the first three parts, namely the rind, the pith and the seeds, all of them are cold, dry, astringent, and strongly so in these qualities. As for the juice of the pomegranate, it is the opposite of these qualities: it is the most delicious and most refined of drinks, closest to temperate balance, and most suited to moderate natures; it strengthens a weak temperament, and it is food in one respect and medicine in another. Thus He, glorified is He, combined in it two opposites that differ, so that the indication of power and mercy in it is more complete and perfect.

Know that the kinds of plants are too numerous to be explained in volumes; for this reason Allah, exalted is He, mentioned these four categories, which are the most noble kinds of plants, and sufficed with mentioning them as an alert to the rest. End of quote.

I say: The hadith "Honour your aunt, the palm" that is mentioned was narrated by Abu Ya'la, Ibn Abi Hatim, al-Uqayli, Ibn 'Adi, Ibn al-Sunni, Abu Nu'aym and Ibn Mardawayh, from 'Ali (may Allah be pleased with him), as in al-Jami' al-Saghir, and it is marked there as weak.

ولَمّا ذَكَرَ تَعالى هَذِهِ البَراهِينَ، مِن دَلائِلِ العالَمِ العُلْوِيِّ والسُّفْلِيِّ، عَلى عَظِيمِ قُدْرَتِهِ، وباهِرِ حِكْمَتِهِ، ووافِرِ نِعْمَتِهِ، واسْتِحْقاقِهِ لِلْأُلُوهِيَّةِ وحْدَهُ - عَقَّبَها بِتَوْبِيخِ مَن أشْرَكَ بِهِ والرَّدِّ عَلَيْهِ بِقَوْلِهِ سُبْحانَهُ:

[p. 2441] القَوْلُ في تَأْوِيلِ قَوْلِهِ تَعالى:

[١٠٠] ﴿وجَعَلُوا لِلَّهِ شُرَكاءَ الجِنَّ وخَلَقَهم وخَرَقُوا لَهُ بَنِينَ وبَناتٍ بِغَيْرِ عِلْمٍ سُبْحانَهُ وتَعالى عَمّا يَصِفُونَ﴾

﴿وجَعَلُوا لِلَّهِ شُرَكاءَ الجِنَّ﴾ أيْ: جَعَلُوهم شُرَكاءَ لَهُ في العِبادَةِ. فَإنْ قِيلَ: فَكَيْفَ عُبِدَتِ الجِنُّ مَعَ أنَّهم إنَّما كانُوا يَعْبُدُونَ الأصْنامَ؟ فالجَوابُ: أنَّهم ما عَبَدُوها إلّا عَنْ طاعَةِ الجِنِّ، وأمَرَهم بِذَلِكَ. كَقَوْلِهِ: ﴿إنْ يَدْعُونَ مِن دُونِهِ إلا إناثًا وإنْ يَدْعُونَ إلا شَيْطانًا مَرِيدًا﴾ [النساء: ١١٧] ﴿لَعَنَهُ اللَّهُ وقالَ لأتَّخِذَنَّ مِن عِبادِكَ نَصِيبًا مَفْرُوضًا﴾ [النساء: ١١٨] ﴿ولأُضِلَّنَّهم ولأُمَنِّيَنَّهم ولآمُرَنَّهم فَلَيُبَتِّكُنَّ آذانَ الأنْعامِ ولآمُرَنَّهم فَلَيُغَيِّرُنَّ خَلْقَ اللَّهِ ومَن يَتَّخِذِ الشَّيْطانَ ولِيًّا مِن دُونِ اللَّهِ فَقَدْ خَسِرَ خُسْرانًا مُبِينًا﴾ [النساء: ١١٩]. وكَقَوْلِهِ تَعالى: ﴿أفَتَتَّخِذُونَهُ وذُرِّيَّتَهُ أوْلِياءَ مِن دُونِي﴾ [الكهف: ٥٠] الآيَةَ. وقالَ إبْراهِيمُ لِأبِيهِ: ﴿يا أبَتِ لا تَعْبُدِ الشَّيْطانَ إنَّ الشَّيْطانَ كانَ لِلرَّحْمَنِ عَصِيًّا﴾ [مريم: ٤٤]. وكَقَوْلِهِ: ﴿ألَمْ أعْهَدْ إلَيْكم يا بَنِي آدَمَ أنْ لا تَعْبُدُوا الشَّيْطانَ إنَّهُ لَكم عَدُوٌّ مُبِينٌ﴾ [يس: ٦٠] ﴿وأنِ اعْبُدُونِي هَذا صِراطٌ مُسْتَقِيمٌ﴾ [يس: ٦١]. وتَقُولُ المَلائِكَةُ يَوْمَ القِيامَةِ: ﴿سُبْحانَكَ أنْتَ ولِيُّنا مِن دُونِهِمْ بَلْ كانُوا يَعْبُدُونَ الجِنَّ أكْثَرُهم بِهِمْ مُؤْمِنُونَ﴾ [سبإ: ٤١].

[p. 2442] وخَلَقَهم حالٌ مِن فاعِلِ: جَعَلُوا، مُؤَكِّدَةٌ لِما في جَعْلِهِمْ ذَلِكَ مِن كَمالِ القَباحَةِ والبُطْلانِ، بِاعْتِبارِ عِلْمِهِمْ بِمَضْمُونِها. أيْ: وقَدْ عَلِمُوا أنَّ اللَّهَ خالِقُهم دُونَ الجِنِّ: (ولَيْسَ مَن يَخْلُقُ كَمَن لا يَخْلُقُ). وقِيلَ: الضَّمِيرُ لِلشُّرَكاءِ. أيْ: والحالُ أنَّهُ تَعالى خَلَقَ الجِنَّ، فَكَيْفَ يَجْعَلُونَ مَخْلُوقَهُ شَرِيكًا لَهُ؟ كَقَوْلِ إبْراهِيمَ: ﴿قالَ أتَعْبُدُونَ ما تَنْحِتُونَ﴾ [الصافات: ٩٥] ﴿واللَّهُ خَلَقَكم وما تَعْمَلُونَ﴾ [الصافات: ٩٦]. أيْ: وإذا كانَ هو المُسْتَقِلَّ بِالخالِقِيَّةِ، وجَبَ أنْ يُفْرَدَ بِالعِبادَةِ، وحْدَهُ لا شَرِيكَ لَهُ.

تَنْبِيهٌ:

ما ذَكَرْناهُ مِن مَعْنى قَوْلِهِ تَعالى: ﴿وجَعَلُوا لِلَّهِ شُرَكاءَ الجِنَّ﴾ أنَّهم أطاعُوا الجِنَّ في عِبادَةِ الأوْثانِ، هو ما قَرَّرَهُ ابْنُ كَثِيرٍ، وأيَّدَهُ بِالنَّظائِرِ المُتَقَدِّمَةِ، ونُقِلَ عَنِ الحَسَنِ، فَتَكُونُ الكِنايَةُ لِمُشْرِكِي العَرَبِ. وقِيلَ: المُرادُ بِالجِنِّ المَلائِكَةُ، فَإنَّهم عَبَدُوهم وقالُوا عَنْهم بَناتُ اللَّهِ. وكِلا الأمْرَيْنِ مُوجِبٌ لِلشَّرِيكِ. أمّا الأوَّلُ فَظاهِرٌ. وأمّا الثّانِي فَلِأنَّ الوَلَدَ كُفْءُ الوالِدِ، فَيُشارِكُهُ في صِفاتِ الأُلُوهِيَّةِ. وتَسْمِيَةُ المَلائِكَةِ (جِنًّا) حَقِيقَةٌ، لِشُمُولِ لَفْظِ الجِنِّ لَهم. وقِيلَ: اسْتِعارَةٌ. أيْ: عَبَدُوا ما هو كالجِنِّ، فَيَكُونُ مَخْلُوقًا مُسْتَتِرًا عَنِ الأعْيُنِ.

وذَهَبَ بَعْضُ السَّلَفِ - مِنهُمُ الكَلْبِيُّ - إلى أنَّها نَزَلَتْ في الثَّنَوِيَّةِ القائِلِينَ بِأنَّ لِلْعالَمِ إلَهَيْنِ: أحَدُهُما خالِقُ الخَيْرِ وكُلِّ نافِعٍ. وثانِيهِما خالِقُ الشَّرِّ وكُلِّ ضارٍّ. ونَقَلَهُ ابْنُ الجَوْزِيِّ عَنِ ابْنِ السّائِبِ. وحَكاهُ الفَخْرُ عَنِ ابْنِ عَبّاسٍ رَضِيَ اللَّهُ عَنْهُ، وأنَّهُ قالَ: نَزَلَتْ في الزَّنادِقَةِ الَّذِينَ قالُوا: إنَّ اللَّهَ وإبْلِيسَ أخَوانِ. فاللَّهُ تَعالى خالِقُ النّاسِ والدَّوابِّ والأنْعامِ والخَيْراتِ؛ وإبْلِيسُ خالِقُ السِّباعِ والحَيّاتِ والعَقارِبِ والشُّرُورِ.

قالَ الرّازِيُّ: وقَوْلُ ابْنِ عَبّاسٍ المَذْكُورِ أحْسَنُ الوُجُوهِ المَذْكُورَةِ في هَذِهِ الآيَةِ، وذَلِكَ [p. 2443] لِأنَّ بِهَذا الوَجْهِ يَحْصُلُ لِهَذِهِ الآيَةِ مَزِيدُ فائِدَةٍ مُغايِرَةٍ لِما سَبَقَ ذِكْرُهُ في هَذِهِ الآياتِ المُتَقَدِّمَةِ.

وقَوّى ابْنُ عَبّاسٍ قَوْلَهُ المَذْكُورَ بِقَوْلِهِ تَعالى: ﴿وجَعَلُوا بَيْنَهُ وبَيْنَ الجِنَّةِ نَسَبًا﴾ [الصافات: ١٥٨]. وإنَّما وُصِفَ بِكَوْنِهِ مِنَ الجِنِّ؛ لِأنَّ لَفْظَ الجِنِّ مُشْتَقٌّ مِنَ الِاسْتِتارِ، والمَلائِكَةُ والرُّوحانِيُّونَ مُسْتَتِرَةٌ مِنَ العُيُونِ، فَلِذَلِكَ أطْلَقَ لَفْظَ الجِنِّ عَلَيْها.

قالَ الفَخْرُ: هَذا مَذْهَبُ المَجُوسِ. وإنَّما قالَ ابْنُ عَبّاسٍ: هَذا قَوْلُ الزَّنادِقَةِ؛ لِأنَّ المَجُوسَ يُلَقَّبُونَ بِالزَّنادِقَةِ؛ لِأنَّ الكِتابَ الَّذِي زَعَمَ زَرادُشْتُ أنَّهُ نَزَلَ عَلَيْهِ مِن عِنْدِ اللَّهِ مُسَمًّى بِ(الزِّنْدِ)، والمَنسُوبُ إلَيْهِ يُسَمّى (زِنْدِيٌّ)، ثُمَّ عُرِّبَ فَقِيلَ: (زِنْدِيقٌ)، ثُمَّ جُمِعَ فَقِيلَ: (زَنادِقَةٌ). واعْلَمْ أنَّ المَجُوسَ قالُوا: كُلُّ ما في هَذا العالَمِ مِنَ الخَيْراتِ فَهو مِن (يَزْدانَ)، وجَمِيعُ ما فِيهِ مِنَ الشُّرُورِ فَهو مِن (أهْرَمَن) (وهُوَ المُسَمّى بِإبْلِيسَ في شَرْعِنا). ثُمَّ اخْتَلَفُوا؛ فالأكْثَرُونَ مِنهم عَلى أنَّ (أهْرَمَن) مُحْدَثٌ، ولَهم في كَيْفِيَّةِ حُدُوثِهِ أقْوالٌ عَجِيبَةٌ. والأقَلُّونَ مِنهم قالُوا: إنَّهُ قَدِيمٌ أزَلِيٌّ. وعَلى القَوْلَيْنِ فَقَدِ اتَّفَقُوا عَلى أنَّهُ شَرِيكُ اللَّهِ في تَدْبِيرِ هَذا العالَمِ، فَخَيْراتُ هَذا العالَمِ مِنَ اللَّهِ تَعالى، وشُرُورُهُ مِن إبْلِيسَ. فَهَذا شَرْحُ ما قالَهُ ابْنُ عَبّاسٍ رَضِيَ اللَّهُ عَنْهُما. وإنَّما جُمِعَ حِينَئِذٍ في الآيَةِ، لِكَوْنِهِ مَعَ أتْباعِهِ كَأنَّهم مَعْبُودُونَ.

ثُمَّ قالَ الرّازِيُّ: وقَوْلُهُ تَعالى: ﴿وخَلَقَهُمْ﴾ إشارَةٌ إلى الدَّلِيلِ القاطِعِ عَلى فَسادِ كَوْنِ إبْلِيسَ شَرِيكًا، وتَقْرِيرُهُ أنّا نَقَلْنا عَنِ المَجُوسِ أنَّ الأكْثَرِينَ مِنهم مُعْتَرِفُونَ بِأنَّ إبْلِيسَ لَيْسَ بِقَدِيمٍ، بَلْ هو مُحْدَثٌ. إذا ثَبَتَ هَذا فَنَقُولُ: إنَّ كُلَّ مُحْدَثٍ فَلَهُ خالِقٌ ومُوجِدٌ، وما ذَلِكَ إلّا اللَّهُ سُبْحانَهُ وتَعالى. فَهَؤُلاءِ المَجُوسُ يَلْزَمُهُمُ القَطْعُ بِأنَّ خالِقَ إبْلِيسَ هو اللَّهُ تَعالى. ولَمّا كانَ إبْلِيسُ أصْلًا لِجَمِيعِ الشُّرُورِ والآفاتِ والمَفاسِدِ والقَبائِحِ، والمَجُوسُ سَلَّمُوا أنَّ خالِقَهُ هو اللَّهُ تَعالى، فَحِينَئِذٍ قَدْ سَلَّمُوا أنَّ إلَهَ العالَمِ هو الخالِقُ لِما هو أصْلُ الشُّرُورِ والقَبائِحِ والمَفاسِدِ. وإذا كانَ كَذَلِكَ امْتَنَعَ عَلَيْهِمْ أنْ يَقُولُوا: لا بُدَّ مِن إلَهَيْنِ، فَسَقَطَ قَوْلُهم. انْتَهى مُلَخَّصًا.

[p. 2444] وقَوْلُهُ تَعالى: ﴿وخَرَقُوا لَهُ﴾ أيِ: اخْتَلَقُوا وافْتَرَوْا لَهُ: ﴿بَنِينَ﴾ كَقَوْلِ أهْلِ الكِتابَيْنِ في المَسِيحِ وعُزَيْرٍ، ﴿وبَناتٍ﴾ كَقَوْلِ بَعْضِ العَرَبِ في المَلائِكَةِ.

قالَ الزَّمَخْشَرِيُّ: يُقالُ: خَلَقَ الإفْكَ وخَرَقَهُ واخْتَلَقَهُ بِمَعْنًى. وسُئِلَ الحَسَنُ عَنْهُ فَقالَ: كَلِمَةٌ عَرَبِيَّةٌ كانَتِ العَرَبُ تَقُولُها. كانَ الرَّجُلُ إذا كَذَبَ كِذْبَةً في نادِي القَوْمِ يَقُولُ لَهُ بَعْضُهُمْ: قَدْ خَرَقَها واللَّهِ! ويَجُوزُ أنْ يَكُونَ مِن (خَرَقَ الثَّوْبَ) إذا شَقَّهُ، أيِ: اشْتَقُّوا لَهُ بَنِينَ وبَناتٍ. وقُرِئَ: ﴿وخَرَّقُوا﴾ بِالتَّشْدِيدِ لِلتَّكْثِيرِ لِقَوْلِهِ ﴿بَنِينَ وبَناتٍ﴾.

﴿بِغَيْرِ عِلْمٍ﴾ أيْ: مِن غَيْرِ أنْ يَعْلَمُوا حَقِيقَةَ ما قالُوهُ مِن خَطَأٍ أوْ صَوابٍ، ولَكِنْ رَمْيًا بِقَوْلٍ عَنْ عَمًى وجَهالَةٍ، مِن غَيْرِ فِكْرٍ ورَوِيَّةٍ، أوْ بِغَيْرِ عِلْمٍ بِمَرْتَبَةِ ما قالُوا، وأنَّهُ مِنَ الشَّناعَةِ والبُطْلانِ بِحَيْثُ لا يُقادَرُ قَدْرُهُ. وفِيهِ ذَمٌّ لَهم بِأنَّهم يَقُولُونَ بِمُجَرَّدِ الرَّأْيِ والهَوى. وفِيهِ إشارَةٌ إلى أنَّهُ لا يَجُوزُ أنْ يُنْسَبَ إلَيْهِ تَعالى إلّا ما جَزَمَ بِهِ، وقامَ عَلَيْهِ الدَّلِيلُ.

ثُمَّ نَزَّهَ ذاتَهُ العَلِيَّةَ عَمّا نَسَبُوهُ إلَيْهِ بِقَوْلِهِ: ﴿سُبْحانَهُ وتَعالى عَمّا يَصِفُونَ﴾ مِن أوْصافِ الحَوادِثِ الخَسِيسَةِ مِنَ المُشارَكَةِ والتَّوْلِيدِ.

Then Allah, exalted is He, proceeded to argue against what they had presumed upon with four proofs. He began with one of them, in His words:

The discussion on the interpretation of His words, exalted is He:

[101] ﴿The Originator of the heavens and the earth. How could He have a son when He has no consort and He created all things, and He is, of all things, Knowing.﴾

﴿The Originator of the heavens and the earth﴾ means: the one who brought them into being without a prior model. It has also been said: meaning the one with no equal in them. Abu al-Su'ud said: the first is the more apparent. The meaning is that He, exalted is He, originates the two realms of the upper and lower world without material, acting absolutely, exempt from being affected in any way.

The parent is the origin of the child and is affected by the transfer of its substance from him, so how could it be possible for Him to have a child?

﴿How could He have a son when He has no consort?﴾ That is: from where and how could He have a son, as they claim, when, according to their own claim, He also has no consort from whom the child would come? The existence of a child without a mother is impossible by necessity, though its existence without a father is possible. Also, a child arises only between two of the same kind, and He, exalted is He, has no like.

His words, exalted is He, ﴿How could He have a son﴾ form a resumptive (new) sentence, serving to affirm His exemption from it, and the circumstantial clause that follows it confirms the impossibility mentioned.

His words, exalted is He, ﴿and He created all things﴾ form another resumptive sentence, serving to establish what was mentioned of impossibility, or it is a second circumstantial clause confirming it. That is: how could He have a son when He has created all things, encompassed by origination and bringing into existence, among the existents, of which is what they named as a son for Him, exalted is He? So how could it be conceived that the created being should be a son to its Creator? This is what Abu al-Su'ud stated.

﴿And He is, of all things, Knowing﴾ means: intensely knowing, eternally and everlastingly. This is also a resumptive sentence, confirming what precedes it of decisive proofs, against their abominable doctrine. That is: He, glorified is He, by His essence knows all knowables; so if He had a son, he would necessarily have to be characterized by His attributes, among them comprehensive knowledge, and this is negated for anyone other than Allah, exalted is He, by consensus.

(p-2446) The discussion on the ta'wil (interpretation) of His saying, exalted is He:

[102] ﴿That is Allah, your Lord. There is no god except Him, the Creator of all things. So worship Him. And He is Guardian over all things.﴾

﴿That﴾ means: the One described by what preceded, whose rank is far above the ranks of those who are associated with Him or to whom begetting is attributed. ﴿Allah, your Lord, there is no god except Him, the Creator of all things, so worship Him﴾ means: by believing in Him alone, for whoever possesses those attributes deserves to be worshipped alone. ﴿And He is Guardian over all things﴾ means: Watcher and Protector, who manages everything other than Himself, provides for them, and safeguards them by night and by day.

**The discussion of His words, Exalted is He:**

[103] ﴿No vision can perceive Him, but He perceives [all] vision. He is the Subtle, the All-Aware.﴾

His words, Exalted is He, ﴿No vision can perceive Him﴾, are a new sentence (*jumlah mustaʾnafah*). It may be emphasizing His words, Exalted is He, ﴿and He is Guardian over all things﴾ (Al-An'am: 102), mentioned to warn that He is a watcher from a place that cannot be seen, so one should beware. Or it may be emphasizing, in the strongest way, what was established before about His transcendence and exaltedness above their falsehoods, by explaining that the ordinary eyes, which are the eyes of the people of this world, cannot see Him, because of His majesty, greatness and magnificence. How, then, could that Great One be attributed to His loftiness? This is because He, Exalted is He, did not create for the people of this worldly creation any capacity to see His holy Being.

The distinguished gnostic, the Greatest Shaykh (Ibn 'Arabi), may his secret be sanctified, said in his *Futuhat*: The reason people are unable to see their Lord in this world is the weakness of the creation of this abode, except for one whom God has strengthened. This is unlike the creation of the Hereafter, which is stronger. The reason for seeing Him, Exalted is He, in a dream is that sleep is the brother of death. And in a hadith: "Indeed, you will not see your Lord until you die." So the Law only negated seeing God in this world while awake. End of quote.

Some of them said: The ordinary eyes of this world cannot perceive Him, Exalted is He, because these eyeballs, as long as they remain with these attributes that they have in this world, cannot perceive God, Exalted is He. They can perceive Him only when their attributes change and their states are transformed.

In the two Sahihs, from the hadith of Abu Musa al-Ash'ari, may God be pleased with him, who said: The Messenger of God ﷺ said: (p-2447) "Indeed God does not sleep, and it is not fitting for Him to sleep. He lowers the scale and raises it. The deeds of the day are raised to Him before the night, and the deeds of the night before the day. His veil is light, or fire; if He were to unveil it, the splendors of His Face would burn away whatever of His creation His sight reaches."

Ibn Kathir said: In the earlier scriptures it is related that God, Exalted is He, said to Moses when he asked to see Him: "O Moses! No living being sees Me but dies, and nothing dry but crumbles." And He, Exalted is He, said: ﴿And when his Lord revealed Himself to the mountain, He made it crumble to dust, and Moses fell down unconscious. When he recovered, he said: Glory be to You! I have turned to You in repentance, and I am the first of the believers﴾ (Al-A'raf: 143).

I say: That the negated perception in this verse is specifically worldly perception needs no proof or evidence. As for whoever, from some sects, such as the Mu'tazilah, understands from this verse that what is negated is perception in both abodes, he has announced his own ignorance of what the Book of God and the widely transmitted Sunnah of His Messenger ﷺ indicate. As for the Book, there is His words: ﴿Faces that day will be radiant﴾ (Al-Qiyamah: 22), ﴿looking at their Lord﴾ (Al-Qiyamah: 23). As for the Sunnah, there is what is related from Jarir ibn 'Abd Allah al-Bajali, who said: "We were sitting with the Prophet ﷺ when he looked at the moon on the night of the full moon and said: 'Indeed you will see your Lord just as you see this moon, and you will not be harmed in seeing Him (p-2448). So if you are able not to be overcome in prayer before the rising of the sun and before its setting, then do so.'" Then he recited: ﴿And glorify your Lord with praise before the rising of the sun and before its setting﴾ (Qaf: 39).

Ibn Kathir said: Reports have been widely transmitted from Abu Sa'id, Abu Hurayrah, Anas, Jarir, Suhayb, Bilal, and many others among the Companions, from the Prophet ﷺ: "The believers will see God in the Hereafter, on the plain of resurrection and in the gardens of Paradise." End of quote.

The Hafiz Ibn Hajar said in *al-Fath*: The textual evidences are abundant that this occurs in the Hereafter for the people of faith and not for others, and that it is prevented in this world. However, it has been disputed regarding our Prophet ﷺ. End of quote.

Ibn Kathir said: The Mother of the Believers, 'A'ishah, may God be pleased with her, used to affirm seeing in the Hereafter and deny it in this world, and she argued with this verse. End of quote.

From Masruq, who said: "I said to 'A'ishah, may God be pleased with her: O Mother! Did Muhammad ﷺ see his Lord? She said: My hair stood on end at what you said! Where are you from three things? Whoever tells you any of them has lied. Whoever tells you that Muhammad saw his Lord (p-2449) has lied. Then she recited: ﴿No vision can perceive Him, but He perceives [all] vision﴾, and ﴿It is not for any human that God should speak to him except by revelation or from behind a veil﴾ (Ash-Shura: 51). Whoever tells you that he knows what will happen tomorrow has lied. Then she recited: ﴿And no soul knows what it will earn tomorrow﴾ (Luqman: 34). Whoever tells you that he concealed [any part of the revelation] has lied. Then she recited: ﴿O Messenger, convey what has been sent down to you from your Lord﴾ (Al-Ma'idah: 67). But he saw Gabriel in his form twice." Recorded by the two Shaykhs (al-Bukhari and Muslim) and al-Tirmidhi.

Ibn 'Abbas differed with her. From him there is an unrestricted affirmation of seeing, and from him that he saw Him with his heart. The question is discussed at length at the beginning of Surah An-Najm, God willing. Some people held that perception is not the same as mere seeing, but rather knowing the essence or encompassing it.

Ibn Kathir said: Others said: There is no contradiction between affirming seeing and negating perception, for perception is more specific than seeing, and negating the more specific does not necessitate negating the more general. Then these people differed about what the negated perception is. It was said: It is knowledge of the reality, for this no one knows except Him, even if the believers see Him, just as one who sees the moon does not perceive its reality, its essence, or its quiddity. The Great One is more deserving of this, and to Him belongs the highest likeness.

Others said: Perception is more specific than seeing, and it is encompassing. They said: Lack of encompassing does not necessitate lack of seeing, just as lack of encompassing knowledge does not necessitate lack of knowledge. God, Exalted is He, said: ﴿And they cannot encompass Him in knowledge﴾ (Ta-Ha: 110).

(p-2450) In Sahih Muslim: "I cannot enumerate praise of You; You are as You have praised Yourself." This does not necessitate the absence of praise, and likewise here. End of quote.

Al-Nasafi said: The Mu'tazilah's clinging to this verse is untenable, because what is negated is perception, not seeing. Perception is standing at the limits and boundaries of the seen thing, and what is impossible for limits and directions is impossible to perceive, not to see. So perception is treated relative to seeing as encompassing is relative to knowledge. Negating encompassment, which entails standing at the limits and boundaries, does not entail negating knowledge of Him, so likewise here. Moreover, the context of the verse, which is praise, requires the affirmation of seeing, since negating perception of what cannot be seen is not praise. Praise lies only in negating perception while seeing is realized, because its negation while seeing is realized is evidence of the removal of the defect of finitude and limits from the Essence. Thus the verse is a proof for us against them. End of quote.

The scholar al-'Adud, in *al-Mawaqif*, excellently treated this verse, cited the doubts of those who deny it, and answered them. For its excellence, we quote his words along with the commentary of al-Sayyid al-Sharif, may his secret be sanctified, and some of its glosses, and his text is:

The first: Among the doubts of those who deny seeing by sight is His words: ﴿No vision can perceive Him﴾.

1. Perception, when attributed to vision, is seeing. The meaning of your saying "I perceived it with my sight" is the meaning of "I saw it." There is no difference except in wording. Or they are two matters that are mutually entailed, such that it is not valid to negate one while affirming the other (p-2451). So one may not say "I saw Him but did not perceive Him with my sight," nor the reverse. The verse negated that vision perceives Him, and this encompasses all sight through the generic *lam* (*al-lam al-jinsiyyah*) in a context of emphasis, at all times. For your saying "So-and-so is perceived by sight" does not express totality of times, so it must express what is opposite to it: that no sight sees Him, neither in this world nor in the Hereafter, for the reasons we mentioned.

2. Also, He praised Himself by being unseen, for He mentioned it among the praises. Whatever attribute's absence is praise, its presence would be a deficiency, which God must be exalted above. Thus it is clear that seeing Him is impossible. We said "from the attributes" to exclude "acts," such as pardoning and retribution, for the former is grace and the latter is justice, and both are perfections.

The answer:

As for the first aspect of the argument from the verse, there are several points:

The first: Perception is seeing in the manner of encompassing the aspects of the seen thing, since its real meaning is attainment and arrival. "Indeed we are overtaken" (*innā la-mudrakūn*) means: we are caught up. "The fruit ripened" (*adraka al-thamarah*) means: it reached the limit of ripeness. "The boy reached maturity" (*adraka al-ghulām*) means: he came of age. Then it was transferred to encompassing seeing, because it is closer to that reality. Seeing qualified by the mode of encompassment is absolutely more specific than unqualified seeing. Therefore, negating encompassing vision of the Originator, Glorified is He, because encompassment is impossible, does not entail negating unqualified vision of Him. As for his saying "one of them cannot be affirmed while the other is negated," this is disputed. Rather, it is valid to say: "I saw Him, but my sight did not perceive Him," meaning: it did not encompass Him from His aspects, even if it is not valid the other way round.

The second: "Perception by sight" (*tudrikuhu al-abṣār*) is a universal affirmative proposition (*mūjibah kulliyyah*), because its subject is a plural defined by the *lam* of totality (*al-lam al-istighrāqiyyah*). Negation has entered upon it and lifted it, and it has lifted the universal affirmative to a particular negative (*sālibah juz'iyyah*). In sum, His words "No vision can perceive Him" allow for the attribution of negation to the whole, by considering first the entry of negation and then the generality coming upon it, which makes it a universal negative (*sālibah kulliyyah*). They also allow for negation of attribution to the whole, by considering generality first and then negation coming upon it, which makes it a particular negative. Given the possibility of the second meaning, no proof remains for you against us, for the sights of unbelievers do not perceive Him, by consensus (p-2452). This is what we say: If it is established that the *lam* in the plural is for generality and totality, well and good; otherwise we reverse the proposition, and claim the verse is a proof for us. We say: "No vision can perceive Him" is an indefinite negative (*sālibah muhmalah*) in the force of a particular, so the meaning is: "some vision cannot perceive Him." Restricting the negation to some implies by inference the affirmation for others. So the verse is a proof for us, not against us. End of quote. However, this is only correct if the indefinite (*muhmalah*) is synonymous with the particular (*juz'iyyah*). Its being in their force does not establish synonymy. For this reason it was objected that the genus within the scope of negation, as in "The man did not come to me," indicates generality by consensus. The possibility lies only in generality of negation, and generality of negation when totality is intended is complete negation; so how can the proposition be reversed under the assumption that the *lam* is for the genus? Even if synonymy were established, we would not dispel the objection, for the verse would then become a proof for us by necessity, since the qualifier of partiality would return to the negation, just as the moderate interlocutor returned the qualifier of generality to it under the assumption of totality. So reflect! Thus in the marginal glosses of al-Halabi and al-Shirwani.

The third: Among those aspects is that the verse, although it generalizes over persons through the totality of the *lam*, does not generalize over times, for it is an absolute negative (*sālibah muṭlaqah*), not a perpetual one (*dā'imah*). We say in accordance with its ruling: it is not seen in this world.

The scholar Hasan Halabi said: As for what the opponent cited earlier to show that it is perpetual, namely that its affirmation does not express generality of times, so it must express what is opposed to it, the answer to this is: that holds only if the opposition between them is contradictory opposition (*taqābul al-tanāqud*), and this is disputed. For the affirmative and negative propositions, when unmodalized, were not laid down in Arabic for two contradictory meanings. Rather, each has interpretations which the speaker takes according to what he intends.

**Fourth:** The verse indicates that sight does not perceive Him, but it does not follow from this that those who see (the *mubsirin*) do not see Him. It is possible that the negation mentioned in the verse is a negation of seeing with the eye (*bil-jarihah*), in the sense of facing and being imprinted upon the sight, as is customary. Therefore, it does not follow that seeing with the eye is negated absolutely. As for the answer to the second point, namely his saying that the Creator is praised by being described as not seen, we say: this is your claim. Where is the evidence for it? If you say: "It was indicated earlier, by its evidence, that it was mentioned in the course of praises, and what is mentioned between them must be praise," we reply: that evidence only indicates praise through negating being perceivable (*al-mubsariyyah*), not through negating seeing, and the difference was explained in the first answer. End.

If it is established that the context of the speech requires that it is praise, then it provides you no evidence for the impossibility of seeing Him. Rather, it provides us with the proof for the validity of seeing Him, because if seeing Him were impossible, praise would not be achieved by negating it of Him, since there is no praise for the non-existent in being not seen, as it has no such attribute. Praise in the non-seeing lies only in one who is unapproachable and fortified by the veil of greatness, as is the case among the witnessed. End.

Al-Khayali (al-Khayali) objected to their statement "there is no praise for the non-existent" by saying: the non-existent's not being praised is because it contains the source of every deficiency, namely non-existence, whereas the origin of all praiseworthy qualities and perfections is existence, and it is devoid of that. Just as sounds and smells are not praised by the impossibility of their being seen, because they are associated with marks of deficiency.

He said: "The truth is that the impossibility of a thing does not prevent praising by its negation, since praise by negating a partner and negating the taking of a son has occurred in the Qur'an, even though both are impossible with respect to the Exalted." End.

Hasan Halabi (Hasan al-Halabi) agreed with him in *Hawashi Sharh al-Mawaqif* (*Marginal Notes on the Commentary of al-Mawaqif*), but he answered that praise in one respect does not require perfection in other respects, and likewise a deficiency in one respect does not contradict praise in another. End.

Qarah Khalil (Qarah Khalil) answered with several points:

The first: the intention of that arguer was the *ilzam* (imposing an argument on the opponent, i.e., a reductio *ad absurdum* directed against the opponent's position), namely against the Mu'tazilites, not the establishment of proof for the permissibility of seeing.

The second: the basis of his speech is custom and language, for when its people wish to praise something they say: "This is among the things that eyes do not perceive," or "among the things that eyes do not see," even though it is ordinarily among the things perceived. So this statement from them indicates the possibility of seeing that thing customarily, indeed even its actual occurrence. This is unlike sounds, smells and the like, for they are not ordinarily among the things perceived by sight, so it is not fitting to praise them by the non-perception of sight, or by their not being seen. Yes! When they wish to praise sounds they say: "No ear has heard them," and when they wish to praise smells they say: "No nose has smelled them."

The third: we said that negating seeing in a context of praise indicates the possibility of seeing, and we did not say that negating anything in a context of praise indicates the possibility of that thing, so that the counter-objection of negating a partner or negating taking a son in a context of praise would apply to us. Moreover, the possibility of what is negated in the counter-example is a deficiency that contradicts divinity, whereas the possibility of what is negated in our present matter is not a deficiency; rather, it is a perfection. End.

Hasan Halabi said: If it is said: "Establishing praise by negating seeing, in the sense of unapproachability and fortification, requires that it not cease, because the cessation of that by which praise is achieved is a deficiency, and so it follows that He is not seen in the Hereafter." The answer: that applies to attributes, whereas praise by negating seeing returns to praise by creating its opposite, and that is of the category of acts, just as the creation of seeing is also of them. End.

We have already explained this at the beginning, and there will come, if God the Exalted wills, a complete and conclusive treatment of this at His saying: ﴿Faces that Day will be radiant﴾ [75:22] ﴿looking at their Lord﴾ [75:23], which is greater in proof and clearer in demonstration. And God is the Granter of success.

As for His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And He perceives the sights﴾, meaning: He sees all visible things and perceives all perceptible things, nothing of them being hidden from Him. ﴿And He is the Subtle, the Aware﴾: that is, the One who deals with His servants with kindness and compassion, ﴿the All-Aware﴾: that is, the Knower of the subtleties of matters and their manifest aspects. It is permitted that the sentence be a justification for what precedes it, according to the method of *laff* (a rhetorical device in which two statements are mentioned together and each is matched with the other's counterpart, the listener being left to connect them), meaning: "sights do not perceive Him because He is the Subtle, and He perceives sights because He is the All-Aware." It was said: then "*al-Latif*" (the Subtle) is a metaphor borrowed from the opposite of *al-kathif* (the dense, the gross), so the hidden thing from perception is likened to it. This is based on the fact that in ordinary usage it is among the attributes of bodies, whereas the truth is that absolute subtlety is not found in a body, since corporeality entails density; its subtlety is only relative. So absolute subtlety is not far-fetched to be ascribed to absolute Light, which is too exalted for the perception of insights, let alone sight, and too lofty for the apprehension of secrets, let alone thoughts, and is exalted above resemblance to forms and likenesses, and is transcended from indwelling of colours and shapes. For perfect subtlety belongs only to one of this description, while describing others as subtle is not absolute, but relative to what is less subtle than them, and they are described as dense in relation to Him. This is how al-Bahai (al-Bahai) verified it in *Sharh al-Asma' al-Husna* (*Commentary on the Beautiful Names*). As for al-Khafaji's (al-Khafaji's) statement: "*al-Latif*, derived from *al-lutf* in the sense of compassion," no connection to it appears here, which is refuted by noting that His saying, exalted is He, ﴿Sights do not perceive Him﴾, was mentioned for intimidation, as we have previously stated, and in that case it is fitting that it be followed by a description of His compassion and mercy, in keeping with the methods of encouragement and warning.

The discussion of the saying of His, the Exalted: [104] ﴿Certainly there have come to you insights from your Lord. So whoever sees, it is for his own soul; and whoever is blind, it is against it. And I am not a guardian over you.﴾

His saying, the Exalted, ﴿Certainly there have come to you insights from your Lord﴾: that is, the signs and proofs by which you perceive guidance from misguidance. It is the plural of (baṣīrah), which is the proof that necessitates seeing a thing and knowing it. It is also permissible that the meaning is: there has come to you from the revelation that which is like insights for the hearts, the plural of (baṣīrah), which is the light by which the heart gains insight, just as sight is a light by which the eye sees.

﴿So whoever sees﴾: that is, sees the truth through those insights and believes in it. ﴿It is for his own soul﴾: that is, it is for his own soul that he sees, because its benefit returns to it. ﴿And whoever is blind﴾: that is, strays from the truth. The expression of it with (ʿamā, blindness) is to disparage him and to repel from it: ﴿it is against it﴾: that is, he is blinded against his own soul, and it is upon it that he harms itself with blindness. ﴿And I am not a guardian over you﴾: that is, not a watcher who observes you and protects you from misguidance. Rather, I am a warner, and Allah protects your deeds and will recompense you for them.

(p-2456) The discussion of His saying, may He be exalted:

[105] ﴿And thus We vary the verses, and so that they may say, "You have studied," and that We may make it clear to a people who know.﴾

﴿And thus We vary the verses﴾ means: We present them in many forms throughout the various passages, so that the proof may be complete against those who oppose. ﴿And so that they may say﴾ in rejecting them: ﴿"You have studied"﴾, i.e., you have read under someone else and learned from him, and by study you have memorized the reports of past peoples. This is like their saying: ﴿"It is dictated to him morning and evening"﴾ [al-Furqan: 5].

It is said: darasa al-kitab yadrusuhu dirasatan, when one reads the book much and makes it easy to memorize. Ibn 'Abbas said: "And so that they may say" means: the people of Makkah, when the Qur'an is recited to them, "(You have studied)" means: you have learned from Yasar and Jabr, who were two slaves from the captives of the Romans. Then you recited to us, claiming that it is from God! Al-Farra' said: its meaning is that you learned from the Jews. Thus in "al-Lubab."

It was also read as "darasta" with an alif and a fatha on the taa', meaning: you studied with another who knows the past reports, like their saying: ﴿"Only a human teaches him." The tongue of the one they point to is foreign﴾ [al-Nahl: 103].

It is also read "darasat" with a fatha on the dal, the ra and the sin, and a sukun on the taa', meaning: they passed away, were brought forth and repeated upon the ears, just as they said: "tales of the ancients." These three readings (p-2457) are mutawatir. In the shadh readings it was read "durisat" as a past passive, meaning: those verses were recited and effaced. It was also read "darrasta" with shadda and in the active voice; the shadda is for intensification or for transitivity, meaning: you taught others the books. It was also read with shadda in the passive. It was read "duwarista" with a damma on the ra, and attributing it to the verses is an exaggeration in erasing them or in reciting them, because the pattern fa'ula with damma belongs to natures and instincts. Ubayy (may Allah be pleased with him) read "darasa," with its subject being the pronoun of the Prophet (ﷺ), or the Book, if it means "was effaced." And "darasna" with the feminine plural nun, both light and heavy. It was read "darisat," meaning "ancient," or meaning "possessing study or studies," like: ʿīshatin radiyah. Its being nominative is because it is the predicate of an omitted subject, i.e., they are darisat.

﴿And that We may make it clear﴾, i.e., the Qur'an, though it has not been mentioned because it is known; or the verses, because they carry the meaning of the Qur'an. ﴿To a people who know﴾, i.e., the truth so that they follow it, and falsehood so that they avoid it.

(p-2458) Two points of caution:

The first: It has been said: the second lam is genuine, and the first is the lam of consequence and outcome, meaning: so that the outcome of their affair becomes that they say, "You have studied," as in His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿So the family of Pharaoh picked him up, that he might become for them an enemy and a sorrow﴾ [al-Qasas: 8]. They did not pick him up for enmity; they picked him up so that he would be a delight of the eye for them, but the outcome of their affair turned to enmity. Likewise, the verses were varied for clarification, not so that they would say, "You have studied"; but this saying came about through the variation of the verses, just as clarification came about, so it is likened to it.

Al-Khafaji said: Abu al-Baqa' and others permitted that it be literal, because the descent of the verses is for misguiding the wretched and guiding the fortunate. He, may He be exalted, said: ﴿He misguides many by it and guides many by it﴾ [al-Baqarah: 26]. Al-Razi said: Taking the lam as consequence is far-fetched, because it is metaphorical; taking it as the lam of purpose is literal, and the literal is stronger than the metaphorical. And what is meant by it is the very thing mentioned in His saying: "He misguides many by it and guides many by it." He said: What confirms this interpretation is His saying: ﴿and that We may make it clear to a people who know﴾, meaning: We have only made it clear to these people. As for those who do not know, We have not made these verses clear to them; and since it was not clarification for them, it is established that its making them astray was for them. End.

It has been said: this lam is the lam of command, and what supports it is that it was read with a sukun on it, as if it were said: "And thus We vary the verses, and let them say what they say," for there is no concern for them and no regard for their saying. It is a command whose meaning is threat, intimidation, and disregard of their saying.

(p-2459) But this is open to question, because what follows it rejects it, since the lam in "li-nubayyinahu" is explicit that it is the lam of kay (purpose). As for the sukun of the lam in the shadh reading, there is no proof in it, for it may be that it was lightened by treating it like kibd, and because it is parenthetical. "Li-nubayyinahu" is connected to an implied verb coordinated with what precedes it; and even if one holds it to be correct, that does not remove it from being contrary to the apparent meaning. Thus in "al-Inayah."

The second: al-Sharif, may his secret be sanctified, said: God's acts have wisdoms and sound benefits branching from them, which are their fruits, even if they are not final causes for them, since without them the agent would not have undertaken the act. Some of the Sunnis agreed with the Mu'tazilah on causation and purpose, the benefit of which returns to the servants, and claimed that this is the doctrine of the jurists and the later scholars.

Having known this, know that the reality of causation and purpose according to the Sunnis is the explanation of what indicates the benefit that follows from the act. As for explaining it as the motive without which the agent would not have performed the act, or denying that this is a condition, that is among the investigations of the theologians and has no connection to language. As for the people of language, it is literal in that sense absolutely. The difference between it and the lam of consequence is that the lam of consequence enters upon what follows from the act and is not a benefit. Whether it is required that the speaker supposes that it does not follow, so that it is in the speech of God without being a report, or not, is a matter of disagreement. Thus in "al-Inayah."

Commentary of al-Qasimi (Mahasin al-Ta'wil) on surah 6, verse 106:

When Exalted is He related the disputes of the polytheists concerning the diversification of the verses (ayat), He followed it with the command to remain steadfast in what he was upon, strengthening his heart and removing what grieves him. So He, glorified is He, said:

The discussion on the interpretation of the words of the Exalted:

[106] ﴿Follow what has been revealed to you from your Lord. There is no deity except Him, and turn away from the polytheists.﴾

﴿Follow what has been revealed to you from your Lord﴾: that is, of the conveying of the message, which is the diversified verses, in exaggeration of establishing the proof. His words ﴿There is no deity except Him﴾ are a parenthetical clause (i'tirad) by which the obligation of following is emphasized, or they are an emphasizing circumstantial clause (hal) relating to "your Lord," meaning: singular in divinity. ﴿And turn away from the polytheists﴾. Abu Muslim said: By turning away is meant abandoning them without warning them, and leaving off admonition. Al-Mahayimi said: That is, do not grieve over them if they persist in polytheism and blindness despite these clear proofs, for He, Exalted is He, intended their remaining in polytheism and blindness, because of the requirement of their predisposition to that.

The discussion concerning His saying, exalted is He:

[107] ﴿And if God had willed, they would not have associated others with Him. We have not appointed you a guardian over them, nor are you a manager over them.﴾

﴿And if God had willed, they would not have associated others with Him﴾ — i.e., even with their readiness (isti'dad) [for faith]; but His way (sunnah) has been to preserve the readinesses (isti'dadat). ﴿Nor have We appointed you a guardian over them﴾ — i.e., although they have a readiness for faith in their natural disposition (fitrah), and they have nullified it, you, although you are one who calls to the rectification of the natural readiness, have not been made one who is in charge of them, guarding their interests, so that you would be one who rectifies their natural readiness.

﴿Nor are you a manager over them﴾ — who arranges their affairs, or who changes them from their readiness to another. Rather, he is entrusted to God, the Exalted, who deals with them according to the requirement of their natural readiness, without changing it. Rather, [the matter] is entrusted to their own choice. This is reported from al-Mahayimi.

Two admonitions:

The first: In His saying, exalted is He, ﴿And if God had willed, they would not have associated others with Him﴾, there is evidence that He, exalted is He, does not will the faith of the disbeliever. However, this is not in the sense that He prevents him from it while He directs Himself towards him, but in the sense that He does not will it from him, due to the absence of His directing his partial choice toward faith and his persistence in disbelief. Al-Zamakhshari interprets it as a will of compulsion and coercion, because in their view the will of choice is absolutely attained. Al-Nihrir said: "This is his crutch in repelling the doctrine of the People of the Sunnah."

(p-2461) The second: Al-Qashani said in his interpretation of His saying, exalted is He, ﴿And if God had willed, they would not have associated others with Him﴾: i.e., everything that occurs occurs only by the will of God. There is no doubt that their readinesses by which they fell into association, and the causes of that — such as the teaching of the fathers, customs and others — also occur by a will from God; otherwise they would not occur. So if they believe in that, it is by the guidance of God; otherwise, make it easy for yourself: We have not appointed you to keep them from error, nor are you one entrusted with them for faith. This does not contradict what He said later, in rebuking them, ﴿Those who associated others with Him will say: "If God had willed, we would not have associated" [al-An'am: 148], because they said that out of obstinacy and to repel faith by that pretext, not out of belief. Their saying that, although it was true in reality, they were in it liars, denying the Messenger, for if they had affirmed it, they would have known that the monotheism of the believers is also by the will of God, and likewise every religion, so they would not have opposed anyone. And if they had known that nothing occurs except by the will of God, they would not have remained polytheists, but would have been monotheists. But they said it for the purpose of denial and obstinacy, and to establish that it is not possible for them to desist from their association; therefore He rebuked them for it, not because it is not so in reality. For they did not perceive the will of God, and that just as He willed their association in the past, He did not will their faith now; since not every one of them is sealed in the heart, as evidenced by the faith of those among them who believed. So why should it not be possible that some of them were ready for faith and monotheism, but they argued by custom and by what they found from their fathers, so they associated; then when they heard the warning and witnessed the signs of monotheism, they yearned for the truth, their veil was lifted, and they affirmed the oneness of God. Therefore He reproached them for their saying, and demanded of them proof that God had willed them thus always, and warned them with the threat against those before them, so that whoever among them had the least readiness, when he is cut off from his argument and hears the threat against those before him among the deniers, his veil is lifted, his heart softens, and he believes; and that will be a granting of success to him and a kindness regarding his affair, for the world of wisdom is built upon causes. As for whoever is among the wretched (p-2462) rejected ones, upon whose hearts a seal is set, he does not raise his head for that, nor lend it an ear. End.

Keep this in mind, for the matter is extremely subtle, and its explanation will come in the following verse, God willing, exalted is He.

The discussion of the interpretation of His words, Exalted is He:

[108] ﴿And do not revile those whom they call upon besides God, lest they revile God in enmity without knowledge. Thus We have made attractive to every community their deeds. Then to their Lord is their return, and He will inform them of what they used to do.﴾

﴿And do not revile those whom they call upon besides God, lest they revile God in enmity without knowledge﴾ means: do not mention their gods, which they worship, with the ugly things that are in them, lest they go beyond bounds to the Exalted Majesty.

ʿAbd al-Razzaq narrated from Qatadah, who said: The Muslims used to revile the idols of the disbelievers, so they were forbidden from doing so for this reason. Al-Zajjaj said: They were forbidden to curse the idols that the polytheists worshipped. End of quote.

Grammar: ﴿alladhina yad'una﴾ is an expression for the gods, and its returning pronoun is implied. The use of ﴿alladhina﴾ (those who) is either according to their claim that they are among the people of knowledge, or based on the principle that reviling their gods is reviling them, as one says: striking the riding animal is slapping its rider. If it is asked: they used to acknowledge God and His greatness, and that they worshipped their gods only so that they would be intercessors with Him, how then would they revile Him? We say: they do not do this explicitly, but their speech leads to it, such as their insulting Him and whoever commands that, for example. It has been explained as: "without knowledge of this," and this is very good. Or: anger and rage may often drive them to revile God explicitly. Do you not see that a Muslim may be carried by the intensity of his anger to disbelief?

﴿ʿAdwan﴾ is a verbal noun, meaning injustice and aggression. One says: ʿadā ʿalayhi ʿadwan, like ḍarban, and ʿudūwan like ʿutuwwan, and ʿadāʾan like ʿazāʾin, and ʿudwānan like subḥānan, when he transgresses and goes beyond bounds. It is an absolute object (of the verb) ﴿tasubbū﴾ from its meaning, because reviling is aggression. Or it is an object of purpose, or an emphatic circumstantial accusative like ﴿bi-ghayri ʿilm﴾, as stated in al-ʿInayah.

Caution:

Ibn al-Faras said regarding the verse: whenever it is feared that reviling the disbelievers and their idols would lead them to revile God, His Messenger, or the Qur'an, it is not permissible to revile them or their religion. He said: this verse is a foundation for the principle of blocking the means (sadd al-dhara'i) to prohibited ends.

Al-Suyuti said: it may also be used as evidence that the obligation of enjoining good and forbidding evil falls away when a greater harm is feared from it. Likewise, every obligatory act whose performance results in a greater harm than the harm of abandoning it.

Some of the Zaydi commentators said: the fruit of the verse is that a good act becomes ugly when its performance produces a harm. Al-Hakim said: they were forbidden from reviling the idols for two reasons:

First: they are inanimate objects that have no sin.

Second: that this leads to the sin of reviling God, Exalted is He.

He said: what we are obliged to do is to make clear our hatred of them, that they are not permissible to worship, that they neither harm nor benefit, and that they do not deserve worship; and this is not reviling. For this reason, the Commander of the Faithful (on the day of Siffin) said: Do not revile them, but mention the ugliness of their deeds. End of quote.

Al-Zamakhshari said: If you say: reviling the gods is a right and an act of obedience, how is the prohibition against it valid, since prohibitions only apply to sins? I say: many an act of obedience is known to lead to harm, and so it leaves being an act of obedience, and therefore it is obligatory to prohibit it, because it is then a sin, not because it is an act of obedience. Like forbidding evil, which is among the greatest acts of obedience; when it is known that it leads to an increase of evil, it turns into a sin, and forbidding it becomes obligatory, just as forbidding evil is obligatory. If you say: it has been narrated from al-Hasan and Ibn Sirin that they attended a funeral, and Muhammad saw women and turned back. Al-Hasan said: if we abandoned obedience for the sake of sin, that would quickly spread in our religion. I say: this is not what we are concerned with; for the attendance of men at a funeral is an act of obedience, and it is not a cause for the attendance of women, for they attend whether men attend or not. This is unlike reviling the gods. It only seemed to Ibn Sirin that it was similar to it, until al-Hasan alerted him to it. End of quote.

From the same source, some of the Zaydi commentators said: know that if the sin is certainly going to occur, whether al-Hasan does it or not, the obligation does not fall away, and the good act does not become ugly. End of quote.

Likewise al-Khafaji said: when an act of obedience leads to a greater sin, and is a cause of it, it is obligatory to abandon it. This is unlike an act of obedience in a situation where there is a sin that cannot be averted. These two often become confused, and for this reason Ibn Sirin did not attend a funeral in which men and women gathered, and al-Hasan disagreed with him because of the difference between them. End of quote.

Al-Razi said: in the verse there is instruction for whoever calls to the religion, lest he occupy himself with what has no benefit for the objective; for describing the idols as inanimate objects that neither harm nor benefit is sufficient to discredit their divinity, so there is no need, in addition to that, to revile them.

﴿Thus We have made attractive to every community﴾ of the past nations, in error, ﴿their deeds. Then to their Lord is their return﴾, that is, by resurrection after death, ﴿and He will inform them﴾, that is, He will tell them, ﴿of what they used to do﴾ in the world. That is by reckoning and recompense for it.

Remarks:

The first: The People of the Sunnah adopted the apparent meaning of the verse, that the one who makes disbelief attractive to the disbeliever and faith attractive to the believer is God, Exalted is He. This is because the act's proceeding from the servant depends on the arising of a motive, and that motive must be by the creation of God, Exalted is He. Al-Razi expanded on this, and cited the feeble interpretations of the Mu'tazilah, so consult him!

The second: In His words, Exalted is He: ﴿then He will inform them﴾ etc., there is a threat of recompense and punishment, like the saying of a man to one he threatens: I will inform you of what you did.

The third: In it there is a secret subtlety, based on a profound wisdom, namely that everything that appears in this mode of existence, of substances and accidents, appears only in a borrowed form that differs from its true form by which it appears in the next mode of existence. Sins are deadly poisons which have appeared in the world in a form that the souls of the disobedient find pleasing, as this noble verse declares. Likewise acts of obedience: although they are the best of goods, they have appeared to people in a hateful form. For this reason the prayer and peace of God be upon him said: "Paradise is surrounded by hardships, and Hellfire is surrounded by desires." So the deeds of the disbelievers have appeared to them in this mode of existence in an adorned form that the deluded find pleasing and the tyrants love. They will appear in the next mode of existence in their true, abhorrent, terrifying form, and then they will know what their deeds really are. So He expressed their manifestation in their true forms by informing them of them, since each of these is a cause of knowing their reality as it is. So let him reflect! Conveyed by Abu al-Suʿud.

The discussion of His saying, Exalted is He:

[109] ﴿And they swore by God with their most earnest oaths that if a sign came to them, they would surely believe in it. Say: Signs are only with God. And what would make you know that when they come, they will not believe?﴾

﴿And they swore by God with their most earnest oaths﴾: *jahda* is a verbal noun (*masdar*) in the position of a circumstantial clause (*hal*). That is, they swore by Him, Exalted is He, exerting themselves in their oaths and expending their utmost effort in confirming them. ﴿If a sign came to them﴾: that is, a miraculous sign (*khariq*) as they had proposed. ﴿They would surely believe in it. Say: Signs are only with God﴾: that is, their matter lies exclusively in His judgment and decree. He disposes of them according to His will, which is founded on far-reaching wisdom. No one's power or will has any bearing on them, so that I could take it upon myself to bring them down by request. This closes the door to proposing signs in the most eloquent and finest manner, by explaining how difficult they are to attain and how exalted their station is. So said Abu al-Su'ud.

(p-2466) ﴿And what would make you know that when they come, they will not believe?﴾ It is read *innaha* with a *kasra*, as a resumptive (*isti'naf*) clause, and the second object is omitted, as if it were said: "And what would make you know their faith?" Then He informed them of what He knew about them, by way of an initial statement. Or it is an answer to a question, as if it were said: "Why were they reproached?" So it was said: "Because when they come, they will not believe!" Or it is based on His saying "And what would make you know," for it is presented in the form of something possible, as if he asked about it with the question of one in doubt, and then gave the reason with His saying "that when they come, they will not believe," definitively, for the opposite side, and as an explanation that the interrogation is not meant in its literal sense. In this there is a denial of the believers' affirmation in a manner that implies a denial of the truthfulness of the polytheists regarding what they swore to. This is a kind of rhetorical magic (*sihr bayani*), subtle in its approach. This holds on the view that the address is to the believers, since they were wishing for the sign to come out of eagerness for their faith. It was also said that the address is to the polytheists, based on the reading "*la tu'minun*" (you will not believe), in which case there is an *iltifat* (shift of address).

It is also read *anna* with a *fatha*. On this reading it was said that the good opinion of the believers toward these obstinate people requires the omission of *la* (not). To illustrate this: if it is said to you, "Honor Zayd, and he will reward you," you say in denying it: "What would make you know that if I honor him, he will reward me?!" If it is said, "Do not honor him, for he will not reward you," you say in denial: "What would make you know that he will not reward me?!" meaning: "And I know from him the reward." So the requirement of the believers' good opinion of the polytheists is that it be said: "And what would make you know that when they come, they will believe?" Thus affirming *la* reverses the meaning, since what is known to you is the occurrence, and you are denying the one who negated it.

The *fatha* reading has been explained in six ways:

Among them: making *la* a superfluous particle (*silah*), as in His saying "What prevented you from prostrating?" and His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And a prohibition upon a city which We have destroyed—that they will not return﴾ [al-Anbiya: 95], meaning: that they will return. Al-Zajjaj weakened this view, on the grounds that what is superfluous is superfluous under all interpretations, and this is not so here, for *la* in the *kasra* reading is not superfluous. Al-Farisi responded: why is it not permissible for it to be superfluous under one of the two interpretations and meaningful under the second? End.

Among them: making *anna* mean *la'alla* (perhaps). Al-Khalil said: the Arabs say, "Go to the market, that you may buy something for us," meaning: "perhaps you may." So it is as if He, Exalted is He, said: "Perhaps when they come, they will not believe." Al-Wahidi said: *anna* meaning *la'alla* is common in their speech. A poet said:

*Show me a steed that died of emaciation, for I see what you see, or a miserly one who lives forever.*

And 'Adi ibn Hatim said:
