*O blamer, what would make you know that my death / is at an hour in the day or at the forenoon of tomorrow?*

What supports this is that *yush'iruKum* and *yudrikum* have the same meaning, and *la'alla* often comes after the verb of knowing, as in: ﴿And what would make you know? Perhaps he would purify himself﴾ [Abasa: 3]. And in the codex of Ubayy: "And what would make you know? Perhaps when they come to them, they will not believe."

Among them: making *anna* mean *hal* (whether).

Among them: making the statement the answer to an omitted oath, based on the fact that *inna* after an oath may be read with a *fatha*. Al-Zamakhshari chose, and the verifying scholars followed him, to take the statement in its apparent sense: the interrogation carries the meaning of negation, and the report of non-knowledge is not a rebuke against them. The meaning is: "And what would make you know that the sign they are proposing, when it comes, they will not believe in it?" That is, I know that when it comes they will not believe in it, and you do not know this.

In *al-Intisaf* it is said: Since the verse, at first glance, conveys that God, Exalted is He, knew their faith, and it rebukes the believers for denying it, while the reality is otherwise, the scholars differed (and he presented something like what we have mentioned among the aspects). Then he said: As for al-Zamakhshari, he perceived that the verse remains in its apparent sense and stays in its proper place, without omission or interpretation. So he said what he said earlier. We clarify its consistency in the earlier example, so that it becomes clear in both its aspects in the verse. We say: if you deprive Zayd because you know he will not reward you, and it is suggested to you to honor him on the basis that the one suggesting thinks he will reward, then you have two states with him: a state in which you deny his claim to know what is known to be otherwise, and a state in which you excuse him for not knowing what you have comprehensively known. If you deny it to him, you say: "What would make you know that he will reward?" And if you excuse him for his not knowing that he will not reward, you say: "What would make you know that he will not reward?" That is: "From where do you know what I know of his not rewarding, when you do not know his matter as I do?" Likewise, in the verse, the discourse is intended to furnish an excuse to the believers for their not knowing the unseen in the knowledge of God, Exalted is He, which is the non-faith of these people. So the entry of *la* becomes correct and determined, and it becomes clear that the cause of the confusion is the mixing of denial with the offering of excuses. End.

In the negation of the cause, which is *ish'ar* (informing), there is an intensification of the negation of the effect, which is *shu'ur* (awareness).

Al-Khafaji said: In negating the effect by this method there is an intensification not found in negating it without it, because in the metaphor (*kinaya*) there is an affirmation of the thing by means of evidence. Within it is an allusion that God knows their non-faith, on the supposition that the sign they proposed comes to them, and an alert that He, Exalted is He, did not send it down because He knew that when it came they would not believe. So the non-sending down is due to their non-faith.

As for *yush'irukum*, *yansurukum* and the like, they have been read with a pure *damma*, with a sukun, and with *ikhtilas* (a rapid, partial vowel).

(p-٢٤٦٩)The discussion of the interpretation of His saying, exalted is He:

[110] ﴿And We turn their hearts and their sight away, just as they did not believe in it the first time, and We leave them in their transgression, wandering blindly.﴾

﴿And We turn their hearts and their sight away﴾ is coordinated with (they do not believe), and falls under the ruling of (what makes you perceive), and is restricted by what it is restricted by. That is: and what makes you perceive that We turn their hearts away from grasping the truth, so that they do not understand it, and their sight away from witnessing it, so that they do not see it? But this is not with their hearts being directed toward it and prepared to accept it. Rather, it is because their hearts have fully turned away from it and their attention has completely abandoned it. For this reason, its mention was delayed after the mention of their not believing, to indicate that they are rooted in disbelief, and to cut off the illusion that their not believing arises from God Most High turning their perceptions by way of compulsion (ijbar, forcing them against their will). This is what Abu al-Su'ud conveyed.

﴿just as they did not believe in it﴾, that is, in what came of the signs. ﴿the first time﴾, that is, before they asked for the signs they proposed. ﴿And We leave them﴾, that is, We let them be, ﴿in their transgression, wandering blindly﴾, that is, moving back and forth in bewilderment, and We do not guide them with the guidance given to believers.

Abu al-Su'ud said: (And We leave them) is coordinated with (they believe), and falls under the ruling of the interrogative of denial (al-istifham al-inkari, a question used to deny), and is restricted by it. It clarifies what is meant by turning the hearts and sights, and it indicates that this is not to be taken literally, namely that God, glorified is He, would turn their perceptions away from the truth while they are directed toward it and prepared for it by way of compulsion. Rather, He leaves them to themselves, after He knew the corruption of their preparedness and their extreme aversion to the truth, and the lack of any effect of divine grace (lutf) upon them at all, and He seals their hearts according to what their preparedness requires, as we have pointed out. End of quotation.

In al-Lubab: In the verse there is evidence that God Most High guides whom He wills and leads astray whom He wills, and that the hearts and the sights are in His hand and under His direction, so He sets upright whichever of them He wills and turns away whichever of them He wills. From this is His saying, may God bless him and grant him peace (ﷺ): "O Turner of hearts, make my heart firm upon Your religion." End of quotation.

Then Allah (exalted is He) clarified their lying in their defiant oaths in the most emphatic and forceful manner, through His saying:

Discussion on the interpretation of His saying, exalted is He:

[111] ﴿And even if We had sent down to them the angels, and the dead had spoken to them, and We had gathered against them every thing in front of them, they would not have believed, unless Allah willed; but most of them are ignorant.﴾

﴿And even if We had sent down to them the angels﴾ meaning: and even if We had not limited Ourselves to granting what they proposed here of a single sign, but had sent down to them the angels, as they said: "Why were the angels not sent down to us?"

﴿and the dead had spoken to them﴾, as they said: "Then bring our fathers, if you are truthful." ﴿And We had gathered﴾, meaning: brought together, ﴿against them every thing﴾ of the animals, the plants and the inanimate objects, ﴿in front of them﴾, meaning: as guarantors of the truth of what they were promised and warned of. ﴿They would not have believed﴾ because of their extreme rebelliousness and transgression, ﴿unless Allah willed﴾, meaning: [unless He willed] their faith, so they would believe. ﴿But most of them are ignorant﴾, meaning: (p-2471) even if they were given every sign they would not believe, and so they swear by Allah with their most solemn oaths to what is hardly going to happen. Or they are ignorant that faith is by the will of Allah, not by supernatural occurrences.

Al-Qashani said: In reality, no weight is given to faith that results from witnessing supernatural occurrences, for it is often merely submission to a perceptible matter and verbal acknowledgement, while there is nothing in the heart of its meaning, like the faith of the companions of al-Samiri. Faith exists only in the heart, as Allah the Exalted said: ﴿The Bedouins say, "We have believed." Say, "You have not believed; but say, 'We have submitted,' for faith has not yet entered your hearts."﴾ [al-Hujurat: 14]

Two points of caution:

The first: ﴿qubulan﴾ is read with a ḍammah on the qāf and the bā' (qubulan, as a plural of qabīl meaning "guarantor," like qalīb and qalb; the other view is that it is a singular, like qubul al-insan and dubur al-insan, "the front and back of a person"). On both views it is a ḥāl (circumstantial accusative) of kull. It is also read with a ḍammah and a sukūn on the bā' as a lightening of the ḍammah, and read with a kasrah on the qāf and a fatḥah on the bā', its being in the accusative as an adverb of place (ẓarf), like their saying: "li-fulān qibala ḥaqq" (I have a right regarding so-and-so). Or as a circumstantial accusative (ḥāl), being a verbal noun (maṣdar), meaning: "in direct witnessing."

The second: In His saying, exalted is He, ﴿unless Allah willed﴾, there is a clear proof against the Mu'tazilah, since it indicates that all things are by the will of Allah, even faith and disbelief. The righteous predecessors of this community and the bearers of its law agreed that whatever Allah wills comes to be, and whatever He does not will does not come to be. The Mu'tazilah resort to a stratagem in their rebuttal by interpreting the negated will as the will of compulsion and necessity. This would only hold for them if the Qur'an followed opinions; but since it is the exemplar and the one to be followed, whoever opposes it and turns away from it is then headed to the Fire, and beyond the truth there is only error.

Then Allah, exalted is He, consoled His Prophet regarding what he was suffering from his people, by having him take as an example those prophets who came before him, peace be upon them. So He, glorified is He, said:

The discussion on the interpretation of His saying, exalted is He:

[112] ﴿And thus We have made for every prophet an enemy: devils of mankind and jinn, inspiring one another with embellished speech as deception. And if your Lord had willed, they would not have done it, so leave them and what they fabricate.﴾

﴿And thus We have made for every prophet an enemy, devils of mankind and jinn﴾ That is: like that appointing which We appointed concerning you, when We made for you enemies who oppose you and do not believe. We made for every prophet who preceded you an enemy from the rebellious ones among mankind and jinn, and they did to them what your enemies did to you, as Allah, exalted is He, said: ﴿Nothing is said to you except what was said to the messengers before you﴾ [Fussilat: 43]. And Waraqah ibn Nawfal said to the Prophet ﷺ: "No man has ever come with the like of what you have come with except that he was opposed."

﴿Inspiring﴾ That is: they cast and whisper: ﴿one another with embellished speech﴾ That is: its deceptive part, whose outward is adorned while its inward is falsehood. ﴿As deception﴾ That is: for the weak, because Allah, exalted is He, made them the people of the veil, and likewise those who remain behind, so that He might subdue them according to the requirement of their readiness. And in the verse there is evidence that the hostility of the disbelievers toward the prophets, peace be upon them, is by the act of Allah, glorified is He, and His creation.

Al-Mahayimi said: So that the proofs may become manifest through their disputing, and their doubts may be removed, and so that it cannot be said that he was a person whom everyone helped in order to devour people's wealth, or to share with them in it.

﴿And if your Lord had willed, they would not have done it﴾ That is: they would not have done that, meaning: opposing the prophets and inspiring adorned falsehoods. This is also evidence against the Mu'tazilah. ﴿So leave them and what they fabricate﴾ That is: of disbelief; for they will come to know.

Then he connected to his saying "ghurūran" (as a deception) a second cause for the inspiring (al-īḥāʾ) by His saying, exalted is He:

The discussion on the interpretation of His saying, exalted is He:

[113] ﴿And that the hearts of those who do not believe in the Hereafter may incline to it, and that they may be pleased with it, and that they may earn what they are earning.﴾

﴿And that the hearts incline to it﴾ means: some of them inspire to others the ornamented speech (zukhruf al-qawl) so that they may deceive them with it, and that the hearts of those who do not believe in the Hereafter may incline to it, because it supports them in their desires. ﴿And that they may be pleased with it﴾ means: for their own selves, after their hearts have inclined to it. ﴿And that they may earn﴾ means: and that they may acquire, as a consequence of their approval of it, ﴿what they are earning﴾, that is, of sins.

Al-Qashani said: So their error grows, and they become openly manifest, and the evils within them come out into action, and they increase in rebellion and transgression against the Prophet, so that the strength of his perfection increases, and the motives of the believers are also stirred by means of it, and those whose preparedness is suited to the Prophet are roused to zeal, and their love for the Prophet and their support of him increase, so that their perfections become manifest upon them.

A subtle point:

He singled out for mention their non-belief in the Hereafter, rather than the other matters that must be believed in, and in which they are disbelievers, to indicate what is the pivot of the inclination of their hearts toward what is cast to them. For the pleasures of the Hereafter are surrounded in this world by hardships, and its pains are adorned with desires. Those who do not believe in it, and in the conditions of what is in it, do not know that behind those hardships are pleasures, and beneath these desires are pains; they only look at what appears to them in this world at first glance. So they are compelled to love desires, of which among the most important are ornamented sayings and the camouflaged falsehoods. As for the believers in it, since they stand upon the reality of the matter and look to the outcomes of affairs, it is not conceivable that they would incline to those ornamentations, due to their knowledge of their falsity and the baseness of their outcome. This is what Abu al-Su'ud conveyed.

(p-2474) The discussion on the interpretation of His saying, exalted is He:

[114] ﴿Shall I seek a judge other than God, when it is He who has sent down to you the Book, fully detailed? And those to whom We gave the Book know that it has been sent down from your Lord in truth, so do not be among the doubters.﴾

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Shall I seek a judge other than God?﴾ is by way of an implied "say" (taqdir al-qawl), as in its counterparts. That is: "Say to them: Shall I seek other than God someone who will judge between me and you and distinguish the one in the right from the one in the wrong?" The meaning is: "Shall I seek a deity (ma'bud)?" For they used to refer their disputes to their idols (tawaghit), and this, in my view, is the clearer reading. Then I found in "Tanwir al-Miqbas" that it restricts itself to this, where he said: "Abtaghi hakaman a'bud rabban" (I seek a judge, I worship a lord). As for the claim that the verse was revealed in response to their saying, "Make between us and you a judge," this is not sound, because they were far from submitting to that.

﴿It is He who has sent down to you the Book﴾, that is, the Qur'an, the miraculous, ﴿fully detailed﴾, that is, clarified within it is the distinction between truth and falsehood, and between the lawful and the unlawful. You were an unlettered people, not knowing what you should do or refrain from.

On the verse there are several issues:

The first: In "al-Iklil" he said: The Kharijites took as evidence His saying, exalted is He, ﴿Shall I seek a judge other than God?﴾ for their rejection of arbitration (tahkim). He said: This is refuted, for reprehensible arbitration is that one seeks a judge who would judge by other than what God, exalted is He, has judged. End of quote.

I say: This is based on the first reading, and you have come to know that the clearer reading is the second, so there is no argument from it, nor any refutation.

The second: They said: "al-Hakam" (the judge/arbiter) is more emphatic than "al-hakim" (the one who judges), and more indicative of firmness (rusukh), because it is not applied except to one who is just and to one from whom judgment has been repeated frequently, unlike "al-hakim."

The third: In the verse there is an indication that the noble Qur'an is sufficient in matters of religion, needing nothing else, through its explanation and its detailing.

﴿And those to whom We gave the Book know that it has been sent down from your Lord in truth﴾: because of the good tidings of you that they have from the earlier prophets, and because it confirms what is with them, even though the Prophet (ﷺ) did not study their books nor mix with their scholars. This is an affirmation that it was sent down from God's presence, by showing that the scholars of the People of the Book in whom the polytheists trusted know its reality and that it was sent down from Him, exalted is He.

﴿So do not be among the doubters﴾: that is, concerning its being sent down from your Lord in truth, on account of most of them denying and disbelieving in it. This is in the mode of stirring up and inciting, like His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And do not be among the polytheists﴾ [Yunus: 105].

Ibn Kathir said: This is like His saying, exalted is He: ﴿If you are in doubt about what We have sent down to you, then ask those who read the Book before you. Indeed the truth has come to you from your Lord, so do not be among the doubters﴾ [Yunus: 94]. He said: This is a conditional, and the condition does not imply its occurrence. For this reason it came from the Messenger of God (ﷺ) that he said: "I do not doubt, nor will I ask." End of quote.

Commentary of al-Qasimi (Mahasin al-Ta'wil) on surah 6, verse 115:

The discussion of His saying, exalted is He:

[115] ﴿And the word of your Lord has been fulfilled in truth and justice. None can alter His words, and He is the All-Hearing, the All-Knowing.﴾

﴿The word of your Lord has been fulfilled﴾ [Hud: 119]. It is also read as "words of your Lord" (kalimat rabbika). That is, His reports, His rulings and His promises have reached their ultimate completion. ﴿In truth﴾ regarding the reports and promises; ﴿and justice﴾ regarding the judgments and rulings.

(p-2476) Al-Qashani said: That is, His decree, exalted is He, in eternity has been completed by what He decreed and determined concerning the submission of whoever submits, the disbelief of whoever disbelieves, the love of whoever loves, and the enmity of whoever is hostile; a decree that is binding, a judgment that is true, conforming to what occurs, and just, in accordance with the fitting of every statement, every perfection and every state, given the readiness of the one from whom it proceeds and its requirement for him. End.

﴿None can alter His words﴾: that is, no one can replace any of them with something more truthful or more just. Or: no one is able to distort them in a widely spread and publicized manner, as was done with the Torah. Moreover, the intended meaning of them is the Qur'an, so this is a guarantee from Him, exalted is He, of its preservation, like His saying: ﴿Indeed, it is We who sent down the Reminder, and indeed, We will be its guardian﴾ [al-Hijr: 9].

Al-Qashani said: That is, none can alter His eternal rulings. End.

Al-Suyuti said in al-Iklil: Those who hold that the Jews and Christians did not alter the wording of the Torah and the Gospel, but only altered its meaning, use this verse as evidence, because the words of Allah cannot be altered. End. This is a narration from Ibn Abbas, which al-Bukhari recorded at the end of his Sahih. Al-Hafiz Ibn Hajar expounded this matter at length in Fath al-Bari. We previously touched on a fragment of this discussion in surah al-Baqarah, so renew your recollection of it.

﴿And He is the All-Hearing﴾ of the statements they utter; ﴿the All-Knowing﴾: that is, of what they conceal.

Then Allah, exalted is He, warned against inclining toward them and acting upon their practices, by His saying:

Discussion on the interpretation of His saying, exalted is He:

[116] ﴿And if you obey most of those on earth, they will mislead you from the way of Allah. They follow not except assumption, and they are not but guessing.﴾

﴿And if you obey most of those on earth﴾ i.e., of the people, and they are the disbelievers, ﴿they will mislead you from the way of Allah﴾ i.e., from the path that leads to Him, by adorning their deceptive ornaments for you and by calling you to what they are upon of following desire, as He said: ﴿They follow not except assumption﴾, which is their assumption that their forefathers were upon the truth, so they imitate them. ﴿And they are not but guessing﴾, lying against Allah, exalted is He, in what they attribute to Him, such as taking a son for Him, making the worship of idols a means of nearness to Him, declaring carrion lawful, and forbidding the baḥāʾir. The particle (in) in it and in what precedes it is negating. Al-kharṣ (conjecture, estimation) means guessing and estimating, and it may be used to express lying and fabrication; its origin is speaking on the basis of assumption and saying what is not certain and verified. This was stated by al-Azharī.

Commentary on the interpretation of His words, may He be exalted:

[117] ﴿Indeed, your Lord is most knowing of who strays from His way, and He is most knowing of those who are guided.﴾

﴿Indeed, your Lord is most knowing of who strays from His way, and He is most knowing of those who are guided.﴾ This is an affirmation of the content of the conditional statement and what follows it, and a confirmation of what it conveys of warning. That is: He is most knowing of both groups, so beware lest you be among the first. Abu al-Su'ud conveyed this.

Note:

Al-Razi said: The opponents of analogy (qiyas) have held fast to this verse, saying: We see that God, exalted is He, has greatly censured the disbelievers in many verses of the Qur'an, because they follow conjecture (zann). Whatever God, exalted is He, makes a cause for censuring the disbelievers must be in the utmost degree of blame. Knowledge through analogy necessitates following conjecture, so it must be blameworthy and forbidden. It cannot be said: since a decisive proof has established that it is a valid proof, acting upon it is acting upon a certain proof, not a conjectural one. For we say: this is refuted in several respects:

First: That decisive proof is either rational or revealed (sam'i). The first is invalid, for reason has no scope in determining whether acting upon analogy is permissible or impermissible, especially according to those who deny that reason determines good and evil. The second is also invalid, for a revealed proof is decisive only if it is mutawatir (widely transmitted), or if its wording does not admit of any other meaning besides this single meaning. Had such a proof existed, people would know by necessity that analogy is a valid proof, and disagreement about it among the community would have ceased. Since that is not found, we know that the decisive proof for the soundness of analogy is absent.

Second: Suppose a decisive proof was found that analogy is a valid proof; nevertheless, acting upon analogy would not be complete except with following conjecture. Its explanation: reliance on analogy rests on two stages. First: the ruling in the place of agreement (al-mahall al-wifaq) is caused by such-and-such. Second: that meaning is present in the place of disagreement (al-mahall al-khilaf). If these two stages are known with certainty and conviction, there is no disagreement among rational people about its soundness. But if their combination, or one of them, is conjectural, then the knowledge of this analogy is not complete except by following conjecture, and in that case it falls under the text indicating that following conjecture is blameworthy. The answer: Why could it not be said that conjecture is a term for a prevailing belief when it is not based on an indicator (amara), and it is like the belief of the disbelievers? As for when the prevailing belief is based on an indicator, this belief is not called conjecture, and by this route the argument falls away. End.

The discussion of the words of His exalted saying:

[118] ﴿So eat of that over which the name of God has been mentioned, if you are believers in His signs.﴾

His exalted saying, ﴿So eat of that over which the name of God has been mentioned﴾, is a command that follows from the prohibition of following those who lead astray, whose misguidance includes making lawful what is unlawful and making unlawful what is lawful. The reason is that they argued with the Muslims and said: "What God slaughters you do not eat, but what you slaughter yourselves you do eat." (Narrated by al-Nasa'i from Ibn 'Abbas.) (p-2479) Then the verse was revealed. The meaning is: eat of that over which the name of God has been mentioned at its slaughter, since His mention removes the impurity of death that would otherwise prevent eating it, not of that over which the name of another has been mentioned, or that which died of its own accord.

﴿If you are believers in His signs﴾, for belief in them requires permitting what He, glorified is He, has made lawful, and avoiding what He has forbidden.

Commentary of al-Qasimi (Mahasin al-Ta'wil) on surah 6, verse 119:

On the interpretation of His saying, exalted is He:

[119] ﴿And what is [the matter] with you that you should not eat of that over which the name of Allah has been mentioned, when He has already detailed for you what He has forbidden to you, except what you are compelled to? Indeed, many [people] mislead [others] by their desires without knowledge. Indeed, your Lord is most knowing of the transgressors.﴾

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And what is [the matter] with you that you should not eat of that over which the name of Allah has been mentioned﴾ is a denunciation of there being any reason for them to abstain from eating what the name of Allah the Exalted has been mentioned over, namely the baheera and the sawaib. That is: what purpose do you have in being scrupulous about eating it, and what prevents you from it?

﴿when He has already detailed for you what He has forbidden to you﴾, that is: He has explained it and made it clear.

Some of the exegetes said: it means in the verse of al-Ma'ida, in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Forbidden to you is carrion﴾ [al-Ma'ida: 3], the verse... It has been objected that al-Ma'ida is among the last of what was revealed at Medina, whereas al-An'am is Meccan. The correct view, then, is that the detailing is either in His saying, exalted is He, after this verse: ﴿Say: I do not find in what has been revealed to me anything forbidden﴾ [al-An'am: 145], the verse... for it was mentioned shortly afterward, and this degree of delay does not prevent it from being the intended meaning; or it was [conveyed] through the tongue of the Messenger, and then revealed afterward in the Qur'an. Both ﴿fassala﴾ and ﴿harrama﴾ have been read in both the active and the passive form. The meaning of the verse is: there is no barrier for you to eating what has been mentioned [over], and He has made clear to you what is forbidden to eat, and this is not among it.

﴿except what you are compelled to﴾, that is: of what has been forbidden to you. That is: except that necessity compels you to eat it because of the severity of hunger, in which case it is permitted to you.

﴿Indeed, many [people] mislead﴾ is read with the ya' both open and with a damma: ﴿[others] by their desires without knowledge﴾, that is: they mislead, so they declare things forbidden and lawful according to their desires and appetites, without any basis in a sacred law.

﴿Indeed, your Lord is most knowing of the transgressors﴾, that is: those who exceed the bounds of truth into falsehood, and of the lawful into the unlawful.

Note:

Al-Razi said: This verse indicates that speaking about religion merely by taqlid (blind imitation) is forbidden, because speaking by taqlid is speaking purely from whim and desire, and the verse indicates that this is forbidden. End.

Some of the Zaydiyya said: The verse indicates the prohibition of issuing fatwas and judgments without evidence, but rather following desire.

The commentary of al-Qasimi (Mahasin al-Ta'wil) on surah 6, verse 120:

When Exalted God had explained that He had detailed the forbidden things (al-muharramat), He followed it with what necessitates abandoning them entirely. So He, glorified is He, said:

The discussion on the interpretation of His, exalted is He, saying:

[120] ﴿And leave the outward and the inward of sin. Indeed, those who earn sin will be recompensed for what they used to commit.﴾

﴿And leave the outward of sin﴾ means: the evil deeds and sayings that are apparent upon the limbs. ﴿And its inward﴾ means: what is concealed within the heart, such as corrupt beliefs and false resolves. Or it means: what is openly committed of sins and what is kept secret and hidden within.

As-Suddi said: its outward is fornication with prostitutes who have banners (dhawat al-rayat), and its inward is with mistresses, female friends and secret lovers (al-akhdan). It is not hidden that the wording is general to every prohibited thing; therefore Qatadah said: that is, its secret and its public, its little and its much, its minor and its major. Like His, exalted is He, saying: ﴿Say: My Lord has only forbidden the indecencies, what is apparent of them and what is concealed﴾ [al-A'raf: 33].

﴿Indeed, those who earn sin will be recompensed for what they used to commit﴾ means: those who acquire (yaktasibun). Al-Shihab said: iqtiraf (committing) in the language means acquiring (iktisab), and it is most often used for evil and sin. Hence it was said: "Confession removes the iqtiraf." It may also occur for good, like His, exalted is He, saying: ﴿And whoever commits a good deed, We increase for him therein in goodness﴾ [al-Shura: 23]. End of quotation.

Muslim and others narrated from Nawwas ibn Sam'an, who said: The Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: "Righteousness is good character, and sin is that which wavers in your soul and you dislike that people should see it."

Al-Hakim said: The verse indicates that the servant is held accountable for the deeds of the heart just as he is held accountable for the deeds of the limbs, i.e., according to the first interpretation of it.

The Commentary of al-Qasimi (Mahasin al-Ta'wil) on Surah 6, Verse 121 (Part 1 of 2)

On the interpretation of His saying, exalted is He:

[121] ﴿And do not eat of that over which the name of Allah has not been mentioned, for indeed, it is grave disobedience. And indeed, the devils inspire their allies to dispute with you. And if you obey them, indeed you are associators [of others with Allah].﴾

﴿And do not eat of that over which the name of Allah has not been mentioned﴾: that is, at the time of its slaughter. That is, by mentioning over it the name of other than Him, meaning it was slaughtered for other than Allah, exalted is He.

﴿And indeed, it is grave disobedience﴾: and "fisq" (grave disobedience) is that which has been dedicated to other than Allah, as in the verse that comes at the end of the surah.

Al-Mahayimi said: ﴿And indeed, it is grave disobedience﴾ means a departure from good to ugliness, by consuming what has been rendered impure by death without anything preventing its effect.

﴿And indeed, the devils inspire﴾: that is, they whisper suggestions ﴿to their allies﴾: that is, from among the disbelievers ﴿to dispute with you﴾: that is, concerning the permissibility of carrion.

﴿And if you obey them﴾: that is, in making lawful what Allah has forbidden, or forbidding what He has made lawful, ﴿indeed you are associators [of others with Allah]﴾: that is, you associate them with Allah in that which is specific to Him, namely the determination of what is lawful and unlawful.

Notes:

First: It has been narrated concerning the occasion of revelation of these verses, from Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him both, that he said: "Some people came to the Prophet ﷺ and said: 'O Messenger of Allah! We eat what we kill, but we do not eat what Allah kills.' So Allah, exalted is He, revealed: ﴿So eat of that over which the name of Allah has been mentioned, if you are believers in His signs﴾ [al-An'am: 118], up to His saying: ﴿And if you obey them, indeed you are associators [of others with Allah].﴾" Narrated by the authors of the Sunan.

In a narration of Abu Dawud concerning His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And indeed, the devils inspire their allies to dispute with you﴾ [p. 2483], he said: They would say: "What Allah slaughters, you do not eat; and what you slaughter yourselves, you eat?" So Allah, exalted is He, revealed: ﴿So eat of that over which the name of Allah has been mentioned﴾ [al-An'am: 118] and ﴿And do not eat of that over which the name of Allah has not been mentioned﴾. Then it was abrogated (nusikha), and He excepted from that, saying: ﴿The food of those who were given the Scripture is lawful for you, and your food is lawful for them﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 5].

In the narration of al-Nasa'i, he said: The polytheists disputed with them, saying: "What Allah slaughters, you do not eat; and what you slaughter, you eat?" Thus it is in Taysir al-Wusul.

Second: The verse indicates the prescription of mentioning the name of Allah at the time of slaughter. It is said: "In the name of Allah," with this noble phrase. And it is said: with any expression that contains glorification of Him, such as "the Most Merciful" and the rest of His beautiful names, based on His saying: ﴿Say: Call upon Allah, or call upon the Most Merciful﴾ [al-Isra': 110], and His saying: ﴿And to Allah belong the most beautiful names, so call upon Him by them﴾ [al-A'raf: 180].

Third: What we have previously put forward, of carrying the verse upon that which is slaughtered for other than Allah, exalted is He, is the most apparent in its interpretation, based on His saying after it: ﴿or a sinful thing over which other than Allah has been invoked﴾, and observing the parallels in the Qur'an is the most fitting means by which the intended meaning is sought.

Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from 'Ata' who said: It was revealed concerning slaughtered animals that Quraysh would slaughter upon idols [p. 2484], and the slaughtered animals of the Magians. Some have tried to strengthen this by making the "waw" in His saying ﴿And indeed, it is grave disobedience﴾ a circumstantial (ha'liyyah) waw, because of the ugliness of conjoining a declarative sentence to an imperative one. He said: The meaning is: "Do not eat it while it is grave disobedience." And "fisq" is general, which is explained by His saying: ﴿that which has been dedicated to other than Allah﴾ [al-Nahl: 115]. So the prohibition is restricted to that which has been dedicated to other than Allah, and what remains beyond it stays lawful, either by implication (mafhum), or by the generality of the evidence for permissibility, or by the default ruling of the original state.

This interpretation has been objected to on the grounds that it entails that the prohibition does not include the eating of carrion, although it is the occasion of revelation; and that the emphasis with "inna" (indeed) and the "lam" (of emphasis) negates that the clause is circumstantial, because such emphasis is only fitting where the purpose is to inform of the certain realization of the matter, or to refute a denial, actual or assumed (as clarified in the science of meanings), whereas the circumstantial clause in commands and prohibitions is based on supposition. It is as if it were said: "Do not eat from it if it is grave disobedience." So it would not be fitting to say: "And indeed, it is grave disobedience," but rather: "And it is grave disobedience."

The first objection is answered by saying that by His saying "And indeed, it is grave disobedience" there entered that which was dedicated to other than Allah, and by His saying "And indeed, the devils ..." etc., there entered carrion. So it is established that this prohibition is restricted to that which was slaughtered on the altars (nusub), or that which died of its own accord.

The second objection is answered by saying that since the intended meaning of "fisq" here is the dedication to other than Allah, the emphasis was fitting, as if it were said: "Do not eat from it when this type of grave disobedience, the ruling on which is established, is realized, while the polytheists deny it." Thus [it is stated] in al-'Inayah.

Something that also strengthens this is His saying: ﴿And indeed, it is grave disobedience﴾, meaning by it departure from obedience to Allah, exalted is He; this is a second possibility in it. And His saying: ﴿indeed you are associators﴾: for whoever eats carrion, or that which was slaughtered on the altars, is committing grave disobedience, and if he does so while deeming it lawful, he becomes a disbeliever. This is unlike that which a Muslim slaughters without mentioning the name of Allah over it, for whoever eats it does not commit grave disobedience nor disbelief, by consensus (ijma') — as al-Razi indicated. And in that case there is no indication in the verse of the prohibition of a Muslim's slaughtered animal over which the mention of Allah's name was omitted, whether intentionally or by forgetfulness.

Abu Dawud narrated in his Marasil from al-Saltt al-Sadusi who said: The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "The slaughtered animal of a Muslim is lawful, whether he mentions the name of Allah or does not mention it; for indeed, if he mentions it, he mentions nothing but the name of Allah."

The Hafiz Ibn Kathir said: This is a mursal (a narration whose chain omits the Companion), and it is strengthened by what al-Daraqutni narrated from Ibn 'Abbas that he said: "If a Muslim slaughters and does not mention the name of Allah, let him eat, for the Muslim has in him a name of the names of Allah, exalted is He."

[p. 2485] Al-Bayhaqi also argued with the hadith of 'A'ishah, may Allah be pleased with her, that: "Some people said to the Prophet ﷺ: 'Indeed, some people bring us meat, and we do not know whether the name of Allah was mentioned over it or not.' He said: 'Mention the name of Allah over it yourselves, and eat it.' She said: 'And they were recent in their conversion from disbelief.'" Narrated by al-Bukhari and al-Nasa'i. He said: If the presence of the mention were a condition, he would not have given them permission except when its occurrence was certain. Likewise al-Khattabi said: In it is evidence that mentioning the name is not a condition for the slaughtered animal, for if it were a condition, the animal would not be rendered permissible by a matter that is doubtful, just as if doubt arose regarding the animal itself, and one did not know whether the valid slaughter had taken place or not. This is what is apparent from the context of the hadith, where the answer in it was: "Mention it yourselves," as if it were said to them: "Do not concern yourselves with that; rather, what should concern you is that you mention the name of Allah and eat." This is from the wise manner of address. Also indicating this is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿The food of those who were given the Scripture is lawful for you﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 5], so He permitted eating from their slaughtered animals, despite the doubt that they mentioned the name of Allah or not.

Now, some people have held fast to the apparent meaning of the verse and went to the view that a slaughtered animal is not lawful if the name of Allah has not been mentioned over it, even if the slaughterer is a Muslim, whether the omission was intentional or due to forgetfulness. They also argued with His saying, exalted is He, in the verse about hunting: ﴿So eat of what they catch for you, and mention the name of Allah over it﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 4], and with the hadiths that came with the command to mention the name at slaughter and hunting [p. 2486], such as the two hadiths of 'Adi ibn Hatim and Abu Tha'labah: "When you release your trained dog and you mention the name of Allah, then eat," and both are in the two Sahihs.

[p. 2487] And the hadith of Rafi' ibn Khadij: "Whatever makes the blood flow and the name of Allah has been mentioned over it, eat it," also in the two Sahihs. And the hadith of Ibn Mas'ud, that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said to the jinn: "For you is every bone over which the name of Allah has been mentioned." Narrated by Muslim.

[p. 2488] And the hadith of Jundub ibn Sufyan al-Bajali, who said: The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "Whoever slaughters before he prays, let him slaughter another in its place; and whoever has not slaughtered until we have prayed, let him slaughter in the name of Allah." Both al-Bukhari and Muslim narrated it.

They said: In these hadiths, permission to eat is made conditional upon the mention of the name, and what is made conditional upon a description ceases to apply when that description is absent, according to those who hold the view of implication (mafhum). And a condition is stronger than a description.

They also argued with the hadith of 'A'ishah mentioned earlier: "Mention it yourselves and eat." They said: The people understood that the mention was indispensable, and feared that it had not been made by those [who brought the meat], due to their recent conversion to Islam. So he commanded them to take precaution with the mention before eating, so that it would serve as a substitute for what was omitted at slaughter, if it had not been made. That is: your mention now makes lawful for you everything of which you do not know whether the name of Allah was mentioned over it or not [p. 2489], provided the slaughterer is one whose slaughter is valid if he mentions the name. They said: It is derived from this that everything found in the markets of the Muslims is to be taken as valid, and likewise what the Muslim Bedouins slaughter, because the general assumption is that they know the mention. End.

Those who carried the verse upon the first interpretation answered: The command in the hadith of 'Adi and Abu Tha'labah is to be understood as recommendation (tanzih), because the two of them used to hunt according to the custom of the Jahiliyyah, so the Prophet ﷺ taught them the rules of hunting and slaughter, its obligatory and recommended aspects, so that they would not fall into any doubtful practice in that regard, and so that they would adopt the most perfect course. As for those who asked about those slaughtered animals, they asked about a matter that had occurred for others, so he informed them of the basic principle of its permissibility.

Ibn al-Tin said: It is possible that what is meant here is the mention at the time of eating, and al-Nawawi affirmed this with certainty.

As for the mention over a slaughter undertaken by others, it is not imposed upon them in that regard; rather, it is only to be treated as invalid if its invalidity becomes clear.

Al-Muhallab said: This hadith is a basis for the view that the mention is not obligatory. Since their mention substituted for the mention at slaughter, this indicates that it is a Sunnah, because a Sunnah cannot substitute for an obligation. End.

Some of those who made the mention a condition for lawfulness went to the permissibility of eating what was left without mention out of forgetfulness, but not intentionally. And he argued with what al-Bayhaqi narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, traced to the Prophet ﷺ: "The Muslim is sufficed by his name; if he forgets to mention it at the time of slaughter, let him mention the name of Allah and eat it." The Hafiz Ibn Kathir said: Its attribution to the Prophet is an error, and the correct version is that it is halted at Ibn 'Abbas, as his own statement; al-Bayhaqi explicitly stated this. He also argued with the hadith transmitted through various chains in Ibn Majah from Ibn 'Abbas, Abu Hurayrah, Abu Dharr, 'Uqbah ibn 'Amir and 'Abdullah ibn 'Amr [p. 2490], from the Prophet ﷺ: "Indeed, Allah has removed from my nation error, forgetfulness, and what they have been coerced into."

And al-Tabarani narrated it from Thawban, traced to the Prophet, with the wording: "Error has been removed from my nation..." the hadith.

Ibn 'Adi narrated from Abu Hurayrah who said: "A man came to the Prophet ﷺ and said: 'O Messenger of Allah! What about a man among us who slaughters and forgets to mention the name?' The Prophet ﷺ said: 'The name of Allah is upon every Muslim.'" Ibn Kathir said: Its chain is weak.

You have already learned the most apparent interpretation of the verse at the outset. And Allah knows best.

Fourth: Ibn Jarir said: The people of knowledge differed concerning this verse: has any of its ruling been abrogated (naskh) or not? Some of them said: nothing of it has been abrogated, and it is muhkam (its ruling is firm) regarding what it intends. This is the view of Mujahid and the general body of scholars.

It has been narrated from al-Hasan al-Basri and 'Ikrimah that He, exalted is He, abrogated from this verse and excepted His saying: ﴿The food of those who were given the Scripture is lawful for you﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 5]. And Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Makhul too that He abrogated it by that and made lawful the food of the People of the Book.

Ibn Jarir said: The correct position is that there is no contradiction between the lawfulness of the food of the People of the Book and the prohibition of what the name of Allah has not been mentioned over.

Ibn Kathir said: What he said is correct. And whoever among the early scholars used the term "naskh" here, he intended "takhsis" (specification). End.

We have already stated in the introduction that it is known from the inductive study of the speech of the Companions and the Successors that they used "naskh" in its linguistic sense, which is the removal of one thing by another, not in the technical sense of the jurists of legal theory (usul). So the meaning of naskh for them is the removal of some of the attributes of a verse by another verse, either by the expiry of the period of application, or by diverting the speech from its apparent meaning to something else, or by clarifying that a certain qualification was incidental, or by specifying a general ruling, and other such matters we have previously mentioned, so remember!

(p-2491) Fifth: al-Zajjaj said: In His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And if you obey them, indeed you are polytheists﴾, there is evidence that whoever makes lawful something that Allah, Exalted is He, has made unlawful, or makes unlawful something that Allah, Exalted is He, has made lawful, is a polytheist. He is called a polytheist only because he has affirmed a legislator other than Allah, Exalted is He, and this is shirk. End of quote.

Ibn Kathir said: ﴿Indeed you are polytheists﴾, meaning: inasmuch as you have turned away from the command and law of Allah for you to the word of another, and you have preferred the other over Him, this is shirk. Like His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿They took their rabbis and their monks as lords besides Allah﴾ [al-Tawbah: 31], the verse. Al-Tirmidhi has narrated in its explanation, "from ʿAdi ibn Hatim, that he said: O Messenger of Allah! They did not worship them. He said: Indeed they made lawful for them what was forbidden, and made forbidden for them what was lawful, and they followed them. That is their worship of them." End of quote.

Sixth: al-Kaʿbi said: The verse is evidence that "faith" (al-iman) is a term for all acts of obedience, even though its meaning in the language is affirmation (al-taṣdiq). Just as Exalted Allah made "shirk" a term for everything that opposes Allah, Exalted is He, even though in the language it is specific to one who believes that Allah has a partner. The proof is that Exalted Allah called the obedience of the believers to the polytheists, in permitting carrion, shirk.

(p-2492) al-Razi objected to him: Why could it not be that what is meant by shirk here is the belief that Allah has a partner in judgment and in legal obligation? By this reckoning, the meaning of this shirk returns to belief alone. End of quote.

Then Exalted is He gave a parable of the believer and the disbeliever, to warn the Muslims away from obeying the polytheists, following His warning against them, with His words, glorified is He:

The discussion on the interpretation of His words, exalted is He:

[122] ﴿Is he who was dead and We gave him life and made for him a light by which he walks among the people like one who is in darkness, not coming out of it? Thus the deeds they used to do were made attractive to the disbelievers.﴾

﴿Is he who was dead and We gave him life and made for him a light by which he walks among the people like one who is in darkness, not coming out of it?﴾ This is a parable of the one whom Allah guided after misguidance and gave sight with the light of proofs and signs, by which he contemplates things and distinguishes between truth and falsehood, and the guided and the astray. [It is likened] to one who was dead and was given life, and what follows from it of the faculties of perception and motion. And the one who remains upon misguidance is like one stumbling in darkness, who never extricates himself from it and never escapes, so he remains perpetually bewildered. ﴿Thus﴾, i.e., like that eloquent adornment: ﴿the deeds they used to do were made attractive to the disbelievers﴾, i.e., the various forms of disbelief and sins. This is why they argued against the truth with them and insisted upon them.

Commentary of al-Qasimi (Mahasin al-Ta'wil) on surah 6, verse 123:

The discussion of His saying, exalted is He:

[123] ﴿And thus We have placed in every city its greatest criminals so that they may plot therein. But they plot only against themselves, and they do not perceive.﴾

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And thus We have placed in every city its greatest criminals so that they may plot therein﴾ is a consolation to the Prophet (ﷺ). That is: just as We placed in Makkah great leaders so that they would scheme against their followers in adorning falsehood and concealing the truth, so We placed in every city to which We sent the messengers its greatest criminals, characterized by the attributes (p-2493) mentioned, having their deeds made attractive to them, persisting in falsehood, disputing the truth with it, so that they would carry out the scheming therein against their followers through deception, in order that they would abandon following the messengers.

Ibn Kathir said: What is meant by "scheming" here is their calling (people) to misguidance through the ornate speech and deeds, like His saying, exalted is He, reporting about the people of Noah: ﴿And they schemed a great scheme﴾ [Nuh: 22], and like His saying, exalted is He: ﴿If only you could see when the wrongdoers are made to stand before their Lord, returning word to one another. Those who were oppressed will say to those who were arrogant, "Were it not for you, we would have been believers."﴾ [Saba': 31] ﴿Those who were arrogant will say to those who were oppressed, "Did we avert you from guidance after it had come to you? Rather, you were criminals."﴾ [Saba': 32] ﴿And those who were oppressed will say to those who were arrogant, "Rather, it was scheming by night and day when you were ordering us to disbelieve in Allah and set up rivals to Him."﴾ [Saba': 33] — the verse.

Al-Zamakhshari said: He singled out the greatest (criminals) because they are the ones who lead to misguidance and who scheme against the people, like His saying: ﴿When We intend to destroy a city, We command its affluent ones﴾ [al-Isra': 16].

﴿But they plot only against themselves, and they do not perceive.﴾ That is: they harm by their scheming only themselves, because its evil recoils upon them, as He, exalted is He, said: ﴿And they will surely carry their burdens and burdens along with their burdens﴾ [al-'Ankabut: 13], and He said: (p-2494) ﴿And of the burdens of those whom they mislead without knowledge. Unquestionably, evil is what they bear﴾ [al-Nahl: 25]. Al-Zamakhshari said: This is a consolation to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), and an advance promise of victory over them.

**Commentary on the Interpretation of His Words, Exalted Is He:**

[124] ﴿When a sign comes to them, they say: "We will never believe until we are given the like of what was given to the messengers of God." God knows best where to place His message. Those who committed crimes will suffer humiliation before God and a severe punishment for their scheming.﴾

﴿When a sign comes to them﴾, i.e., a proof and a decisive argument. ﴿They say: "We will never believe until we are given the like of what was given to the messengers of God"﴾, i.e., of the revelation and the miracles that confirm it. Like His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And those who do not expect to meet Us say: "Why have the angels not been sent down to us, or do we not see our Lord?"﴾ [al-Furqan: 21], and so on.

And His saying, glorified is He: ﴿Rather, each one of them wants to be given scrolls spread out﴾ [al-Muddaththir: 52].

﴿God knows best where to place His message﴾ is a resumed statement serving as a rebuke to them, and to show that He chooses for prophethood only the one whom He knows to be fit for it: one who is suited to be illuminated by the lights of His knowledge and entrusted with the hidden secrets of His mystery, such that if they were revealed to another, the soul of that other would overflow, or his intellect would be carried away by their majesty and greatness. So He knows best the place where He puts it among them.

Al-Imam Ahmad narrated from Wathila ibn al-Asqa', may Allah be pleased with him, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Indeed Allah, Mighty and Majestic, chose Isma'il from the offspring of Ibrahim. He chose from the children of Isma'il the children of Kinanah. He chose from the children of Kinanah Quraysh, and He chose from Quraysh the Banu Hashim. And He chose me from the Banu Hashim." Muslim alone also narrated it.

Al-Imam Ahmad also narrated from al-Muttalib ibn Abi Wada'a, from al-Abbas, from the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), who said: "Indeed Allah created creation and placed me in the best of His creation. He divided them into two groups and placed me in the best group. He created the tribes and placed me in the best tribe. He made them into houses and placed me in the best of them as a house. So I am the best of you in house and the best of you in person."

﴿Those who committed crimes will suffer humiliation﴾, i.e., abasement and disgrace after their arrogance and their pride, ﴿before God﴾, i.e., on the Day of Resurrection, as a recompense for their contesting Him, exalted is He, in His greatness by rejecting His signs and His message, and for their objecting to Him in His choosing for the message someone other than them. ﴿And a severe punishment﴾, meaning in the Hereafter, ﴿for their scheming﴾ in the world, by harming the prophets.

Ibn Kathir said: Since scheming is usually hidden, consisting of subtle contrivance in deception and treachery, they were met with a severe punishment from Allah on the Day of Resurrection, as a fitting recompense. ﴿And your Lord does not wrong anyone﴾. It is reported in the two Sahihs from the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) that he said: "On the Day of Resurrection, a banner will be raised for every treacherous person at his backside, and it will be said: 'This is the treachery of so-and-so, son of so-and-so.'"

(p-٢٤٩٦) The wisdom in this is that since treachery is hidden and people are not aware of it, on the Day of Resurrection it becomes a banner displayed over its doer for what he did. End of quotation.

The discussion on the interpretation of His saying, exalted is He:

[125] ﴿Whoever Allah wills to guide, He expands his breast to Islam; and whoever He wills to leave astray, He makes his breast constricted and tight, as though he were climbing up into the sky. Thus Allah places defilement upon those who do not believe.﴾

﴿Whoever Allah wills to guide﴾, i.e., to monotheism (tawhid, affirmation of God's oneness): ﴿He expands﴾, i.e., widens, ﴿his breast to Islam﴾ by polishing it with the light of guidance, so that it accepts the light of truth, as He, exalted is He, said: ﴿But Allah has endeared to you the faith and made it pleasing in your hearts﴾ [al-Hujurat: 7].

(p-2497) ʿAbd al-Razzaq narrated that the Prophet (ﷺ) was asked about this verse: "How does He expand his breast?" He said: "It is a light that is cast into it, and so it expands." They said: "Is there a sign by which one can recognize it?" He said: "Turning in repentance toward the abode of eternity, withdrawing from the abode of delusion, and preparing for death before the encounter with death." Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim also narrated it. Ibn Kathir said: "The hadith has chains that are mursal (where a Companion is omitted from the chain) and muttasil (continuous), each strengthening the others."

﴿And whoever He wills to leave astray, He makes his breast constricted and tight﴾, i.e., extremely constricted, so that it has no room for correct beliefs about Allah and the matters of the Hereafter.

Abu al-Baqa said: "Ḥarajan (with a kasra on the rāʾ) is an attribute of ḍayyiqan, or a third object (mafʿūl thālith), just as it is permissible for a subject to be described by several predicates, or all of them may be in the position of one predicate (ḥulwun ḥāmiḍun, 'sweet and sour'). In every case, it emphasizes the meaning. It is also read with a fatḥa on the rāʾ, as a verbal noun (maṣdar), meaning: possessing constriction. It has also been said that it is the plural of ḥarajah, like qaṣabah and qaṣab, and the hāʾ in it is for intensification." End of quote.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿as though he were climbing up into the sky﴾, i.e., he laboriously attempts to ascend toward the sky, while his nature pulls him down to the earth. He is compared, for the sake of emphasizing the tightness of his breast, to one who attempts something impossible, because climbing into the sky is a proverb for what is impossible and far beyond capability, and what capability cannot reach. It has also been said that the meaning is: as though he were ascending into the sky, in aversion to the truth and in fleeing far away from it. The original form of yaṣṣaʿʿadu (يَصَّعَّدُ) is yatasaʿʿadu, from ṣuʿūd (ascent).

﴿Thus Allah places defilement upon those who do not believe﴾, in beliefs and in morals. Rijs (defilement) is what is loathed of deeds, and it is so named for the sake of intensifying the condemnation of it.

(p-2498) On the interpretation of His saying, exalted is He:

[126] ﴿And this is the path of your Lord, straight. We have detailed the verses for a people who remember.﴾

﴿And this﴾ i.e., the clarification that the Qur'an has brought, or the path of tawhid (monotheism) and the submission of one's face to God. ﴿The path of your Lord﴾ i.e., His way which He has approved; ﴿straight﴾ with no inclination in it toward excess (ifrat) or deficiency (tafrit) in beliefs, morals, and deeds. Or: with no crookedness in it toward looking to other than Him and associating partners with Him.

﴿We have detailed the verses for a people who remember﴾ i.e., the knowledge and realities that are deposited in their innate capacities (isti'dad), so that they may be guided by them.

The discussion on the interpretation of His saying, exalted is He (al-Qawl fi ta'wil qawlihi ta'ala, interpretation, i.e. the explanatory exposition of a verse):

[127] ﴿For them is the abode of peace with their Lord, and He is their Protector because of what they used to do.﴾

﴿For them is the abode of peace﴾ means: safety from what is disliked, and it is Paradise, because they are in the station of nearness. ﴿With their Lord, and He is their Protector﴾ means He takes charge of them with His love and places them in security. ﴿Because of what they used to do﴾ means: by reason of their good deeds in following His path.

Commentary of al-Qasimi (Mahasin al-Ta'wil) on surah 6, verse 128:

The discussion of the interpretation of His words, exalted is He:

[128] ﴿On the Day He gathers them all together, [He will say]: "O assembly of jinn, you have taken much from mankind." And their allies among mankind will say: "Our Lord, we benefited from one another, and we have reached our term which You appointed for us." He will say: "The Fire is your abode, wherein you will abide eternally, except as God wills. Indeed your Lord is Wise, Knowing."﴾

﴿On the Day He gathers them all together﴾ meaning: Mention, O Muhammad, in what you relate to them and warn them of, the Day We gather them all together, namely the jinn and their allies among mankind who used to worship them in the world, seek refuge with them, obey them, and whose some inspire to others ornate speech as deception.

(p-2499) ﴿O assembly of jinn﴾ meaning: We will say, "O assembly of jinn!" namely the devils. Al-Mahayimi said: He singled them out for the address because they are the origin of deceit. ﴿You have taken much from mankind﴾ meaning: from their misguidance and their leading astray. Or "from them," by your making them your followers, your adorning and beautifying for them the transient goods of this world and the bodily pleasures, and your whispering to them of sins, so they were gathered with you. This is by way of rebuke and reproach. ﴿And their allies among mankind will say﴾ meaning: those who obeyed them and took them as allies: ﴿"Our Lord, we benefited from one another"﴾. Al-Hasan said: The benefiting of some of them from others was only that the jinn were obeyed and the humans were aware. That is: the jinn gained honor from them and were worshipped, while humans, through their whispering, enjoyed preferring immediate desires over distant pleasures. ﴿And we have reached our term which You appointed for us﴾ meaning: by death, or by the bodily resurrection in the most hideous form and the worst state.

Abu al-Su'ud said: They said this in acknowledgment of what they did of obeying the devils, following desire, and denying the resurrection, and as a display of regret over it, sorrow over their condition, and submission to their Lord. Perhaps the restriction to relating the speech of the misguided is to indicate that the misleaders have been utterly silenced and were unable to speak at all.

﴿He will say: "The Fire is your abode"﴾ meaning: your dwelling place, just as the Abode of Peace is the abode of the believers.

﴿Abiding therein eternally, except as God wills﴾ Al-Qashani said: That is, except for the time of His will that they be lightened, or that whoever among you whose punishment is not caused by firmly rooted polytheism in his belief be saved.

Al-Mahayimi said: That is, except for the time of His will to move you from it to the zamharir (extreme cold), your moving from one desire to another.

Al-Zamakhshari said: That is, they will be made to abide in the torment of the Fire forever, the whole of eternity, except for the times in which they are transferred from the torment of the Fire to the torment of the zamharir. It is narrated that they will be made to enter a valley containing such zamharir that it separates some of their joints from others, so they howl and seek to be returned to the Blazing Fire. Or it may be from the speech of (p-2500) the one who has been wronged, who has overcome his enemy, and who keeps gnashing his teeth at him, while the enemy asks him to ease his grip on his throat: "May God destroy me if I ease my grip on you except when I will." He knows that he will only will to satisfy himself against him to the utmost of what he is able, through reproach and severity. So his saying "except when I will" is among the most severe threats, together with mockery of the one threatened, since it comes out in the form of an exception that holds out hope. End.

Al-Khafaji said: Since the address is to the disbelievers, and they will not come out of the Fire, because what precedes it is an explanation of their state, it is far-fetched to make it inclusive of the disobedient so that the exception would be valid with respect to them; moreover, the use of "ma" for rational beings is rare. They have explained it by saying that the intended meaning is transfer from the Fire to the zamharir, or hyperbole regarding eternity, meaning that it will not cease except during the time of God's will, which is something that does not occur when it is presented in the form of an exit, which holds out hope to them, as mockery and as intensifying the matter upon them. "Ma" here is a temporal verbal-source particle. Or the excepted thing is the time of their being given respite before entering. The first was rejected on the grounds that it shifts "the Fire" from its specific meaning, the abode of punishment, to its lexical meaning. It was answered that there is no harm in such a shift when a necessity calls for it. It was said in reply that the objector does not accept the necessity, since other interpretations are possible, and moreover his saying "your abode" requires what the objector maintains, according to the apparent sense. Abu Hayyan rejected the last view, saying that in an exception the time of the excluded and the excluded-from must be the same. So if you say, "The people stood except Zayd," it means: "except Zayd, who did not stand." It is not valid for the meaning to be: "except Zayd, who will not stand in the future." Likewise, "I will strike the people except Zayd" means: "except Zayd, for I will not strike him in the future," and it is not valid for the meaning to be: "except Zayd, for I did not strike him before," unless it is a disjunctive exception, in which case it is permissible, as in His saying: "They will not taste death therein except the first death" (44:56), for they did indeed taste it. You may say that the one who holds this view is committed to its being disjunctive, as in the verse he mentioned, and there is no objection to that, given the occurrence of its like in the Qur'an, though this is open to question. It was also said: this is a heedlessness regarding the interpretation of eternity (khulud) as everlasting duration, and everlasting duration does not require entry. End.

Al-Nasir said in al-Intisaf: The eternal abiding of the disbelievers in the torment has been established with certainty, so scholars have taken great care in discussing the exception in this verse and its counterpart in Surah Hud. Some of them held that it encompasses the disobedient among the monotheists and the disbelievers, with the excepted being the disobedient, since they will not abide eternally. You know its remoteness.

Then he said: Some held that this exception is limited by the will of lifting the punishment, that is: they will abide eternally unless God wills otherwise, if He had willed. Its benefit is to show His power and to proclaim that their abiding was only because God had willed it, though it was rationally permissible in His will that He not punish them, and if He punished them He would not make them abide eternally, and that this is not an obligation upon Him, but rather a consequence of His will and desire, exalted and majestic is He. In this sense it also repels the position of the Mu'tazilah, who claim that the eternal abiding of the disbelievers is obligatory upon God by the requirement of wisdom, and that it is impossible by reason for Him to will otherwise.

Al-Zajjaj took a subtle view, which becomes evident only with elaboration. He said: The intended meaning, and God knows best, is: except what He wills of increase in punishment. He did not explain the reason for the exception. The excepted, on this interpretation, does not differ from the excepted-from in the ruling. We shall clarify it: punishment, God forbid, is of varying degrees. As if the meaning were that they abide eternally in the kind of punishment, except what your Lord wills of an increase reaching the ultimate limit and the utmost extremity, so that, by reaching the limit and by being so distinct from the other kinds of punishment in severity, it is counted as not of the kind of punishment and as outside it. When something reaches its limit in their estimation, they express it by its opposite, as was mentioned earlier regarding expressing the frequency of an act by "rubba" and "qad," which are both designed for the opposite of frequency, namely paucity; and this is a common usage in the Arabic language. Abu al-Tayyib has hovered around this when he said:

"You have been so generous that Hatim nearly becomes stingy in comparison, and from joy there is weeping."

So when these people are transferred to the extremity of punishment and the utmost severity, they have reached the point where they nearly exit the absolute name of punishment, so that treating it in speech as something different becomes valid. This is a good interpretation, which can hardly be understood from al-Zajjaj's words except after this elaboration.

In the Tafsir of Ibn 'Abbas, may God be pleased with him, there is something that supports it. End.

There are other interpretations of the verse:

Among them: what is reported from Ibn 'Abbas, may God be pleased with both of them, that He excepted a people whose knowledge preceded that they would submit and believe in the Prophet (ﷺ). This is based on the view that the exception is not part of the reported speech, and that "ma" means "man."

(p-2503) Among them: that the doors of Paradise will be opened for them, and they will come out of the Fire; but when they turn to enter, they will be shut in their faces as mockery of them. This is the meaning of His saying: "Today those who believed will laugh at the disbelievers" (83:34). Al-Sharif al-Murtada said in al-Durar: If it is asked, "What is the benefit of this act, and what is the wisdom in it?" we say: The wisdom in it is evident, for it is more grievous to their souls and more severe in what they dislike, and it is a kind of the punishment they deserve by their evil deeds; for whoever hopes for deliverance and escape from what is disliked, and whose eagerness for that is intense, then is kept from relief and returned to what is disliked, his punishment will be harder and more severe than the punishment of one who has no path to hope. Thus in al-Inayah.

Among them: that this exception is an allusion to the annihilation of the Fire, meaning: except the time of His will for its annihilation and the cessation of its punishment.

Al-Suyuti said in al-Durr al-Manthur: Ibn al-Mundhir reported from al-Hasan who said: Umar, may God be pleased with him, said: "If the people of the Fire remained in the Fire as long as the sands of 'Aligh, there would still be a day for them on which they would come out." 'Abd ibn Humayd also reported it from al-Hasan.

Shaykh al-Islam Ibn Taymiyyah, may God have mercy on him, said: This has been related from Umar, Ibn Mas'ud, Abu Hurayrah, Abu Sa'id, and others. End. A group has championed this view. They said: What has come regarding eternal abiding in it, perpetuity, and non-exit, and that its torment is lasting, is all a true and accepted matter with no dispute. This requires eternal abiding in the abode of punishment as long as it endures, and only the people of monotheism will come out of it while it endures. There is a difference between one who leaves a prison, which remains in its state, and one whose imprisonment is nullified by the ruin and dissolution of the prison. Imam Ibn al-Qayyim has elaborately investigated this in his book "Hadi al-Arwah," and with his great championing of this view, and his citing of twenty-five proofs for it, he did not affirm it, where he said: As for the everlastingness of Paradise, that it does not perish or vanish, this is known necessarily, and no one has said it perishes. Whoever says so, like the Jahmiyyah, is astray, an innovator, deviating from the truth, and has no predecessor in that. As for the everlastingness of the Fire, there are two well-known views among the early and later scholars, and the more correct view is that it also does not perish. End.

It will come, God willing, to elaborate this matter in the verse of Hud.

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim have reported from Ibn 'Abbas regarding this verse that he said: It is not fitting for anyone to pass judgment upon God regarding His creation: He does not cause them to enter Paradise or the Fire.

﴿Indeed your Lord is Wise﴾ so He punishes only as wisdom requires, ﴿Knowing﴾ that is: of whom is punished for his disbelief so that his punishment endures, or for his evil deeds, so that he is punished according to them and then delivered from it.

The discussion concerning His words, may He be exalted:

[129] ﴿And thus do We make some of the wrongdoers allies of others, because of what they used to earn.﴾

﴿And thus do We make some of the wrongdoers﴾ — that is, from among mankind — ﴿allies of others﴾, meaning We place them in such a state that they become allies to one another through misguidance and leading astray, just as the devils and the misguided among mankind do. ﴿Because of what they used to earn﴾ — that is, because of their persistence in earning it, namely disbelief and sins.

Al-Razi said:

Because kinship (al-jinsiyyah) is the cause of joining together. Wicked souls join with what resembles them in wickedness. The same applies to pure souls: every person concerns himself with the affairs of those who resemble him in support, aid and strengthening.

(p-2505) A note:

Al-Suyuti said in al-Iklil: the verse carries the meaning of the hadith: "As you are, so will you be ruled over," which Ibn Qani' recorded in Mu'jam al-Sahabah from the hadith of Abu Bakrah. End of quote.

In al-Jami' al-Saghir, he attributed its takhrij to al-Daylami in al-Firdaws (from Abu Bakrah), and to al-Bayhaqi, from Abu Ishaq al-Subai'i as a mursal report — and it was marked as weak.

It is related in al-Durr al-Manthur, from Mansur ibn al-Aswad, who said: I asked al-A'mash about His words, may He be exalted: ﴿And thus do We make some of the wrongdoers allies of others﴾. What did you hear them saying about it? He said: I heard them saying: When people become corrupt, the worst of them are put in authority over them.

He also recorded similar reports from Malik ibn Dinar, Ka'b, and al-Hasan.

Abu al-Layth al-Samarqandi said in his Tafsir: It is also said concerning the meaning of the verse: We set some of the wrongdoers upon others, so that he destroys him or humiliates him. He said: This is a statement of threat to the wrongdoer, so that he refrains from his wrongdoing. The verse includes every wrongdoer: a shepherd in his flock, a merchant in his trade, a thief, and others.

Al-Fudayl ibn Iyad said: When you see a wrongdoer taking revenge on a wrongdoer, stop and look at it in wonder.

Ibn Kathir said: The meaning of the noble verse: just as We appointed over these losers from mankind that group of jinn who misled them, so We do with the wrongdoers. We set some of them over others, destroy some of them by means of others, and take vengeance on some of them through others, as a recompense for their wrongdoing and transgression.

The Commentary of al-Qasimi (Mahasin al-Ta'wil) on Surah 6 (al-An'am), verse 130:

Then Allah, may He be exalted, explained what will happen in terms of the rebuke of the disbelievers from both groups on the Day of Resurrection, following the explanation of the rebuke of the jinn for misleading and leading astray mankind. Know that they will have no way to deny, so they will bear witness against themselves to their disbelief, and that they were not punished except through the proof (hujjah). Thus Allah, may He be exalted, said:

(p-2506) The discussion on the interpretation of the words of Allah, may He be exalted:

[130] ﴿O assembly of jinn and mankind! Did there not come to you messengers from among you, relating to you My verses and warning you of the meeting of this your day?" They will say, "We testify against ourselves." The worldly life deceived them, and they will testify against themselves that they were disbelievers.﴾

﴿O assembly of jinn and mankind! Did there not come to you﴾, that is, in the world: ﴿messengers from among you, relating to you My verses﴾ with the commands and prohibitions: ﴿and warning you﴾, frightening you: ﴿of the meeting of this your day﴾, which is the Day of Gathering, in which they have witnessed the various kinds of terrors. ﴿They will say﴾, meaning the jinn and mankind: ﴿We testify against ourselves﴾, that is: we acknowledge the coming of the messengers and their warning, and the denial of their call, as detailed in His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿They said, "Yes, there came to us a warner, but we denied and said, 'Allah has not sent down anything. You are only in great error.'"﴾ [al-Mulk: 9]. ﴿The worldly life deceived them﴾, that is: by what it contained of splendor and bliss, and this is an explanation of what led them in the world to disbelief. ﴿And they will testify against themselves﴾, that is: in the Hereafter. Al-Mahayimi said: after the testimony of their limbs, ﴿that they were disbelievers﴾, that is: in the world, by what the messengers brought them.

Remarks:

The first: Those who said that Allah sent messengers from among the jinn cited His saying, ﴿Did there not come to you messengers from among you?﴾ Ibn Jarir related this from al-Dahhak ibn Muzahim, but most scholars hold that there was no messenger from among the jinn, and that the messengers were only from mankind. Mujahid, Ibn Jurayj, and many other imams of the early and later generations stated this explicitly.

Ibn 'Abbas said: The messengers are from the children of Adam, and from the jinn there are warners (nudhur). They answered the apparent meaning of the verse by saying that there is an elision (mudaf) in it, i.e., "from among you", meaning from among mankind. Or it is the attribution of what belongs to some to the whole, as in His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿From both of them come out the pearl and the coral﴾ [al-Rahman: 22], whereas they come out only from one of them, namely the salt water and not the sweet. This is permissible because their mention has been combined in His saying: ﴿He released the two seas, meeting side by side﴾ [al-Rahman: 19], and this is permissible in whatever is united in its origin. Therefore, when the mention of the jinn was combined with mankind, it was permissible to address both with what applies to one of the two groups, namely mankind. This is the view of al-Farra' and al-Zajjaj.

Abu al-Su'ud said: The meaning is: Did there not come to you messengers from your whole company, but not in the sense that they are of the kind of both groups together, rather from mankind alone. They were described as being from both, either to emphasize the obligation to follow them and to indicate the closeness of the two in essence, and their unity in obligation and address, as if they were of one kind. That is why one of them could mislead the other. Or because the intended meaning of "messengers" includes the messengers of the messengers. It is established that the jinn listened to the Qur'an and warned their people with it, as expressed in His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And when We directed to you a company of jinn listening to the Qur'an﴾ [al-Ahqaf: 29], up to His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿They turned back to their people as warners﴾ [al-Ahqaf: 29]. End of quotation.
